posters.P001:
Over the last few decades, it has been established that desialylation significantly enhances the atherogenic properties of
low-density lipoproteins (LDL). Consequently, human sialidases responsible for LDL desialylation represent promising
therapeutic targets for atherosclerosis prevention and treatment.
Flavonoids are natural compounds with diverse biological activities, including the inhibition of microbial sialidases. This
study evaluates the capacity of dietary flavonoids to inhibit human sialidase NEU1 using an integrated in silico and in
vitro approach.
We performed a virtual screening on 148 flavonoids from the PubChem database combining molecular docking
and machine learning-based IC50 prediction. Docking into the NEU1 catalytic site (PDB ID: 1VCU) was performed
using AutoDock Vina (v1.2.5). For the IC50 prediction we used an ElasticNet model trained on Morgan fingerprints
for 208 ChEMBL-sourced compounds (R2 = 0.76).
Based on binding energies, ML predictions, and commercial availability, avicularin and epigallocatechin were
selected for in vitro validation.
Inhibitory effects were assessed via fluorogenic 4-MUNANA substrate cleavage assay. Epigallocatechin and
avicularin exhibited IC50 values of 11.6 µM and 71.6 µM, respectively. Given their low toxicity and availability, these
compounds represent promising functional food additives for atherosclerosis prevention.
The work is supported with the RSF grant #25-25-00364
posters.P002:
Rational design of multi-target drugs remains a central challenge in polypharmacology due to conflicting biological
objectives and the high computational cost of candidate evaluations. Existing deep generative methods frequently
suffer from sample inefficiency, requiring excessive oracle calls to identify quality candidates. Here, we present a
sample-efficient generative framework that designs potent multi-target drugs while minimizing costly evaluations. The
framework integrates chemical language modeling with reinforcement learning and preference-based optimization. By
employing nested optimization loops, Pareto-based ranking, and Direct Preference Optimization, it intensively reuses
previously evaluated molecules from memory buffers, providing a stable, oracle-free alignment signal without
handcrafted reward shaping. Under a strict budget of 30,000 oracle calls for a MEK1/CDK6 dual-target task, our
method substantially outperformed established baselines, yielding 6,642 unique dual-active hits and 5,681 novel
scaffolds. It demonstrated high scalability in a complex five-kinase design task, identifying 4,063 unique hits. Notably,
hyperparameter-optimized variants maintained superior early-stage efficiency even under a severely restricted budget
of 5,000 calls. Independent Boltz-2 predictions and 3D molecular docking confirmed the structural plausibility and
robust binding affinities of the candidates. These findings establish the proposed method as a robust and
data-efficient foundation for polypharmacological drug discovery under realistic computational constraints.
posters.P003:
Cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9) is a major drug-metabolizing enzyme in the human liver and exhibits extensive
genetic polymorphism. Some variants show altered metabolic activity toward specific substrates, resulting in
interindividual differences in drug efficacy and adverse drug reactions. Understanding the structural basis of these
functional changes is essential for drug development and precision medicine. However, the structural mechanisms
underlying altered substrate metabolism in many CYP2C9 variants, particularly rare alleles, remain poorly understood.
In this study, we investigate the structural effects of CYP2C9 polymorphisms using both available experimental
structures and computationally generated variant models. Variant structures were generated using Rosetta-based
modeling, and their structural reproducibility was compared against existing crystal structures. Structural analyses were
performed focusing on the substrate-binding pocket, active-site geometry, and access tunnels, which play key roles in
substrate binding and catalysis. In addition, analyses of substrate binding modes are being conducted to explore
possible relationships between structural changes and altered metabolic activity. Through these ongoing analyses, we
aim to establish a framework for evaluating the impact of CYP2C9 polymorphisms on drug metabolism from a
structural perspective and to support future prediction of variant-dependent functional changes.
posters.P004:
Hankuk University of Foreign Studies
Ordinal side-effect frequencies provide more granular safety information than binary occurrence labels, but sparse
annotations hinder generalization to unseen drugs. Structural representations may miss functional pharmacology,
whereas natural-language descriptions offer richer context but risk encoding side effects. We evaluated whether
leakage-controlled DrugBank descriptions add complementary signal under five-fold drug-disjoint evaluation.
We analyzed 49,160 SIDER-derived drug-side-effect pairs with ordinal frequency labels, spanning 773 drugs and 2,717
side effects (SEs). Identity mapping and rule-based/contextual review yielded descriptions for 724 drugs; missing
descriptions were mask-gated. Using fixed UMLS-derived SE embeddings, we separately projected 1,536-dimensional
SDF- and DrugBank-derived drug embeddings and formed drug-SE interaction features using element-wise products
and absolute differences. A factorial design toggled both drug channels and an additive training-fold-derived SE prior;
coverage-matched shuffling broke drug-description identity.
Across four matched contrasts, descriptions improved pooled quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.0449 (95% CI,
0.0297–0.0592) and reduced mean absolute error (MAE) by 0.0525; effects were favorable in all five folds. With all
factors enabled, matched descriptions outperformed shuffled text by 0.0773 QWK, improving every fold. The
SDF-plus-description model achieved QWK 0.5532 and MAE 0.8181. Factorial and identity-shuffled controls indicated
drug-matched text effects, while subadditive interactions suggested partial redundancy with SDF-derived
representations.
posters.P005:
Hankuk University of Foreign Studies
Drug response varies substantially across cell lines even within the same cancer type, making accurate prediction of
this heterogeneity a central challenge in precision oncology. Although various computational methods have been
proposed, fundamental limitations remain. First, cell lines within the same drug–cancer pair often show heterogeneous
IC50 profiles, making cell-specific prediction difficult. Drug-level averages can explain much of the prediction variance,
causing cell-specific signals to be overlooked. Second, many existing methods do not fully capture drug mechanisms
of action (MoA) or target-gene-level responses. However, gene-level interpretability remains largely unexplored. To
address these limitations, we propose PAMoA (Prior-augmented Attention for MoA interpretability), which integrates
biological target priors into a target-aware attention mechanism. By focusing the gene search space on drug-target
signals, PAMoA mitigates drug-mean bias while capturing cell-specific responses and providing gene- and
pathway-level interpretability through attention scores. Evaluations on GDSC dataset demonstrate that PAMoA
substantially outperforms conventional baselines (Random Forest and ElasticNet), achieving a mean MSE of 1.0894±(R2 = 0.887). Ablation studies confirm the contributions of target priors and attention mechanisms, while top-ranked
genes closely align with known drug targets and associated pathways. Overall, PAMoA provides a target-aware
framework that unifies drug response prediction and biological interpretation for preclinical drug screening.

Drug response prediction (DRP) is a crucial biomedical challenge for discovering and repurposing anticancer drugs
tailored to heterogeneous genomic profiles. The growing volume of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data
offers unprecedented opportunities to investigate the fine-grained mechanisms of innate and acquired drug resistance
within specific cell subpopulations and the complex tumor microenvironment. However, unlike bulk analyses,
single-cell studies typically lack definitive sensitivity indicators like half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), and the
available data is highly fragmented across public databases. Consequently, existing DRP models are predominantly
trained on in vitro bulk transcriptomics and remain unvalidated against large-scale single-cell cohorts. To address this
gap, we evaluated several prominent DRP models using 17 publicly available monotherapy scRNA-seq collections. To
better reflect physiological responses, these cohorts comprised surgically resected tumors, patient-derived organoids
(PDOs), and xenografts (PDXs), capturing both preclinical and translational contexts. By inputting scRNA-seq profiles
transformed into pseudo-bulk counts per identified cell cluster, we found that current DRP algorithms exhibit limited
efficacy in discerning sensitive from resistant subpopulations. Ultimately, this study highlights critical limitations in
existing models and underscores the urgent need for DRP frameworks optimized for single-cell resolution.

Accurate assessment of drug toxicity remains a major challenge in drug development. Discrepancies between
preclinical models and human toxicity outcomes primarily contribute to safety failures. Here, we present a novel
framework that leverages genotype-phenotype differences (GPD)—defined as variations in how genetic factors
influence traits across species (or organisms)—to enhance toxicity assessment. We found GPD to be significantly
associated with severe adverse events in clinical settings. Incorporating GPD features into a machine learning model
for drug toxicity assessment enhances predictive performance compared to current state-of-the-art chemical-based
approaches. Our method enables the identification of drugs with toxicity risks that were previously unrecognized
based on their chemical properties. GPD features are particularly effective in detecting drugs linked to nervous system
and cardiovascular toxicity, two leading causes of clinical drug failure. Additionally, chronological validation
demonstrates that our model can accurately forecast future toxicity from historical data, underscoring its practical
utility in the real world. These findings highlight the pivotal role of GPD in addressing translational gaps and offer a
promising strategy for more reliable toxicity assessment of candidate drugs.

RNA is an attractive therapeutic target beyond the druggable proteome, but scarce RNA-ligand data and limited
RNA-focused libraries constrain the design of RNA-targeted small molecules. Generative Active Learning (GAL)
addresses this by iteratively generating candidates, selecting molecules for oracle evaluation via an acquisition
function, and updating the model with newly acquired data. However, existing GAL approaches fix the acquisition
strategy across rounds. We propose an agentic GAL framework that determines the acquisition strategy through
multi-agent debate. In each round, an Orchestration Agent summarizes the search state such as predictive uncertainty,
scaffold diversity, and top-candidate improvement as shared context. An Exploration Agent argues for broad chemical
space coverage while an Exploitation Agent argues for refinement of top hits. The Orchestration Agent mediates this
multi-turn debate and determines the acquisition function and allocates a scaffold-specific oracle budget. We apply
our framework to de novo optimization of small molecules targeting pre-miR-21, using LOGICS as the generator, an
ECFP-based random forest as the surrogate, and a DeepRNA-DTI ensemble as the oracle. The framework will be
compared against fixed acquisition strategies under identical oracle budgets in terms of predicted activity, scaffold
novelty, and sample efficiency. Agent deliberation additionally provides rationales for each acquisition decision.
posters.P009:
Precision oncology depends on knowing how a given tumour will respond to a given compound. However, profiling
every compound against every cancer cell line is prohibitively costly. Machine learning models can be trained to
predict such responses. An example is models trained on L1000 perturbation data which use relevant drug
information. However, how much this information contributes to the model remains largely untested. Here we test this
by benchmarking seven published models spanning graph, variational, diffusion and transformer architectures on a
curated L1000 subset (78,453 profiles, 8,276 compounds) with drug inputs full, zeroed and shuffled. In all the models,
ablating the drug input negligibly changed 31 evaluation metrics. Furthermore, a drug-free baseline which depends
only on levels of gene expression before drug treatment, was as good as the best model. Keeping this baseline fixed,
we trained a second network to predict the drug-specific effect for each gene. Under a drug-blind split, our residual
architecture outperformed the drug-free baseline and the retrained best published model, while ablating the drug
inputs removed this gain. Our approach thus separates the contribution of drug information from that of basal cell
state and exploits it to predict unprofiled compounds.

Drug-induced transcriptomic profiles provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular
responses to pharmacological perturbations. However, the vast combinatorial space of drugs, doses, and cell lines
makes comprehensive experimental profiling impractical. Here, we present a computational framework for predicting
drug-induced gene expression profiles by learning gene-level Hill-slope equations, enabling the modelling of the
nonlinear dynamics inherent to dose-response relationships.
Across comprehensive evaluations, our framework consistently outperformed existing approaches, with particularly
strong performance in challenging settings involving previously unseen drugs and cell lines. Importantly, the predicted
transcriptomic profiles preserved both drug-specific and cell-type-specific biological signals, as demonstrated through
network analysis and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. Furthermore, incorporating the predicted drug-induced profiles
improved cancer drug response prediction, particularly for drugs not observed during model training, a longstanding
challenge in computational drug response modelling.
Together, these results demonstrate that modelling nonlinear dose-dependent transcriptomic responses can provide
biologically informative predictions and expand the utility of transcriptomic data for drug response modelling,
including in settings where experimental measurements are unavailable.

High attrition rates of drug candidates during clinical evaluation highlight the critical need for accurate ADMET
assessment in the early stages of drug development. Despite recent advances in deep-learning-based molecular
property prediction, achieving robust predictive generalizability across heterogeneous ADMET endpoints remains
challenging. To address this limitation, we present an ADMET-centric foundation model that leverages multimodal
contrastive pre-training between chemical structures and ADMET profiles.
Our framework comprises three stages. First, we construct a densely labeled ADMET profile by integrating
experimental ADMET data from multiple sources, followed by missing-value imputation using machine learning
models. Second, during pre-training, the model learns a joint representation by aligning chemical structural features
with the imputed ADMET profile space through contrastive learning. Lastly, the pre-trained chemical structure encoder
is further fine-tuned to predict downstream ADMET endpoints.
Comprehensive evaluations show that our model outperforms both existing uni-modal and multi-modal molecular
representation baselines across a broad spectrum of ADMET endpoints. Significantly, integrating ADMET profile
context and chemical structures during pre-training improves the representation quality for biologically intricate
clinical endpoints.
posters.P012:
Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs) offer an innovative therapeutic paradigm by harnessing cellular degradation
machinery to eliminate historically undruggable disease targets. While computational approaches increasingly aid in
silico activity prediction, current deep learning models remain hindered by limited benchmark data, inadequate
representations of multi-body interaction dynamics, and deterministic outputs lacking confidence estimation. To
resolve these bottlenecks, we introduce RP-PROTAC, an interpretable framework grounded in PROTAC structural
biology. We first curate an expanded bioactivity benchmark comprising 8,789 labeled interactions, an approximate
six-fold increase over prior datasets. Mirroring the canonical ternary complex mechanism, RP-PROTAC explicitly
partitions molecules into warhead, linker, and E3-ligand moieties, modeling their granular cross-interactions with
proteins of interest and E3 ligases via hierarchical multi-head cross-attention. Additionally, it quantifies both aleatoric
and epistemic uncertainties using variance regularization and deep ensembles to evaluate prediction reliability.
Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RP-PROTAC consistently outperforms existing baselines across unseen pairs,
target proteins, and chemical scaffolds (AUPR/AUROC of 0.866/0.804, 0.842/0.701, and 0.676/0.627), achieving up to
8.4% AUPR and 17.2% AUROC gains. Furthermore, uncertainty-based filtering elevates AUROC from 0.642 to 0.691 on
unseen PROTACs, confirming well-calibrated error awareness. These findings establish RP-PROTAC as a dependable
bioinformatics platform for accelerating data-driven candidate prioritization in targeted drug discovery.

Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is an essential treatment for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, peritoneal
fibrosis (PF), a common complication of PD, significantly impairs its efficacy and increases the risk of peritonitis,
cardiovascular diseases, and the progression of CKD. Here, we analyzed the proteome of human peritoneal
mesothelial cells (hPMCs) from CKD patients and conducted drug connectivity analyses to identify key biomolecules
linked to PF, particularly focusing on the RhoA protein. hPMCs were isolated from PD effluent and were treated with 2
ng/mL rTGF-β for 48 hours to induce fibrosis. Tandem mass tag-based quantitative proteomic analysis was conducted
to investigate the global proteome profile of hPMCs. Identified differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were subjected
to pathway analysis using the KEGG Database and drug connectivity analysis using the Proteomic Atlas for Small
Molecule Perturbagens Database to identify potential drug targets. A total of 8,961 proteins were quantified in hPMCs.
Treatment with rTGF-β induced a significant increase in the expression of key extracellular matrix proteins, including
FN1, COL1A1, and TAGLN. DEPs were further selected based on their increased expression in response to rTGF-β
treatment for drug connectivity analysis. Potential therapeutic candidates were identified, including inhibitors of RhoA,
PDGFR, and tyrosine kinase, which may counteract the gene expression patterns associated with PF. Notably, RhoA, an
important GTPase that regulates myofibroblast differentiation, was found to be highly expressed in hPMCs,
highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for PF. These findings suggest that targeting RHOA, along with other
identified inhibitors, could offer promising therapeutic strategies for mitigating PF.
posters.P014:
Pusan National University
Screening ultra-large chemical libraries requires identifying high-affinity ligands from only a small fraction of the
available compounds while avoiding redundant selections from structurally similar chemical scaffolds. This creates a
challenging active learning problem in which limited docking budgets must support both efficient hit retrieval and
exploration of chemical space. We present a virtual screening framework that combines locality-sensitive hashing
(LSH), ranking-based surrogate learning, and Bayesian optimization.
LSH is used to organize molecular representations into hash-based groups and to construct structurally diverse initial
samples without exhaustive pairwise comparisons. The ranking-based surrogate model then learns relative priorities
among compounds instead of predicting absolute docking scores, directly supporting top-candidate retrieval.
Acquisition functions then iteratively select new compounds by balancing predicted priority and uncertainty
throughout screening.
The framework was evaluated on large-scale molecular libraries, including ZINC 138M, using fixed docking budgets
and metrics for top-ranked retrieval, scaffold diversity, and exploration coverage. On ZINC 138M, the proposed
strategy achieved approximately 27-fold higher top-1% retrieval than random sampling while increasing the number
of unique scaffolds by approximately 6%. These results show that ranking and hashing can complement active
learning to improve both efficiency and diversity in ultra-large virtual screening under severely constrained molecular
evaluation budgets.
posters.P015:
RNA is an increasingly important therapeutic target, making efficient in silico screening of large compound libraries
essential for RNA drug discovery. Molecular docking requires a separate physical calculation per target–ligand pair,
limiting scalability to billion-compound libraries. Dense-retrieval methods such as DrugCLIP improve efficiency by
embedding targets and ligands in a shared space for nearest-neighbor search, but compress each into a single global
representation, limiting their ability to capture motif-mediated RNA–ligand recognition.
Here we introduce HotCoil, an RNA-specific virtual screening method that combines CLIP-style contrastive learning
with unbalanced entropic optimal transport (UOT) to score RNA–ligand compatibility without experimental structures.
Nucleotide- and atom-level embeddings are integrated by bilinear cross-attention and pooled into global RNA/ligand
and local motif/fragment representations. The global branch scores molecule-level compatibility by cosine similarity,
whereas the local branch uses UOT to align predicted secondary-structure motifs with BRICS fragments; their weighted
sum defines the final score. On RNAmigos2, HotCoil matches structure-based docking in retrieval performance while
achieving stronger early enrichment with orders of magnitude less computation. On the PNU test set, it ranks
high-affinity binders above weaker binders, suggesting its scores reflect relative binding strength. UOT transport plans
and attention maps additionally provide motif- and nucleotide-level interpretability.

Accurate molecular activity prediction is essential for identifying promising drug candidates and accelerating drug
discovery. Many deep learning-based methods have been successfully applied across various chemical domains
through pretraining-based knowledge transfer strategies that leverage large-scale unlabeled datasets. However, these
methods often struggle with activity prediction involving activity cliffs, where structurally similar molecules exhibit
substantial differences in biological activity.
To address this challenge, we propose a molecular activity prediction framework that leverages hierarchical molecular
representations incorporating both atom- and fragment-level contexts. First, the proposed model is trained to learn
context-aware discrete codebooks at both levels, which capture the chemical properties and local structural patterns
of molecules. The local structural information from both levels is integrated into a global molecular representation
through a heterogeneous augmented graph encoder.
The proposed model achieves the best performance on activity benchmarks across 30 macromolecular targets, while
demonstrating robust performance on activity cliff molecules. Furthermore, it also shows comparable performance to
state-of-the-art models in various molecular property prediction tasks and pretrained embedding analyses, suggesting
its potential applicability to diverse molecular tasks through hierarchical molecular representations that preserve local
information at both fine- and coarse-grained levels.
posters.P017:

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterised by the absence of estrogen
receptor, progesterone receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, resulting in limited therapeutic
options. Cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9), a transcriptional regulator involved in oncogenic and anti-apoptotic gene
expression, represents a potential therapeutic target in TNBC. This study investigated natural flavonoids as potential
CDK9 inhibitors using an integrated computational approach. The human CDK9 sequence (UniProt P50750) was
modelled using SWISS-MODEL, I-TASSER and AlphaFold 3, followed by structural validation using ERRAT and
PROCHECK. Five flavonoids were docked into the ATP-binding pocket, and the top-ranked complex underwent 100ns
molecular dynamics simulation. AlphaFold 3 Model 1 demonstrated the best overall quality, with an ERRAT score of
98.442% and 85.9% residues in the most favoured Ramachandran region. Luteolin showed the strongest docking
affinity (-9.23 kcal/mol), compared with ATP (-9.01 kcal/mol), forming hydrogen bonds with Asp109 and Asp167 and
hydrophobic interactions with Gly26, Val33, Leu156 and Ala166. Molecular dynamics indicated stable behaviour of the
central kinase domain, while terminal regions displayed greater flexibility. These findings identify luteolin as a
promising computational lead for further CDK9 validation in TNBC.

Evaluation of the binding affinities of drugs to proteins including off-targets is essential for identifying drug
pharmacological actions. Docking simulation is one of the widely used approaches for evaluating binding affinities,
but it requires three-dimensional structures of proteins. Only a small fraction of the human proteome has been
structurally determined by experiment. Here, we propose novel computational methods to predict the therapeutic
indications and side effects of drug candidate compounds from the binding affinities to human protein structures on
a proteome-wide scale. Large-scale docking simulations were performed for 7,582 drugs with 19,135 human protein
structures revealed by AlphaFold, including experimentally unresolved proteins, and the binding free energies were
calculated, and the proteome-wide binding affinity score (PBAS) profiles were constructed. Using the PBAS profiles
with template matching and machine learning models, we predicted therapeutic effects for 559 diseases and side
effects for 285 toxicities. The PBAS profiles outperformed chemical substructure profiles and existing target protein
profiles. The method further enabled the prediction of therapeutic effects even when the three-dimensional structures
of the proteins had not been experimentally determined, and successfully extracted proteins associated with side
effects. The PBAS profiles will be useful in various applications in drug discovery.

Early prediction of toxicity and biological activity is essential for reducing the high attrition rate in drug development.
However, existing molecular representation learning methods predominantly rely on a single view of the molecule,
capturing only a limited aspect of its chemical information. Specifically, graph-based methods learn atom-level and
graph-level information but provide limited supervision at the fragment level, while fingerprints remain fixed auxiliary
features rather than learned representations. To address these limitations, we propose HiFi-Mol, a multi-view
framework in which two complementary encoders are pretrained independently and subsequently integrated for
downstream property prediction. The graph encoder is trained with fragment-aware masking and multi-resolution
supervision to acquire fragment-level representations while preserving atom-level and graph-level information. In
parallel, the fingerprint encoder tokenizes the active bits of seven fingerprint families and learns their contextual
dependencies jointly with SMILES tokens through masked language modeling. Evaluated on MoleculeNet under the
scaffold split, HiFi-Mol improves the average ROC-AUC across eight classification tasks by 2.77% over the strongest
baseline and achieves competitive performance on three regression tasks. Further analyses indicate that
fragment-aware masking enhances the quality of graph representations, and that the graph and fingerprint encoders
exhibit dataset-dependent strengths.
posters.P020:
Campups
Modeling molecular toxicity requires integrating heterogeneous representations that capture complementary structural
and chemical properties. We present MEMOL, a multimodal learning framework for drug toxicity prediction that
combines molecular images, graphs, and fingerprints through mixture-of-experts-guided attention. These modalities
are encoded by a vision transformer, a graph neural network, and a pretrained autoencoder, respectively. The resulting
embeddings are refined through self-attention and fused through cross-attention, allowing the model to capture both
modality-specific patterns and cross-modal dependencies. Unlike conventional fusion strategies, MEMOL incorporates
sparse mixture-of-experts routing directly into both self-attention and cross-attention modules, enabling adaptive
expert selection during intra- and inter-modality representation learning. We evaluated MEMOL on five benchmark
datasets including cardiotoxicity, drug-induced liver injury, skin reaction, carcinogenicity, and an extended liver injury.
MEMOL consistently outperformed conventional machine learning and recent deep learning baselines, with
improvements of up to 8.33% AUROC and 9.11% AUPRC over the strongest competing model. Additional analyses
showed that integrating all three modalities yielded the most robust performance, and ablation studies confirmed that
sparse expert routing in both self-attention and cross-attention was more effective than standard attention or dense
expert configurations. Our results highlight sparse expert-guided attention as a promising multimodal representation
learning strategy for molecular property prediction.
posters.P021:
Predicting human oral pharmacokinetics (PK) from molecular structure would accelerate early drug discovery, but most
structure-based models predict only isolated summary parameters and miss the full concentration-time course that
efficacy and safety depend on.
First, it builds a fully traceable, reproducible dataset of human oral concentration-time profiles, curated from the
literature through systematic digitization, harmonization, and quality control, so the observed concentrations can be
learned and validated.
Second, it shows that predicting the whole profile directly from structure is not merely a richer output but a better
learning target: summary parameters recovered from the predicted profile were more accurate than regressing each
separately under identical conditions, and this advantage grew as data became scarcer.
Third, it pinpoints the bottleneck: the shared temporal shape is learned reliably, whereas compound-specific absolute
exposure dominates the error, reflecting formulation, absorption, first-pass metabolism, and clearance, which structure
cannot capture.
Thus molecular structure encodes meaningful features of human oral PK trajectories and offers an early exposure prior
for compound prioritization and ADME planning from structure and dose alone.
posters.P022:
Medicine, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul, Korea
Traumatic brain injury involves complex molecular responses, making the systematic prioritization of drug repurposing
candidates challenging. We propose a drug repurposing framework that integrates disease-relevant Gene Ontology
biological processes, recovery-oriented metric learning, and biomedical knowledge graph information.
Disease-relevant biological processes were selected based on semantic similarity to traumatic brain injury
pathophysiology descriptions, and gene expression profiles were transformed into biological process-level features
using gene set variation analysis. A metric-learning model was then trained to construct an embedding space
reflecting the recovery direction from the disease state toward the normal state. An axis-aware recovery score was
defined to account for both projection along the recovery axis and off-axis deviation. In traumatic brain injury gene
expression data, levetiracetam and N-acetylcysteine showed relatively high axis-aware recovery scores. These scores
were combined with similarities between candidate and experimental drugs based on Hetionet target-binding and
gene-regulation relationships for candidate prioritization, with both drugs ranking among the top candidates. These
results suggest that integrating transcriptomic recovery patterns with knowledge graph-based drug similarity may
provide a useful strategy for prioritizing drug repurposing candidates for traumatic brain injury.
posters.P023:
Rare and intractable diseases have unmet therapeutic needs, yet many are not represented in any medical knowledge
graph (KG), precluding existing graph-based drug repurposing methods. We propose a zero-shot drug repurposing
framework that integrates KG-absent diseases into a disease network, using traumatic brain injury (TBI), an intractable
disease, as a case study. We integrated a disease ontology hierarchy with a KG to construct a disease network based
on semantic similarity. After augmenting sparse disease-gene features using neighboring diseases, we iteratively
predicted gene features of the target disease and converted them into Gene Ontology biological process profiles. The
target disease was incorporated into the network via link prediction, and predicted disease-drug associations from
multiple seeds were aggregated into a drug ranking. TBI was incorporated primarily through links to cerebrovascular
diseases. Top-ranked drugs included statins, antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents, corticosteroids, and tetracycline
antibiotics, which are associated with vascular injury and neuroinflammation in TBI. In validation, where diseases with
known associations were isolated from the KG, the framework recovered their disease-disease and disease-drug
associations. It also performed consistently on KEGG, an independent KG, demonstrating generalizability. This
framework can provide biologically plausible drug candidates for rare and intractable diseases lacking KG
representation.

Accurate prediction of molecular properties, including ADMET endpoints, is central to drug discovery, yet
substructure-level interpretation remains challenging. We introduce a model integrating atom-level molecular graphs
and substructure-level junction trees through membership-constrained bidirectional cross-attention: substructures
attend only to their member atoms, and atoms attend only to substructures containing them. Each molecule's two
representations form a positive pair for augmentation-free contrastive pretraining on ZINC250k. Against 23 baselines
on nine MoleculeNet datasets, our model achieved the best average rank under random splits (1.78; first on seven
datasets) and the second-best under scaffold splits. On the MoleculeACE activity-cliff benchmark (30 targets), it
achieved the lowest overall and cliff-restricted mean RMSEs among 24 methods (0.749 and 0.816, respectively).
Ablations showed performance gains from both the membership constraint and pretraining. Across all nine datasets,
substructure-to-atom attention shifted with layer depth from carbon atoms toward heteroatoms, while
atom-to-substructure attention shifted from ring substructures toward smaller bond-based substructures. These
patterns were already present in the pretrained model. In all nine datasets, masking higher-attention substructures
tended to cause larger prediction changes. For all 30 targets, attention differences within activity-cliff pairs were
concentrated near modified atoms. The model combines competitive predictive performance with directly inspectable
atom-substructure attention.

Protein kinases are major therapeutic targets in drug discovery [1,2], but early identification of potent and selective kinase inhibitors
remains challenging because (i) few computational tools support systematic screening across a broad kinase panel, (ii) integrated
assessment of off-target liabilities within a single framework is lacking, and (iii) most AI-driven methods predict only binary
interactions rather than quantitative binding affinities [3,4]. To address these limitations, we developed DeepKinomeWeb, an
integrated web-based platform for quantitative kinase inhibitor screening and selectivity profiling [5].
DeepKinomeWeb is built upon DeepKinome, a 20-layer CNN regression model that predicts kinase–compound binding affinity as percent inhibition across a panel of 229 kinases [6]. On the L1000 test dataset, DeepKinome achieved an RMSE of 1.157, Pearson r of
0.743, and R² of 0.535, outperforming nine competing AI models with statistical significance (three-fold CV, Welch's t-test, P < 0.01).
The platform further provides binding affinity heatmap visualization, selectivity index (SI) calculation, promiscuity/specificity radar plots,
AutoDock Vina-based docking analysis [7], and ADMET profiling [8].
Users submit compounds via PubChem CIDs or SDF files [9], and the platform automatically generates an integrated analysis report. In a case study using three FDA-approved kinase inhibitors absent from the training data—brigatinib (Type I), ponatinib (Type II), and
sunitinib (Type I/II)—DeepKinomeWeb correctly distinguished selective and broad-spectrum profiles through predicted affinity
heatmaps, docking poses, ADMET properties, and SI rankings. Statistical validation confirmed that FDA-approved on-target pairs
exhibited significantly higher SImean than off-target pairs (median 1.058 vs. 0.997; n = 422 vs. 154,480; Wilcoxon P = 2.48 × 10⁻⁹), and
DeepKinome ranked approved target kinases closer to the top than AutoDock Vina alone. These results suggest that DeepKinomeWeb can serve as a practical decision-support platform for prioritizing kinase inhibitor candidates and reducing downstream experimental
burden.

The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a major obstacle in the development of therapeutics targeting the central nervous
system, particularly the brain. Although the BBB protects the brain from exogenous substances, a drug must cross this
barrier at an adequate level to exert its intended pharmacological effect. Consequently, predicting BBB permeability is
an important early-stage task in drug discovery. Numerous deep-learning models have been developed for this
purpose, most of which learn from molecular structural data. However, molecules with highly similar structures can
exhibit substantially different permeability profiles. To address this challenge, we propose a learning strategy that
combines a graph representation model pretrained on largescale compound data with scaffold-aware contrastive
learning, yielding a competitive alternative to existing state-of-the-art models.

Precision medicine aims to identify optimal treatments based on the molecular profiles of individual patients.
However, predicting drug response remains a major challenge due to intratumoral heterogeneity. To fully capture this
biological complexity, integrating comprehensive multi-omics profiles has become essential, driving the necessity for
methodologies that can leverage complex biological and chemical data modalities. In this study, we propose
OmicsDRP, a dual-branch deep learning model that predicts drug response by integrating cellular multi-omics profiles
and drug structures. This architecture enables each branch to learn informative representations from distinct data
modalities, thereby effectively capturing cross-modality interactions governing drug sensitivity. Through
cross-validation on the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) dataset, OmicsDRP demonstrates consistent
improvements in predictive performance over conventional machine learning methods and exhibits competitive
predictive accuracy compared to existing drug response prediction models. Furthermore, comprehensive
interpretability analyses—including latent embedding visualizations and feature-level SHAP analysis—reveal
biologically meaningful insights aligned with known drug targets and mechanisms of action, validating the model's
reliability at the molecular level. In summary, OmicsDRP presents a reliable framework for precision oncology by
combining robust predictive performance with biological interpretability.

Large-scale transcriptomic datasets generated from bioactive compounds and herbal medicines are scattered across
numerous public repositories, which complicates integrative analysis. To address this challenge, we systematically
collected transcriptomic datasets from multiple public resources and uniformly processed them through quality
control, normalization, and differential expression analyses. This effort resulted in a unified perturbation transcriptome
database comprising more than 20,000 small-molecule treatments, 40 herbal formula/extract treatments, and 1,500
natural product ingredient treatments across diverse cell lines and tissues.
For each treatment-induced gene expression signature, enrichment analyses were performed against curated pathway
gene sets, disease signatures, and drug-induced transcriptomic signatures using complementary statistical approaches,
including hypergeometric and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests.
Our collected data provide a foundation for developing predictive models of drug interactions, molecular targets,
mechanisms of action, and potential therapeutic indications.

Pusan National University
Background and Objectives: The Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) provides customized claims
data for selected drugs and study periods, supporting targeted investigations of potential adverse drug events.
However, study-specific data extraction and access requirements limit the feasibility of extending this approach to
systematic safety screening across a broad range of drugs. Annual patient samples offer an alternative, but their
one-year observation periods constrain sequence symmetry analysis (SSA). We aimed to develop an automated SSA
framework tailored to these datasets.
Methods: HIRA National Patient Sample datasets from 2017 to 2024 were analyzed separately by year, without
patient-level linkage across years. Each dataset included claims for approximately 2–3% of healthcare users in Korea.
We screened the 1,000 most frequently prescribed drugs in 2024. First observed prescriptions and diagnoses were
defined as index and marker events, respectively, and drug–disease sequences were assessed for temporal asymmetry.
Results: We present an automated SSA framework that integrates event identification and drug–disease pair screening
within independent annual datasets, enabling systematic evaluation of temporal associations under a one-year
observation constraint.
Conclusions: This framework provides a basis for large-scale pharmacovigilance using annual claims samples. External
validation will assess signal detection performance and inform methodological refinement.

Persistent sexual, neurological and somatic symptoms following discontinuation of 5α-reductase inhibitors (5ARIs) and
selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) share a substantially overlapping symptom profile which motivated the
hypothesis of a common neuroendocrine mechanism based on shared genetic susceptibility to the conditions
described as post-5ARI syndrome (P5ARIS) and post-SSRI sexual dysfunction (PSSD). Whether susceptibility to these
conditions is genetically correlated is unknown, and no adequately powered genetic study of either has been reported.
Lacking an explicit endpoint definition, we are building representative, or ‘proxy’ cohorts of individuals suffering from
P5ARIS and PSSD, and initially specified P5ARIS alone as the target phenotype in FinnGen (n ≈ 520,000). Combining 1
mg prescriptions and 5 mg purchasers restricted to first exposure before age 45 yielded less than 1000 exposed men,
of which well below 100 fulfilled P5ARIS case definition.
Genome-wide association analysis of 961 PSSD cases against 23323 exposed, discontinued comparison subjects identified
no variant reaching genome-wide significance (p < 5×10⁻⁸). A secondary definition requiring sustained hormonal
treatment alone, without a second symptom domain, gave 1008 cases against the same comparison group, yielding 14
significant variants. Genetic correlation between the two definitions tests whether they represent one condition.
Since neither arm is adequately powered alone, we specify post-drug syndrome as an umbrella phenotype, arguing
that the mechanism converging distinct pharmacological classes on one symptom profile determines who is affected
based on a common genetic susceptibility.
posters.P032:
Toxicities missed in preclinical animal studies underlie many clinical trial failures and post-marketing withdrawals.
Computational toxicity prediction has relied largely on chemical structure, and target safety assessment on human
genetic evidence alone. Yet orthologous genes can occupy different network positions, so perturbing the same target
in mouse and human need not have the same consequence. Attributing such differences to biology first requires
separating them from differences in data coverage. We built separate human and mouse knowledge graphs, each
linking small-molecule drugs to targets, protein-protein interactions, gene-phenotype annotations and preclinical
toxicity findings. Orthology is held outside the graphs as a mapping, not an edge, so cross-species differences can be
measured. This design quantifies the coverage gap. Among 16,505 one-to-one orthologous pairs, each supported by
both NCBI and MGI, 97.9% of human genes carry interaction data against 73.5% of their mouse counterparts, and
where both are covered, median degree is 94 versus 5. Conversely, 79.8% of mouse genes carry phenotype
annotations against 30.1% in human, reflecting targeted knockout curation versus annotation confined to Mendelian
disease genes. The gap is data-type-specific; conflating it with biology misreads missing data as species differences.
This work provides a species-resolved framework for interpreting preclinical-to-clinical translation.
posters.P033:
HITS Incorporation
Distinguishing class-wide from molecule-specific drug toxicity requires weeks of manual literature synthesis.
LLM-based agents could accelerate this, but their claims are often untraceable to a source, limiting their reliability in
biomedicine. We present HyperKG, a biomedical knowledge graph of 12.9M nodes and 191M edges from 200+
sources, coupled to a multi-agent framework for graph traversal, literature retrieval, and workflow planning. Every
edge records its source database, so multi-hop paths from drugs and their targets to clinical phenotypes remain
traceable at each step.
We tested whether the framework recovers a known mechanism among four CETP inhibitors, of which only torcetrapib
caused excess mortality in phase III. Given only the compound names, the agent compared their graph
neighborhoods and isolated an off-target neighborhood unique to torcetrapib (CYP11B2, aldosterone, EDN1). These
entities guided literature queries that recovered the upstream L-type calcium channel mechanism absent from the
graph, showing that graph traversal and retrieval fill complementary gaps.
Ablation across retrieval-only, graph-only, and graph-guided conditions, with a negative control, evaluates accuracy,
mechanism recall, and grounding. By anchoring hypotheses to source-attributed paths, this framework makes agentic
hypothesis generation auditable.

Pooling MRI data from multiple sites allows larger samples to be assembled and may improve the generalizability of
machine leanring analyses. However, non-biological variability arising from site-related differences can affect both the
performance and interpretation of neuroimaging-based disease classification. For multi-site classification of normal
cognition (NC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), it remains unclear whether
harmonization can reduce site effects while preserving disease-related biological information and maintaining
predictive performance.
We analyzed T1-weighted MRI volumetric data from 1,305 participants across nine sites and compared multi-class
classification performance before and after harmonization. To avoid data leakage in the machine learning pipeline,
harmonization parameters were estimated only within the training set. Model performance was then evaluated using
leave-one-site-out validation, in which each site was held out in turn as unseen test site. Finally, permutation feature
importance was used to identify the brain regions that contributed most to diagnostic classification.
This study evaluates the effects of harmonization on MRI-based volumetric classification within a validation framework
designed to prevent data leakage, while identifying interpretable regional brain features associated with NC, MCI, and
AD.

As whole genome sequencing (WGS) emerges as a standard technology in genome research and medicine, the
demand for rapid and accurate genomic data analysis continues to grow. We developed GenomeBoost Server (GBS), a
high-performance platform for efficient WGS/WES data analysis that integrates specialized hardware design with
highly optimized software. Leveraging hardware-software co-optimization, GBS enabled rapid processing, achieving up
to 4.9 WGS samples per hour for 30x variant calling in benchmarking experiments. Notably, variant calling results
generated by GBS showed 100% concordance with those obtained using GATK best practices, demonstrating full
compatibility with established analytical standards. These results demonstrate that the integration of optimized
hardware and software can substantially accelerate WGS analysis while maintaining analytical concordance. GBS
facilitates the identification of genetic variations and the discovery of insights that support progress in both genome
research and medicine.

Single-cell transcriptomic ageing prediction is confounded by batch effects from technical difference, which are
entangled with the biological signal. This study aims to segregate the ageing signal from these dataset-intrinsic
confounders.
To train to isolate aging-related signals from cohorts and datasets, we constructed integrated PBMC data consisting of
five publicly available single-cell datasets containing six immune cell types. (1,825 donors, age range 19–97 years). as a
measure the degree of aging, we used a publicly available pretrained single-cell foundation model as the backbone
and adapted it to the downstream task of age prediction via parameter-efficient fine-tuning. To mitigate cross-dataset
imbalance and cohort–batch confounding, our model introduces a domain-alignment component that learns
representations of aging invariant to dataset origin.
In the first instance, evaluating the model trained with CD8T cells, the mean absolute error (MAE) was 5.08 years in
the internal cross-validation. On an independent external validation cohort, it achieved an MAE of 16.52 years. Under
identical data-splitting and preprocessing protocols, our framework consistently outperformed a conventional
regression model on both internal and external datasets.
This study proposes a domain-aligned fine-tuning strategy for single-cell foundation models, providing a scalable
route to transcriptomic aging clocks in immunosenescence.

Large language models (LLMs) pretrained on large-scale biomedical corpora have become powerful tools for encoding
functional knowledge of genes. However, it remains unclear how gene representation and embedding strategies
influence the capacity of gene embeddings to capture biologically meaningful information. Here, we developed
GEbench to evaluate gene representations and embedding models across pathway-level, LLM generation, and
genome-scale biological tasks. We evaluated five input strategies, including Ensembl identifiers, gene symbols, NCBI
summaries, LLM-refined NCBI summaries, and LLM-generated functional descriptions. These inputs were transformed
by BioLinkBERT, Qwen-Enc, Qwen-7B, Mistral-7B, and BioMistral-7B for gene embedding generation. In a benchmark
of 680 genes from five pathways, functional descriptions, especially LLM-generated descriptions, achieved the
strongest performance across all input strategies, with ARI values of 0.49–0.60 and a maximum MacroF1 of 0.88.
Among gene embedding models, Qwen-Enc showed the strongest overall pathway-level performance. For the
LLM-generated functional descriptions, DeepSeek-V4-Flash was the strongest generation model. Genome-scale
analyses further showed that LLM-generated representations better preserved GO-BP semantic similarity and improved
GO-BP/KEGG annotation and PPI prediction. Overall, our study provides the GEbench framework to evaluate gene
embeddings for functional content representation, highlighting LLM-generated descriptions as an effective strategy to
generate meaningful gene embeddings across diverse genomic tasks.

Designing and executing a CRISPR-Cas genome-editing experiment requires chaining together many computational
steps - choosing a target gene, designing and ranking guide RNAs (gRNAs), assessing off-target risk, and quantifying
editing outcomes from sequencing data - each traditionally served by a separate tool with its own inputs, formats,
and expertise requirements. This fragmentation raises the barrier to entry and makes complete workflows slow and
hard to reproduce. Here we present an integrated web platform that unifies the entire genome-editing cycle and
exposes its computational modules through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling them to be directly
integrated with agentic AI systems. Through MCP, AI agents can interpret researchers' natural-language requests,
select and invoke appropriate genome-editing tools, coordinate multi-step workflows, and return the resulting
analyses, allowing the platform to serve as a standardized computational backend for AI-assisted genome-editing
workflows. Central to this release, its off-target engine has been re-engineered (Cas-OFFinder 2). Including GPU
acceleration, unlimited mismatches, and flexible PAMs, it is far faster than the original and, critically, keeps a nearly
constant runtime regardless of how many guides are queried, so screening one or hundreds of gRNAs costs
essentially the same. It also exhaustively enumerates off-targets containing DNA and RNA bulges (indels) that earlier
versions often missed, producing more complete specificity profiles.

General-purpose LLMs lack sufficient Korean-language capability and Korea-specific agricultural bioscience knowledge
and cannot access the National Agricultural Biotechnology Information Center (NABIC), Korea’s national omics
platform. We are developing NABIC-LLM, an on-premises system integrating domain adaptation with
evidence-grounded retrieval. A versioned canonical Parquet corpus comprised 26,711 Korean- and English-language
full-text articles and yielded 481,968 question-answer pairs and 29,480 chain-of-thought samples. Four open-weight
candidates—Model Q (27B), E (33B), G (31B), and A (72B)—were screened for version, interface, and training
compatibility. The selected checkpoint will receive domain-text LoRA-CPT and instruction-data LoRA-SFT.
Stage-specific evaluation retains Base, CPT, SFT, and RAG raw metrics for knowledge, adaptation, retention, question
answering, instruction following, retrieval, and grounding. A pre-RAG pilot assessed language, terminology, reasoning,
and deployment suitability using normalized metrics (S = Σwᵢzᵢ). Model Q led the composite, whereas Model A led
Base KMMLU; the reversal is exploratory and does not determine selection. Literature is retrieved through hybrid
dense-BM25 LanceDB search, while NABIC genomic and phenotypic records are accessed via read-only Model Context
Protocol tools. By unifying traceable evidence from Korean agricultural literature and national omics records,
NABIC-LLM helps agricultural researchers find evidence, verify provenance, and formulate data-informed questions.
posters.P040:
Genomic foundation models adopt architectures from natural language processing without examining whether they
suit the target domain. Prokaryotic genomes have distinctive properties: functional structure is predominantly local,
from codons within genes to operons spanning kilobases and genomic islands over hundreds of kilobases, while
long-range regularity reflects shared ancestry rather than compositional rules. With only four letters, prokaryotic DNA
carries far less information per position than text, making the choice of sequence operator especially consequential.
We propose that this choice should be derived from the biology of the target genome. Prokaryotic DNA replication is
directional and error-prone; these two properties imply an operator with self-correcting memory and order-sensitive
transitions. We trained a ~300M-parameter bidirectional foundation model on ~60,000 high-quality prokaryotic
genomes at single-nucleotide resolution, selecting an architecture whose computational properties match these
requirements. Systematic ablation confirms that order-sensitive transitions are biologically important: a variant without
this property requires ~2.4× more training tokens to reach the same gene function quality, and the advantage grows
with scale. Our model rivals models up to 13× larger on gene function and taxonomic classification at less than a
third of their training data, demonstrating domain-derived architecture as a productive principle for prokaryotic
genome foundation models.

With the rapid influx of biological data, the ecosystem of analytical tools has become increasingly complex. While
recent attempts leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate workflow code generation from natural
language, pure LLM-based approaches often suffer from hallucinations and offer little control over parameter tuning
and reproducibility. To address these hurdles, we built ComfyBioflow. We introduced a Tool Selection Registry (TSR)
layer to enforce strict tool-mapping rules, eliminating LLM hallucinations. Furthermore, we integrated ComfyUI—a
visual node-graph GUI platform that represents complex computational pipelines as intuitive, interconnected blocks.
This allows researchers to inspect step-by-step data flows and fine-tune parameters on the fly without writing code.
When applied to standard genomic pipelines like RNA-seq and variant calling, ComfyBioflow successfully combines
the ease of natural-language interaction with the rigor of reproducible, traceable workflow execution.

Q-omics (https://qomics.ai) is a consensus-based omics discovery platform that enables researchers to identify
therapeutic targets, biomarkers and disease mechanisms without bioinformatics expertise.
The platform integrates over 1 billion multi-omics measurements and over 30 billion statistically significant
associations across somatic mutation, DNA methylation, RNA expression, proteomics, drug response, CRISPR/shRNA
dependency, patient survival and the tumor microenvironment.
Bio-LDM, the first ontology-gated AI model for omics, outperforms state-of-the-art models on omics prediction tasks,
and uniquely enables systematic interpretation of context-specific gene-gene relationships. It jointly learns from omics
data and quantitative gene relationships derived from biological ontologies to identify phenotype-specific functional
interactions, gene modules and network hotspots. This enables the discovery of target–biomarker pairs and synthetic
lethal vulnerabilities.
Natural-language workflows translate biological questions into executable multi-omics analyses and evidence-backed
hypotheses. Users can move directly from a question to target prioritization, gene-pair biomarker discovery and
mechanistic interpretation.
By connecting literature, large-scale omics evidence and ontology-guided gene networks, Q-omics provides an
accessible framework for generating, prioritizing, and validating actionable hypotheses.

The concept of AI co-scientists are widespread but few are accessible to researchers yet. Here, we present Qoka, an
All-in-one AI research platform that integrates the entire research process into a single, easy-to-use application. Qoka
provides hypothesis and method search, project overview and roadmap creation, literature search and summarization
across sources, natural-language analysis pipelines that run on an on-premises server, AI-assisted research notes with
version history, and manuscript writing with automated peer review. With these features, researchers can check
whether a hypothesis has already been proposed and find methods to test it, create a project overview and roadmap,
review the literature and obtain concise summaries, build and run analyses and check their results, keep and edit
notes, and write and review a manuscript, all by describing what they want in natural language.Qoka's guided,
step-by-step interface and automatic setup remove the need for any technical configuration. By lowering these
barriers, Qoka aims to let researchers focus on scientific questions rather than on tools. The beta version of Qoka is
freely available at https://qoka.org.

In the case of large-scale spatial and single-cell omics data analysis, often count matrices easily exceed system
memory size, which hinders efficient computation. Here we present GeneQuant, a novel method for compressing
large-scale count matrices via data quantization. GeneQuant quantizes count matrices by minimizing a Lagrangian
cost combining weighted distortion with measured code length. GeneQuant enables analysis of large-scale datasets
with compressed representation without full decompression of dataset. In this work, we demonstrate the efficacy of
GeneQuant with a SSAM dataset comprises 1,922,990 voxels and 5,006 genes, which results in only 1.01 GB for data
storage, compared with 7.10 GB using Zarr v3 store with zstd compression. For downstream analysis, the memory
footprint within GPU was 2.96 GB, compared to original SSAM analysis with 38.5 GB, resulting in 13.0-fold
compression ratio with 98.0% of similarity to the original analysis results.

AI models are increasingly deployed in healthcare as black boxes: their training data and inner workings are
inaccessible, and many medical models output only labels without confidence scores. Accuracy verification requires
fully labelled test sets, an often costly process; this work investigates whether it can instead be achieved with partially
labelled, unseen test data. We propose a framework in which an auxiliary classifier, termed an oracle, learns to predict
whether the target classifier f is correct on each sample; averaging these predictions estimates f's accuracy. Two oracle
variants are developed, using f's predicted labels alone or, when available, its label probabilities. The oracle is trained
iteratively, prioritising samples misclassified by f or near its decision boundary to minimise labelling cost, and
integrates label-based agreement and input-perturbation stability signals through a gated meta-classifier robust to

Conventional single-cell analyses enable precise measurement of cellular gene expression but lose spatial information,
including tissue location and neighboring cellular environments. Understanding disease mechanisms at the tissue level
therefore requires models that jointly capture gene expression and spatial context. Spatial transcriptomics data are
also strongly affected by batch effects arising from differences in platforms, tissues, resolution, and experimental
conditions, while individual cohorts are often limited in size. Foundation models trained on large and diverse
spatial-omics datasets may address these limitations by learning transferable biological representations. Accordingly,
recent foundation-model development has increasingly incorporated spatial transcriptomics data alongside single-cell
data to capture spatial context. Despite the rapidly growing number of foundation models, there is still limited
systematic insight into which models perform best for particular applications and which downstream tasks their
embeddings can support. Here, we address this gap through a unified benchmark comprising five cancer types, 12
Xenium samples, and 3.26 million cells. We evaluated six foundation models and two non-foundation-model baselines,
PCA and scVI, across four representative tasks using frozen embeddings and common task-specific probes.

included in the benchmark—achieved the highest performance in niche classification and was the only model to
exceed a macro-F1 score of 0.5. Overall, this study aims to characterize the task-specific strengths of spatial
transcriptomics foundation models and provide practical guidance for selecting and applying these models across
diverse downstream analyses.

interface, they lack embedded complex molecular network structures. To address this, we present BioGraPhE, a
framework for embedding multi-omics knowledge graphs (KGs) into large language models (LLMs). We constructed a
regulatory KG centered on NF-B signaling by integrating patient-derived RNA-seq, inferred transcription factor
activities, protein-protein interactions, and curated pathways. We then evaluated two LLM-querying architectures: a

prompting. Our results demonstrate that the GraphRAG agent achieved high accuracy (95.92%) when reasoning over
complete graphs. While G-Retriever initially faced subgraph extraction bottlenecks, its predictive performance

Sleep-dependent memory consolidation relies on coordinated slow oscillation–spindle activity during non-REM sleep,
making precise real-time detection essential for targeted memory reactivation (TMR). However, most existing TMR
pipelines depend on research-grade polysomnography and offline analysis, limiting translation to consumer hardware.
This project developed and evaluated a non-look-ahead closed-loop TMR pipeline using consumer-grade frontal EEG.
First, a real-time sleep staging model was benchmarked against expert labels, YASA, and Huawei Watch on a full-night
Muse 2 recording, achieving 69.4% epoch-level agreement. Second, MaskingSpindleNet, a hybrid dilated CNN and
masked Transformer encoder, was trained on frontal EEG windows using pseudo-labels from an offline central-channel
spindle detector. On nine held-out subjects, the model achieved AUC-ROC of 0.841, recall of 0.759, and specificity of

accepted cue delivery, with a median latency of 1.10 s. Third, a real-time slow-oscillation upstate detector based on
forward-pass filtering, zero-crossing detection, and amplitude thresholding achieved mean event precision of 0.774 ±
0.036 against a YASA silver standard, with 7/9 subjects reaching precision ≥ 0.75. These results demonstrate the
feasibility of consumer EEG-based, real-time neurophysiological gating for closed-loop TMR and provide a foundation
for future human memory-consolidation studies.

and sequence design. The Kazusa Codon Usage Database (CUTG) has not been updated since 2007 and therefore no longer reflects

machine-readable standards, structured metadata, and persistent accession identifiers. However, this scale also encompasses
heterogeneity among submitter-derived records in taxonomic assignment, assembly status, annotation, and provenance, making
scalable, transparent quality assessment essential for reproducible secondary analysis.

integrate DDBJ/INSDC records with RefSeq reference data while distinguishing CDS validity from annotation and provenance evidence
rather than reducing heterogeneous information to a single quality score. Users will be able to define comparisons by taxon, gene,
organelle or replicon, translation-table context, source, and quality level, and generate codon-usage profiles, bias measures, and
comparative visualizations, with downloadable datasets and API access. These functions will support studies of codon evolution and
within- and between-species variation, as well as codon optimization for heterologous expression and therapeutic sequence design.

complete nucleotide sequences. INSDC's scale, taxonomic breadth, and interoperable standards provide a strong foundation for
biological AI, while genome- and CDS-level representations preserve complementary biological contexts for genome-scale
representation learning and codon-aware modeling. Together, these resources are intended to support task-specific AI-ready dataset
construction and controlled studies of how taxonomic composition, sequence representation, and curation influence model
generalization and biological interpretation.

Realistic synthetic patient data can accelerate validation of research, development of (AI) models, and in-silico trials,
while reducing privacy concerns and data-access constraints. However, there is limited guidance on holistic
performance evaluations for synthetic healthcare data. Moreover, most studies on tabular datasets evaluate large-N
datasets with moderate/low-p, leaving small-sample, high-dimensional scenarios, common in healthcare settings,
largely underexplored.
We present an evaluation framework for tabular synthetic healthcare data, spanning marginal fidelity, bivariate
dependence, multivariate similarity, prediction-based distinguishability, and privacy risk, with every metric interpreted
against a real-to-real bootstrap reference and assessed for stability and generalizability. We compared synthpop, vine
copulas, conditional tabular GAN (ctGAN), and variational autoencoders (VAE) across three healthcare datasets: clinical
trial proteomics (N=80, p=350), breast cancer proteomics (N=841, p=222), and electronic health records (N=19,903,
p=58).
Synthpop was most robust in the large-sample dataset, and vine copula was most competitive at higher
dimensionality. High marginal fidelity did not imply multivariate fidelity, and no method reproduced joint structure or
tail behaviour in the small-sample, high-dimensional setting. Privacy distances were at or above reference for most
generators. Realistic synthetic healthcare data therefore require regime-specific method selection and evaluation
across complementary metric families. The complete framework will made available through GitHub.

In silico perturbation modeling is advancing rapidly, with growing numbers of methods and benchmarks, yet the field
moves faster in comparing models than in establishing what these comparisons mean. Benchmark outcomes are
shaped not only by model predictions but also by the perturbation signal in data, what metrics capture, and whether
transcriptomic agreement preserves biologically relevant information. Here, we examine these components. Using
controlled prediction-corruption experiments, we show common metrics have distinct blind spots: correlation-based
metrics can remain high despite severe loss of perturbation magnitude or responsive-gene fidelity, whereas
distributional metrics detect population-level distortions but are sensitive to technical scaling and non-specific effects.
Across 19 public single-cell perturbation datasets, perturbation coverage, response strength, and systematic variation
strongly influence outcomes and can alter model rankings; restricting evaluation to datasets with stronger,
perturbation-specific signals reshapes conclusions from indiscriminate aggregation. Using gene essentiality as an
independent endpoint, we find high benchmark scores do not imply preservation of biologically relevant information.
Reliable benchmarking thus requires explicit attention to dataset properties, metric behavior, and biological relevance.
Rather than treating benchmark scores as self-evident measures of quality, our work offers a framework for
interpreting current evaluations and a practical path toward biologically grounded perturbation models.

Functional enrichment analysis (FEA) is widely used to interpret gene sets derived from high-throughput biomedical
data by identifying over-represented biological functions using methods such as SEA, GSEA, and MEA, with significance
typically assessed via enrichment P-values. However, most existing tools focus on single-result visualization and lack
support for interactive loading and systematic comparison across multiple datasets or enrichment methods, limiting
cross-study interpretability and functional benchmarking. To address this limitation, we developed FeaVis, a web-based
interactive Shiny application for multi-dataset functional enrichment visualization, comparison, and interpretation. FeaVis
enables users to dynamically load multiple enrichment result datasets and perform cross-dataset comparative analysis
through interactive filtering, function-level querying, and unified dot-plot visualization. In addition, FeaVis incorporates
AI-assisted result interpretation to help prioritize biologically relevant functions and highlight shared or divergent
enrichment patterns across datasets, facilitating more efficient exploration of functional signals. This integrated design
supports iterative analysis, improves comparability across enrichment methods and studies, and enhances biological
insight extraction from complex gene lists. FeaVis is implemented as a fully deployed Shiny web application and is
publicly accessible via an institutional server: https://biocoreapps.bsd.uchicago.edu/apps/app/feavisapp

while protecting patient privacy. We developed a framework in which a trusted administrator generates MedSigLIP
chest radiograph embeddings and encrypts them alongside 33 clinical and genomic variables using CKKS
homomorphic encryption, retaining the decryption key. An honest-but-curious server performs exact matching,

Advances in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering have increased the demand for identifying enzymatic
reactions that can be utilized for the biosynthesis of value-added chemicals. In parallel, computational approaches for
predicting enzyme–substrate relationships and enzyme properties have been actively developed. However, information
on experimentally characterized enzymatic reactions remains scattered across the scientific literature, making its
systematic and large-scale utilization challenging. To address this limitation, we developed a text-mining-based
approach to identify enzyme–chemical reaction relationships from the scientific literature and organize them into a
structured database. Our pipeline processes PubMed abstracts through three steps: named entity recognition (NER) to
detect enzyme and chemical mentions, named entity normalization (NEN) to map these mentions to standardized
identifiers, and relation extraction (RE) to determine enzyme–substrate–product relationships. The resulting database is

prognostic information. Public kidney-transplant transcriptomic datasets were collected using an LLM-assisted curation

deposition, distribution, and management of agricultural life-science omics data in Korea. The increasing volume and
heterogeneity of agricultural omics data require standardized metadata management, cross-institutional data
exchange, data integrity control, and reproducible computational access. In 2026, NABIC is being upgraded to NABIC

Predicting single-cell responses to drugs and genetic perturbations could support drug discovery and target
prioritization. However, noisy gene expression and heterogeneous cellular responses complicate prediction and
interpretation. We present a conditional flow matching framework that models perturbation responses using
independent, low-dimensional pathway representations. By summarizing coordinated variation among biologically
related genes, these representations aim to reduce sensitivity to gene-level noise and facilitate response sharing
across perturbations. Our model learns pathway-specific vector fields and combines them through weights
conditioned on cellular state, perturbation information, and integration time. To account for state-dependent
heterogeneity, generation is conditioned on initial control-cell states, while Leiden clusters derived from training
treated cells provide auxiliary supervision for response subpopulations and their proportions. This design aims to
capture how baseline heterogeneity shapes distinct response subpopulations. The framework learns from unpaired
control and treated populations without prescribing a branching topology. Pathway-specific weighted vector
contributions provide a basis for interpreting modeled expression changes across subpopulations and along
computational trajectories. Evaluation will focus on generalization to unseen perturbations and preservation of
population diversity, using separate protocols that hold out drug identities or genetic targets. Our goal is to generate
heterogeneous cellular responses while making the model’s pathway-level contributions accessible for analysis.

Genomic foundation models capture sequence regularities, yet existing interpretability tools rarely ask where in the
layer stack a biological grammar becomes stable.
We introduce GDTR (Genomic Deep-Thinking Ratio), a training-free residual-stream lens that assigns each nucleotide
token a settling depth c(t): the first layer at which its representation stabilizes against the post-final-norm reference.
On Evo 2 7B, splice donor and acceptor sites settle approximately two layers earlier than intronic contexts,
enhancer-like cCREs show a smaller but measurable shift, and a chr22 calibration transfers to held-out chr17.
Perturbing canonical splice donors shows that the signal is bidirectional: disrupting the central GT motif deepens
settling, whereas shuffling the flanking grammar makes the preserved motif settle earlier. Differential GDTR further
reveals consequence-associated peak-disruption depths across ClinVar variants, with synonymous substitutions
peaking deepest but with broad class overlap.
GDTR therefore provides a layer-wise interpretability axis for genomic foundation models, complementary to existing
prediction and variant-scoring tools.
