Alzheimer disease (AD) involves multiple co-occurring neuropathologies — tau (Braak), amyloid-β (Thal), TDP-43
(LATE-NC) and α-synuclein (Lewy bodies) — that affect distinct brain cell types, while single-nucleus transcriptomes also
carry substantial technical and inter-individual variation. A central challenge is to separate disease programs shared
across individuals from donor-specific molecular variation. We developed PRISM, a module-structured model that
decomposes cell-type-specific transcriptional variation into neuropathology-associated patterns shared across donors
and donor-specific baseline variation. PRISM also includes an explicit donor-specific pathology-response component, so
that its contribution can be tested directly. We applied PRISM to 2,773,812 nuclei from the dorsolateral prefrontal and
middle temporal cortex of 89 SEA-AD donors, using donor-disjoint training (64), validation (16) and locked test (9)
partitions. PRISM recovered cell-type-resolved module organization in unseen donors: in the locked test,
general-module recovery was positive in all 24 cell types, and the direction of AD-associated module changes was
preserved in 23 of 24 cell types. Ablations indicated a small but reproducible contribution of donor-specific baseline
information, whereas donor-specific pathology-response effects were not supported beyond the shared response.

found that common-pathology fingerprints were stable and pathology-axis-specific across unseen donors while
retaining distinct cell-type-dependent shapes. These results suggest that AD transcriptomes contain a reproducible
shared neuropathology organization expressed through cell-type-specific modules, together with measurable
donor-specific baseline variation. PRISM provides an interpretable framework for separating these components without
equating model-derived geometry with causal disease progression.

efforts to translate individual genomic profiles into disease prediction. Genomic language models (gLMs), which learn
sequence representations directly from DNA, have emerged as promising approaches for capturing regulatory and
functional signals. However, their utility for sample-level disease prediction remains unclear. Here, we benchmarked
seven gLMs for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using de novo variants from whole-genome sequencing data of

clinical failure. In hair loss, particularly androgenetic alopecia, therapeutic options remain limited to a few approved

Missense variants constitute a major class of disease-associated genetic variation. By altering amino acid sequences,
these variants can reshape protein structure, perturb protein–protein interactions, and ultimately influence gene
expression changes that drive disease phenotypes. Therefore, characterizing these effects requires scalable approaches,
yet experimental methods remain costly and low-throughput. Virtual cell models offer a scalable alternative for
predicting transcriptomic responses to perturbations in silico; however, most are not designed for missense variants,
and systematic evaluation remains limited.
Here, we benchmarked eight virtual cell models on the task of predicting single-cell transcriptomic profiles of TP53
missense variants using TISCC-seq data. Each variant was encoded by MSA Transformer-derived protein representation
and provided as a variant-level perturbation input. Beyond commonly used quantitative metrics, we evaluated whether
predictions preserved variant-specific biology, including pathway responses and functional effects. We further
predicted transcriptomic responses for all possible TP53 missense variants and compared them with measurements
from two independent saturation mutagenesis screens of TP53.
Across evaluations, scFoundation showed the best overall performance in capturing TP53 missense variant effects.
Together, our findings highlight the importance of evaluating variant-specific responses and we provide a framework
for assessing virtual cell models for predicting transcriptomic responses to missense variants.

individual-level gene expression. AlphaGenome, a state-of-the-art S2F model, excels across a range of sequence-based

Postzygotic mosaic variants can establish cancerized fields within normal tissues, providing a genetic basis for field
cancerization. Patients harboring such variants would be classified as sporadic cases, lacking family history and
germline variant findings, potentially leaving their cancer susceptibility underrecognized. However, conventional
tumor-normal analysis often misses these variants because shared signals are removed during germline subtraction
and low-VAF alleles are difficult to call at standard coverage. To address this, we developed a tumor-informed
detection pipeline for standard-depth WES (~50–100×) that recovers tumor-normal shared variants in cancer driver
genes while distinguishing them from germline variants, technical artifacts, and tumor-in-normal contamination.
Applied to the TCGA breast cancer cohort (n=661), the pipeline identified candidate mosaic driver variants in a subset
of patients, including PIK3CA and MLLT10. Because tumor-normal sharing alone cannot establish a genuine cancerized
field, we further evaluated variants to distinguish true field formation from independent hotspot recurrence and
non-carcinogenic clonal expansion in normal tissue. This framework enables systematic recovery and evaluation of
mosaic field events and, when extended across cancer types, could define their contribution to tumor initiation and
clarify how cancers arise from precancerized normal tissue.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) accounts for ~90% of malignant pancreatic tumors, and five-year survival
remains below 13%. Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) are widely used for drug response studies because they
preserve tumor architecture and heterogeneity in vivo. During engraftment, however, human stromal and immune
cells are replaced by murine tissue, and clonal selection may occur. It therefore remains unclear how faithfully PDXs
retain the genomic features of the original tumor.
We established PDXs from primary tumors of 12 patients with PDAC and performed whole-exome sequencing on
matched blood, primary tumor, and PDX samples, using blood as the normal control. In PDXs, detection rates of
major driver mutations were generally higher, most notably for KRAS and TP53. Variant allele frequencies (VAFs) of
PDAC driver mutations were also significantly elevated, which may partly explain the increased detection rates. Despite
these shifts, VAF-based pairwise correlations between each primary tumor and its matched PDX remained strong,
indicating that patient-specific mutational profiles were largely preserved.
Taken together, these findings are consistent with clonal selection during engraftment and a higher tumor cell fraction
in PDXs. Such changes should be considered when extrapolating genomic findings from PDXs to patient tumors.

Background/Aim: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has transformed the treatment of advanced hepatocellular
carcinoma (HCC), yet reliable blood-based prognostic biomarkers remain limited. We investigated whether plasma
proteome profiling could identify a clinically applicable prognostic biomarker for HCC patients receiving ICB.
Methods: Plasma samples from patients with HCC receiving ICB were analyzed by targeted proteomics in a discovery
cohort. Cox proportional hazards regression identified candidate biomarkers, which were evaluated in an independent
validation cohort. Multivariate Cox regression assessed whether the validated biomarker was prognostic independent
of established clinical variables. Its cell type-specific expression was further examined using a publicly available
peripheral blood single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset.
Results: Plasma proteomics identified proteins associated with progression-free survival and treatment response in the
discovery cohort. Independent validation confirmed one biomarker that consistently stratified patient prognosis and
remained associated with outcome after adjustment for clinical variables. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis
demonstrated concordant differential expression of the corresponding gene in myeloid cells, supporting the plasma
proteomic findings.
Conclusion: Plasma proteomics identified and independently validated a blood-based prognostic biomarker for
patients with HCC receiving ICB. The biomarker provided prognostic information beyond established clinical variables
and may improve patient stratification for HCC immunotherapy.

Background: Breast cancer PAM50 subtypes are inferred from bulk transcriptomic profiles reflecting mixtures of
malignant epithelial and tumor microenvironment (TME) cells. We investigated how variation in epithelial subtype
composition and TME inclusion affects breast cancer molecular classification.
Methods: Publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing data comprising 100,064 cells with PAM50 subtype
annotations were used to generate pseudo-bulk tumors. LumA and LumB epithelial cells were mixed at 11 proportions
(100:0 to 0:100), with 30 independently sampled replicates per ratio, generating 330 pseudo-bulks per tumor.
Subtypes were independently assigned using PAM50, a 50-gene centroid-based classifier, and AIMS, a single-sample
predictor. TME cells were subsequently incorporated into each pseudo-bulk mixture to assess their impact on subtype
classification.
Results: Bulk subtype assignments shifted from LumA toward LumB with increasing LumB epithelial proportions. AIMS
showed overall agreement with PAM50, although PAM50 was more sensitive to changes in epithelial composition,
while AIMS was more strongly influenced by the major epithelial subtype. Notably, TME addition shifted classifications
toward the original bulk PAM50 subtype in several tumors, highlighting the contribution of non-epithelial signals to
bulk molecular subtyping.
Conclusions: Both epithelial heterogeneity and TME composition can influence transcriptome-based breast cancer
subtyping. These findings highlight the importance of tumor purity and microenvironmental composition in bulk
molecular subtyping.

Carcinosarcoma is an ultra-rare and highly heterogeneous malignancy composed of both carcinomatous and
sarcomatous components. Although these components can be recognized histologically, their molecular organization
and functional interplay remain poorly understood, and it remains unclear whether carcinosarcoma should be
therapeutically approached as a carcinoma or sarcoma. To computationally resolve this heterogeneity, we analyzed
pretreatment RNA-sequencing profiles from patients with carcinosarcoma enrolled in a prospective immune
checkpoint inhibitor trial.

treatment outcome. We therefore applied non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), an unsupervised learning approach
that simultaneously identifies coordinated gene-expression programs and sample-level patterns within high￾dimensional transcriptomic data. Without incorporating clinical response into the clustering process, NMF separated
the tumors into two distinct molecular states. Notably, patients with favorable responses to immune checkpoint
blockade were preferentially enriched in one cluster, which was characterized by metabolic programs potentially
supporting antitumor immune activity and prolonged progression-free survival.

relevant tumor states that are not readily captured by response-directed analyses. NMF-based stratification provides a
computational framework for dissecting the complex biology of carcinosarcoma and understanding heterogeneity in
immunotherapy response.

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are functionally heterogeneous components of the hepatocellular carcinoma
(HCC) microenvironment, but the reproducibility, clinical relevance, and regulatory basis of their cellular states remain
incompletely understood. By integrating five independent HCC single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, we identified
three reproducible CAF states: antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs), inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs), and myofibroblastic CAFs

datasets. In TCGA-LIHC, higher inferred apCAF abundance was associated with favorable survival, whereas higher
inferred mCAF abundance was associated with adverse survival; iCAF abundance showed no significant association.

perturbation of candidate regulators supported directional changes in CAF state composition, while spatial regulatory
network scores predominantly localized to the corresponding CAF niches. Collectively, these results establish a
reproducible and clinically divergent CAF landscape in HCC shaped by state-specific regulatory programs, providing a
rationale for investigating stromal state modulation as a therapeutic strategy.

Background: Measurable residual disease (MRD) is the strongest predictor of outcome in adult T-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) but its genomic correlates at diagnosis are undefined. We describe the chromosomal
microarray (CMA) landscape of a single-protocol adult cohort stratified by MRD status.

MRD-positive and duplications and cnLOH in MRD-negative disease. Near-ETP (early T-cell precursor) patients showed

genomic-scar scores, but a scar records past repair failure rather than a tumour's current molecular state. We asked

across cancers, and whether tumours reaching HRD through BRCA1 promoter methylation share the transcriptional
state of mutation-driven tumours.

programmes were tissue-dependent. Among HR-wild-type tumours, 11/89 (12.4%) HRD-positive versus 1/494 (0.2%)
HRD-negative breast cases carried BRCA1 promoter hypermethylation (p = 6.4×10⁻⁹); the subgroup reproduced in

Introduction: Breast cancer is one of the most common malignancies in women and remains a major cause of
cancer-related mortality worldwide. It comprises multiple molecular subtypes, including estrogen
receptor-positive/HER2-negative (ER+/HER2−) breast cancer and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which differ in
tumor biology, therapeutic response, and clinical outcome. Despite this heterogeneity, breast cancer progression and
metastasis may involve shared molecular alterations across subtypes. This study tested the hypothesis that genes
consistently dysregulated across ER+/HER2− and TNBC tissues may serve as common molecular markers of breast
cancer progression and metastatic potential.
Materials and Methods: The publicly available gene-expression dataset GSE58135 was reanalyzed. The dataset
included 42 primary TNBC tumors, 42 primary ER+/HER2− tumors, 30 uninvolved breast tissue samples adjacent to
ER+/HER2− tumors, 21 uninvolved breast tissue samples adjacent to TNBC tumors, and 5 normal breast tissue
samples obtained from reduction mammoplasty procedures in individuals without known breast cancer. Principal
component analysis was used to assess global transcriptional differences among sample groups. Tumor and adjacent
uninvolved tissues from the same patients were matched, yielding 30 paired ER+/HER2− tumor-adjacent samples and
18 paired TNBC tumor-adjacent samples. Differential expression analyses were performed across tumor, paired
adjacent, and normal tissue comparisons. Differentially expressed genes were cross-compared to identify consistently
dysregulated candidates. Gene Ontology (GO) analyses were performed to characterize pathways associated with
these candidates and their potential roles in tumor progression.
Results: Cross-comparison of differential expression results identified TDO2 as a metabolic marker consistently
upregulated across all evaluated comparisons. TDO2 expression was elevated in ER+/HER2− tumors relative to both
normal breast tissue and paired adjacent tissue and was similarly increased in TNBC tumors relative to normal tissue
and paired adjacent tissue. TDO2 expression was also elevated in uninvolved breast tissue adjacent to both ER+/HER2 − and TNBC tumors compared with normal breast tissue from individuals without cancer. TDO2 encodes tryptophan
2,3-dioxygenase, a heme-containing enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of tryptophan catabolism
through the kynurenine pathway. GO analysis identified pathways associated with TDO2 dysregulation and suggested
a potential role in breast cancer progression and metastasis.
Conclusion: TDO2 was consistently upregulated in both ER+/HER2− and TNBC tumors and was also elevated in
uninvolved tissues adjacent to tumors, indicating that TDO2 dysregulation may represent a shared molecular feature
associated with breast cancer progression across distinct subtypes. These findings support TDO2 as a potential
biomarker of breast cancer progression and metastasis and as a candidate therapeutic target. Further functional and
pharmacologic studies are warranted to evaluate TDO2-directed therapeutic strategies in breast cancer.

Background: Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Ate/Bev) is the first-line standard for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma
(HCC) but benefits only a subset of patients, creating a need for pretreatment models to guide patient selection. We
developed an XGBoost model and explored whether it captures treatment-relevant biology or generic prognosis,
using external validation in Ate/Bev cohorts and comparison with tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)-treated controls.
Methods: Of 949 screened patients, 737 were analyzed. From 18 baseline variables, univariate Cox screening and
recursive feature elimination yielded six routinely available blood-based predictors. XGBoost was trained to predict
clinical benefit in 354 Ate/Bev-treated patients from Korea and Austria. Clinical benefit was complete or partial
response, or stable disease with progression-free survival (PFS) of at least 6 months. External validation used the phase
3 IMbrave150 trial (n = 99) and a real-world cohort (n = 184). Treatment specificity was assessed in the IMbrave150
sorafenib arm (n = 28) and a lenvatinib-treated real-world cohort (n = 72), and by treatment-prediction interaction
across IMbrave150 arms.
Results: In the Ate/Bev validation cohorts, XGBoost achieved AUCs of 0.70 and 0.67 with the lowest Brier scores
among comparator models and remained prognostic for overall survival (OS) after covariate adjustment. In the TKI
cohorts, this discrimination did not extend (lenvatinib AUC 0.56). In survival analyses, XGBoost stratified neither OS nor
PFS in either cohort, whereas established prognostic scores did in the same cohorts. Within IMbrave150, the PFS
benefit of Ate/Bev over sorafenib was greater in patients predicted to benefit (interaction P = 0.045 for PFS and 0.194
for OS).
Conclusion: Benchmarking against alternative-regimen controls is a practical test of treatment specificity. Loss of
discrimination under TKI therapy suggests the model encodes Ate/Bev-relevant signal, although the small control
cohorts and an interaction significant for PFS but not OS keep this finding exploratory.

Introduction: Advances in targeted and immune therapies for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) reinforce the need for
individualized treatment. However, tissue biopsy is not mandatory in HCC, limiting tissue availability for genomic
profiling. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling may overcome this limitation. We evaluated genomic concordance
between ctDNA and tumor tissue and the clinical utility of ctDNA in advanced HCC treated with atezolizumab plus
bevacizumab (atezo/bev).
Methods: Pretreatment plasma was prospectively collected from 130 patients with advanced HCC who underwent
tissue-based sequencing before systemic therapy (June 2020–October 2022). Tumor tissue and ctDNA were sequenced
using the Oncomine Comprehensive Assay and Guardant360, respectively.
Results: Compared with tissue sequencing, ctDNA profiling showed 72.6% (69/95; 95% CI, 62.9–80.6%) sensitivity and
75.0% (69/92; 95% CI, 65.3–82.7%) positive predictive value. When tissue and plasma were collected within 30 days,
sensitivity increased to 96.3% (26/27; 95% CI, 81.7–99.3%). In patients receiving first-line atezo/bev, higher ctDNA
maximum variant allele frequency (maxVAF) was independently associated with poorer survival.
Conclusion: In advanced HCC, ctDNA profiling showed acceptable concordance with tissue sequencing and may offer
an alternative for genomic profiling when tissue is unavailable. ctDNA maxVAF may serve as a prognostic biomarker in
patients receiving first-line atezo/bev.

The tumor–normal interface represents a unique spatial compartment where colorectal cancer (CRC) directly interacts
with non-neoplastic mucosa. While previous studies have focused on intratumoral regions or the invasive front, the
biological organization of the interface remains poorly understood. We aimed to define spatially organized immune
programs across the interface using single-cell–resolved spatial transcriptomics. Using the Xenium platform, we
analyzed matched tumor core and interface regions from 10 CRCs, including five microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H)
and five microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors. Key findings were supported by immunohistochemistry and public
scRNA-seq dataset of over 300 patients. The tumor–normal interface was biologically distinct from both the tumor
core and invasive front. Regardless of microsatellite status, the non-invaded side preserved a homeostatic mucosal
immune program characterized by B and plasma cell enrichment and expression of CCL15, CXCL14, and CCL28,
whereas the tumor-facing side showed subtype-specific immune organization. MSI-H tumors maintained intratumoral
immune activation associated with CXCL9/10/11 expression, cytotoxic lymphocyte enrichment, and immune-associated
niches. Notably, MSS tumors were not uniformly immune-cold, retaining immune activity at the interface despite
immune-depleted tumor cores. Spatial trajectory analysis revealed that immune exclusion in MSS tumors reflects
restricted propagation of immune programs rather than their absence. These spatial programs were accompanied by
niche-specific signaling, including IL15–IL2RB in MSI-H and VEGFA–FLT1 in MSS. Our findings identify the tumor– normal interface as a gatekeeper of immune activity in CRC. These results provide a framework for understanding
immune activation and exclusion, highlighting interface-associated programs as potential therapeutic targets,
particularly in MSS tumors.

Background: Endometrial carcinoma (EC) is classified into four molecular subtypes with distinct prognoses. The no specific
molecular profile (NSMP) subtype, representing approximately 50% of cases, lacks defining molecular features of other
subtypes and shows substantial heterogeneity in clinical outcomes. We sought to identify transcriptomic biomarkers
associated with recurrence in NSMP ECs.
Methods: We conducted whole-exome sequencing (WES) and whole-transcriptome sequencing (WTS) on 54 stage I ECs,
including 27 NSMP cases. Molecular subtypes were assigned based on mutation profiles and immunohistochemical findings.
Candidate genes associated with recurrence were identified through transcriptomic analysis and validated in TCGA-UCEC
dataset. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis was used to characterize the cellular origin of candidate biomarkers and their
associated immune microenvironment.
Results: Recurrence-free survival differed significantly across molecular subtypes (p<0.05). Within the NSMP subgroup, PRR7
expression was strongly associated with recurrence (p<0.001). Single-cell analysis identified PRR7-positive epithelial cells with
enriched ciliary organization programs and suppressed inflammatory and cytokine response pathways, indicating an
immune-suppressed microenvironment. This stratification may reflect distinct patterns of immune infiltration, indicating that
the prognostic value derives from epithelial cell state and immune composition.
Conclusions: We identify an epithelial-derived transcriptomic signature associated with recurrence in NSMP ECs. PRR7
expression defines a malignant epithelial cell state associated with immune suppression and may serve as a biomarker for recurrence risk stratification in NSMP EC.
Keywords: Endometrial carcinoma, No specific molecular profile, Recurrence, Transcriptomic biomarker, Tumor
microenvironment

Tumor transcriptomic characteristics and clinical progression may be influenced by sex, highlighting the need for
sex-aware prognostic prediction. However, it remains unclear whether transcriptomic prognostic signals identified in
one sex are transferable to the other and whether these signals reflect sex itself or underlying molecular tumor
subtypes. We aimed to identify prognostic signals transferable between males and females and transcriptomic
candidate biomarkers with sex-differential effects in lower-grade glioma. We independently derived transcriptomic
principal components in male and female patients from TCGA-LGG, performed TransCompR-inspired cross-sex
projection and Cox survival analyses, adjusted for molecular subtypes defined by IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion,
and validated the findings in an independent CGGA cohort. Female-derived PC2 improved prognostic prediction in
males compared with a clinical-only model, but this improvement disappeared after molecular subtype adjustment. In
contrast, the sex-differential prognostic association of APOBEC3F remained consistent across TCGA and CGGA after
adjustment for molecular subtype and PC2. These findings support the use of sex-aware cross-population
transcriptomic analysis to distinguish prognostic signals explained by molecular subtype from independent
sex-differential candidate biomarkers.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) metastases share driver mutations with their primaries, but whether
metastasis changes which full-length isoform a gene uses remains unresolved, because short reads rarely reconstruct
complete isoforms. We sequenced matched primary tumours and liver metastases from 10 patients with PacBio long
reads and compared gene expression, isoform expression and usage within patient. To minimise normal-liver
contamination, candidates were filtered against normal-liver expression and usage. Usage changed for 173 isoforms,
88% without a gene-level change. Of 21 liver-gained isoforms with concordant abundance gain, only RPS6KA3 FSM02
passed the filters and was supported by independent cohorts. FSM02 differs from the canonical isoform at its 5' end,
which replaces the N-terminus while keeping both kinase domains. Its abundance rose in all 10 patients, and median
usage rose from 0.10 in primaries to 0.42 in liver metastases (9 of 10, p = 0.004), with total RPS6KA3 unchanged,
becoming dominant in 5 patients. The within-patient rise in FSM02 usage correlated with the fall in Hallmark EMT
score (rho = -0.81, p = 0.005), also after albumin adjustment (rho = -0.73). Paired long-read sequencing reveals
isoform remodelling hidden at the gene level and links RPS6KA3 FSM02 to reduced EMT in PDAC liver metastasis.

Cancer driver gene (CDG) prediction is essential for understanding tumorigenesis and identifying potential therapeutic
targets, but remains challenging due to heterogeneous molecular information and complex biological networks. Here,
we present ORBIT, a geometry-aware deep learning framework that integrates multi-omics profiles, protein sequence
representations, and functional gene-set information for CDG prediction. ORBIT employs cross-attention-based
multimodal fusion and context-adaptive graph reweighting to integrate complementary biological signals and capture
cancer-specific interaction patterns. Hyperbolic graph convolution models the hierarchical structure of biological
networks, while bi-prototype contrastive learning guides the representation space using driver- and
non-driver-associated functional prototypes. We evaluated ORBIT across multiple biological networks against seven
state-of-the-art CDG prediction methods. Across 15 cancer types, ORBIT achieved the highest AUPRC in all evaluated
cancer types, demonstrating robust performance under severe class imbalance. Further analyses showed that
hyperbolic representations better captured biological network structure, while functional enrichment and
drug-sensitivity analyses supported the biological and potential therapeutic relevance of highly ranked candidates.
Overall, ORBIT provides a geometry-aware framework for integrating heterogeneous biological information and
enabling robust identification of cancer driver genes.

Bladder cancer exhibits distinct sex disparities, with men having a fourfold higher incidence while women are more
likely to present with aggressive tumors and worse outcomes. The molecular mechanisms underlying these differences
remain poorly understood, and sex-specific therapeutic strategies are lacking. Here, we performed an integrative
multi-omics analysis of muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) to characterize sex-based molecular differences. We
assembled a meta-cohort of publicly available MIBC datasets, including TCGA and additional genomic and
transcriptomic cohorts, and analyzed somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene and protein expression, and
pathway activity. The tumor microenvironment (TME) was assessed using multiple deconvolution and
immune-response prediction approaches, and findings were examined across independent cohorts. We observed
sex-associated differences in genomic alterations and transcriptional programs that converged on key signaling
pathways linked to immune regulation. Male and female tumors displayed distinct pathway activity patterns associated
with contrasting immune microenvironment phenotypes and potential implications for immunotherapy response.
These findings suggest that sex-dependent signaling programs may contribute to TME heterogeneity in MIBC and
provide a basis for sex-informed biomarker discovery and precision treatment strategies.

Pediatric brain tumors (pBTs) are the most common solid malignancies and the leading cause of cancer-related
mortality in children and adolescents. These tumors exhibit profound inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity in their
tumor immune microenvironments (TIMEs), yet their shared immunological features remain poorly understood. To
systematically characterize these landscapes, we integrate multi-omics data—comprising DNA methylation, RNA-seq,
somatic mutations, and copy number alterations—from 503 patients in the Children’s Brain Tumor Network (CBTN). By
inferring immune cell compositions through DNA methylation-based deconvolution, we identified three pan-pBT
immune clusters (IC1-3) that transcend traditional histological boundaries. While IC1 and IC2 demonstrate distinct
immune-active profiles, IC3 is characterized by broad immune depletion, with a marked reduction in CD4+ effector T
cells. Crucially, this immune-cold IC3 phenotype emerges as an independent predictor of poor survival. Transcriptomic
analysis predicts cluster-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities: the highly proliferative IC2 is susceptible to cell cycle kinase
inhibitors, whereas IC3 exhibits a profound dependency on DNA replication stress checkpoints. Together, this study
provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex pBT TIME, guiding future prognostic assessments
and tailored therapeutic strategies.

Understanding the cell of origin (COO) across cancer types is essential for elucidating tumorigenesis and advancing
diagnostic and therapeutic approaches in oncology. Prior work has shown that chromatin accessibility patterns of the
COO influence the genomic distribution of somatic mutations in cancer. In this study, we integrated machine learning
with 559 single-cell chromatin accessibility profiles and 2,734 whole-genome sequencing samples to infer the COO of
36 cancer subtypes with high robustness and accuracy. Our framework recapitulates established anatomical and
cellular origins across multiple cancers, often at the level of specific cell subsets. Notably, our results suggest that
basal cells may serve as the COO for small cell lung cancer, challenging the conventional neuroendocrine origin
model. In addition, we identify distinct cellular trajectories associated with different histological subtypes and reveal an
intermediate metaplastic state during tumorigenesis in several gastrointestinal cancers. These findings provide insights
with potential relevance for cancer prevention, early detection, and therapeutic stratification.

Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have emerged as highly effective cancer therapies, clinical benefits
remain limited to a subset of patients and cancer types due to treatment resistance. In this study, we used an
integrated single-cell RNA sequencing atlas of ICI-treated patients, comprising 110 patients across nine cancer types.
We applied sample-wise non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) separately within each cell type to identify gene
expression programs and grouped recurrent programs across samples to define cell type-specific meta-programs
(MPs). The identified MPs captured variation in transcriptional states within each cell type beyond discrete cell subtype
classification. Analysis of MP co-occurrence and ligand–receptor crosstalk revealed that MPs representing related
biological states showed correlated abundance patterns across samples. Furthermore, clinical evaluations demonstrated
that several cell type-specific MPs showed significant associations with survival outcomes across cancer types. In
summary, this study analyzed the non-malignant tumor microenvironment (TME) at a pan-cancer level using
scRNA-seq data from ICI-treated patients and evaluated the clinical relevance of cell type-specific MPs. These findings
provide a basis for understanding tumor microenvironmental features associated with ICI response.

Rectal cancer patients receiving preoperative radiotherapy show heterogeneous responses, ranging from complete
pathological regression to substantial residual disease. To establish a bioinformatic framework for identifying
circulating biomarkers predictive of radiotherapy response, we designed a longitudinal study of plasma extracellular
vesicle (EV)-miRNAs collected before radiotherapy (T0), after radiotherapy (T1), and after surgery (T2), using residual

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is an age-associated expansion of hematopoietic stem cells
carrying somatic mutations. Recent studies show that immune cells derived from CHIP clones infiltrate solid tumors, a
phenomenon termed tumor-infiltrating clonal hematopoiesis (TI-CH). We investigated TI-CH and its clinical relevance
in Korean patients with pancreatic cancer. We analyzed paired tumor and blood whole-exome sequencing data from
205 patients. Somatic mutations in a predefined set of CHIP-associated genes were detected in the blood of 26
patients (12.7%), including 18 (8.8%) with identical mutations in their tumors (TI-CH) and eight (3.9%) with mutations
detected only in blood (blood-only CHIP). CHIP was associated with shorter overall and event-free survival, with
poorer outcomes particularly evident in patients with TI-CH. Transcriptomic deconvolution indicated myeloid
abundance in TI-CH tumors. In an independent whole-genome sequencing cohort of 29 patients, we identified two
TI-CH and two blood-only CHIP cases. One patient carried a TET2 nonsense mutation detectable in blood and in both
biopsy and surgical tumor specimens by whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing. These findings support the
presence of TI-CH in Korean pancreatic cancer patients and its association with adverse outcomes, suggesting that
TI-CH may influence the tumor microenvironment and serve as a potential prognostic biomarker.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) requires rapid therapeutic decision-making at diagnosis, yet current risk stratification
systems based on cytogenetic and molecular profiling do not fully capture disease heterogeneity and can be difficult
to implement in routine clinical settings. We aimed to develop a clinically interpretable prognostic model to estimate
2-year mortality risk using a limited set of gene expression measurements. We analyzed RNA-seq data from 1,887
patients across four independent AML cohorts. Gene expression values were normalized using combinations of stable
reference genes to derive relative expression, thereby reducing platform variability and batch effects. Automated
machine learning (AutoML) with AutoGluon was applied for model discovery and feature identification, followed by
construction of a simplified logistic regression model to ensure interpretability. The final formula incorporated four
genes (CD109, DOCK1, PLXNC1, and SCD) together with patient age. The logistic regression model achieved a mean
LOCO-CV AUC of 0.720, while the final model trained on the full dataset achieved an AUC of 0.727. Robust
performance was maintained in an independent external validation cohort (AUC = 0.721), with stronger predictive
performance observed in adult-dominant cohorts. This compact and interpretable model enables estimation of 2-year
mortality risk using a small number of gene measurements, supporting rapid treatment decision-making at diagnosis
and facilitating practical clinical implementation.

1Pusan National University. 2 Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology
Background: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detects gene expression within intact tissue, but a probe
designed to target a specific microbial transcript can also bind host and co-residing microbe transcripts, and few
mismatches are often insufficient to prevent non-specific binding. Sequence similarity across diverse microbes and
their host drives off-target hybridization, yet existing tools screen specificity only within the target organism.
Methods: SHARP-FISH generates candidate probes using a sliding window approach, filters them according to
user-specified thermodynamic parameters, aligns the remaining candidates against both the host transcriptome and
co-occurring microbial genomes, and applies a final filter based on user-defined mismatch and k-mer tolerances.
Results: SHARP-FISH matched OligoMiner on shared host-filtering but, under stricter parameters, flagged 3, 23, and 28
probes OligoMiner retained in the S. hygroscopicus, B. thetaiotaomicron, and gut samples, all with indel off-targets
Bowtie2 missed. Within-organism mode recovered 23 of 52 specific probes for the paralog-rich H4C1. On the
SEER-FISH dataset, SHARP-FISH flagged the strongest cross-hybridization event, PS binding PD1 at 65.9% of on-target
signal, and cleared eight specific probes.
Conclusion: Simultaneous background screening detects cross-hybridization risk probes overlooked by single-target
pipelines. The tool is freely available at https://mpd.pnucolab.com

, Hugo Sámano-Sánchez1,2 1Centre of Biomedical Systems and Informatics,Zhejiang University-University of Edinburgh Institute, Zhejiang University School

Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) contribute to protein regulation and flexibility, but their evolutionary patterns
are difficult to interpret because IDR abundance is influenced by nucleotide composition, length, and gene-family
history. We investigated how IDR fraction varies across relative lineage categories and whether protein language
models (PLMs) identify age-related properties beyond traditional sequence composition information.
We analyzed yeast species using IDR predictions, orthology assignments, phylogenetic relationships, and PLM
representations. Whole-protein, IDR, and ordered-region representations were compared across orthologue pairs.
Controls matched length and nucleotide or amino-acid composition.
IDR fraction and its relationship with coding-sequence GC differed across lineage categories. The pattern appeared
across predictors but varied in strength. Relationships between IDR fraction and representation divergence also
differed among whole-protein, IDR, and ordered-region analyses. Differences between actual proteins and
composition-matched controls varied with family homology age and persisted across controls.
These findings show that sequence composition, predicted disorder, duplication history, and family age require
separate consideration. While our results suggest that yeast genes show age-related PLM patterns, PLM distances
described representation differences rather than factual evolutionary information.

Advances in sequencing, genome assembly, and bioinformatics have increased access to bacterial genomes from a
wide range of repositories. However, many recently published genome catalogs focus on specific habitats or narrowly
defined sources, while several global catalogs include medium-quality genomes that may reduce the reliability of
downstream comparative analyses. Here, we present UNIBERSE (The Unified Bacterial Reference Genomes), a
comprehensive global bacterial genome catalog constructed from near-complete (NC) or higher-quality genomes. We
collected approximately 6.1 million NC bacterial genomes from multiple public repositories and classified them into
201,416 species-level clusters. Using UNIBERSE, we examined bacterial distribution patterns across habitats and
identified species that were habitat-specific or broadly distributed. We also investigated associations between various
genomic features and habitats. UNIBERSE can provide a high-quality reference for studying bacterial diversity,
evolutionary relationships and ecological distributions. It may serve as a useful resource for comparative genomics and
large-scale studies of bacterial ecology.
posters.P108:
National Institute of Agricultural Sciences
Jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA) are major phytohormones that induce plant defense responses through
distinct signaling pathways. Although both hormones have essential roles in stress adaptation, temporal transcriptional
responses and tissue-specific regulation mechanisms are incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the
molecular response in soybean (Glycine max) leaves and roots following JA and SA treatment. Samples were collected
at 0, 1, 3, 7, and 24 h after treatment and RNA sequencing was conducted to investigate gene expression patterns.
Transcriptome analysis revealed that JA and SA induce distinct temporal expression and biological processes. JA
treatment rapidly induced hormone signaling related and defense responsive genes at 1 h, while extensive metabolic
reprogramming and photosynthesis were pronounced at 24 h. In contrast, SA signaling pathway and defense were
induced in the early response of SA treatment, and photosynthesis, antioxidant metabolism, and carbohydrate
metabolism responded later. Protein folding, chaperone activation and stress response pathways were strongly
enriched at 24 h, indicating protein homeostasis and recovery were activated. These results demonstrate that JA and
SA induce distinct pathways across tissues and time points, coordinating defense responses. Our findings provide a
comprehensive view of transcriptomic dynamics depending on phytohormone in soybean and provide a guideline for
understanding the molecular mechanism of phytohormone-mediated stress response.
posters.P109:
Jeonbuk National University, Republic of Korea
Age-appropriate maturation of the gut microbiota is closely associated with healthy childhood development, yet the
coordinated changes in microbial community composition and organization that accompany this process remain
poorly understood. We estimated gut microbiota maturation using a microbial age model trained on gut microbiota
profiles from healthy Italian children (n = 94). Individuals were stratified into groups with higher and lower relative
microbiota maturation, and their taxonomic composition and microbial association networks were compared. Network
analysis identified maturation-associated microbial subnetworks that distinguished the two groups. The higher￾maturation group exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity, densely connected microbial subnetworks, and highly
connected hub genera, including Alistipes_A_871404 and Acetatifactor. These subnetworks showed lower connectivity
in the lower maturation group and even lower connectivity in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease. These findings
indicate that childhood gut microbiota maturation involves not only age-associated taxonomic shifts but also the
emergence of structured microbial community organization. Disruption of maturation-associated microbial subnetworks
represents a shared ecological signature linking lower microbiota maturation with disease-associated dysbiosis. Our
findings provide an ecological framework for understanding gut microbiota maturation and establish a foundation for
developing microbiota-based biomarkers and interventions to support healthy gut microbiota development during
childhood.

, Sandra Beleza1
1University of Leicester, United-Kingdom. 2Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council
Within-host bacterial populations undergo demographic and evolutionary changes that can affect the genetic
variation observed during infection. To represent these processes, we developed a forward-in-time SLiM framework
simulating bacterial populations under different conditions, including founding population sizes, infection durations,
horizontal gene transfer (HGT) and selection. Clonal (founding n=1) and nonclonal (founding n=1000) infections were
simulated for 10, 40 and 80 years, with 25 replicates per condition. The resulting genetic variation was first examined
using the site frequency spectrum (SFS) and Tajima’s D. Relate was then used to assess how the inferred demographic
history compared with the known population history from the forward-in-time simulations. Relate recovered the
general pattern of population expansion towards the present, although the inferred effective population sizes differed
from the simulated census population, particularly further back in time.

Comparative studies of vertebrate brains have elucidated the evolution of morphological diversity; yet, the
fundamental chordate brain blueprint and the emergence of vertebrate-specific innovations remain elusive. To
reconstruct the cellular and molecular origins of brain architecture in chordates, we combined single-nucleus RNA-seq
with spatial transcriptomics to generate a three-dimensional cell atlas of the central nervous system (CNS) in the
early-branching chordate amphioxus. This atlas reveals a tripartite anterior-posterior organization comprising a rostral
retinal/hypothalamic region, a di-mesencephalic domain, and a caudal hindbrain/spinal cord. Challenging previous
views, we identify cell clusters resembling the vertebrate zona limitans intrathalamica and midbrain-hindbrain
boundary regions that demarcate major brain compartments. Conversely, the absence of telencephalic marker
expression in the amphioxus rostral forebrain suggests that the telencephalon is a vertebrate innovation. Collectively,
our findings establish a spatial transcriptomic framework for the amphioxus CNS, providing crucial insight into the
evolutionary origins of vertebrate brain complexity.
posters.P112:
Microbiome studies have primarily characterized variation at the species level, despite substantial genomic diversity
among strains that may underlie ecological adaptation and host association. Strain-level population structure remains
comparatively underexplored in the oral microbiome. Here, we investigated associations of geography and host age
with within-species diversity by combining phylogeny-aware single-nucleotide variant (SNV) analysis with pangenome￾based gene presence/absence analysis across 241 species from the Human Reference Oral Microbiome (HROM)
genome collection. Geographic screening identified China-enriched lineages in eight species. In Prevotella shahii, a
polysaccharide utilization locus containing SusC/SusD-family proteins, a GH95 glycoside hydrolase, and a FecR-family
regulator comprised less than 1% of callable coding sites but accounted for 12.7% of China-associated missense
variants, with the signal reproducible across independent cohorts. Pangenome analysis revealed additional gene￾content differentiation, including depletion of iutA in the P. shahii China-enriched lineage and marked depletion of
thiamine biosynthesis genes in a China-enriched lineage of Rothia mucilaginosa_A. Systematic phylogenetic screening
also identified widespread age-associated population structure, with childhood enrichment predominating among
significant lineages. Together, these results indicate that geography and age are associated with strain-level
population structure in the oral microbiome, while geographic differentiation extends across both allelic and accessory
gene-content variation.
posters.P113:
Research Institute of Molecular Alchemy, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Gyeongnam 52828, South Korea
Understanding gene expression across different tissues is essential for studying plant development and adaptation. In
rice (Oryza sativa), large-scale bulk RNA-seq datasets have been generated across diverse tissues and developmental
stages, but methods to integrate these heterogeneous datasets and extract shared regulatory patterns remain limited.
Here, we present RiceExFormer, a Transformer-based model pre-trained on 2,798 bulk RNA-seq samples from 54 rice
tissue types to learn generalizable representations of gene expression. Instead of treating each sample independently,
the model is trained with three self-supervised objectives: masked expression reconstruction, masked gene identity
prediction, and contrastive learning across augmented transcriptomic views. This allows the model to capture both
expression levels and co-regulation patterns. The learned representations reflect meaningful biological structure:
tissues with similar developmental origins cluster together, and the model's gene attention concentrates on
tissue-variable genes. Notably, the representation generalizes across independent studies, organizing samples from
unseen datasets by tissue more consistently than raw expression. In addition, experiments with different gene
vocabulary sizes (1,000–20,000 genes) show that using highly variable genes leads to better tissue discrimination than
using the full transcriptome, indicating that expression variability is more important than gene coverage. RiceExFormer
shows that self-supervised learning on bulk RNA-seq data can capture biologically meaningful patterns and provides a
useful representation framework for downstream tasks such as phenotype prediction, regulatory analysis, and gene
function annotation.

Dodders (Cuscuta) exhibit substantial variation in genome size, and C. japonica has been reported to possess an
exceptionally large genome. However, the genomic basis of this expansion remains unclear. Here, we present a draft
assembly of a putative C. japonica lineage collected in Muju, South Korea, and evaluate alternative assembly models
because its genome size and ploidy remain uncertain.
Using an automatically inferred coverage of 68×, the default assembly spanned 37.6 Gb and recovered 97.2% of
conserved single-copy orthologs, with 56.4% detected as duplicated. However, 13.9% of reliable read-derived k-mers
were absent. An alternative assembly using the dominant 34× k-mer peak as the expected coverage increased the
assembly size to 45.3 Gb, recovered 97.3% of conserved orthologs with 81.9% duplication, and reduced missing
reliable k-mers to 0.059%.
Most duplicated orthologs occurred on contigs with expected read depth, and many corresponding regions showed
approximately 1:1 synteny. These patterns suggest that much of the duplicated sequence cannot be explained by
residual haplotigs alone and may reflect divergent subgenomes or highly divergent haplotypes. Further cytogenetic
and comparative analyses will be required to determine the genomic basis of the exceptionally large genome.

Cuscuta (dodders) comprises approximately 220 obligate parasitic plants that damage crops worldwide. As these
species reduce or abandon photosynthesis, their plastid genomes undergo accelerated gene loss, offering a system for
studying the genomic consequences of parasitism. Yet plastomes exist for only a small fraction of species, and no
resource brings phylogenomic, comparative, and distributional data together in one place.
We compiled plastomes for 35 Cuscuta species and three outgroups, three re-sequenced in our laboratory, and built
CuscutaDB, a freely accessible web database requiring no registration or software. Orthologous groups were identified
with OrthoFinder and Bayesian phylogenetic inference with BEAST2. CuscutaDB organizes these results into eight
interactive tabs covering species browsing, phylogeny, side-by-side genome comparison, a gene-loss heatmap,
GBIF-linked distribution mapping, and one-click data download.
Plastome sizes span 61–125 kb (mean 88.4 kb), and the phylogeny recovers all four subgenera as monophyletic
(posterior probability 1.0), with gene retention declining from Monogynella through Cuscuta s.str. and Pachystigma
toward Grammica. All 4,807 occurrence records and underlying datasets are downloadable in standard formats.
By consolidating curated plastome data within a single interactive interface, CuscutaDB lowers the barrier to
comparative and evolutionary research on this agronomically important parasitic genus.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic
drugs (DMARDs), yet inter-individual variability in treatment response remains a major clinical challenge and validated
baseline predictors are lacking. Although the oral cavity is an active immunological interface implicated in RA
pathogenesis, its multi-kingdom microbial composition, spanning bacteria, viruses, and fungi, has not been
systematically examined in relation to treatment response. We performed whole-metagenome shotgun sequencing on
tongue-dorsum swabs from 77 participants, comprising 43 treatment-naïve patients with RA and 34 osteoarthritis (OA)
controls, and stratified patients with RA by EULAR criteria into good and non-good responders. In this poster, we will
show that response was not associated with global diversity or overall bacterial and fungal community structure;
instead, signals emerged at the species, functional, and cross-kingdom levels. We will present species-level taxonomic
signatures separating the response groups, and an OA-referenced comparison indicating that good responders
resemble a non-autoimmune baseline. We will further highlight nucleotide catabolism and anaerobic fermentation
pathways enriched in non-good responders and positively correlated with baseline systemic inflammatory markers,
together with a coordinated phage–host module enriched in good responders. Finally, a multi-kingdom random forest
classifier achieved an AUROC of 0.822, outperforming single-kingdom models.

Capsicum annuum is an economically valued crop characterized by diverse fruit traits and capsaicinoid-derived
pungency. However, genomic resources for Philippine cultivars remain limited. In this study, we generated a
chromosome-scale genome assembly of a Philippine C. annuum cultivar (CaPhR) and characterized major genes
associated with pungency. PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads were assembled using hifiasm-UL,
followed by haplotig purging and Omni-C-based scaffolding. The final assembly was approximately 3.10 Gb, with
99.64% of the sequence anchored to 12 chromosome-scale pseudomolecules and 99.4% complete BUSCOs. Repeat
annotation showed that 83.43% of the genome consisted of repetitive sequences, while gene prediction identified
38,163 protein-coding genes. Major capsaicinoid biosynthesis genes, including Pun1/AT3, pAMT, Pun3/CaMYB31, and
CaKR1, were identified for further comparative and expression analyses. This chromosome-scale genome provides a
valuable genomic resource for investigating pungency-related traits and supporting future Capsicum genetic
improvement.
posters.P118:
Pusan National University
The hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the presence of amyloid and tau pathology. However, the accompanying
cellular processes exhibit regional heterogeneity and are lost when tissue is dissociated or averaged in bulk methods.
Spatial transcriptomics preserves this spatial organization. Additionally, whether microbial sequences reported in AD
brain tissue represent true tissue-associated organisms or contamination introduced during sample handling remains
an unresolved question. Addressing this requires observing microbial signals within their spatial context rather than in
pooled homogenates, which is feasible only when RNA capture is not restricted to polyadenylated transcripts.
To address this, we generated spatial transcriptomics data using Stereo-seq OMNI FFPE—a polyA-independent
platform that records host and non-host transcripts within a shared coordinate system. Seven 2 mm punches from a
tissue microarray were mounted on a single chip, comprising six neocortical sections from one non-demented control
and three AD donors, alongside one hippocampal section. Host downstream analysis follows a standard spatial
workflow including quality control, normalization, batch correction, unsupervised clustering, spatial domain and
neighborhood analysis, and differential expression. Cell types are annotated using CeLLMan, an agentic annotation
framework that infers cell identity from mRNA signals via a knowledge graph of marker genes. Microbial profiling
proceeds via sequence-level verification, in which reads assigned to microbial taxa are screened against host and
artifactual sequence sources, with surviving candidates confirmed by orthogonal alignment to reference genomes.
Candidates from both layers will be carried forward to orthogonal validation, including immunohistochemistry on
adjacent sections and independent detection of microbial candidates.
posters.P119:
University
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a multifactorial disease in which the gut microbiome plays a crucial role. In
addition to bacteria, fungi contribute to barrier function and immune modulation. Gut microbes form complex
interaction networks, and interactions between bacteria and fungi may influence community structure. This study
aimed to investigate changes in bacteria-fungi interaction networks across IBD progression (healthy, high-risk, and IBD
groups).
Using SPIEC-EASI, heterogeneous co-occurrence networks were inferred for each group based on 16S and ITS gene
feature tables. While the total numbers of nodes and edges increased from healthy to high-risk and IBD groups, the
number and proportion of heterogeneous edges decreased. Notably, Rhodotorula exhibited high betweenness
centrality in the healthy network but showed reduced connectivity in the high-risk and IBD networks. Rhodotorula
expresses cell wall molecules similar to those of Saccharomyces spp., suggesting a potential association with beneficial
microbial community characteristics.
These preliminary findings suggest that bacteria-fungi interaction patterns may change during IBD progression, with
altered heterogeneous connectivity and loss of fungal taxa potentially reflecting changes in microbial network
organization. Further investigation is required to confirm these observed patterns using additional statistical analyses
and complementary analytical approaches. Further studies may provide a better understanding of the potential role of
bacteria-fungi interactions in IBD progression.
posters.P120:
Depressive disorder is associated with dysregulation of the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems, which contribute
to mood regulation. Recent studies on the gut-brain axis have suggested that the gut microbiome may serve as a
potential diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target for neuropsychiatric disorders. However, the specific taxonomic
and functional alterations in the gut microbiota associated with depressive disorder remain unclear. Therefore, this
study aims to identify common taxonomic and functional alterations associated with depressive disorder, with a focus
on functional redundancy within the gut microbiome.
Taxonomic and functional profiles were characterized using MetaPhlAn4 and HUMAnN3 with metagenomic data
obtained from The Microsetta Initiative, including individuals with depressive disorder and healthy controls.
Differentially abundant taxa and metabolic pathways were identified between the groups. Taxon-level contributions to
altered pathways were examined to assess functional redundancy, alongside comparisons of taxonomic and functional
diversity. MaAsLin3 and ANCOM-BC2 were used to adjust for age, sex, BMI, and medication status, and results from
the two complementary models were compared to evaluate consistency and method-specific patterns of differential
associations.
This study is expected to enhance our understanding of gut-brain axis-related pathophysiology in depressive disorder
and to provide a basis for future microbiome-targeted therapeutic research.
posters.P121:
2DECODEBIOME Co., Ltd. Incheon 21983, Republic of Korea
Fungal communities are increasingly implicated in human health, yet species-level profiling from whole-metagenome
shotgun (WMS) data remains challenging because of low fungal abundance and incomplete, non-site-specific
reference collections. We developed MycobiomeDB, body-site-specific fungal genome databases for the gut, oral
cavity, skin, and vagina. From 16,365 fungal genomes collected from NCBI and JGI, we retained 4,094 near-complete
species representatives and further filtered them using mapping evidence from 24,282 public WMS samples and
ecological manual curation. The final databases contained 766 gut, 259 oral, 642 skin, and 112 vaginal species. Among
1,150 species, only 86 (7%) were shared across all four sites, whereas 777 (68%) were site-specific. In 72 simulated
communities, bacterial depletion followed by Kraken2 and Bracken achieved 0.998 recall, 0.873 precision, a 0.927 F1
score, and 0.996 mean Bray-Curtis similarity to ground truth, with robust performance across sequencing depth, fungal
load, and community complexity. In real datasets, this workflow detected disease-associated mycobiome differences in
more cohorts and profiled more oral and skin samples than MiCoP or EukDetect. It was also 7- to 24-fold faster than
MiCoP, providing an accurate, sensitive, and efficient framework for human mycobiome profiling, while enabling
body-site-aware fungal profiling across major human-associated microbial ecosystems in WMS datasets.

Domestic dogs have coexisted with humans for thousands of years, yet the genomic diversity of their gut microbiome
and virome, and its implications for One Health, remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed 1,752 shotgun
metagenomes from 15 countries to construct the Dog Reference Gut Microbiome (DRGM), comprising 33,893
metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 931 prokaryotic species. Integrating viral identification with
genome binning to rescue fragmented contigs, we further generated the Dog Reference Gut Virome (DRGV): 20,875
viral MAGs clustered into 12,125 species-level operational taxonomic units. Both the canine microbiome and virome
resembled their human counterparts more closely than those of mice in taxonomic composition and functional
potential. Human-shared bacterial species showed significantly greater metabolic independence and carried more
antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), particularly against clinically important antibiotic classes. Companion dogs
overlapped more with the human gut microbiome than non-companion dogs, and companion-associated species
were preferentially shared with humans, displayed higher metabolic independence, and harbored a greater ARG
burden. These findings establish genome-resolved bacterial and viral references for the dog gut, identify
human-shared lineages as key ecological and functional links between canine and human gut ecosystems, and
highlight companion dogs as models for One Health antimicrobial resistance research.

Metformin is the most widely used pharmacological agent for type 2 diabetes (T2D), yet glycemic response varies
substantially among individuals. Whether this heterogeneity reflects treatment-induced microbiome remodeling or
pre-existing microbial ecology remains unclear. We performed longitudinal multi-kingdom shotgun metagenomic
profiling of fecal samples from 56 Korean individuals with newly diagnosed, drug-naive T2D and 29 healthy controls.
T2D samples were collected before metformin initiation and after 10 days and 3 months of treatment, and response
was defined by >1% HbA1c reduction at 3 months. Metformin produced little community-wide restructuring across
bacterial, fungal, viral, or functional profiles, although selected taxa showed time-dependent changes. By contrast,
baseline microbiome features differed between future responders and non-responders. Responders showed greater
acetate-production and butyrate-associated downstream-processing potential, whereas non-responders were enriched
for oral- and mucosal-associated bacteria overlapping with T2D-associated taxa. A predefined ectopic oral species
panel showed higher baseline burden and richness in non-responders and distinguished response groups with
moderate discriminatory performance (AUROC 0.705-0.727). These findings suggest that metformin response is shaped
less by broad microbial remodeling after treatment than by the pre-treatment gut ecological state.
posters.P124:
Background: Disruption of oral microbial homeostasis has been closely linked to various human diseases, making it a
promising non-invasive marker for health surveillance. However, defining universal oral microbial homeostasis remains
challenging due to profound inter-individual heterogeneity and limited global-scale reference data.
Methods: Publicly available oral microbiome datasets were integrated through standardized quality control, taxonomic
harmonization, and metadata curation. Descriptive analyses were performed to characterize microbial communities
across sample types, geographical regions, and sequencing settings. Health-associated microbial features were
explored across populations as candidate components of a future homeostasis framework.
Results: The integrated data comprised 62,435 samples (16S: 55,072; WGS: 7,363) from 610 cohorts spanning 62
countries and 15 regions, representing 17 sample types, and covering 3,693 genera (16S: 1,182; WGS: 2,511) and
14,061 species (WGS). For both sequencing approaches, sample type had a stronger marginal effect on alpha- and
beta-diversity than geographical region did. Differential abundance analysis identified 8 and 9 genera significantly and
consistently enriched in healthy and unhealthy groups, respectively, across sequencing approaches. Co-abundance
network analyses further identified more significant microbial correlations in the unhealthy than healthy group.
Conclusion: This global-scale resource provides a foundation for future development of a population-generalizable
framework for quantifying oral microbial homeostasis.
posters.P125:
Microbiome profiling is a critical step in microbiome studies, yet different computational workflows may generate
substantially different ecological and taxonomic profiles from the same sequencing data. We evaluated the impact of
two commonly used microbiome analysis workflows by independently processing an identical microbiome dataset
derived from human fecal samples. The two workflows generated broadly similar microbiome profiles at the
community level, indicating that major biological patterns were reproducible across analytical approaches. However,
pipeline-dependent differences were observed in observed richness and Shannon diversity, demonstrating that
alpha-diversity estimates were sensitive to bioinformatic processing choices. Beta-diversity analysis showed substantial
overlap between pipelines but also revealed a measurable pipeline effect, suggesting differences in the reconstructed
community structure. Taxonomic profiling identified concordant dominant taxa across both workflows, while
discrepancies were observed in the detection and relative abundance of several individual taxa. Our findings support
that bioinformatic pipeline selection represents an important source of technical variability in microbiome studies and
underscore the need for transparent reporting, careful workflow validation, and caution when comparing results
generated using different analytical pipelines.

Comprehensive functional characterization of the gut microbiome requires moving beyond taxonomic profiling to
capture the dynamic molecular activities of microbial communities. While metagenomics reveals the gene repertoire, it
cannot distinguish active from dormant members or quantifygene expression. Here we present META-Insight, an
end-to-end multimodal meta-omics framework that systematically links three molecular layers of the central dogma:
whole-metagenome sequencing for individual genome reconstruction and functional potential, metatranscriptome
(metaRNA-Seq) for mRNA synthesis, and metatranslatome (metaRibo-Seq) for protein production. The framework
employs a MAG-centric, sample-specific PanGenes reference that combines genes reconstructed from metagenomes
and those of pangenome representatives derived from a curated reference genome collection spanning the strain
diversity of species present in each sample. By augmenting sample-derived gene content with this reference diversity,
PanGenes consistently outperforms de novo catalog-based profiling that depends on assembled contigs and scaffolds
only in read mapping rate, gene-family recall, and KEGG ortholog accuracy across four CAMI II gold-standard
benchmarks. Detailed procedures cover meta-omics sequencing strategies, whole metagenome assembly and binning
tools for improved MAG quality, metatranscriptome library preparation, and metatranslatome profiling with
translation-efficiency estimation. By constructing a directional evidence chain along the microbial central dogma,
META-Insight advances mechanistic insight into microbiome function.

Abiotic stresses are primary constraints on global crop productivity, reducing yields by up to 80%. While traditional
phenotypic sensing detects stress only after physiological symptoms emerge and often fails to discriminate specific
stressor types, transcriptomic profiling offers a high-dimensional solution, capturing rapid and sensitive molecular
shifts. In this study, we developed AbiOmics, the first end-to-end machine learning pipeline specifically designed to
identify and discriminate among multiple stressors. This approach represents a previously undocumented method for
stress specification using large-scale transcriptomic big data. We identified 320 stress-specific marker genes using a
curated collection of 1,243 transcriptomes of Arabidopsis samples treated with four major abiotic stresses, salt, cold,
heat, and drought. A single-layer perceptron model trained on these features achieved 91% accuracy during five-fold
cross-validation and 93% accuracy on an independent test set. The model demonstrated an unprecedented capacity
to generalize to multi-stress conditions, identifying concurrent signatures in combinatorial salt-and-heat treatments. By
integrating marker identification with SHAP-based biological interpretation, AbiOmics provides a rigorously validated
diagnostic tool superior to conventional sensing. This framework establishes a high-confidence labeling strategy for
AI-driven crop management and precision breeding to mitigate climate change impacts.

Comparative genomics treats fungal biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) inventories as properties of an organism and
reads presence/absence differences between strains as biological variation. If the same strain is independently
sequenced and assembled, it is unclear how often assemblies disagree about BGC presence. We developed an
alignment-free framework using FracMinHash sketches of canonical k-mers and containment, derived the estimator's
conditional sampling law, and obtained a closed-form operating envelope relating divergence, partial overlap, k-mer
length, and the matching threshold. Benchmarked against a generative model that transforms real intervals preserving
correspondence, the envelope predicted matching success across 80 parameter combinations without fitted
parameters; an empirical null of 37,430 non-homologous pairs produced no false matches, and a matched
alignment-based method recovered the same 190 components. Across five verified strain groups, the per-assembly
miss rate was 6.18% (95% CI 4.48–8.29%), where 2.93 points were fragmentation across contigs. At this error rate,
three assemblies per group cannot resolve presence-frequency differences, and ten assemblies resolve only differences
≳0.30. The alignment-free framework makes BGC correspondence across independent assemblies reproducibly
measurable. Comparative BGC studies should verify strain identity, propagate detection error, and prioritize assembly
continuity over gene-model variation.

Metagenomic study of rhizosphere microbial and viral communities is challenging. High-quality DNA is hard to
extract, plant DNA dilutes the microbial signal and Antarctic soils have low biomass, so metagenomes can
undersample the community and its interactions. We developed a pipeline and applied it to three Antarctic plant
rhizospheres (Colobanthus quitensis, Deschampsia antarctica and Poa annua). It starts with nanopore adaptive
sampling, which rejects plant DNA during sequencing. Plant DNA made up 1.1–1.9% of mapped reads, leaving 10.8 of
11 Gb of microbial sequence. The community was reproducible between technical replicates (r=0.999), with
Pseudomonadota (39%) and Actinomycetota (30%) among classified reads and Streptomyces the most abundant
genus in every plant. From the same reads, metaFlye, geNomad and CheckV recovered 320 viral sequences in 308
vOTUs, including 29 proviruses, and one phage genome was free in one rhizosphere and integrated in another. Phold
annotated 35.5% of viral proteins from predicted structure (2.4× geNomad, 11× KOfam) and performed equally well
on proviruses and free viruses. Tiered curation identified four high-confidence and eight probable auxiliary metabolic
genes, none involved in carbon cycling. Phage-encoded WhiB, Pup and GcrA regulators mirror the actinobacterial
community, linking both communities.

Conserved gene clusters often coordinate related functions, but many remain uncharacterized. Spacedust discovers
conserved gene clusters by combining sensitive protein comparison with gene-neighborhood conservation. However,
extending this approach to predicted protein structures requires microbial proteins to be connected to their source
genomes.
Here, we apply this approach to the bacterial and archaeal protein fraction from the AlphaFold Protein Structure
Database. We developed a workflow that links microbial AlphaFold Database entries through UniProt proteome
accession to their GTDB or Genbank genome assemblies. The workflow mapped 133.5 million proteins and produced
a Spacedust-ready dataset of 50,264 genomes. A Skani-based Average-Nucleotide-Identity clustering pipeline reduced
this set to 36,207 representative genomes. We demonstrate Spacedust’s scalability with an all-versus-all analysis of
10,000 microbial genomes, identifying 2,129,604 non-redundant conserved gene clusters covering 80 percent of the
21.4 million genes.
This work expands the discovery of conserved gene clusters to the predicted protein structure universe, allowing
genomic conservation to be explored across the microbial protein space.
posters.P131:

Small open reading frames (smORFs) encoding proteins of up to 100 amino acids are widespread in microorganisms
and participate in diverse cellular processes. However, their global diversity and functional repertoire remain poorly
characterized, largely because short coding sequences are frequently overlooked by traditional gene prediction and
annotation approaches. Here, we constructed the Global Microbial smORFs Catalog (GMSC) by integrating 63,410
publicly available metagenomes from 75 habitats with 87,920 high-quality microbial genomes. GMSC contains
approximately 965 million non-redundant smORFs with extensive annotations, including 43 million high-confidence
sequences supported by computational and experimental evidence. Notably, even small protein families conserved
across diverse taxa and habitats remain largely functionally uncharacterized, revealing a substantial unexplored
functional space. We also developed GMSC-mapper for small protein identification in microbial genomes. However, its
reliance on sequence similarity limits the identification of low-homology or previously unseen small proteins. To
address the limitations of existing identification and annotation approaches, we further developed spBERT, a
pre-trained language model for identifying and functionally annotating microbial small proteins directly from genomic
sequences. Trained on a global collection of 176 million smORF families, spBERT outperforms existing methods across
diverse microbial lineages and habitats. Additionally, spBERT captures attention-associated sequence features,
including the Shine-Dalgarno motif, that are relevant to smORF recognition. Applying spBERT to GMSC provided
functional predictions for more than two million previously unannotated small protein families. Together, GMSC and
spBERT provide a global resource and an AI-based framework for advancing the discovery and functional
characterization of microbial small proteins.

Flax (Linum usitatissimum L.) is an important oilseed crop, and its seed composition is a key target for quality
improvement. This study characterized relationships among 11 seed quality traits, including protein and oil contents,
five fatty acids, and four lignans, and identified associated variants through a genome-wide association study (GWAS).
A total of four datasets were analyzed including year-specific phenotypes (2024 and 2025) and best linear unbiased
predictions for 172 accessions, and 2025 phenotypes for 401 accessions. Protein and oil contents were negatively
correlated in both years (r = −0.55 to −0.40). Correlations ranged from −0.88 to 0.50 among fatty acids and from −
0.02 to 0.46 among lignans. GWAS was performed using a mixed linear model, FarmCPU, and BLINK with
approximately 48,000 SNPs. Significant SNP-trait associations with fatty acid traits were detected in all four datasets,
whereas associations for protein, oil, and lignan-related traits varied by trait and model. These findings provide
insights into the genetic architecture of flax seed quality traits and support quality improvement.
