Genome annotations for non-model insects are frequently incomplete, inconsistent, or redundant, limiting the interpretation of gene
function and the reliability of downstream comparative analyses. This challenge is particularly important for species that are ecologically
significant but remain underrepresented in genomic resources. Here, we describe an ongoing effort to develop an evidence-based
structural annotation for the harlequin ladybird, Harmonia axyridis (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae), an important biological control agent, a globally invasive species, crucial for agriculture, and an emerging system for studying insect development and adaptation.
Using the publicly available chromosome-level genome assembly GCA_914767665.1, we are systematically integrating transcriptomic
and comparative protein evidence to improve gene-model definition. Public RNA-seq datasets are being collected from the NCBI
Sequence Read Archive and span the species’ life cycle, including larval instars, pupae, and adult tissues. Following uniform quality
control and genome-guided alignment, the resulting transcriptomic evidence is combined with Arthropoda protein homology through
the BRAKER4 ETP framework. This approach is designed to improve the identification of exon–intron structures, coding regions,
alternative transcripts, and lowly or stage-specifically expressed genes while minimizing redundant predictions.
To evaluate the robustness of the annotation, we are comparing complementary strategies involving evidence-based gene prediction,
transcriptome-guided reconstruction, consensus merging, targeted recovery of candidate missing loci, and transcript deduplication.
Annotation quality is being assessed using conserved insect orthologs, expression support, structural consistency, and comparison with
existing reference resources. In parallel, we are developing HarmoniaBase, a JBrowse2-based genome browser that brings together
gene models, transcript isoforms, and RNA-seq evidence in a unified, navigable resource. This project will provide an openly accessible genomic foundation for H. axyridis and establish a reproducible workflow for improving
annotations in other non-model insects. By connecting public data, computational annotation, and accessible visualization, we aim to
help close the annotation gap that currently limits functional and comparative genomics across Metazoa.
posters.P134:
Kanazawa University
Conventional metagenomic source classification assigns samples to predefined environmental categories, limiting its
ability to represent intermediate or previously unrepresented sources. This study presents a contrastive
representation-learning framework that maps taxonomic composition into a continuous latent space for environmental
source inference. A study-balanced dataset of 27,684 genus-level count tables from 153 studies, comprising 2,648
genera across five representative environmental categories, was used for evaluation. Genus-level profiles were
square-root transformed and sample-wise L2 normalized, and an encoder was trained to bring samples from the same
source closer while separating samples from different sources. The learned representation achieved a macro-F1 score
of 0.889 for environmental classification, compared with 0.845 for an SVD-based baseline. Leave-one-environment-out
evaluation further demonstrated discrimination of held-out environmental sources, with AUROC values ranging from
0.85 to 0.93. In addition, distances among source categories in latent space reflected continuous relationships among
environmental microbiomes rather than only discrete class boundaries. These results indicate that contrastive
representation learning can provide an interpretable source space for metagenomic profiles, supporting environmental
source inference beyond conventional closed-set classification and improving the characterization of previously
unrepresented source profiles.
posters.P135:
Anam Hospital, Korea University College of Medicine,, Korea
Crop wild relatives (CWRs) provide valuable genetic and ecological diversity for improving crop resilience to
climate-related stresses. Advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and multi-omics have
revealed constitutive and inducible regulatory responses, tissue- and time-dependent expression programs, metabolic
adjustments, and physiological traits associated with drought, heat, salinity, flooding, and related stresses. However,
the current evidence base is highly heterogeneous across species and accessions, stress regimes, tissues, developmental
stages, sampling times, molecular layers, reference genomes, and levels of validation. This review synthesizes
representative CWR omics studies and argues that the major challenge is no longer simply generating more data, but
connecting evidence in biologically and technically meaningful ways. We highlight key sources of fragmentation,
including variable stress definitions, incomplete tissue and temporal alignment, inconsistent multi-omics matching,
reference and orthology issues, and uneven links to functional or agronomic validation. Future studies should prioritize
biologically aligned experimental designs, transparent sample correspondence, interoperable analytical frameworks,
reusable metadata, systems-level interpretation, and staged validation from molecular discovery to crop performance
under realistic conditions. Building better-connected evidence will improve the translation of naturally evolved CWR
diversity into practical resources for climate-resilient agriculture and strengthen its contribution to sustainable crop
improvement.
posters.P136:
al-Farabi Kazakh National University
The inverted-repeat-lacking clade (IRLC) of Fabaceae includes major forage and pulse crops, yet nuclear and
mitochondrial signals are rarely compared in a dated framework. We reconstructed IRLC relationships using nuclear
ITS (18 taxa) and mitochondrial atp1 (17 taxa) GenBank sequences, plus outgroups. Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian
trees were inferred for each marker and a partitioned concatenated matrix (16 shared taxa, 2,402 bp). Divergence
times were estimated in BEAST X using uncorrelated lognormal relaxed clocks and three secondary calibrations.
Marker concordance was assessed with Robinson–Foulds distance and Townsend informativeness profiles. Both
markers recovered Robinia as sister to the IRLC and Onobrychis as its earliest-diverging lineage, with monophyletic
Fabeae and Medicago. Topological discordance was moderate (normalized RF = 0.36) and confined to poorly
supported nodes. ITS contained 249 parsimony-informative sites versus 67 in atp1 and showed higher estimated
informativeness across all depths, whereas atp1 informativeness peaked near 17 Ma. Relative to ITS, concatenation
raised support for Fabeae and Trifolium + Medicago to PP = 1.0. The IRLC crown was dated to 34.9 Ma (95% HPD
31.2–38.6), with Fabeae, Trifolium and Medicago diverging in the Miocene (8–16 Ma). Integrating nuclear and
mitochondrial signals improved phylogenetic resolution and provided a dated framework for IRLC diversification.
posters.P137:

Domestic cats are important companion animals and serve as models for many inherited diseases. Cats-I
(https://cat.annotation.jp) is a genome database based on AnAms1.0, a chromosome-scale assembly of an American
Shorthair cat. Cats-I provides KEGG and InterPro annotations on individual gene pages and as downloadable GFF3 and
TSV files. It also provides a genome browser for AnAms1.0 and felCat9, the previous reference genome.
To further improve Cats-I, we implemented two updates. First, we expanded functional annotation resources. New
pages summarize KEGG pathways, KOG categories, and Gene Ontology (GO) terms assigned to protein-coding genes.
We also incorporated descriptions corresponding to GO terms into the gene annotations for the current domestic cat
reference assembly, Fca126, and 15 other vertebrate genomes obtained from Ensembl. As a result, Cats-I now provides
46% more functional annotation records than the previous version.
Second, we introduced JBrowse 2 as a new genome browser supporting AnAms1.0, felCat9, and Fca126. It also
visualizes synteny among these three assemblies, enabling direct comparison of corresponding genomic regions.
These features will help researchers identify genes by function and compare genomic loci across domestic cat
assemblies. This update also provides a foundation for expanding Cats-I to additional high-quality cat genomes.

Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) have traditionally emphasized transcription factors, whereas upstream chromatin￾regulatory factors that establish accessible regulatory regions remain largely unmodeled. We developed CRANE-GRN
(Chromatin Remodeling Activity Network Extension), a cofactor-aware framework that extends enhancer-centered
GRNs by inferring which chromatin-regulatory modules are associated with enhancer accessibility in individual cells.
CRANE-GRN combines single-cell RNA and ATAC data with public ChIP-seq. An iterative Random Forest identifies
recurrent factor combinations whose binding patterns predict accessibility. RNA expression of module members
provides prior-like regulatory feasibility, while accessibility of module-supported regions provides likelihood-like
chromatin evidence. Their Bayesian-inspired integration yields cell-specific module activity estimates linked to
SCENIC+ eRegulons. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells, integrated activity preserved lineage-specific RNA context
and improved lineage concordance over accessibility evidence alone. In ovarian cancer, module support was
concordant with eRegulon activity and predicted ARID1A-associated regions showed greater loss of accessibility after
ARID1A knockout. In endometrial cancer, CRANE-GRN recovered transcriptional differences consistent with
conventional analyses while revealing tumor-associated changes in upstream module usage and regulatory rewiring
that were not resolvable from expression alone. CRANE-GRN provides an interpretable framework for tracing
enhancer-centered GRNs to candidate upstream chromatin-regulatory mechanisms.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory neurodegenerative disorder affecting approximately 2.8 million people
worldwide, causing physical and cognitive impairments that severely impact their quality of life. Because genetic
studies of MS have largely focused on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) or other isolated variants, investigating
other forms of variation, such as short tandem repeats (STRs), in combination with neighboring SNPs may provide
unexplored biological insight. Given the technical complexity of integrating multi-allelic STRs with SNPs, this study
developed an adaptable computational pipeline to analyze joint STR-SNP haplotypes in more than 40,000 individuals
from the UK Biobank (UKBB) cohort, including MS cases and controls. The framework identifies SNP haplotypes and
corresponding STR alleles together with their observed population frequencies and distributions within the cohort.
Ultimately, this pipeline establishes a methodology for studying fine-scale genomic variation and provides a
foundation for future investigation of STRs and SNPs in the context of complex disease heritability.

DNA N6-methyladenine (6mA) is a prevalent bacterial epigenetic modification that plays key roles in bacterial survival
and host-microbe interactions. Although the Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) Revio platform enables direct output of
high-fidelity (HiFi/CCS) reads, computational methods optimized for direct 6mA detection from Revio HiFi data remain
largely undeveloped. To address this gap, we developed BACH, a deep learning framework for strand-specific,
single-molecule 6mA calling from PacBio Revio HiFi reads. BACH integrates sequence context and kinetic signals using
an attention-based recurrent neural network to estimate the read-level 6mA probabilities. On a benchmark dataset
covering 13 unique 6mA motifs across six bacterial species, BACH achieved exceptional accuracy (AUC-ROC: 0.997;
AUC-PR: 0.995), outperforming the Jasmine tool. When applied to Caulobacter vibrioides, BACH successfully recovered
all three known 6mA motifs at single-molecule resolution and identified consistently hypomethylated GANTC sites
upstream of iron transport genes. These results demonstrate BACH’s ability to resolve both single-molecule patterns
and site-specific epigenetic regulation. Together, BACH provides a practical and reliable framework for 6mA detection
from Revio HiFi data, facilitating meta-epigenomic profiling across complex bacterial communities.

Technological advancement in mapping the protein-RNA interaction network is key in understanding
post-transcriptional regulation. Yet, it is unclear whether the associated computational tools align with the technical
noise in the data generation process and provide certain statistical guarantees for downstream analysis. Here, we
reassess existing computational tools for handling CLIP-seq data and propose a full nonparametric approach for
identifying interaction sites of RNA-binding proteins (RBP). Our method only requires size-matched input data which is
then used to directly control false discovery rate. We find that our method is statistically robust and reproducible by
accounting for the sequence depth and zero-inflation in genome-wide site identification. Reanalyzing ENCODE
CLIP-seq data of 120 RBPs in K562 cells and 103 RBPs in HepG2 cells, we examined the performance of our method in
the context of mitochondrial RNA, noncoding RNA, RNA modification, and RNA splicing. Lastly, we linked the function
of RBP interaction sites by incorporating genetic information of variant databases including ClinVar, COSMIC, and
GTEx, thereby providing mechanistic insights for functional genomics in RNA biology.

Together with N6-methyladenosine and pseudouridine, N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) has been reported as one of the most
abundant mRNA modifications. As such, sequencing technologies have been developed to map the modification sites
and its functional role in RNA regulation. However, recent computational discussions have raised potential limitations
of ac4C data interpretation. This challenge thus calls for the investigation of reliable statistical frameworks handling
sequencing data for ac4C modification. To address this, we examined existing data preprocessing workflows and
identified its statistical limitations including the usage of Fisher’s exact test for p-value computation. We propose an
alternative statistical method that models sequencing error and library depth. Reanalysis of RedaC:T-seq in HeLa cells
revealed 1,877 mRNA acetylation sites, suggesting possible selective regulation of specific mRNAs. Of these sites, we
find the enrichment of ac4C consensus motif which is consistent with previous reports of RNA acetylation. In all, this
computational exercise provides alternative avenues for exploring the functional role of mRNA acetylation and
highlights the importance of data analysis for RNA modifications.

Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) are essential for disease modeling, drug screening, and cell therapy. However,
prolonged in vitro culture compromises their stability by accumulating genetic and epigenetic changes that increase
heterogeneity. The specific epigenetic mechanisms, particularly histone modifications, driving this instability remain
poorly understood. We analyzed scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data from a hESC long-term culture dataset to
investigate passage-dependent histone alterations. We found that epigenetic drift precedes transcriptional changes,
with significant chromatin remodeling occurring in early passages while transcription remains stable. In later passages,
cells exhibit metabolic and stress-related shifts, including increased stress responses, elevated lipid metabolism, and
decreased replication. With increasing passages, cells undergo dynamic epigenetic reprogramming via upregulation of
specific histone modifiers (e.g., KDM6A, KDM5C, ASXL1) and DNMT3B-induced chromatin repression. We are
extending our analysis to early passages (under P100) and utilizing induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) datasets to
confirm reproducibility. Furthermore, integrated analysis of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data will link epigenetic
alterations with gene expression, focusing on the regulatory impact of histone modifiers. Ultimately, our study
elucidates global epigenetic changes of cell instability during long-term culture, providing new perspectives on
overcoming acquired epigenetic vulnerabilities.

Background: Preeclampsia (PE) is a serious pregnancy disorder that affects both the mother and baby. Changes in
gene expression and genetic regulation may contribute to the development of PE. In this study, we investigated the
genetic regulation of placental gene expression at the annotated gene 5’-regions and transcript far 5’end (TFEs) levels.
Methods: Placental samples from the Finnish Genetics of Preeclampsia Consortium (FINNPEC) were analyzed using
single-cell tagged reverse transcription (STRT) RNA-seq. Gene expression was quantified using annotated gene
5’-regions and TFEs. Maternal and fetal genotypes were analyzed separately using cis-expression quantitative trait
locus (cis-eQTL) analysis. Pathway enrichment analysis and cell type deconvolution were also performed.
Results: Immune-related pathways were enriched in PE placentas and Hofbauer cell proportions were reduced
compared with normotensive pregnancies. Gene 5’-region-based eQTL analysis identified several candidate loci, but
no significant interaction eQTLs after multiple testing correction. In contrast, TFE-based analysis identified two
significant interaction eQTLs, suggesting that genetic regulation in PE may be better detected using TFE than
annotated gene 5’-regions.
Conclusions: Our findings show that combining analyses of annotated gene 5’ regions and TFEs provides a more
detailed view of genetic regulation in the placenta. This approach may help identify genes and regulatory variants
associated with preeclampsia.
posters.P145:
Pusan National University
Circular RNAs (circRNAs) participate in post-transcriptional regulation through interactions with microRNAs (miRNAs),
yet miRNA binding sites on full-length circRNA isoforms remain difficult to predict. Isoform-specific context and
sequence continuity across the back-splice junction (BSJ) further complicate this task. We formulate circRNA–miRNA
binding-site prediction as a miRNA-conditioned nucleotide-level sequence-labeling task and introduce circMAC, which
combines global attention, Mamba-based sequential modeling, circular convolution for local motif extraction, and
miRNA conditioned cross-attention. Given a full-length circRNA isoform and a mature miRNA, circMAC predicts
per-nucleotide binding probabilities and is initialized through base-pairing prediction (BPP) pretraining. Using 27,512
circRNA–miRNA pairs with curated AGO-CLIP-supported binding-site annotations, we evaluated circMAC against
pretrained RNA language models, conventional sequence encoders, and rule-based screening approaches. On the
pair-disjoint benchmark, circMAC achieved an F1-macro of 0.762, AUROC of 0.902, and AUPRC of 0.545,
outperforming all evaluated baselines. circMAC also retained the strongest overall performance under stricter
isoform-disjoint and BSJ-disjoint evaluations. Ablation studies supported complementary contributions of sequential,
global, and local sequence modeling. Aggregate analysis showed enrichment of predicted probability around
annotated binding-site regions. These results support full-length, miRNA-conditioned circular isoform modeling for
nucleotide-resolution circRNA–miRNA binding-site localization.

Nuclear speckles are among the most prominent membraneless organelles in the nucleus, enriched in diverse splicing
factors and RNA-processing machinery. Despite their functional importance, the lack of comprehensive profiling of
speckle–genome interactions across cell types limits our understanding of their functional roles and dynamic
regulation. To overcome this limitation, we previously developed HiCAN, a tool for inferring speckle–genome
interactions from Hi-C contact maps. However, the original HiCAN is not suitable for quantitative comparisons across
cell types, as it is strongly affected by experimental batch effects and interchromosomal translocation signals in Hi-C
contact maps. Here, we introduce HiCAN2, which enables quantitative comparison of speckle–genome interactions
across diverse cell types. HiCAN2 reduces the influence of interchromosomal translocation signals on Hi-C contact
maps by modelling genomic region-specific interchromosomal contact frequencies as background. Leveraging HiCAN2
results across 359 publicly available Hi-C and Micro-C datasets, we developed a normalization framework that models
the dependence of HiCAN2 measurements on library quality. We confirmed that HiCAN2 shows comparable accuracy
to experimental approaches, including SON TSA-seq and SON CUT&RUN, in measuring speckle–genome interactions.
Using HiCAN2, we demonstrate that while the core structure of speckle–genome interactions is conserved across cell
types, consistent with previous reports, speckle–genome interactions are dynamically regulated across cell types,
cancer types, and differentiation stages. We further aim to compare HiCAN2 results with TSA-seq, CUT&RUN, and
ORCA imaging to characterize the strengths and limitations of each approach for detecting speckle–genome
interactions. Together, HiCAN2 enables systematic profiling and quantitative comparison of speckle–genome
interactions across public chromatin conformation datasets and provides a global view of their dynamic regulation
across cell states.
posters.P147:

CRISPR screening has enabled systematic investigation of gene function by linking targeted genetic perturbations to
cellular phenotypes. Single-cell CRISPR screening approaches, exemplified by Perturb-seq, have extended this
framework by enabling transcriptomic responses to hundreds of genetic perturbations to be measured simultaneously
at single-cell resolution. However, the information contained in single-cell RNA sequencing data remains underutilized,
as most Perturb-seq analyses focus primarily on gene expression while largely overlooking other layers of RNA
regulation, including alternative splicing. In this study, we developed an algorithm to quantify RNA splicing alterations
at single-cell resolution. The method measures the deviation of cellular splicing patterns from a reference splicing
state and generates a standardized splicing divergence score, enabling systematic identification of cells and
perturbations associated with altered RNA splicing. By applying this framework to CRISPR-based Perturb-seq datasets,
we identified multiple gene perturbations associated with substantial changes in RNA splicing across different cellular
contexts. These included perturbations of well-established core components of the spliceosome, while also
highlighting additional candidate genes whose roles in RNA splicing regulation have not been extensively
characterized. Together, these results establish a computational framework for extracting RNA splicing phenotypes
from single-cell CRISPR screening data. By extending Perturb-seq analysis beyond conventional gene expression
measurements, this approach enables systematic identification and prioritization of regulators associated with RNA
splicing and provides an additional dimension for the functional interpretation of large-scale genetic perturbation
screens.

Nuclear speckles are membrane-less compartments closely associated with active transcription and RNA processing. Although
transcriptionally active regions tend to be associated with speckles, transcriptional activity does not fully account for variation
in speckle proximity across the genome. In this context, the zinc finger proteins MAZ and CTCF have both been linked to
speckle-associated genome positioning, yet whether they act through shared or distinct mechanisms remains unclear. MAZ
and CTCF make distinct, context-dependent contributions to speckle-proximal genome organization. Using public Hi-C
datasets from mESC, MAZ- and CTCF-dependent changes in speckle proximity were compared with HiCAN. MAZ loss resulted
in an approximately four-fold greater reduction in genome–speckle proximity than CTCF depletion, while a subset of regions
showed shared responses to both perturbations. To directly compare their effects within the same cellular context, a dual-degron system was established in SEM cells, which show high basal expression of both MAZ and CTCF and allow acute
individual or combined depletion. Hi-C followed by HiCAN analysis revealed clear changes in genome–speckle organization
after CTCF depletion, whereas MAZ depletion produced little to no measurable effect. This limited MAZ response was explained by an alternatively spliced, early-terminated isoform that lacks the degron-targeted C-terminus and compensates
for loss of the canonical isoform. Splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) are therefore being used to suppress this residual
isoform and assess the effect of more complete MAZ depletion. For CTCF, deep TSA-seq was further performed to directly measure speckle proximity, refine the perturbation effects inferred from Hi-C, and explore finer-scale, potentially loop-like
organization of speckle-associated chromatin. Finally, speckle-targeted TurboID will compare MAZ- and CTCF-associated
protein environments to investigate the molecular basis of their shared and distinct effects on speckle proximity. Together,
these analyses aim to define the features that determine region-specific dependency of speckle-proximal chromatin on MAZ
and CTCF.

Inspection of 3D genome organization can elucidate underlying mechanism of gene expression which is mediated by
the contacts between regulatory elements on the genome. However, due to experimental limitations, it is difficult to
verify 3D genome information for all situations such as rare cell types within the tissue. To overcome these limitations
in computational method, several deep learning methods which utilize DNA sequence and epigenome feature to
predict Hi-C contact map were proposed. Despite such advances, due to the nature of the Hi-C contact map
generation method that relies on transposed convolution, a blurry image is generated. In this study, we developed
codeFormer-based framework that conducts blind restoration of Hi-C contact map by learning a mapping of low
quality generated image to high quality real image. By using a vector quantized-variational autoencoder for the
quantization of the Hi-C contact map, blur caused by convolution is minimized, and a transformer is used to enable
mapping that preserves the global features of the contact map. The model was implemented with a performer
architecture to handle long sequences that are difficult to handle with a standard transformer. In baseline
measurement tests using reconstruction of the same Hi-C contact map, 90% codebook accuracy was recorded. In
integration tests with the actual Hi-C prediction model, the VGG-19 perception loss was reduced by approximately 0.1.
The proposed method in this study operates faster than diffusion models that require a step-wise diffusion process
and can be applied regardless of the type of prediction model, which can facilitate systematic analysis and contribute
to expanding the capacity of 3D genome research.
posters.P150:
Nuclear speckles are dynamic, membraneless nuclear organelles key to RNA metabolism, encompassing alternative
splicing and RNA export. Recent studies highlight their role as spatial hubs coordinating active chromosomal
interactions. Despite their importance, how compositional heterogeneity varies across cell types and links to cellular
phenotypes or genome architecture remains unexplored. In this study, we identified four nuclear speckle types that
actively drive cell-state transitions by reshaping 3D genome architecture, rather than passively reflecting transcription.
Using Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and HiCAN, we decomposed speckle variability into discrete functional
types and evaluated their 3D speckle-genome interactions. Cell lines grouped into the same speckle composition
category displayed conserved 3D spatial genomic similarity at speckle-associated regions, indicating that speckle types
act as functional frameworks for lineage-specific 3D genome organization. Notably, these speckle types were
successfully recapitulated in in vivo systems. Leveraging these insights, we are investigating candidate trans-acting
factors driving type-specific nuclear speckle-genome interactions. Together, our findings highlight nuclear speckle
heterogeneity as a modular determinant coupling cell lineage identity to spatial genome architecture.

The steroid hormone, 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), orchestrates insect metamorphosis via transcriptional reprogramming.
However, it remains unclear how 20E dynamically remodels chromatin accessibility to regulate transcription. We
combined ATAC-seq and RNA-seq to characterize the temporal dynamics of chromatin accessibility in Drosophila S2
cells after 20E treatment. Although 20E rapidly reshaped chromatin accessibility at transcription start sites and
enhancers during the early response, prolonged treatment reduced accessibility signals in regulatory regions,
accompanied by an increased proportion of short DNA fragments. Integrative analysis revealed that increased
promoter accessibility was associated with gene activation, whereas reduced enhancer accessibility was linked to
transcriptional repression. Genes exhibiting rapid changes in chromatin accessibility displayed greater transcriptional
responses than those with delayed remodeling. We also identified enhancer-switching events associated with
20E-responsive gene regulation, demonstrating that dynamic enhancer remodeling likely regulates miR-282
expression. Our findings provide a genome-wide framework for understanding dynamic chromatin remodeling during
hormone-induced transcriptional responses.

RNA modifications (RMs) are critical for diverse biological processes, but the lack of accurate, quantitative detection
methods has limited their study. A large-scale and high-quality training dataset is an essential component for accurate
deep learning, but such dataset has been absent for RM detection, resulting in low accuracies. We developed DeepRM
(Deep learning for RNA Modification), a sophisticated deep learning framework powered by Nanopore sequencing.
DeepRM dataset is a massive- scale, three orders of magnitude larger than the comparable previous ones, and
unprecedentedly high-quality dataset that closely mirrors endogenous transcript environments. Accordingly, DeepRM
detects RM sites and measures their modification stoichiometries with a near-perfect accuracy. Using DeepRM, we
constructed a comprehensive, human m6A atlas at a single-molecule resolution that reveals a large number of
previously underappreciated non-canonical m6A sites and differentially modified transcripts, highlighting the
complexity and dynamic nature of the human epitranscriptome. DeepRM is freely available, providing a unique,
powerful opportunity for understanding the biological functions of RMs. DeepRM can also be expanded to various
other RMs and organisms, potentially becoming a future standard for investigating the epitranscriptome.

Helpless T cells are cytotoxic T lymphocytes that develop without CD4+ T-cell help, exhibiting reduced cytotoxicity,
exhaustion marker upregulation, and impaired memory differentiation. Despite these features, the transcriptional
programs underlying this divergence between Helped and Helpless CD8+ T cells remain poorly characterized.
To address this gap, J15 transgenic CD8+ T cells from an H60-specific, MHC class I-restricted murine model were
profiled by scRNA-seq across multiple time points. Following initial DEG/GSEA screening, differentiation trajectories
were inferred with scFates, trajectory-associated gene modules identified using Hotspot, condition-specific GRNs
reconstructed via SCENIC, and regulon activities cross-validated with decoupleR, in a hierarchical, resolution-refining
pipeline.
This integrated approach revealed that trajectory bifurcation points coincided with distinct gene modules linked to
condition-specific regulons, corroborated by decoupleR, converging on a unified regulatory axis defining the
exhaustion-associated transcriptional identity of Helpless relative to Helped CD8+ T cells.
By synthesizing these complementary outputs, we interpret Helpless CD8+ T cell differentiation as a coherent,
multidimensional process, unifying independently derived signals into this single regulatory axis. It offers a foundation
for extending the framework to exhaustion-driven conditions such as cancer and other T-cell exhaustion-associated
pathologies, informing future strategies to restore effector T cell function.

Ovarian cancer (OV) is a heterogeneous tumor with the highest mortality rate among gynecological malignancies. Its
survival rate has no significant improvements with emerging treatments, indicating a need for novel diagnosis and
treatment targets of OV. Alternative splicing (AS) is known to play important roles in the progression of ovarian
cancer, while long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are recently reported as splicing regulators to perform functions in
tumor development. The role of lncRNAs in the abnormal splicing of OV has not yet been understood, thus we
performed a genome-wide analysis to identify splicing-regulatory lncRNAs with pathogenic characteristics. In the
present work, from 207 differentially expressed lncRNAs and 1 201 abnormal splicing events, 2 545 co-expression pairs
were found. We further established regulatory networks of lncRNAs on abnormal splicing through integrating known
interactions between lncRNA and other regulators (splicing factor, transcription factor, microRNA). Utilizing the restart
random walk algorithm (RWR) optimized by seed points of oncogenes, we identified 29 hub splicing-regulatory
lncRNAs. Among them, a total of 15 lncRNAs are significantly associated with the OV survival. In summary, our study
provides novel biomarkers, explores the functions of lncRNAs in splicing regulation, and presents new insights into the
underlying mechanism of OV.

Bacterial small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are key regulators of gene expression and microbial adaptation, yet their
genome-wide identification remains challenging due to limited sequence conservation, structural diversity, and
heterogeneous genomic contexts. Here, we present the development of a comprehensive, multi-modal dataset to
support machine learning-based sRNA identification across diverse bacterial genomes.
We are compiling a curated dataset covering over 1,000 bacterial species with experimentally validated sRNAs, paired
with matched negative non-sRNA genomic regions. For each candidate, we capture the sRNA sequence, flanking
regions, predicted secondary-structure characteristics, and genomic context. Features include distances to upstream
and downstream transcription start sites (TSSs), same- and opposite-strand genes and ORFs, ORF overlap, bacterial
lineage, k-mer composition, GC content, thermodynamic stability, coding potential, ribosome-binding-site signals, and
sequence conservation.
The resulting dataset provides the foundation for training and benchmarking explainable machine learning and deep
learning models, including implementations of Random Forest, XGBoost, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
Models will be evaluated on independent test sets, and the best-performing model will be deployed through an
open-source web tool for standardized sRNA annotation.
This project is funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Marie
Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement No. 101283050, BACRNA.

Cell fate reprogramming induced by exogenous transcription factors, such as OSKM-mediated pluripotency induction or GMT-mediated cardiac reprogramming, provides a powerful model for studying transcriptional state transitions. However, the
broader set of genes that can substitute for, cooperate with, or function downstream of canonical reprogramming factors
remains incompletely defined. We present FateDriver, a dual-view graph neural network that ranks candidate driver genes
from single-cell RNA sequencing data before and after TF induction, jointly modeling a pseudotime-aware cell graph and a gene graph built from co-expression and NicheNet-derived regulatory priors. The model learns cell and gene embeddings in a shared latent space via a tier-aware hybrid ranking objective distinguishing canonical factors, direct TF-targets, and
non-drivers. Across OSKM-induced fibroblast-to-iPSC and GMT-induced fibroblast-to-cardiomyocyte datasets, FateDriver
recovered known drivers more accurately than existing models, with predicted genes showing activation more consistent with
actual reprogramming dynamics. In an OSKM-induced fibroblast reprogramming dataset, fibroblasts formed two pseudotime￾distinct clusters representing separate starting states, and FateDriver predicted switch-on pluripotency genes from the earlier
cluster versus switch-off MET-barrier genes from the later cluster, showing that the model captures state-specific transition
programs rather than assuming a single starting point. In an in vivo OSKM-induced intestinal epithelial reprogramming
dataset, FateDriver independently modeled transitions from each candidate source population to newly emerged
atrophy-induced villus epithelial cells (aVECs) and revival stem cells (revSCs), identifying enterocytes (ECs) as the likely source of aVEC and transit-amplifying (TA) cells as the likely source of revSC, consistent with lineage and marker-based evidence.
These results establish FateDriver as a tractable framework for nominating reprogramming regulators, characterizing
state-dependent transitions, and tracing unknown cell origins, pending experimental validation.

Conserved non-coding elements (CNEs) are important components of gene regulation, yet their rapid sequence
divergence makes the detection of deeply conserved CNEs challenging using conventional sequence comparison.
Here, we developed a sensitive profile hidden Markov model (profile-HMM)-based approach for detecting highly
diverged CNE and constructed a large-scale CNE database comprising approximately 27,000 CNE families conserved
across diverse vertebrate lineages. Applying this approach to the zebrafish genome identified approximately 39,000
CNEs. Benchmark using epigenomic datasets of developmental zebrafish revealed strong enrichment of chromatin
accessibility and active regulatory signals around the centers of predicted CNEs, supporting their potential regulatory
relevance. We further applied our method to the abalone genome to investigate conservation beyond vertebrates and
found 217 CNE hits representing 133 CNE families that showed significant associations with conserved genomic
neighborhoods. Our results demonstrate that optimized sequence comparison methods can provide a powerful means
of detecting conserved elements across deep evolutionary distances, revealing signatures of an ancient gene
regulatory system that date back to the last common ancestor of bilaterians.
posters.P158:
Background: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is fundamental to cell identity and disease. Although
enhancer-promoter interactions drive gene expression, how proximal promoters integrate regulatory signals from
distal elements remains poorly understood.
Methods: We developed a computational framework using a graph-embedding approach to model Cofactor￾Transcription Factor (TF)-Gene interactions within 3D transcriptional domains. Analyzing large-scale public human NGS
datasets, our pipeline combines greedy regression modeling to identify critical regulators with graph embedding to
classify co-regulated genes.
Results: This approach uncovered highly organized regulatory networks assigned to specific biological functions.
Notably, cofactors were frequently co-expressed not only with their interacting TFs but also with the target genes
regulated by those TFs, highlighting a tightly coordinated regulatory mechanism.
Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate the essential functional role of cofactors in integrating proximal and distal
regulatory activities within the 3D genome. This study provides a versatile, data-driven computational framework for
dissecting complex 3D genome architecture, offering broad insights into transcriptional regulation in health and
disease.
posters.P159:
Soongsil University
Gene co-expression networks (GCNs) capture context-dependent relationships between genes, but the extent to which
their organization is encoded by upstream regulatory information remains unclear. Here we present MultiCoNet, a
framework that reconstructs cell-line-specific GCNs from DNA sequence, H3K27ac-associated regulatory signals and
three-dimensional chromatin features, without using gene expression as model input. Across 16 cell lines, MultiCoNet
outperformed chromatin-only reconstruction and recovered both shared and context-specific network organization.
We developed the topology-adjusted Label-native Residual Connectivity Score (taLRCS) to quantify gene-level
deviations from recurrent connectivity and derive pathway-level context profiles. Recurrent connectivity was associated
with DepMap dependency breadth in both observed and reconstructed networks, whereas taLRCS-derived pathway
profiles correctly identified cell-line context in 15 of 16 cases. H3K27ac-associated information did not simply
strengthen predicted connectivity; instead, it reshaped context-dependent partner preferences and improved recovery
of recurrent-versus-context-specific gene roles. These effects preserved both the amplitude and relative geometry of
pathway-level context profiles despite limited recovery of exact co-expression neighbours.
By contrast, models transferred to an unseen cell line recovered substantial co-expression structure without reliably
recovering its context-specific identity. Together, these results distinguish reconstruction of individual edges from
recovery of higher-order network context, and show how multimodal regulatory information can encode biologically
relevant organization in GCNs.
posters.P160:
University of Malta
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression through sequence-dependent interactions with target RNAs.
Characterizing evolutionary constraints across miRNA sequences may help identify positions that tolerate variation and
inform target prediction. Here, we apply PHACTn, a training-free phylogenetic framework, to map nucleotide tolerance
across human miRNA precursors.
Our approach combines ortholog alignments, a consensus species tree and gap-aware ancestral reconstruction to
estimate tolerance for each possible nucleotide at every position. Unlike nucleotide frequencies alone, the framework
accounts for shared ancestry and the evolutionary distance of observed substitutions. We generated profiles for 331
miRNA precursors and mapped them onto annotated regions, providing a basis for comparing seed sequences, other
mature-miRNA positions and surrounding precursor regions. Consensus-tree scoring increased positional contrast in
many mature-miRNA profiles, while some remained uniform.
We further explored these profiles as inputs to miRNA–target prediction alongside sequence and target-site
evolutionary information. Preliminary models achieved test-set AUPRC values up to 0.890, although gains were not
consistent for left-out miRNAs.
Together, these analyses provide a resource for examining nucleotide tolerance across miRNA sequences and
evaluating its contribution to target prediction.
posters.P161:
Noncoding variants can influence plant phenotypes by altering transcription factor (TF) binding, but identifying the affected
TF, relevant cell type and candidate target gene remains challenging. We are developing araFINCH, a computational
framework for inferring the regulatory impact of noncoding variants in Arabidopsis.
To identify the affected TF of noncoding variants, we trained TF-specific BPNet models using publicly available DAP-seq and
ampDAP-seq data, as the first module of araFINCH. We evaluated their predictive performance on held-out chromosomes
using Pearson correlation and Jensen–Shannon distance-based score. Contribution-based motif discovery and comparison
with reference motifs provide additional assessment of learned sequence features. To provide relevant cell type and candidate
target genes of each variant, we designed the second module of araFINCH, that integrates predicted TF-binding changes with
cell-type-resolved chromatin accessibility profiles using the collection of snATAC-seq and shared Hi-C contact data through an ABC-inspired activity-by-contact framework. The resulting report prioritizes candidate variant–TF–cell type–regulatory
element–target gene relationships and provides the underlying binding and chromatin evidence.
In the user interface, araFINCH accepts a genomic coordinate and an alternative allele, automatically retrieves the reference
sequence and compares both alleles across available TF models. Predicted binding changes are quantified using log2 fold
changes in binding magnitude and Jensen–Shannon divergence between binding profiles. araFINCH also supports local
insertions and deletions of up to 800 bp under default configuration, including comparisons of binding profiles at shared
genomic positions. Complementary in silico mutagenesis, contribution-based analyses and motif-spacing analyses support
investigation of variant-sensitive nucleotides and TF-specific sequence features. For those variants potentially impactful for TF
binding, araFINCH further suggest the candidate cellular contexts and target genes in the final report.
Overall, araFINCH provides cell-type-informed prioritization of regulatory hypotheses which is experimentally testable with
genome editing, allele-specific binding assays, and allele-specific reporter analyses in the Arabidopsis system.

Germline variants modulate transcription in a context-dependent manner, yet how epigenomic remodeling during
tumorigenesis reshapes these regulatory effects remains poorly understood. We integrated promoter-targeted bisulfite
sequencing with RNA-seq in paired tumor and normal-adjacent tissue (NAT) from 80 colorectal cancer (CRC) patients,
thereby controlling for germline background, and mapped expression and methylation quantitative trait loci (eQTLs
and mQTLs). Both eQTL and mQTL landscapes exhibited pronounced tissue-state specificity, and tumor-specific
eGenes were significantly enriched in hallmark oncogenic pathways, including WNT and MAPK signaling. At loci
harboring both eQTL and mQTL signals, methylation mediated genotype effects on expression in only a minority of
cases, indicating that a linear SNP–methylation–expression cascade inadequately explains these relationships. In
contrast, methylation-modulated eQTL (memo-eQTL) mapping, which explicitly models genotype × methylation (G×M)
interactions, identified 18 and 73 genes in NAT and tumor, respectively, with no triplet reaching significance in both
states. For NAT-defined triplets, the patient-level shift in interaction burden from NAT to matched tumor was
significantly greater in stage III than stage I–II disease. These findings demonstrate that promoter-proximal G×M
interactions are extensively reconfigured between normal and malignant colorectal tissue and link NAT-defined G×M
interactions to disease progression.

A large-scale single-nucleus ATAC-seq (snATAC-seq) dataset has become a central resource for interpreting GWAS
variants in cis-regulatory elements (CRE). However, in multi-sample analysis, weak CRE signals are indistinguishable
from technical noise and are therefore progressively removed by the conventional snATAC-seq pipeline. We present a
sequence- and centroid-mapping-based workflow for multi-sample CRE discovery, which calls peaks permissively,
aligns summits across samples to derive representative coordinates, and identifies functional CREs based on their
sequence predictability in gapped-k-mer-based light-weight models rather than statistical significance alone. Our
workflow recovered CREs that the conventional pipeline had discarded, and partitioned heritability analysis confirmed
the recovered CREs as trait-linked regulatory signals. In human embryonic heart samples, recovery was highest in
trophectoderm, the rarest cell type, and across cardiovascular traits, 37 of 40 trait–cell-type pairs showed increased
enrichment. We are now applying this workflow to large-scale PBMC data to construct a high-resolution regulatory
map of immune cells. By conducting partitioned heritability analyses across levels of hierarchical organization, we are
investigating whether each immunological complex trait is best explained at a distinct resolution. Together, the
cell-state-level CRE map provides a resolution unattainable by gene-level analysis and allows interpretation of the cell
states in which noncoding regulatory variants act.

Membranous nephropathy (MN) is an autoantibody-mediated glomerulonephritis with a variable clinical course, yet
the molecular basis of relapse and treatment resistance remains undefined. We hypothesized that chromatin priming
stratifies MN prognosis, reasoning that trained immunity deposits epigenetic memory that can shape
immunosuppressive-therapy response. We profiled PBMCs from 12 individuals using paired single-cell RNA and ATAC
sequencing (4 healthy controls; 4 in sustained remission confirmed at follow-up; 4 relapsing or refractory). Across
17,559 cells spanning 10 cell types, we scored 46 gene programs independently in RNA and ATAC, aggregating ATAC
signal to genes through cell-type-matched and CRISPR-informed enhancer-gene links. In pseudobulk PCA, chromatin
profile discriminated remission from healthy controls more than transcription did, whereas transcription better
discriminated relapsing/refractory disease. Relative to healthy controls, remission monocytes exhibited a priming-like
signature: increased chromatin accessibility without a corresponding transcriptional change. This signature was
particularly pronounced in a BCG-induced trained-immunity program, while relapsing/refractory disease showed lower
accessibility and higher transcription. The remission pattern extended to Hallmark IFN-γ and TNFα–NF-κB programs,
which gained accessibility in remission but were transcriptionally attenuated in relapsing/refractory disease. Together,
MN clinical courses leave distinct regulatory signatures across transcription and chromatin, positioning epigenomic
priming as a candidate prognostic layer beyond expression.

Predicting biological function from genetic sequences requires extrapolating experimental data gathered from a
minuscule fraction of possible sequences to the entire sequence space, a challenge that has never been fully
addressed for any full-length protein or non-coding RNA sequences. Despite the importance of RNA structure in
determining RNA functionality, previous attempts at functional prediction for RNA cis-regulatory elements, such as
mapping UTR sequence to mRNA decay rates, have been conducted without incorporating RNA structural information
during the learning process. Here, I present a neural network that predicts functional activity from any RNA sequence
with consideration of RNA structure. This model is designed to simultaneously predict both RNA secondary structure
and functional activity, enabling the neural network to effectively learn structural information during the training
process. This joint prediction approach allows for better integration of RNA structural features that directly impact
functionality, improving the model's ability to capture the structure-function relationship. When trained on
high-throughput in vitro primary microRNA cleavage assay data, this model accurately predicts how efficiently any
RNA sequence is cleaved by the Microprocessor, a gene regulator consisting of a DROSHA and two DGCR8 proteins,
that processes hundreds of specific transcripts to initiate microRNA biogenesis. This model promises to unravel RNA
structure-dependent gene regulation at an unprecedented scale and resolution, showcasing the power of deep
learning to generalize experimental knowledge to broader biological contexts.

Alternative transcription initiation (ATI) reshapes protein N-termini, yet genome-wide detection typically requires 5′ -end sequencing, which is unavailable for large clinical cohorts. We developed a pipeline that calls unannotated 5′ -extension ATI events in individual patients from standard RNA-seq. The pipeline scans 161,532 windows upstream of
annotated internal exons, scores each by window depth, gene expression, window-to-exon coverage ratio and
intra-gene intronic background, and removes events observed in 705 normal samples or explained by annotated
isoforms. Built-in safeguards recount calls using uniquely mapped reads directly from BAM files and exclude tumors
with aberrant intronic background. Across four TCGA cohorts (1,938 tumors), the pipeline identified 1,533 candidate
windows in 1,120 genes, 82% of which were specific to a single cancer type. Benchmarked against splice-junction
evidence not used for calling, it recovered an unannotated ROR1 ATI in all 21 junction-supported melanomas while
calling 98.7% of junction-negative tumors negative, improving recovery from 62% under the original expression cutoff.

first among 23 cancer types, and the melanoma candidate HKDC1 was confirmed by CAGE in melanoma cells. This
pipeline turns existing tumor RNA-seq into a resource for patient-level ATI discovery and multi-omics integration.

Acquired resistance to third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer
(NSCLC) is characterized by multiple resistance-associated alterations whose cellular co-occurrence cannot be resolved by
bulk sequencing. We profiled post-progression tumors from five patients, including two who progressed on first-line and
three on second-line third-generation EGFR-TKIs, together with two TKI-resistant cell lines, using Tapestri single-cell DNA
sequencing. Joint SNV-CNA analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction resolved clonal architecture and lineage relationships.
We identified three major clonal patterns: retention of the founding EGFR driver mutation, emergence of an EGFR-independent lineage, and loss of the mutant EGFR allele. Distinct branch-specific alterations involved bypass receptor
signaling, MAPK–RAS and PI3K pathways, and cell-cycle regulation. Polyclonal divergence was also observed in vitro, with
divergent EGFR copy-number states among HCC827 subclones under TKI pressure. Despite lineage heterogeneity, alterations
disrupting cell-cycle regulation and tumor-suppressor function recurred across multiple lineages within individual tumors.
These findings demonstrate complex post-treatment evolutionary trajectories involving the coexistence of distinct
resistance-associated clones and shared pathway alterations, and provide insights into future therapeutic strategies targeting
both lineage-specific and convergent resistance mechanisms.

Cell-type-resolved linking of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) to their target genes enables the translation of genome￾ide association study (GWAS) loci into causal variants and effector genes. However, existing approaches primarily
capture CRE-gene links that distinguish cell types, and therefore overlook regulatory interactions that vary across
individuals and cell states. Here, we generated CRE-gene maps of 14 kidney cell types from 23 single-cell multiome
samples across life stages and disease states. Using sequence-assisted multi-sample (SAMS) CRE mapping, we
identified ~600,000 CREs (1.2-fold more than a conventional pipeline) and linked them to target genes by
within-cell-type co-variation. Connected CREs explained more kidney trait heritability than CREs prioritized by
cell-type-specific accessibility or by gene expression, especially in injury-associated PT-VCAM1+ cells, and were
enriched for variants colocalized between eGFR GWAS and tubule eQTL. Only 49.6% of fine-mapped eGFR variants

and linked an additional 15.5% of variants to target genes. Kidney function genes without eQTL support had more
CREs and cell-type-dependent associations between expression and eGFR, indicating a complex regulatory
architecture. Together, within-cell-type CRE-gene mapping links kidney functional variants to effector genes beyond
eQTL coverage.

Advanced colorectal adenoma (ACA) is a pre-cancerous lesion associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer,
one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Both adenomas and adenocarcinomas arise from the
epithelium. Characterizing the transcriptional and regulatory states of epithelial cells within ACA is essential for
understanding early colorectal tumorigenesis and informing future prevention strategies. Here, we profiled ACA tissues
collected from ten Korean donors using 10X Genomics single-nucleus sequencing, generating nine paired
single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin
sequencing (snATAC-seq) data and one snRNA-seq data. An integrated analysis resolved nine epithelial populations,
including stem-like cells, transit-amplifying cells, colonocytes, and goblet cells. Tumor-related transcriptional signatures
differed significantly across these populations, although the magnitude of these differences was generally small.
Motif-accessibility and regulatory network analyses further identified distinct regulatory patterns across epithelial
populations. An immature colonocyte population with elevated DUOX2 expression exhibited prominent AP-1
motif-associated chromatin accessibility and inferred FOS/FOSL2-associated regulatory features. These findings
characterize epithelial heterogeneity in ACA and describe an AP-1-associated regulatory state in immature colonocytes
with elevated DUOX2 expression, providing a basis for further investigation into the biological significance of this state
in pre-cancerous lesions.

Altered linear splicing and circRNA abundance have both been reported in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but
whether and how ALS alters circRNA processing beyond abundance remains unclear. We analyzed total RNA-seq data
from 320 Answer ALS iPSC-derived spinal neuron samples (283 ALS and 37 controls), examining multiple dimensions
of circRNA processing.
At the global level, the circRNA-processing features examined were largely preserved in ALS. For example,
depth-controlled analysis showed no clear ALS-wide increase in rare or control-unseen back-splice junctions (BSJs) or
in alternative-BSJ dispersion.
In contrast, event-level analysis identified locus-specific alterations across distinct dimensions of circRNA processing.
These included altered alternative BSJ usage at SNX25 and reduced detection frequency of a TRIP4 circRNA. Of 233
events with sufficient paired circular and linear coverage, 3 showed significant interactions between ALS status and
circular versus linear splice-site usage, indicating that disease-associated shifts in use of the same splice sites can
differ between circular and linear products.
Together, these findings indicate global preservation of circRNA processing alongside selective locus-specific
alterations in ALS. The identified events provide candidates for investigating disease-associated mechanisms
underlying circular RNA processing and splice-site choice beyond changes captured by conventional analyses of
circRNA abundance or linear splicing.

The T2T-CHM13 reference provides complete centromere sequences, but extensive variation in alpha-satellite arrays among
individuals and haplotypes means that sample-specific centromeric sequences and structures may not be represented.
Structural variants (SVs) connecting alpha-satellite to non-centromeric sequence have rarely been reported, and their
detection and localization remain challenging. Conventional long-read SV callers may filter out repeat alignments with low
mapping quality (MAPQ), whereas single-breakend approaches retain junction candidates without necessarily resolving anchor
placement. Here, we developed a two-path framework that compares anchor coordinates from direct read-to-reference
alignments with coordinates projected through sample-specific genome assemblies. We applied this framework to candidate
junctions supported by reads with alpha-satellite-containing soft-clipped sequences in normal and tumor samples. Junctions
with concordant coordinates were grouped into events within each sample and characterized using contig alignment
structure. A substantial proportion of alpha-satellite-associated candidates showed discordant coordinates, with discordance
markedly more frequent than among candidates with non-alpha clipped sequences. Discordance was concentrated at young
transposable element anchors, particularly L1HS, and persisted among alignments with MAPQ 60. Realignment of
read-derived L1 segments to an L1HS copy panel revealed poor copy discrimination despite high MAPQ in the original
alignments. In a representative case, an apparent chromosome-arm L1HS–alpha junction was better explained by an L1
embedded within a centromeric array on another chromosome in the corresponding assembly. Among concordant events,
insertions in normal samples predominantly involved pre-existing alpha-satellite loci, including the euchromatic alpha-satellite
island at 2q21, whereas tumor samples also contained candidate alpha-satellite–arm rearrangements. These findings show
that high MAPQ does not guarantee accurate localization of alpha-satellite-associated junctions and highlight the value of
sample-specific assemblies for distinguishing variation at pre-existing alpha-satellite loci from candidate alpha-satellite–arm rearrangements.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia (SCZ), and bipolar disorder (BD) are highly heritable psychiatric
disorders with accumulating evidence for early developmental origins. While understanding the causal mechanisms is
critical, reliance on post-onset samples makes primary etiological factors hard to distinguish from secondary cellular
changes. To address this limitation, we mapped regulatory links among disease-associated variants, genes, and cellular
functions across excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, and glial cells at prenatal, pediatric, and adult stages,
generating context-specific landscapes of risk variant-gene-function axes. These risk axes comprised 11,946 variants,
342 genes, and 22 functions, converging on five broad categories: immune system, neural development, synaptic
function, gene expression, and cellular homeostasis. Function-level comparisons revealed prominent pre-onset disease
associations for SCZ risk axes in neurons and BD risk axes in glia, with more moderate associations for ASD risk axes
in neurons. By prioritizing variants based on predicted motif disruption and genomic element activity, we provided
mechanistic insights into how pre-onset variants may perturb cellular functions. Comparisons of pre-onset risk axes
across disorders can reveal shared etiological factors potentially contributing to comorbidity. Our framework provides
a foundation for identifying pre-onset biomarkers and therapeutic targets for ASD, SCZ, and BD, ultimately facilitating
earlier intervention strategies.

Federated genomic analysis keeps patient data local, but removes the coordinator's ability to confirm that each site
ran the agreed variant-calling pipeline. Existing methods validate that aggregate results approximate the centralized
setting; none verify per-site execution. Because processing choices change variant calls, divergence in thresholds,
versions or normalization propagates silently into pooled results.
We formalize per-site execution equivalence in a protocol where each site emits, per stage, three deterministic
summaries: a set-level structural digest, a canonicalized parameter digest, and a distributional sketch. A coordinator
detects divergence, attributes it, and localizes it to the first divergent stage; no raw data leaves a site. Set-level digests
make variant-presence queries impossible.
On synthetic three-site data the protocol flagged no clean replicate (0/30) and detected threshold and normalization
divergence (10/10 each), localizing each correctly with the expected cascade. It detected a non-conforming
configuration shared by all sites (10/10), invisible to consensus. A hidden offset behind agreed parameters was caught
only above a measured floor, and the distributional layer proved a coarse backstop.
What is new is the target rather than the primitive: per-site execution equivalence, verified from deterministic
summaries and localized to a stage. Limitations are honest-but-careless sites, a synthetic proof-of-concept, and
undefended forgery.

Background: Although long-read sequencing resolves many alignment ambiguities, short-read sequencing remains
widely used. We characterized misalignment-induced variant errors using assembly-derived simulated reads with
known ground-truth locations.
Methods: We simulated 30× whole-genome sequencing with error-free 150-bp paired-end reads for 232 normal
human genomes. Reads were classified as misaligned when their alignments did not overlap their ground-truth
locations. Variants were called using a conventional HaplotypeCaller pipeline. False-positive (FP) and false-negative
(FN) variants were defined by concordant classification across three reference callsets: PAV, dipcall, and
HaplotypeCaller calls from reads realigned to ground-truth locations. Cohort allele frequencies (AFs) were calculated
from the intersection of reference callsets.
Results: Misaligned-read regions and FP/FN counts were consistently greater in Africans. gnomAD AFs exceeded
cohort AFs for FP variants but were lower for FN variants. 22 FP and 13 FN variants were known pathogenic variants
or loss-of-function variants in genes with loss-of-function disease mechanisms. Among them, one FP occurred in a
dominant disease gene with non-benign gnomAD AF; five FP had gnomAD AFs >5% despite cohort AFs of 0,
receiving benign, conflicting, or incompletely penetrant pathogenic ClinVar interpretations; and nine FN were known
pathogenic variants.
Conclusion: Misalignment can systematically distort population AFs and obscure clinically relevant variants.

Flow-based whole-genome sequencing (WGS) using the Ultima Genomics (UG) platform enables scalable
genome-wide tumor profiling at reduced cost. However, while considerable effort has focused on somatic variant
calling and platform-specific sequencing errors, downstream frameworks for systematic interpretation of genome-wide
biomarkers remain insufficiently standardized. Here, we present a post-calling analytical framework extending
interpretation of Ultima Genomics WGS data beyond variant detection. The workflow integrates somatic SNV/indel,
copy-number, and structural variant data with functional and clinical annotation, followed by tumor mutational burden
(TMB), mutational signatures, microsatellite instability (MSI), chromosomal instability (CIN), and homologous
recombination deficiency (HRD) analyses. HRD was assessed using three independent methods, revealing substantial
discordance among classifiers due to differences in underlying genomic features and modeling approaches. To
address this variability, we developed a gastric cancer-specific consensus framework integrating scar-based, mutational
signature, and machine learning-derived evidence into a unified interpretation of HRD status. These findings highlight
HRD as a model-dependent biomarker requiring tumor-specific calibration and context-aware interpretation. Overall,
the proposed workflow provides a scalable approach for downstream interpretation of flow-based WGS, integrating
genome-wide biomarkers with clinically relevant annotation.

A key computational step in reference-based variant calling is distinguishing true genetic variants from sequencing
errors. Advanced tools and workflows have been developed to handle this by computational modelling of technical
errors from the sequencing machines. However, these recalibration workflows have largely been evaluated for human
data only and its exact applicability for non-human data remains unknown. Here, we conducted a systematic
evaluation of variant calling on human, rice, sheep, and chickpea data, and found that existing workflows introduce
unexpected statistical bias, thus leading to suboptimal variant calls for non-human data. To address this problem, we
present simple guidelines for constructing a “pseudo-”database (pseudoDB) of genetic variants as a scalable and
portable solution for recalibration and variant calling. With human data, our pseudoDB-based workflow performs
comparably to existing dbSNP-based GATK3 workflows and those using DeepVariant, Strelka2, and FreeBayes. We
extend this to other non-human genomes, namely cattle, brown bear, swan goose, African oil palm, Komodo dragon,
and stevia, altogether resulting in the identification of up to 242.0% unique genetic variants. The majority of newly
identified variants are within the non-coding regions, hinting at the rich diversity of genome regulation in the
non-human population. Our pseudoDB-based workflow is agnostic to reference genomes and modular for easy
integration with other computational workflows for human and non-human resequencing data.

Ribosome profiling has become a central tool for identifying open reading frames (ORFs) by enabling transcriptome￾ide, subcodon-resolution snapshots of active translation. However, existing computational tools struggle with the
statistical sparsity and variability of ribosome occupancy patterns and thus result in unreliable ORF discovery. Here, we
propose a non-parametric statistical framework that successfully controls the false discovery rate (FDR) by modeling
the codon periodicity in a data-dependent manner. By applying our method on ribosome-bound and matched mRNA
control experiments, we show that our p-value estimator achieves reliable statistical calibration. In fact, our method
leads to the identification of 3.11-fold greater number of high-confidence non-canonical ORFs than existing
computational tools. Further integrative analyses of mass spectrometry data confirm the de novo discovery of 4,105
ORFs of which 291 have not been previously annotated in UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot. Together, these results demonstrate
that our method accounts for the statistical bias and variation inherent in ribosome occupancy patterns, revealing the
complex regulation involving non-canonical start codons, internal ORFs, and alternative translation initiation.

Microsatellite markers are widely used in population genetics and ploidy assessment, but identifying highly
polymorphic loci remains labor-intensive. We developed an integrated genome-wide bioinformatics workflow
combining GMATA and HipSTR to discover and prioritize microsatellite markers from publicly available Pacific oyster
(Magallana gigas) genomic resources. A reference genome and eight whole-genome resequencing datasets were
processed for microsatellite discovery, read mapping, genotyping, and quality-based filtering. GMATA identified 56,132
candidate loci, of which HipSTR successfully genotyped 749. Subsequent filtering yielded 30 polymorphic candidates,
and 14 loci were experimentally validated in 96 diploid individuals from three South Korean populations. The markers
showed high amplification success, strong polymorphism, and low null-allele frequencies. Genotyping of 28 known
triploids achieved 100% triploidy detection, with selected loci identifying three-allele genotypes in up to 92.86% of

genotyping can efficiently identify robust markers for genetic analysis and ploidy verification, while also supporting
the potential of non-invasive eDNA-based genotyping in aquaculture.

In Korean rice breeding, cultivar evaluation increasingly requires integrated interpretation of agronomic performance,
pedigree relationships, and genomic marker evidence as breeding targets expand to stress resilience, disease
resistance, grain quality, and consumer-oriented traits. However, phenotypic, pedigree, genotype, and genome-wide
association study (GWAS) resources remain fragmented, limiting their direct use for cultivar evaluation and breeding
decisions. We developed RiceDBreeder, a web-based breeding informatics platform integrating curated phenotypic
data from 8,831 Korean rice variety records, digitized pedigree information for 843 cultivars, resequencing-derived
genotypes for 475 cultivars, and trait-associated markers from published GWAS resources. By matching GWAS Atlas
SNP coordinates with Korean cultivar VCF data and retaining loci carrying GWAS-reported minor alleles, RiceDBreeder
provides 3,670 GWAS-linked loci for trait-guided marker inspection. The platform supports phenotype-based
candidate filtering, pedigree-based cultivar selection, phenotype distribution profiling, and genotype comparison at
GWAS-linked loci. Example analyses show that predefined trait targets, including short and broad grain phenotypes,
can identify matching candidate materials and enable comparison of shared or group-specific allele patterns among
selected cultivars. RiceDBreeder provides a traceable phenotype–pedigree–genotype framework to support breeder￾irected candidate prioritization, parental line evaluation, and crossing-design planning in Korean rice improvement

Genomic prediction (GP) can accelerate genetic improvement in breeding programs, but prediction accuracy may be
limited when large SNP panels contain many markers with little relevance to the target trait. This study aimed to
identify optimal SNP pre-selection strategies for improving genomic prediction accuracy of morphological traits by
evaluating prediction performance using different SNP subsets and the full SNP panel. More than 200 individuals
genotyped with over 10,000 SNP markers were analyzed. Various SNP pre-selection approaches, including
GWAS-based and complementary marker selection methods, were evaluated to identify informative subsets of markers
associated with the target traits. Genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) models were constructed using the
full SNP panel and each selected subset, and prediction accuracy was evaluated by cross-validation. The SNP
pre-selection strategies optimized in this study may provide useful guidance for improving genomic prediction

sequencing, but the impact of PCR-derived heteroduplexes on UMI integrity remains poorly characterized. We

additionally analyzed public multi-strain amplicon and single-genotype transcriptome datasets. Among 2,585,624

and reverse single-strand consensus reads showed Hamming-distance peaks corresponding precisely to the 18-bp

Migraine and schizophrenia are complex neurogenetic disorders with heterogeneous, polygenic architecture that likely
reflects combination of rare high-impact variants, cumulative common-variants, and epigenetic modifications. Despite
extensive genome-wide association studies (GWASs), a substantial proportion of disease heritability remains
unexplained. While previous studies identified genetic causation for familial forms of migraine and schizophrenia, the
interplay between common and rare variants underlying the diseases has not been investigated. We aim to establish a
comprehensive analytical framework that jointly evaluates rare variant burden, GWAS-derived common variant
contributions, polygenic risk, and epigenetic signatures in a whole-exome sequencing (WES) cohort (N = 193)
comprising migraine cases, schizophrenia cases, and unaffected family members. WES data was processed following
GATK best-practices for germline variant calling. Rare variant prioritization identified shared variants across multiplex
families. Variant burden was analyzed using sequence kernel association test (SKAT) to identify gene-level associations.
GWAS-derived common variants were assessed, polygenic risk scores calculated using PLINK. Combining rare and
common variant analyses, this framework offers a scalable and generalizable approach to dissecting the layered
genetic architecture underlying complex neurogenetic diseases. Applying it to phenotypically distinct conditions but
overlapping mechanistic hypotheses may reveal contributory pathways, informing future strategies for risk
stratification, and functional prioritization.

Highly identical segmental genome duplications (SDs) contribute to disease and evolution within species. However, SD
comparisons to map traits that are associated with their variants between individuals remain limited by computational
costs. To address this, we developed an alignment-free method to identify SDs and trace their evolutionary
trajectories at the pangenome scale. Our method partitions genomes into overlapping sliding windows and generates
k-mer sketches to compute sequence similarity without alignment. In SD simulations on random sequences, our
method achieved an F1 score of 0.99 while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude and requiring 2% of the
memory used by existing SD profilers. By leveraging this efficiency, we applied our method to four plant pangenomes
totaling 95.26 Gb that have been challenging to profile with existing methods. Among them, 79.4% of grapevine and
78.7% of Arabidopsis thaliana SDs were fixed among strains or ecotypes. In contrast, 23.6% of tomato SDs and 1.8%
of rice SDs were fixed, indicating that fixation rates of SDs may vary across plant genomes. Our method profiles SD
dynamics and provides speed and accuracy for large-scale duplication identification in the era of high-quality
pangenomes.

Human DNA replication relies on multiple conserved DNA polymerases. While the contributions of the replicative
polymerases (Polα, Polδ and Polε) to bulk DNA synthesis are well established, the roles of other polymerases remain
less clear. Error-prone polymerases (e.g. Polη, Polκ and Polθ) are traditionally associated with DNA damage tolerance
and repair, where they provide flexibility at the cost of fidelity. However, accumulating evidence suggests that they
may contribute more broadly to genome replication.

sequencing (Pu-seq), which identifies the locations of ribonucleotides incorporated by polymerase mutants via
high-throughput sequencing. Under unperturbed conditions, Polη and Polκ both exhibit a lagging strand bias, with
evidence of partial functional redundancy. Strand-biased usage of Polη depends on PCNA and may reflect stochastic
competition between polymerases. Unlike Polκ, Pol η usage increases in late-replicating domains in a PCNA
ubiquitylation-dependent manner supporting variability in DNA polymerase usage as replication progresses. In cancer
genomes, characteristic Polη mutations are enriched in late-replicating regions and correlate with RAD18 expression,
consistent with an association between PCNA ubiquitylation and Polη-mediated mutagenesis. Building on these
findings, we are developing AI-assisted approaches to identify cancer-associated polymerase variants for functional
characterisation.

Low-coverage genotyping-by-sequencing (0.5–5×) underpins crop breeding but leaves 30–90% of genotypes missing.
