break Markov conditioning and major-allele bias erases the rare variants (MAF < 5%) critical for breeding. We present
QuImputer, which reformulates imputation as energy minimization over a linkage disequilibrium (LD) network: each
missing SNP becomes a qubit in an Ising Hamiltonian whose couplings encode LD strength and physical distance, and
the optimal allelic configuration is obtained by Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), optimizing
entire windows simultaneously. QuImputer complements rather than replaces HMMs as a local deep optimizer for rare
variants and high-missingness windows. In in-silico blind masking tests on 100 high-coverage rice (Oryza sativa)
accessions across all 12 chromosomes (2.22 billion genotypes), QuImputer exceeded Beagle 5.4 concordance at MAF 1
–5% (+0.40 pp) and 5–10% (+0.90 pp), consistently across chromosomes, a 30-combination parameter grid and five
masking seeds. On the IBM Fez 156-qubit Heron processor, imputation matched the classical exact solver perfectly
(concordance 1.0000) at 10–25 qubits, with fidelity governed by circuit depth rather than qubit count. QUBO-based
local optimization is therefore a practical route to rare-variant recovery on current quantum hardware.

Transposable element consensus sequences are usually built by clustering copies within a single reference genome.
This works for young, intact elements but fails for ancient, degraded repeats such as MER130, whose copies are
fragmented, diverged, and poorly captured by de novo models.
I developed an orthology-guided pipeline across 302 tetrapod RefSeq genomes (142 mammals, 84 archosaurs, 39
lepidosaurs, 22 amphibians, 15 turtles): nhmmer detection, gene anchoring (overlap/closest), syntenic gathering,
phylogeny-aware locus validation, and per-cluster ancestral reconstruction (locus extend + PRANK).
I identified 78,885 MER130 hits (28,665 genic; 49,997 intergenic), organized into 1,069 host-gene anchor groups and
1,213 orthologous locus clusters. Most anchors are lineage-restricted (median 4 species, 4 hits) and cannot be read as
tetrapod-wide shared ancestry. Fourteen loci each span ≥200 species as one cluster—ARHGAP15 and DGKB retain
hundreds of copies in ~270/302 species (~90%), indicating one ancient insertion still recognizable across amniotes. A
few neighborhoods record several independent insertions (e.g. KHDRBS2, three loci), separating true re-invasion from
fragmentation of a single copy. Together, these validated locus clusters yield ancestral MER130 sequences that are
more representative than single-genome consensus models and define which insertions are ancient and widely shared
versus lineage-restricted.

One-to-many global alignment is the problem of finding, over N target sequences, every target whose edit distance
to a query sequence is at most a threshold k, and it arises in many applications. Heuristic methods may miss the
optimal alignment, so applications that cannot tolerate misses require exactness. Repeating an exact pairwise aligner
takes time proportional to N, whereas existing methods that use a tree structure over the targets grow exponentially
with k.
I propose DT-Patricia, which runs a diagonal transition algorithm on a Patricia tree, so that the computation over
prefixes shared by several targets is performed only once, making the search exact and scalable in N. Here σ is the
alphabet size and M an upper bound of the number of target characters a search can reach. The search takes O(Nk2+
σNk+kM) time, so the running time is quadratic in the threshold, not exponential. DT-Patricia also supports affine gap
penalties, with the same complexity.
On synthetic DNA sets the running time grew more slowly than in proportion to N, so the advantage over per-target
alignment widened as the target set grew. Evaluation on real sequence data is in progress.

Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is a powerful molecular diagnostic technique that uses up to six
primers to amplify nucleic acid templates under constant temperature conditions. Unlike conventional PCR which relies
on a single primer pair, LAMP requires coordinated multi-site binding and formation of stem-loop structures under
isothermal conditions. While LAMP is ideal for rapid detection without sophisticated laboratory equipment, its
multi-primer thermodynamics and high mismatch tolerance make it prone to false-positive amplification when primer
design is suboptimal. To overcome these limitations, we present EasyLAMP, a machine learning-assisted platform that
captures high-dimensional, nonlinear dependencies among primer sequences, template context and experimental
conditions to predict fluorescence amplification curves and curve-derived performance metrics. The predictive model
is integrated with a curated primer database that collects fluorescence amplification curves and a user-friendly primer
design interface. We validated the scoring system, optimisation workflow and taxonomy-aware discrimination by
designing primer sets for pathogens of current global concern, including Bundibugyo ebolavirus, Andes hantavirus
and Nipah virus strains. By providing data-driven ranking of LAMP primer sets, EasyLAMP can accelerate assay
development for point-of-care diagnostics and outbreak preparedness.

Trace reconstruction is a central challenge in DNA data storage, where the original DNA strand is recovered from
multiple noisy reads affected by insertions, deletions, and substitutions. Existing methods often rely on restrictive error
models, sequential decoding, or locally defined consensus operations, limiting their ability to reconstruct sequences
under complex and heterogeneous noise. In this work, we introduce DART, a diffusion and autoregressive framework
for DNA trace reconstruction. Our approach represents reconstruction as the reversal of a discrete corruption process
conditioned on an unordered set of noisy reads. A diffusion-based component iteratively constructs a global
consensus representation, while an autoregressive refinement module models local dependencies and resolves
remaining sequence ambiguities. This combination enables the model to jointly exploit evidence across reads while
preserving dependencies along the reconstructed strand. We evaluate DART on synthetic sequencing channels and
real DNA storage datasets across a range of read coverages and error rates. The results show that DART consistently
achieves lower reconstruction error than existing alignment-based and deep-learning baselines, with particularly
strong improvements under low-coverage and high-error conditions. These findings demonstrate that combining
discrete diffusion with autoregressive refinement provides an effective and robust approach to trace reconstruction for
DNA data storage.

Recent advances in RNA–RNA interaction detection employ small-molecule crosslinkers, such as psoralen, to capture
proximal nucleotides. These experiments generate chimeric reads that map to two regions of a reference sequence.
Existing methods cluster these reads under the assumption that crosslinked nucleotides occur near the center of the
mapped read spans. However, our analysis of data from different RNA–RNA crosslinking protocols, including PARIS
and COMRADES, shows that the locations of known base pairs relative to the read spans vary between protocols and
can even lie outside the read spans. The existing clustering methods omit this protocol-induced bias. In this work, we
introduce BlockBluster2D, a computational method that clusters nearby chimeric reads into crosslinked regions, also
known as duplex groups, while preserving an estimate of base-pair interaction likelihood. Each read is modeled as a
two-dimensional probability distribution over potential base-pair locations and adjusted for protocol-specific
positional bias. This allows for density-based clustering using peaks in the total density function. These peaks within
duplex groups frequently align with known base pairs in evaluated reference structures. Thus, unlike binary
duplex-group representations, BlockBluster2D provides position-specific pairing probabilities that can serve as
weighted constraints for RNA structure prediction

Somatic mosaic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) arising during development are shared among the tissues
descended from the cell in which they arose, yet their low allele fractions make them hard to detect. Sequencing
multiple tissues from the same individual can recover such variants, but existing callers either analyze each sample
separately, missing signal spread across many samples, or pool the reads, diluting variants confined to a subset of
samples. Here we present MosaicSync, which uses variational inference to jointly genotype all samples from the same
individual. Because n samples define 4
n genotype configurations per site, MosaicSync discards sites at which a
germline genotype is most probable, ranks the remaining samples by their mosaic evidence, and admits only
configurations in which the top k carry the variant, reducing the space to n+1. Joint genotyping therefore scales
linearly with the number of samples. MosaicSync also estimates across all sites how many samples typically share a
mosaic variant and uses this distribution as a prior, rescuing variants too weak to call in any single sample. On a
synthetic cell-line-mixture exome standard and a real 27-tissue whole-genome dataset, MosaicSync detected
low-fraction variants that single-sample and read-pooling callers missed, held precision and recall together where
competing methods traded one for the other, and identified the carrying samples most accurately, with its advantage
greatest at the low allele fractions that dominate genuine tissue mosaicism. Multi-sample joint genotyping is therefore
an effective and computationally efficient strategy for characterizing mosaicism in normal tissues.

Accurate coding sequence prediction in short prokaryotic metagenomic sequences, such as Illumina reads, remains
challenging due to sequence fragmentation, unknown sequence origins, and sequencing errors.
Here we introduce DeepCDS, a deep learning-based \textit{ab initio} coding sequence predictor trained on short
prokaryotic sequences with and without simulated Illumina-like sequencing errors. DeepCDS integrates ESM-2 protein
language model embeddings with nucleotide-level information to predict complete and fragmented coding sequence
regions.
Benchmarking on 215 phylogenetically diverse prokaryotic organisms demonstrates that DeepCDS consistently
outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in coding sequence detection across sequence lengths from 75bp to
1000bp, including improved identification of both canonical and non-canonical start codons as well as stop codons,
and greater robustness to different sequencing error profiles. DeepCDS also remains operational on sequences shorter
than existing tools support. We additionally evaluate DeepCDS on a simulated metagenomic dataset from the Critical
Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation initiative, where it likewise achieves the strongest performance among
tested tools. These findings demonstrate that protein language models capture distinct signals relevant for
nucleotide-level coding sequence detection, especially at very short lengths. Ultimately, DeepCDS may help uncover
the functional potential of the vast microbial diversity that remains genomically uncharacterized. The DeepCDS 1.0
webserver is available at: https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/DeepCDS-1.0/.

Tandem repeat expansion disorders can be difficult to diagnose when expansions exceed 200 repeats, as standard
methods (for example, Southern blot and modified PCR) often fail. We present a Cas9-targeted nanopore sequencing
workflow and an automated analysis pipeline, RepeatLab, for accurate repeat-length estimation, structure assessment,
and high-resolution methylation profiling. Validated on 13 myotonic dystrophy type 1 samples, 4 healthy controls, and
4 cell lines, this approach demonstrates improved sensitivity and accuracy for large expansions. Key refinements
include an alternative basecalling strategy for extended repeats and a repeat-length calling algorithm that remains
robust at lower sequencing throughput. The platform also automatically reports methylation near the DMPK repeat
region, including five CpG site groups that could inform more nuanced clinical evaluations. This integrated workflow
offers a rapid, cost-effective diagnostic solution with a turnaround time under 24 h and costs comparable to standard
assays. Its compatibility with readily available computational resources enhances accessibility and scalability.
posters.P194:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by substantial genetic and neurobiological heterogeneity, yet the biological
pathways and functional brain circuits through which this heterogeneity emerges remain incompletely understood. In this
study, we aimed to dissect the polygenic risk of MDD at the biological pathway level and investigate whether pathway-based
polygenic risk scores (Pb-PRSs) are linked to MDD through alterations in resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC). Using UK
Biobank participants of European ancestry aged <65 years, we identified MDD-associated functional connectivity patterns and
defined disease-related biological pathways based on independent MDD genome-wide association study data.
Pb-PRSs were then constructed for each pathway and evaluated using mediation analysis. We observed alterations in circuits
involving the default mode network (DMN), hippocampus, and putamen, which have been repeatedly implicated in MDD,
including changes in DMN–hippocampus and DMN–putamen connectivity. Altered connectivity between the putamen and
visual regions was also identified, suggesting a potential role for striatal–visual circuitry in MDD. At the genetic level, MDD
risk was associated with diverse biological processes, including neurodevelopment and synaptic function, neuronal excitability,
immune processes, RNA regulation, and proteostasis. Several Pb-PRSs showed indirect associations with MDD through
specific functional connections, suggesting that distinct components of polygenic risk may contribute to disease susceptibility
through different functional brain circuits. These findings indicate that the polygenic architecture of MDD may be linked to
disease risk through multiple pathway-to-circuit mechanisms rather than a single neural pathway.
By integrating pathway-specific genetic risk, functional brain connectivity, and individual-level mediation profiles, this
framework also enables patient clustering to explore MDD archetypes that may reflect distinct genetic and neural circuit
mechanisms. Overall, this study provides an integrative framework for understanding the biological heterogeneity of MDD
and for supporting biologically informed patient stratification

Meiotic crossovers ensure accurate chromosome segregation and generate genomic diversity, but crossover number is
constrained to 1-3 per chromosome pair and distribution is shaped by chromatin accessibility and DNA
polymorphisms. Genome-wide crossover mapping in diploids has been enabled by short-read sequencing, but
polyploid studies have relied mainly on cytology. Here, we combined Illumina short-read and Nanopore long-read
sequencing to map high-resolution crossovers in progeny from Arabidopsis autotetraploid crosses, using SNP allele
frequency analysis of individual plants and SNP pattern analysis of long reads. Neo-autotetraploids were generated via
microRNA-induced silencing of OSD1. Crossovers per bivalent increased 27.7% in wild-type Col 4n × Ler 4n F2 versus
diploid Col 2n × Ler 2n F2, and 58.8% in recq4a recq4b (4n vs. 2n), showing polyploidization increases crossover
number, with a larger effect in recq4a recq4b. Neo- and established autotetraploids showed similar crossover
numbers, though Col 4n × Ler 4n had higher aneuploidy than Wa-1 × Col 4n. This approach enables precise
crossover mapping in polyploids, facilitating crossover evolution studies.
posters.P196:
Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentation patterns reflect cancer-associated alterations, but conventional
fragmentomic approaches typically rely on predefined features such as fragment length and end motifs. We evaluated
individual-level cancer detection using cfDNA fragment sequence embeddings from a pretrained DNA foundation
model.
We analyzed 1,496 individuals, including patients across five cancer types and healthy controls. Each fragment was
encoded into a 472-dimensional embedding using Caduceus. Performance was evaluated using stratified five-fold
cross-validation. For each embedding dimension, six summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, median
absolute deviation, and the 25th and 75th percentiles) were computed across fragments and concatenated into a
2,832-dimensional feature vector. A multilayer perceptron using these features achieved an AUROC of 0.892,
compared to 0.878 for a Set Transformer and 0.520 for max/min pooling, using 100,000 fragments per individual.
Increasing the number of fragments to 2 million improved the AUROC to 0.928. Linear discriminant analysis showed a
corresponding improvement, from 0.482 to 0.866. Discriminative power also increased with cancer stage (stage I:
0.785; stage IV: 0.908). These findings suggest that distributional summaries of cfDNA sequence embeddings capture
cancer-associated information and that increasing fragment input improves cancer detection performance.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) induce oxidative DNA damage, including the formation of 8-oxoguanine (8oG), a
mutagenic lesion resulting in G>T mutations via 8oG:A base pairing. To estimate regional oxidative genome damage
with 8oG modifications in whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, we extended and revised the global imbalance
value (GIV), which measures strand-biased imbalanced variants as a single value per sample and is therefore unable to
indicate where the damage occurs. Initially, the genome is partitioned into 50-bp blocks whose variant counts are
stored in compressed HDF5; Aggregated block reproduced G>T GIV values (mean R² = 0.99; n = 24) with reduced
runtime (>5-fold; n =13) compared with the conventional calculation, when applied to liver hepatocellular carcinoma
(LIHC) WGS data. To assess the biological relevance of the calculated regional G>T GIV values, we used oxidation
regions, identified by 8oG immunoprecipitation sequencing (8oG-IP), in WGS data from diethylnitrosamine
(DEN)-induced rat hepatocellular carcinoma models. After coverage and count filtering, 350-bp IP-enriched intervals
tended to show higher local GIV than non-enriched control intervals before tumorigenesis (P<0.007; one-sided
median-based permutation test). Then, we developed a deep learning model to predict oxidized genomic regions
from sequence embeddings, wherein adding local GIV features increased the Pearson correlation (from 0.31 to 0.53;
on chr20 with a 100-kbp span). Overall, our work presents a bioinformatics method to estimate regional oxidative
genome damage without performing 8oG-specific experiments. The resulting local metric may help discover
potentially important oxidative damage regions in ROS-induced diseases and their usage as prognostic biomarkers.

Sample mislabeling is a persistent quality-control challenge in next-generation sequencing (NGS) studies, yet existing
SNP-based tools are designed exclusively for human data, and comparable approaches are needed as NGS expands
across non-human organisms. We present a scalable framework extending SNP-based sample identification beyond
human studies. We surveyed species registered in the European Variation Archive and selected 16 spanning mammals,
birds, fish, insects, and plants. Reference SNP panels for each species were curated from public genotyping and variant
databases, then filtered and spatially binned. We assessed performance across panel sizes using permutation testing:
SNPs were resampled at random 100 times per size to test robustness to SNP selection. Most species achieved 99– 100% sensitivity and specificity with as few as 1,000–5,000 SNPs. In one public dataset, a sample pair showed only
~65% genotype concordance, far below the 90–98% of confirmed matches, suggesting an undetected mislabeling
event. We also found that some sample sets contain individuals too genetically similar to distinguish, such as inbred
or clonal lines, and developed a diagnostic metric flagging such cases without prior knowledge of true sample
identity. This framework enables robust sample identification across the growing multi-species NGS landscape,
underscoring the need for identity verification beyond human studies.
posters.P199:
Cell-free RNA (cfRNA) liquid biopsy inherently exhibits a low signal-to-noise ratio due to high background
compositional variance and technical variability stemming from pre-analytical and experimental factors. Our
comprehensive variance analyses across public datasets indicate that technical variations and batch effects consistently
exceed disease-related variance. Furthermore, conventional mean-based case-control comparisons often obscure
patient-specific signals due to the high intra-group heterogeneity of complex diseases. In small cohorts, this
heterogeneity renders group mean estimates unstable and highly dependent on cohort composition. To address these
structural limitations, we propose a normative modeling framework optimized for whole-transcriptome
sequencing-based cell-free messenger RNA (cf-mRNA) data. This approach constructs a conditional normative
distribution from a large-scale healthy control reference integrated across multiple public cohorts, utilizing
multidimensional technical bias metrics derived directly from the sample data as covariates. The model quantifies the
deviation of each gene in disease samples from this conditional distribution. Through 5-fold cross-validation, the
framework demonstrated statistical calibration on unseen healthy samples. Application to a pancreatic cancer cohort
successfully identified pancreas-specific and cancer-associated marker genes undetected by standard group-level
analyses. These results suggest that our framework mitigates population-level signal cancellation and enhances
disease signal detection in heterogeneous cfRNA data. Ultimately, this study provides an analytical alternative for
integrating diverse public datasets to discover patient-specific biomarker candidates.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron loss and
cytoplasmic aggregation of phosphorylated TDP-43 (pTDP-43). Most ALS cases occur sporadically, exhibit substantial genetic
and molecular heterogeneity, and lack clearly defined genetic contributors to pathogenesis. To investigate whether clonal
somatic mosaicism in motor neurons contributes to sporadic ALS (sALS), we performed whole-genome sequencing of
laser-captured motor cortex neurons with pTDP-43 aggregates from 26 patients with sALS, alongside pTDP-43
aggregation-negative neurons from 8 neurotypical controls. Integrative analysis of somatic mutations, transcriptomic profiles,
and clinicopathological features identified a distinct genomic subgroup of sALS, termed ALS-high (13 of 26 cases),
characterized by a significant increase in somatic single-nucleotide variants enriched for mutational signatures of oxidative
damage. These mutations were detected in both pTDP-43 aggregation-positive and -negative motor neurons, and their
features were consistent with a possible developmental origin. The ALS-high subgroup further corresponded to a known
molecular subtype of sALS with oxidative stress-associated transcriptomic profiles and exhibited more rapid progression of
pTDP-43 aggregation, suggesting that oxidative stress-induced somatic mutations arising during neuronal development
predispose motor cortex neurons to pTDP-43 pathology. Together, our findings indicate that clonal somatic mosaicism in
motor neurons may contribute to selective vulnerability to pTDP-43 pathology and underlie molecular heterogeneity in sALS.

Population-specific allele frequencies are essential for variant interpretation, but restricted access to Korean clinical
whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data has limited their reuse. We present the Korea Variant Archive (KVar), a public
resource within the Korea BioData Station (K-BDS) that shares cohort-level variant summaries while source reads
remain in the access-controlled Korea Sequence Read Archive (KRA). KVar links BioProject, BioSample, Study, Dataset,
and Variant records, assigns ks-prefixed identifiers, and cross-references human variants to dbSNP, dbVar, and ClinVar.
Users can search by coordinate, gene, rsID, or KVar identifier, download variant data, and compare Korean cohort
frequencies with gnomAD, KOVA II, and 61KJPN in an integrated genome browser. KVar includes 376 Korean
individuals across one normal and five disease cohorts and contains records spanning ten species. To illustrate its use,
we analyzed the normal cohort and four disease cohorts, totaling 369 individuals. Among disease-cohort alleles
passing a <1% threshold for available gnomAD and KOVA frequencies, we identified 3,119 high-confidence predicted
loss-of-function and 4,519 predicted damaging alleles; 222 and 85, respectively, matched ClinVar pathogenic or likely
pathogenic records. KVar makes Korean cohort variation discoverable and supports variant interpretation and
follow-up.

Reference-guided chromosome-scale assembly requires scaffolding and telomere checks, but manual inspection is
time-consuming and hard to interpret, and few lightweight tools automate these steps.
We developed two pure-Python tools. Synscaf uses GENESPACE synteny blocks to assign, orient, order and join draft
contigs onto reference chromosomes, and converts gene annotations to the new coordinates. Each run verifies that all
input sequences are preserved, and joining can be skipped when the karyotype is unknown. Synscaf-estimate predicts
cutoff effects from synteny blocks alone, avoiding repeated runs and guiding parameter choice. Teloviz draws tidk
telomeric-repeat windows as chromosome ideograms, calls telomere caps using user-set thresholds, flags short
contigs prone to false two-ended calls, and overlays rDNA arrays.
On a draft assembly of a dog breed, fully automated scaffolding retained BUSCO completeness comparable to manual
curation (95.1% vs 94.5%), with gene models carried through the coordinate conversion. Teloviz visualized tidk and
barrnap results, showing both telomeres capped on 29 of 39 chromosomes and rDNA arrays on three, consistent with
cytogenetic reports.
Requiring no additional sequencing data such as Hi-C, both tools are simple to run, record all parameters, and
produce publication-ready figures, enabling transparent and reproducible chromosome-scale assembly.

Telomere-to-telomere (T2T) references and long-read sequencing have improved variant discovery in repetitive
regions, yet their effect on genotyping short tandem repeats (STRs), a disease-associated variant class, has not been
systematically benchmarked. We genotyped STRs in three individuals with matched 150-bp paired-end short reads
(ExpansionHunter) and PacBio HiFi long reads (TRGT) against GRCh38, CHM13, and KOREF, a complete Korean
reference matching the individuals' ancestry. The GRCh38-curated TRExplorer catalog was lifted over to each
reference, yielding 4,705,577 tandem repeat loci, and genotypes differing by at most one repeat unit were considered
concordant. We compared genotypes from the same data across references and between platforms on the same
reference. Cross-reference concordance was high and differed only slightly: 97.785% between CHM13 and KOREF
versus 97.367% for pairs involving GRCh38. Short-read genotypes were more consistent across references than
long-read genotypes (97.755% vs. 97.258%), with short-read concordance highest between CHM13 and KOREF
(98.064%). In contrast, short- and long-read genotypes on the same reference agreed at below 90%, lowest on
GRCh38 (GRCh38, 86.982%; CHM13, 87.452%; KOREF, 87.584%). Thus, complete references only slightly improve
cross-reference consistency, short-read genotypes are slightly more robust to reference choice, and sequencing
platform and caller, rather than reference, account for most genotype discordance.

Therapeutic mRNA potency depends on sequence identity, transcript completeness, and poly(A) length. Each requires
monitoring from development through manufacturing, typically by separate assays. Nanopore direct RNA sequencing
(DRS) measures all three on the same molecules in one run. However, N¹-methylpseudouridine (m¹Ψ), the uridine
substitute in most therapeutic mRNAs, alters ionic current and translocation kinetics, biasing basecalling and poly(A)
estimation.
We present mRNAspect, a pipeline combining analysis alongside sequencing, a basecaller fine-tuned on six IVT
constructs with cDNA-IVT libraries to call m¹Ψ as U, and a poly(A) estimator that excludes positions with m¹Ψ at the
motor-protein site when estimating translocation rates for converting poly(A) dwell time into length.
Across four held-out m¹Ψ constructs, fine-tuning reduced median per-read error 2.2-fold (19.3% to 8.6%; unmodified
4.0%) and consensus mismatches 6.2-fold. For the worst-affected construct, median per-read reference coverage rose
from 91.7% to 99.0%, matching unmodified mRNA. Across all four, correction raised median poly(A) lengths from 91– 93% to 99.4–99.8% of template-encoded length. Each 3-min batch (~6,000 reads) took ~40 s on two RTX 2080 Ti.
mRNAspect makes DRS a real-time, single-assay readout of all three attributes for m¹Ψ-modified mRNA.

Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a central mediator of inflammatory and autoimmune disease, and peptides capable of inducing
IL-6 secretion play a dual role in both disease pathogenesis and therapeutic peptide design. Experimental
identification of IL-6-inducing peptides is low-throughput and resource-intensive, motivating computational prediction
approaches. However, existing machine learning (ML) predictors rely on a limited number of sequence encoders and
lack systematic feature selection, leaving much of the sequence-derived feature space unexplored. We proposed a ML
architecture that generated 4,353 features from 59 sequence encoders spanning compositional, physicochemical, and
structural properties. Then, a heuristic subset selection algorithm was applied to identify an optimal, non-redundant
70-feature subset. We developed seven ML classifiers, and the best-performing model, extremely randomized trees,
yielded an MCC of 0.621, an F1-score of 0.662, and accuracy of 0.927 on the independent test set. The model
outperforms state-of-the-art predictor, PredIL6, by 18.51% in MCC and 2.8% in accuracy. Feature importance analysis
further revealed that dipeptide deviation from expected mean features, particularly those involving leucine, serine, and
proline, are the strongest features for prediction. Our method offers improved predictive performance and biological
interpretability, supporting future discovery of immunomodulatory peptides and therapeutic development.

Oral mucosal diseases are traditionally classified as distinct clinical entities; however, whether they share a common
breakdown of tissue homeostasis remains unclear. Here, by integrating large-scale single-cell and spatial
transcriptomic data across inflammatory, premalignant, and malignant lesions, we establish a quantitative framework
for oral mucosal homeostasis. We define epithelial meta-program architectures and derive a single-sample epithelial
homeostasis index (seHIX) that captures coordinated shifts in program activity and contextual variability along a
continuous spectrum of disease severity. At single-cell resolution, we identify a state-agnostic baseline core that
anchors epithelial stability and develop a single-cell epithelial homeostasis index (scHIX) to quantify anchor loss.
Coupling epithelial deviation with immune–stromal remodeling reveals structured ecosystem axes that contextualize
pathological divergence. By integrating these layers, we construct a systemic homeostasis index (sysHIX) that stratifies
disease severity and generalizes across other stratified squamous epithelia. Together, our study reframes oral mucosal
disease as an ecosystem-level failure of homeostasis and provides a quantitative framework to interpret its progressive
destabilization.

Accurate identification of virulence factors (VFs) is essential for understanding bacterial pathogenicity and monitoring
pandemic strains. However, existing approaches provide limited insights into strains with highly dissimilar sequences
as they rely heavily on protein sequence representations, including handcrafted features and protein language model
embeddings. Here, we present VFTextSeq, a machine learning model framework that improves prediction performance
by leveraging distinct features from protein sequences, biological texts, and structure-aware homology search results.
The biological descriptions are retrieved from sequence search engines of InterProScan and MMseqs2, which provide
protein signatures and the least common ancestor information of a query protein from respective databases.
Structure-aware homology search with TEA-MMseqs2 enables the identification of distant homologs. With the
integrated representation of sequence, text description, and homology search, VFTextSeq demonstrates robust
generalization against sequences with low sequence similarity to training data. Our approach can be applied to other
protein-related downstream tasks since biological descriptions and provide affluent domain information beyond
protein sequence.

Metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs)-based approach is increasingly used in metagenomic sequencing for
antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. However, factors such as low species abundance, repetitive sequence
elements and mobile genetic elements inherently disrupt standard assembly and binning algorithms. Whether and to
what extend these factors cause the systematic loss of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) remain unqualified. Here,
we developed a systematic benchmarking framework to evaluate these blind spots across the MAG-based analytical
workflow. We designated blaKPC as a representing plasmid-borne ARG model for MAG-based AMR surveillance, based
on a global prevalence analysis. Using matched carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae metagenomes and
isolate-confirmed ground truth, we showed that MAG-based approaches suffer from a systematic ARG loss. Ablation
experiments revealed that every stage, including binning, post-binning refinement and MAG quality-control,
introduces technical biases, underscoring critical need for binning-independent strategies. To address this, we
established detection limits for binning-independent read- and contig-level approaches in a real-world AMR
surveillance scenario. Population-scale MAG-based and binning-independent strategies comparison indicated that this
blind spot extends to a broader range of ARGs, including blaCTX-M, sul2, and tet(A). These findings distinguish
biological rarity from technical artifacts, providing practical guidance and explicit detection thresholds for reliable
metagenomic ARG surveillance.

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitors, are central to
rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treatment, yet clinical responses remain heterogeneous. To identify baseline immune features
associated with DMARD response, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells
from patients with RA before clinically indicated treatment and integrated cell-state, gene-network, and in silico
perturbation analyses. Responders showed dominant type I IFN programs, with enrichment of interferon-classical
monocytes expressing interferon-stimulated genes such as SIGLEC1 and IFI6. In contrast, non-responders exhibited
type II IFN and TNF-linked inflammatory circuits involving MAIT and NK cells, consistent with persistent immune
activation. Co-expression networks also diverged, showing coherent myeloid networks in responders and convergent
lymphoid networks in non-responders, where IRF8 emerged as a hub associated with poor clinical improvement. In
silico perturbation suggested that SIGLEC1 helps sustain the responder-associated type I IFN monocyte program, as its
perturbation shifted cells toward a non-responder-like state. These findings indicate that type I versus type II
interferon engagement shapes baseline peripheral immune architecture associated with DMARD response, supporting
therapeutic stratification in RA.
posters.P210:
Designing a multi-epitope vaccine (MEV) means chaining a dozen mutually incompatible predictors by hand, which is
slow, error-prone and hard to reproduce.
MEVD integrates that workflow and exposes it as 23 Model Context Protocol tools, so an LLM agent can invoke any
single stage or an entire design from one call. Covered stages are T-cell (NetMHCpan-4.2/NetMHCIIpan-4.3, 27-allele
IEDB reference panels) and B-cell (BepiPred-3.0 with DiscoTope-3.0 on Boltz-2 models) epitope prediction,
allergenicity/toxicity filtering, clustering, population-coverage-driven selection, construct assembly, and physicochemical,
solubility and structural characterization. Each predictor runs in its own environment behind a host-wide job queue,
with cached, resumable runs fingerprinted by model-weight hashes.
This integration makes a design question answerable that manual workflows cannot reach: does epitope order matter?
MEVD optimizes within-class order by Bayesian optimization (BO), maximizing NetSolP-predicted solubility under a
usability floor. For a 317-aa SARS-CoV-2 spike construct (5+5+5 epitopes) we scored all 1,728,000 orders exhaustively:
the canonical order sat near the median (0.500) while the optimum reached 0.776. BO recovered that exact optimum
within 64 evaluations, 0.004% of the space, outperforming equal-budget random search on average at every budget.
Agent-drivable, reproducible MEV design yields constructs with markedly better predicted solubility, now awaiting
experimental test.

Autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed for bioinformatics analysis. However, it is still unclear whether
these agents reproduce the judgment of an analyst or only the mechanics of a pipeline. In this study, we added a viral
variant composition task to BioAgent Bench and adopted its evaluation framework, which combines deterministic
scoring against a ground truth derived from a human analysis with an LLM judge that examines the trace of the
agent. The task uses publicly available sequencing data of four commercial varicella zoster virus (VZV) vaccines. The
agent aligns human depleted reads to the parental Oka reference, reports SNVs across the whole genome for each
product, and quantifies 42 loci that are associated with attenuation. The prompt specifies the deliverables but does
not specify the method, so the choice of aligner, filtering criteria, and calling criteria is left to the agent. We
performed three replicate runs together with three perturbation conditions, which were an inflated prompt, the
addition of decoy reads, and a corrupted reference.
The agent completed the analysis in all of the runs. Reproducibility followed the extent to which the specification
reached. The 42 specified loci showed agreement across the runs, whereas discovery across the whole genome, which
was left open, diverged. Under the perturbation conditions, the agent responded appropriately to the two conditions
whose evidence was present in its workspace. It refused to produce any output from the decoy reads, and it
recovered an intact reference for the corrupted one. The condition that modified only the prompt left nothing that
could be inspected, and it was therefore not detectable. However, both conditions that produced deliverables showed
degradation at the specified loci without any indication from the agent. Detecting a compromised input and
recognizing the error in its own output therefore appear to be separate abilities.

The human gut virome is a ubiquitous and dynamic component of the intestinal microbiome with substantial impact
on human health. Although prior studies have reported virome-disease associations, findings remain fragmented
across cohorts due to inconsistent analytical methods and incomplete reference resources. Here, we present Human
Reference Gut Virome (HRGV), a comprehensive catalog comprising 857,289 high-confident viral genomes with ≥ 50%
completeness, representing 251,038 species-level viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) and expanding
species-level gut viral diversity by _57% relative to prior references. Viral binning-derived genomes, which account for
25.5% of the catalog, increased mean estimated completeness by ~60% compared with contig-level assemblies and
rescued ~850k sequences that failed contig-level QC. Using structure-informed alignment, we assigned functions to
~59% of 14.0 million nonredundant viral proteins derived from 542 million predicted coding sequences (CDS). HRGV
enabled host linkage for 91% of viral genomes by integrating sequence alignment and CRISPR spacer hits,
demonstrating that broad host ranges are common. Finally, leveraging HRGV, we characterized dynamics of gut
virome dysbiosis, host connectivity, and functional potential across over 30 human diseases. The disease-associated
viral genus markers effectively discriminated disease status with a mean AUROC of 0.745, and ~30 % of genus-level
markers were composed exclusively of binning-derived genomes, underscoring the pivotal role of viral binning for
discovering disease-associated viral signatures.

Host immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection give rise to a wide range of symptom severities, which in turn drive
changes in Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cell (PBMC) composition. However, due to variability across both individual
patients and infecting viral variants, key markers common to disease severity remain unclear.

in the Republic of Korea during 2021 (B.1.497, B.1.619.1, and Delta; n=196). We first examined how PBMC gene
expression changed with increasing symptom severity (mild, moderate, severe/critical), independent of variant. We
then stratified patients by severity and compared gene expression between variant pairs within each stratum to
identify variant-specific markers.

reduced expression of TNF/NF-κB and Type I interferon-related genes. Variant-specific differences were most
pronounced within the severe/critical stratum: B.1.619.1 showed reduced Type II interferon-related gene expression
relative to B.1.497 in late infection, while Delta showed reduced Type I interferon-related gene expression relative to
B.1.619.1 in early infection, both concentrated in key innate and cytotoxic immune populations.

severe COVID-19 symptoms. The variant-specific interferon signatures identified within the severe/critical stratum are
considered important markers for determining the replacement and spread of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants.

microbial changes underlying the transition from a healthy to a diseased state remain understudied, largely because
most previous studies focus on comparisons between patients with established IBD and healthy controls. This study

In our prior study, we generated extensive datasets of the SARS-CoV-2 translatome and transcriptome at early (0, 1, 2, and 4
hours) and late (12, 16, 24, and 36 hours) post-infection (hpi) time points in Calu-3 cells to examine temporal changes in
gene expression induced by viral infection. Our analyses revealed a previously unidentified translation initiation site located in
the leader sequence, termed TIS-L. Given that TIS-L is present in the 5ʹUTRs of all SARS-CoV-2 genomic and subgenomic

SARS-CoV-2 replication and could serve as a promising target for antiviral therapy, highlighting non-AUG translation initiation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in SARS-CoV-2.

Interactions between therapeutic antibodies and unintended proteins could raise safety concerns but knowing such
off-targets remains very difficult. Antibodies often recognize a protein through a combination of linear peptides
(conformational epitopes). Here we developed a structure-based computational workflow to extract potential
off-target proteins at the proteome scale and evaluated it using a known antibody–off-target pair.

membrane-associated and secreted proteins as off-target candidates. The structure of the antigenic region (epitope)
recognized by tralokinumab was obtained from the existing structure with IL-13 (PDBID: 5L6Y) and used as a structural
query. Candidate proteins were screened by TM-align to identify proteins with structurally similar region, followed by
filtering based on local structural consistency, solvent accessibility, and alignment coverage. The residue
correspondences were then refined, and the structural similarity of the resulting candidates was evaluated.

structural similarity to the reference epitope (RMSD 0.37 Å). Importantly, a reported off-target protein (IL-4) was

information for accurately narrowing down potential antibody off-targets.

Liver fibrosis in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development, yet
how fibrosis-related transcriptional states established in nonmalignant liver are represented in HCC remains unclear.
Prognostic studies in HCC have largely focused on prognostic signatures from tumor or adjacent liver tissue, but
cross-state continuity and prognostic relevance of fibrosis-associated transcriptional states are insufficiently
characterized. We adapted a systems modeling framework called Translatable Components Regression (TransComp-R),
initially developed for cross-species translation, to transfer an unsupervised transcriptional component basis learned
from nonmalignant CHB liver into independent HCC cohorts. Within the basis, the component most strongly
associated with fibrosis stage was defined as the fibrosis axis, while the full component set was used for penalized Cox
modeling of overall survival. The fibrosis axis was consistently elevated in tumors relative to adjacent liver across HCC
cohorts, whereas prognostic weights were distributed across other CHB-derived components rather than concentrated
on this axis. We identified that fibrosis-associated transcriptional continuity and prognostic risk in HCC are separable
within the CHB-derived basis. Cross-state translation may therefore provide a framework for tracing disease-associated
molecular variation across nonmalignant and malignant states, supporting interpretation of how such variation relates
to HCC progression.

Background: Being in an intensive care unit (ICU) reflects both patient need and hospital resource allocation, such as
beds, treatment instruments and human resources. A model trained on ICU transfer therefore learns an allocation
process as well as a clinical one. We aimed to compare mortality across care settings on a common critical care need
scale.
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 17,737 bacteremia admissions at two Korean tertiary hospitals (2013–2024).
Critical care need was defined as any of four events requiring ICU-level care within 72 hours. We developed a
missingness-aware recurrent neural network that calculates a daily need score from the preceding 24 hours of vital
signs and laboratory results.
Results: The model achieved an AUROC of 0.93 on a held-out test set. The proportion of daily assessments made in
an ICU rose with the need score: 3%, 39% and 81% at scores 0.00–0.20, 0.20–0.50 and 0.50–1.00. At comparable
scores, 72-hour mortality was higher on general wards than in ICUs: 8.9% versus 3.2% at 0.20–0.50, and 31.6% versus
7.3% at 0.50–1.00.
Conclusions: At comparable predicted need, mortality was substantially higher on general wards than in ICUs. A
need-based score, rather than one trained on ICU transfer, may help identify ward patients who require ICU-level care.

Background: Peripheral immune changes associated with herbal treatment and clinical response in Long COVID
remain poorly understood. We investigated longitudinal immune remodeling in patients receiving three herbal
interventions.
Methods: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on 80 peripheral-blood samples collected from patients with
Long COVID at baseline, Month 3, or Month 6, together with two healthy-control samples. After quality control,
318,044 singlet cells were retained. Raw UMI counts were aggregated by participant, timepoint, and cell type and
analyzed using REBEL mixed-effects models and Hallmark pathway enrichment.

interferon-related programs. BIT showed few significant changes, whereas CBD demonstrated broader inflammatory,
interferon, metabolic, and cytokine-signaling enrichment, particularly in monocytes. KOG responders showed relative
attenuation of inflammatory and interferon programs compared with nonresponders. KOG-associated transcriptional
remodeling continued through Month 6. RORB and MZF1-AS1 were the two gene-level findings that remained
significant after false-discovery-rate correction.

KOG was associated with attenuation of persistent inflammatory and interferon signaling, while CBD showed broader
monocyte-centered immune activation.

Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is a major driver of chronic liver disease mortality. Particularly in Asian patients, where vertical
transmission is the primary route of infection, a robust state of immune tolerance is established. Consequently, current
nucleotide analogue-based treatments can merely suppress viral replication without eradicating virus-infected hepatocytes
(vHEPs), a limitation directly connected to insufficient immune activation. Clinically, this challenge is most profound in “Grey
Zone” patients, who exhibit a striking biochemical dissociation characterized by persistenty minor liver damage despite
maintaining high viral loads. To decode these elusive immunopathologies, we mapped the sub-cellular spatial transcriptomic
landscape of the hepatic microenvironment utilizing the Xenium platform with a custom viral transcript panel.
By conducting in situ transcriptomic profiling of CHB liver tissue, we divided Grey Zone patients into an Immune Tolerant (IT)
cohort (high viral load, minimal liver damage) and an Indeterminate Phase (IP) cohort. Pseudobulk differentially expressed
gene (DEG) analysis revealed a robust upregulation of Interferon Stimulated Genes (ISGs) in the Active cohort compared to
the Normal group. Interestingly, the IT cohort also exhibited a partial upregulation of ISGs. Subsequent gene-set scoring with
ISG signatures clearly distinguished these responses. While type I ISG signatures were upregulated in both Active and IT
cohorts, the type II ISG signature was significantly suppressed exclusively in IT patients. Similarly, TCR activation signatures were markedly downregulated in the IT cohort. This result suggests that although IT hepatocytes successfully detect the virus,
the subsequent adaptive immune activation is actively inhibited. Spatial neighborhood analysis surrounding vHEPs further
highlighted this functional divergence. In the Active cohort, cells neighboring vHEPs exhibited significant upregulation of
pathways related to apoptosis and type II ISG, reflecting the active immune-mediated clearance of infected cells. Conversely,
the IT cohort showed an upregulation of lipid metabolic pathways within these specific neighborhoods, indicating active viral
propagation into adjacent uninfected hepatocytes without triggering cell death. Finally, spatial niche analysis identified an
immune-infiltrated hepatocyte niche, which was significantly increased in the Active cohort. This confirms that robust T
cell-mediated clearance occurs exclusively in the Active phase.
In conclusion, we redefines the Immune Tolerant (IT) phase within the CHB "Grey Zone" not merely as a passive
immunological ignorance, but as an actively maintained, spatially organized microenvironmental failure. While the Active
phase is characterized by the robust formation of immune-infiltrated necroinflammatory niches driven by type II ISG
signatures and T cell-mediated apoptosis, IT hepatocytes actively subvert this clearance by halting the adaptive immune
cascade and exploiting localized lipid metabolic pathways. These sub-cellular spatial blueprints resolve the clinical paradox of
high viremia without overt liver damage, providing precise, niche-targeted immunological insights that serve as a critical
foundation for early intervention and functionally curative strategies in Indeterminate CHB patients.

Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) enables comprehensive characterization of somatic alterations and genomic
biomarkers, but integrated interpretation remains challenging because clinically relevant evidence is distributed across
heterogeneous bioinformatics tools and output formats. We developed an automated tumor-normal WGS
interpretation and reporting pipeline for precision oncology using Ultima UG100 data.
Starting from post-alignment files, the workflow integrates somatic SNV/InDel calling, copy-number alteration analysis,
structural variant and fusion interpretation, microsatellite instability, homologous recombination deficiency, tumor
mutational burden, mutational signature profiling, and genome-wide visualization. Somatic alterations are annotated
using curated oncology knowledge bases with tumor-type-specific and pan-cancer therapeutic evidence, while
module-level outputs are standardized into a unified data structure.

relevant alterations, driver events, genomic instability metrics, mutational signatures, and genome-wide alteration
patterns. To date, it has been applied to approximately 130 patients with stage III–IV cancers from five participating
hospitals within a nationwide multicenter precision oncology study involving 14 medical institutions. By integrating
multi-class genomic analysis, knowledge-based therapeutic annotation, standardized data integration, and automated
reporting within a single workflow, the pipeline enables consistent and scalable tumor-normal WGS interpretation for
precision oncology research.

Peripheral immune composition varies substantially across individuals, yet the extent to which age and sex contribute
to this variation in Asian populations remains incompletely defined. To characterize these demographic effects at
single-cell resolution, we analyzed version 2 of the Asian Immune Diversity Atlas. The Indian cohort was excluded
because of its limited age range, resulting in a final dataset of approximately 1.12 million peripheral blood
mononuclear cells from 589 healthy individuals representing four Asian countries.
We assessed variation in both major immune-cell populations and their constituent subtypes across age and sex.
Age-associated differences were considerably more evident at the subtype level than at the major-cell-type level,
suggesting that broad immune-cell classifications can mask substantial within-lineage remodeling. This pattern was
particularly prominent in T-cell populations. Increasing age was associated with a progressive reduction in naïve T-cell
subsets together with an expansion of memory- and effector-like populations, with the strongest redistribution
observed within the CD8+ T-cell compartment.
Sex was also associated with distinct immune-cell composition. Females showed relatively higher proportions of B cells
and CD4+ T cells, whereas NK cells were more abundant in males. In contrast, the overall proportion of CD8+ T cells
showed comparatively limited differences between sexes. These patterns indicate that age and sex influence peripheral
immune composition through partially distinct and cell-type-dependent processes.
Together, our findings provide a single-cell reference of demographic variation in peripheral immune composition
across Asian populations. In particular, the pronounced age-associated changes observed at the subtype level
highlight the importance of resolving immune populations beyond broad lineage classifications when evaluating
physiological immune variation and disease-associated immune alterations.

Immunosenescence, the age-related decline in immune function, is characterized by changes in immune-cell
composition and protein expression, which can reduce vaccine responses and increase disease susceptibility. Because
immune aging varies substantially among individuals of the same chronological age, accurately estimating immune
age may provide a more informative measure of immune-system status. However, previous approaches have largely
relied on sample-level summary statistics, such as cell-type proportions or mean protein expression, potentially
overlooking heterogeneous age-related cellular states within individual immune-cell population.
To address these limitations, we propose FAGE, a deep learning model for predicting immune age from CyTOF
profiles. We curated 182.8 million cells from 560 healthy samples across nine ImmPort studies. FAGE encodes
protein-expression profiles of individual cells, groups phenotypically similar cells using vector quantization, and
aggregates cell-group representations using a Transformer to generate a sample-level embedding for age prediction.
FAGE achieved a mean absolute error of 6.78 years, representing a 7.8% improvement over a baseline model.
Moreover, integrated gradients and attention score analyses identified naïve T cell populations as major contributors
to age prediction. These results demonstrate that FAGE captures interpretable, cell-level patterns of immune aging
while enabling accurate estimation of individual immune age from CyTOF data.

Proteins mediate nearly all biological processes, and their functional efficacy—collectively defined as fitness—is
intricately tied to their three-dimensional structure. Optimizing fitness, which encompasses vital properties like
thermostability, is crucial in therapeutic development to improve solubility and clinical efficacy. While single-mutation
effects are well characterized, combinatorial variants introduce extreme complexity due to non-additive epistatic
interactions, complicating rational design.

space, our research couples a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with Bayesian Optimization (BO). The VAE embeds

the empirical burden inherent to protein engineering, providing a scalable, data-driven strategy for the targeted
discovery of novel protein architectures.

prediction engine for genome-scale metabolic modeling, for prioritizing enzyme candidates in pathway design, and
for scoring directed evolution candidates.

All-atom co-folding models such as AlphaFold3, Chai-1, Boltz-1/2, Protenix, and RoseTTAFold-All-Atom have rapidly
become central to AI-driven structural biology, promising to replace classical docking for structure-based molecular
design. Yet across 2025-2026, independent benchmark studies (including large-scale, low-homology evaluations) have
converged on a troubling pattern: high leaderboard accuracy that collapses once test cases are decoupled from
training data, raising doubts about real-world design utility. We conducted a structured synthesis of co-folding
benchmark literature (2024-2026), cross-mapping evaluation dimensions - training overlap and memorization,
binding-pocket similarity, ligand novelty, physical plausibility, and affinity calibration - against reported outcomes
across five major models and four independent benchmark efforts. The synthesis reveals convergent, independently
replicated evidence of memorization-driven overfitting, a four-mode taxonomy of generalization failure (data leakage,
pocket-similarity dependence, physics violations, affinity miscalibration), and an evidence map identifying which
molecular-design contexts - de novo ligands, allosteric and cryptic sites, antibody interfaces, low-homology targets - are least trustworthy today. We propose a practitioner-facing co-folding trust framework for pairing specific design
tasks with the current evidence base, and flag priority benchmarking gaps for the next generation of models entering
AI-driven structural biology and drug-design pipelines.

Glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) is a validated target in tauopathy and Alzheimer's disease, but blood-brain
barrier (BBB) constraints drive high attrition in central nervous system (CNS) drug development, and CADD pipelines
for CNS kinases rely on a single pharmacophore from one co-crystallized complex, limiting chemical diversity. To
reduce this bias, we applied a multi-chemotype pharmacophore intersection strategy: forty GSK-3β inhibitors (IC50 <
1,000 nM) from BindingDB were clustered by Tanimoto similarity (≥ 0.80) into four chemotypes, each yielding an
independent pharmacophore; compounds satisfying all hypotheses were retained and compared against a
single-hypothesis control (most potent inhibitor). Both screens used a 52,760-compound BBB-permeable library,
followed by docking, a pose-consistency filter, 100-ns MD simulation, and MM-GBSA decomposition benchmarked
against AR-A014418 (1Q5K). Individual hypotheses retrieved between 0 and 19,653 compounds; intersection screening
retained 506 compounds, reduced to 447 after property filtering, versus 27/28 control hits. Pose-consistency filtering
yielded 26 intersection and 2 control compounds above the reference score. Across 100 ns of MD, 8
intersection-derived compounds remained stable (RMSD < 3 Å), whereas the control compound drifted to 7.72 Å;
docking score and stability were uncorrelated (r = -0.139, p = 0.51). ZINC08790378 and ZINC12883218 satisfied all
criteria and are proposed as leading candidates.

Protein-protein interactions are central to understanding biological processes. Predicting interaction partners is
extremely valuable for avoiding costly, time-consuming experiments. AlphaFold has shown an unsurpassed ability to
predict protein-protein interactions accurately. However, a protein can also form homomeric interactions, i.e. interact
with itself. When identifying homodimers, AlphaFold yielded a significantly higher false-positive rate than when
identifying heterodimers. True Positive Rate (TPR) at 1% False Positive Rate (FPR) drops from 81% for heterodimers to
22% for homodimers. When we investigated the high-scoring false positives, i.e., non-homodimers with high
AlphaFold scores that were predicted as such, we found that their homologs were enriched for homomultimeric
proteins, indicating that stoichiometry is not always conserved among homologs. We split our dataset into a training
and test set and with a simple logistic regression model that combines AlphaFold scores with stoichiometry
information among homologs and interface features from the predicted structures. This logistic regression model was
able to increase the performance on the test set from 27% TPR (at 1% FPR) to 36%. Without homology stoichiometry
information, no improvement was seen. The higher number of high-scoring false predictions for homodimers indicates
that homodimer prediction still has significant room for improvement.

Conventional differential expression (DE) methods model sampling variability and mean–variance dependence but do not
explicitly consider where an observed expression change occurs within the normal expression range of each gene. Because
genes differ substantially in their baseline expression distributions and regulatory ranges, identical absolute or fold changes
may represent different levels of biological perturbation. We hypothesized that gene-specific expression distributions across normal biological contexts encode an effective expression range associated with gene-specific regulatory and functional
constraints.
We developed the Effective Expression Index (EEI), which maps observed expression to its relative position within a gene-specific reference distribution. Reference distributions were constructed from 33k normal bulk transcriptomes collected
from GTEx and ARCHS4. To reduce study-specific variation while preserving biological structure, expression profiles were
integrated using a dual-latent adversarial autoencoder that separates biological and batch-associated representations. Each
gene was then modeled using a zero-inflated Gamma or Gamma-mixture distribution with a data-driven expression threshold.
EEI is derived from the resulting gene-specific cumulative distribution, such that an equivalent change in expression can produce different EEI shifts depending on its position within the gene's reference distribution.
We evaluated whether gene-specific distributional properties were associated with gene function and whether EEI improved
differential expression analysis. Benchmark analyses assessed false-positive control, recovery of known transcription factor–
target relationships in genetic perturbation datasets, and reproducibility of consensus differentially expressed genes across
independent batches or datasets. These analyses tested whether EEI can distinguish expression changes that are numerically
large from those that are large relative to the normal expression range of the corresponding gene.
EEI provides a gene-specific reference framework for transcriptomic comparison by incorporating the endogenous expression
range of each gene into differential analysis. This formulation complements conventional count-based statistical models and
enables expression changes to be interpreted relative to gene-specific reference distributions.

Protein–metal ion interactions are essential for enzymatic catalysis, molecular regulation, and protein stability. However,
available structures of metal ion-binding sites are highly imbalanced across ion types, limiting the sensitivity of structure-based
prediction methods, particularly for rare metal ions. This study developed ion-specific unconditional diffusion models to
reconstruct protein–metal ion-binding microenvironments and establish a foundation for generating new structural
representations. From non-redundant X-ray crystal structures in the Protein Data Bank (clustered at 30% sequence identity
using CD-HIT), metal-binding templates were curated across 18 metal ion types, defined by having at least two coordinating
residues (via O, N, or S atoms) within 3.5 Å of the metal ion. Each sample comprised four coordinating entities containing 2–4
interacting amino acids, with vacant positions represented by coordinating water molecules, parameterized by 164 spatial and
physicochemical features. Specifically, these features define the local coordination frame using unit vectors of backbone atoms
(C , N, and C) and the metal-interacting atom, pairwise interatomic distances, and key inter-vector angles, including vectors
from C to the metal ion and the C atom, alongside interaction types (backbone, side-chain, or water-mediated) and
physicochemical descriptors of amino-acid. Separate diffusion models were trained for each metal ion using five-fold
cross-validation. Out-of-fold reconstruction ensured rigorous evaluation on unseen data across structural geometry, amino-acid
identity, and interaction class. Across the 18 ion-specific datasets, the mean structural RMSD remained between 0.96 and 1.51
Å, with mean angular errors ranging from 4.9° to 16.2°, demonstrating that reconstructed geometries preserved local
orientations of coordinating atoms. Furthermore, the models accurately recovered binding chemistry, achieving an overall exact
amino-acid–interaction pair accuracy of 87.1% (macro-averaged accuracies of 89.3% for amino acids and 95.5% for interaction
types; recalls of 93.9% for backbone, 99.9% for side-chain, and >99.9% for water-mediated interactions). These findings
demonstrate that diffusion models can robustly capture both the geometric coordination and biochemical characteristics of
metal-binding microenvironments, providing a principled approach to augment underrepresented structural templates.

Enzyme discovery sometimes involves reactions whose products have not been identified. For recalcitrant substrates,
incomplete product information can make it difficult to identify enzymes that may contribute to their degradation. To
assess enzyme–substrate pairs in this setting, we developed a classifier using protein sequences and substrate SMILES
without requiring product information.After substrate SMILES annotation and removal of duplicate pairs and exact
train–test pair overlaps, the dataset comprised 2,056,290 training pairs (1,027,911 positive and 1,028,379 negative) and
228,228 held-out test pairs (113,918 positive and 114,310 negative). Across these sets, it represented 321,184 unique
proteins and 12,678 unique substrates. The model integrated ESMC-600M protein representations and IBM
MoLFormer-XL substrate representations using bidirectional cross-attention blocks. 4-fold cross-validation grouped by
protein determined the model checkpoints. Test predictions from the four models were averaged.The test set
contained no exact EC numbers present in the training set. The ensemble achieved an AUROC of 0.8825, precision of
0.9508, recall of 0.5092, and an F1 score of 0.6632. The lower recall indicate a need to improve model performance.
Comparisons with published methods, including EZSpecificity, are ongoing.

Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) are essential for understanding biological processes and developing therapeutics. Recent
PPI prediction models have increasingly leveraged sequence-based protein representation models to jointly encode paired
protein chains. Existing approaches either depend on paired multiple sequence alignments and full structure prediction, as in
AlphaFold-Multimer, or compress each protein into a single pooled embedding before any interaction is modeled, leaving no mechanism to actively search two sequences for the residues that form their interface. We address this with a small set of
learnable queries that act as interaction probes, attending to both frozen protein language model embeddings and distilling
the interface into a compact, length-independent representation, inspired by a lightweight querying transformer.
We introduce LQ-PPI (Learnable Queries for PPI), a lightweight transformer built on learnable queries that is specifically
designed to capture interaction signals within protein complexes. In LQ-PPI, the learnable queries iteratively attend to the
residue embeddings of both proteins, regardless of sequence length, and distill their interaction signals into a fixed-size latent
space. This design substantially reduces the number of trainable parameters while allowing the model to focus its capacity on
inter-protein interactions.
Trained and evaluated on a strictly partitioned split designed to prevent data leakage between training and test proteins,
LQ-PPI achieved an accuracy of 76.77% on binary contact classification. Moreover, without generating any 3D structure and
using only MLP heads, LQ-PPI achieved a distance-based lDDT (dLDDT) of 0.7176 and an accuracy of 24.64% in classifying
contact residues.
These results suggest that the learnable queries of LQ-PPI can extract interaction-relevant information from frozen protein
language model embeddings, highlighting their potential as general-purpose interaction representations for diverse
downstream tasks.

RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is the most conserved enzyme in RNA-virus replication and a proven antiviral target,
yet most inhibitors act at its catalytic centre, which is highly susceptible to resistance mutations. Conserved pockets
distal to the active site could enable allosteric inhibition with a higher barrier to escape, but whether such sites exist
across the Coronaviridae, and whether they can be engaged, has not been established.
Here, we identify a putative conserved allosteric pocket in the Coronaviridae polymerase and design de novo binders
against it. Palmcore sequences from PalmDB were matched to nsp12 references by MMseqs2 and modelled with
ColabFold; conservation mapping and consensus pocket detection across 72 palmcore and 39 nsp12 models yielded
seven pockets, from which we targeted the most solvent-exposed site. Of ~4,100 binders generated with
Proteina-Complexa, 80 structurally distinct designs survived filtering for full-length steric compatibility, pocket
engagement and fold diversity; five were confirmed independently by ESMFold2 and Protenix v2, achieving a high
ipSAE interface score of 0.87. Unconstrained generation could not reach this site, suggesting a cryptic pocket.
These designs will be tested experimentally for whether this pan-Coronaviridae pocket allosterically modulates
polymerase activity, providing a conservation-guided targeting approach to other RNA-virus polymerases.

Antigen-antibody interactions mediate specific immune responses. A mimotope is a peptide that mimics the
conformation of an epitope—the specific region of a protein that interacts with antibodies or T-cell receptors. In
particular, designing mimotopes that bind to the CDRs of a monoclonal antibody (mAb) can facilitate the
development of novel antigens. These antigens may elicit high-affinity antibodies upon immunization, potentially
reducing costs and enhancing efficacy compared to the passive administration of expensive mAbs. Despite the
emergence of AI-based algorithms for protein binder design, success rates of mimotope designs remain limited due
to intrinsic structural diversity. Cyclic peptides can serve as a promising design strategy by preserving target specificity
while enhancing structural stability through conformational constraint. Here we present MimoPrism, a computational
pipeline for cyclic mimotope design and in silico evaluation for candidate selection to carry out empirical screening
and validation. Using a target structure of peptide-mAb complex as one-shot input, MimoPrism generates de novo
mimotopes by leveraging multiple generative AI models, including RFpeptide and CyclicMPNN. We tested MimoPrism
with malaria CSP-mAb complexes (e.g. Fab311 and L9). Final candidates were selected using a scoring function
encoding diverse parameters encompassing physicochemical properties, CDR interactions, and structure prediction
scores from ESMFold2 and AlphaFold3.

Thermodynamic RNA folding provides the objective function for mRNA design and inverse folding, which evaluate
millions of candidate sequences, and the central step of structure-probing analysis. Its O(N³) cost has forced a choice
between exact tools too slow to call repeateldy and the linear-time LinearFold and LinearPartition, whose beam
searching let approximate energy evaluations. Here we present GARFold, a GPU program in Triton and Python that
runs the complete folding recursions with wavefront parallelism, efficient memory access, and dynamic batching. In
optimized batch, GARFold accelerates minimum free energy and partition function calculations by 81–201-fold and
104–355-fold over a single CPU thread of ViennaRNA RNAfold, reproduces ViennaRNA results within floating-point
precision, and outpaces LinearFold and LinearPartition at every tested length (16–4,096 nt). As the folding engine of
three published pipelines, GARFold completed RiboTree codon optimization 8.5–39.9-fold faster with lower average
unpaired probability than LinearPartition, finished DesiRNA designs of 3,700 nt that overflow in ViennaRNA, and
folded SHAPE-constrained human transcripts in 28 minutes on an RTX 4080, 2.5-fold faster than ViennaRNA on a
96-thread server. Folding on a single desktop GPU brings transcriptome-scale RNA design within reach of more
laboratories and could speed the development of personalized mRNA vaccines and RNA therapeutics.

Background: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen responsible for infections ranging from mild skin
infections to severe, life-threatening disease. Increasing antimicrobial resistance underscores the need for new
therapeutic and preventive strategies. A better understanding of how S. aureus adapts to different host environments
during early infection may reveal novel pathogenic mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
Methods: We investigated human- and rodent-adapted S. aureus strains in a murine infection model across different
anatomical sites. In vivo bacterial whole-transcriptome sequencing was combined with profiling of the host immune
response to characterize bacterial adaptation and identify physiological pathways associated with infection.
Results: Overall transcriptional responses were substantially conserved across strains and tissue types, although
important differences in virulence mechanisms were observed. Central carbohydrate metabolism, oxidative
phosphorylation, and protein synthesis were reduced, suggesting a shift away from growth-oriented processes during
infection. In contrast, siderophore biosynthesis and metal-ion transport were strongly upregulated, indicating
increased nutrient acquisition under host-imposed limitations. Multiple virulence factors were also upregulated in
tissue- and strain-dependent patterns.
Conclusions: These findings provide insight into the adaptive and pathogenic strategies employed by S. aureus during
early infection. The identified metabolic and virulence-associated pathways provide candidates for further investigation
and may reveal novel therapeutic targets. Future work will focus on defining strain- and tissue-specific responses and
identifying previously uncharacterized virulence factors.

Accurate identification of cell-cycle phases is essential for understanding cell proliferation programs, such as
tumorigenesis, and cellular senescence. However, the limited gold-standard data, the low transcriptomic activity in G0
cells, and technical sparsity in single-cell and spatial assays collectively hamper the accuracy of existing tools. Here, we
developed TranSCycle, which employs Transformer-based framework for cell-cycle identification in scRNA-seq and
spatial transcriptomics. Leveraging 856 gold-standard cells, TranSCycle simulated 43,304 cells along the cell-cycle
pseudotime to train a robust predictive model. Extensive benchmarks revealed that TranSCycle outperformed existing
methods (e.g. Seurat and Revelio) across diverse datasets, achieving 99.6% accuracy in detecting cell-cycle phases. In
scRNA-seq, TranSCycle revealed that 99.6% of doxorubicin-induced cells were in G0 phase, and KRAS inhibition
increased the proportion of G0 cells. In spatial transcriptomics, TranSCycle constructed a pan-cancer spatial
transcriptomic atlas from various cancer types, uncovering the border-enriched G0 cells which forms a senescent
barrier. In hepatocellular carcinoma CAR-T therapy dataset, TranSCycle identified G0-mediated resistance to CAR-T
therapy. These findings highlight the efficient performance of TranSCycle in cell-cycle detection and its broad
applicability for downstream cell proliferation and senescence analyses.

cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) states, yet the signaling axis linking inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs), malignant epithelial
cells, and myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) remains poorly resolved. We integrated three public single-cell RNA
sequencing datasets (GSE154778, GSE155698, GSE205013; 189,238 quality-controlled cells, 41 PDAC patients) using
