Cancers cells show phenotypic heterogeneity, with differences between and within genomic subpopulations (subclones) of cancer cells arising due to a combination of genomics, epigenomics and microenvironmental stimuli. However, there exist no systematic investigations into the transcriptomic similarities within and between genomic subclones and any potential
transcriptomic subpopulations therein. We analysed multi-sample public single cell RNA sequencing datasets from four cancers. For each sample we identified genomic subclones by clustering in a reduced-dimension version of the inferred
single-cell copy number aberration matrix. For samples with detectable subclones, transcriptomic subclusters were identified
within each subclone. Their respective differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and subjected to
overrepresentation analysis to detect enrichment of specific gene sets involving signalling pathways and cancer states.
Similarity between subcluster pairs was calculated by overlapping their respective DEG or gene set lists. We found that
subclusters from different subclones were often more similar to each other and exhibited shared phenotypes, as compared to
subclusters within the same subclone. Using multi-sample cancer datasets from four different cancer types, our study
suggests that subpopulations from genomically distinct cancer populations can show convergent behaviour, potentially due
to signalling or other environmental stimuli.

single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the human substantia nigra (SN) across the PD continuum, control, incidental Lewy

intercellular and microenvironment that may underlie selective dopaminergic vulnerability and guide the development of
ancestry-informed therapeutic strategies.

Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), caused by Pkd1 or Pkd2 mutation, is characterized by
fluid-filled renal cysts. As ADPKD progression varies in humans, cystogenic progression in mouse models is strictly
dictated by the timing of Pkd inactivation. Knockout before postnatal day 13 (P13) drives early-onset cystogenesis,
whereas knockout after P13 results in late-onset disease. However, the vulnerable cell states associated with
cystogenic development and progression remain poorly understood. To decipher the transcriptomic profiles defining
cystogenic progression, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on wild-type mouse kidneys
across postnatal stages (P13, P15, and adult). Analysis of tubular epithelial cells revealed a dynamic transition of the
epithelial proliferation program between P13 and P15. Specifically, tubular epithelial cells at P13 exhibit a transient
mitotic state characterized by a hyperproliferative cellular signature alongside DNA replication and repair processes,
which rapidly resolves into genomic stabilization and an epithelial maturation program at P15. By defining this normal
transcriptional signature across distinct renal lineages, we delineate a transient, cyst-prone proliferative state
susceptible to Pkd inactivation. These findings provide novel insights into epithelial cell state transitions and
susceptibility to Pkd perturbation, offering a mechanistic basis for understanding variable ADPKD onset and
cystogenesis in individuals.

Organoids are stem cell–derived models that recapitulate the physiological state of human tissue development and
disease. However, liver organoids remain functionally immature, and their developmental states are difficult to assess.
Here we developed a single-cell framework that estimates hepatocyte maturation in liver organoids against a human
fetal liver atlas.
We mapped organoid single-cell transcriptomes onto the fetal liver atlas assigning a post-conceptional week (PCW)
score to predict their developmental age. To validate this scoring metric, we defined in vivo differentiation trajectories
from transcription factor and pathway activities across fetal and adult livers. Low-scoring organoids occupied the early
trajectory, dominated by proliferative regulators such as MYC, whereas high-scoring organoids shifted toward
canonical hepatocyte regulators including HNF4A and HNF1A. Pathway activity followed the same ordering, from cell
cycle programs to adult hepatic functions (bile acid metabolism, xenobiotic metabolism, and coagulation). Notably,
these functions remained below the levels of primary adult hepatocytes even in the highest-scoring organoids,
delineating the residual gap to full maturity.
Collectively, this study places liver organoids on a quantitative scale of hepatocyte maturation. Beyond assigning a
developmental state, the framework resolves which components of the adult hepatic program remain unattained,
providing potential targets for advancing liver organoid differentiation.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) comprises Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), yet marked biological
heterogeneity exists within and across these diagnoses. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revealed complex
intestinal cellular compositions, particularly among immune and epithelial populations, but how these populations
collectively organize into distinct tissue-level states remains unclear. We asked whether sample-level cellular
composition could reveal biologically distinct intestinal states beyond conventional IBD classification. We analyzed
intestinal scRNA-seq profiles from the Taurus IBD cohort. Following cell-type annotation, cellular abundances were
summarized at the sample level, transformed to account for their compositional nature, and analyzed using
unsupervised clustering to identify recurrent cellular states. Five major tissue-level cellular states emerged,
distinguished by coordinated variation across immune, epithelial, stromal, and endothelial compartments. These states
represented distinct cellular ecosystems characterized by differential contributions of T-cell, plasma-cell, myeloid,
epithelial, and stromal populations, revealing cellular heterogeneity beyond CD and UC diagnoses. This sample-level
framework provides a basis for linking intestinal cellular states to clinical outcomes and anti-TNF treatment response.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is widely used for dimensionality reduction in single-cell RNA sequencing
(scRNA-seq), but sparsity and technical perturbations can destabilize its embeddings. We developed five
distance-weighted generalizations of multivariate Kendall's tau PCA and benchmarked them against standard PCA and
four existing robust methods. Replicated Splatter simulations examined dropout, synthetic doublets, and gene-subset
mean shifts, while three public scRNA-seq datasets were evaluated under repeated cell subsampling. Performance
depended on perturbation type. Principal component pursuit (PCP) achieved the highest mean Gaussian mixture
model (GMM) ARI and NMI in all synthetic-doublet and gene-subset mean-shift conditions but deteriorated as
dropout strengthened. At the strongest simulated dropout setting, Kendall's tau PCA still yielded the highest mean
GMM ARI and NMI, although the values were only 0.23 and 0.19, respectively. The proposed variants preserved
subspaces across many conditions, but their clustering performance differed by weighting function. Real-data rankings
also varied across datasets, and label-free subspace stability did not align consistently with clustering reproducibility.
These findings show that robust PCA methods should be selected according to anticipated perturbations and
downstream analyses rather than a single global ranking.

Assigning cell types from spatial transcriptomics data relies on cell segmentation, which is difficult to achieve
accurately. Here we introduce an agentic AI framework that infers cell types directly from mRNA signals without cell
segmentation or neighborhood aggregation. The framework deploys one specialized agent per organism and organ
combination, each of which mines PubMed to construct a knowledge graph of cell-type marker genes and assigns cell
identities from expression signals alone, adapting its reasoning to the tissue it specializes in. We tested our approach
on sequencing-based platforms Visium HD and Stereo-seq and imaging-based platforms Xenium and MERFISH. The
framework recovers cell-type distributions with accuracy matching or exceeding segmentation-dependent methods
across platforms, organs, and organisms. This segmentation-free, agentic approach offers a scalable route to cell-type
annotation across spatial and single-cell transcriptomics.
posters.P272:
InnoCORE AI-CRED Institute, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)
Selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons is a pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the
molecular mechanisms underlying this selective vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we report that two
distinct dysregulated glial programs enriched for immune-response and metabolic stress pathways are closely
associated with dopaminergic neuron vulnerability and these are commonly dysregulated across individuals.
Specifically, we create single-nuclear transcriptome atlas across multiple brain regions from the same donor and also
integrate large-scale postmortem single-nucleus transcriptomic datasets from more than 477 human brain specimens
across PD, Alzheimer's disease (AD), and neurotypical controls. Applying a deep learning-based integration framework
with meta-program analysis identifies PD-associated oligodendrocyte and astrocyte programs that strongly correlate
with the depletion of vulnerable dopaminergic neuronal populations. Importantly, spatial transcriptomic analyses
revealed that these disease-associated glial programs were not independently distributed, but instead spatially
converged within pathogenic brain regions. Together, our findings illuminate how coordinated glial dysfunction may
contribute to selective dopaminergic neuronal loss in PD.

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative movement disorder characterized by the progressive accumulation of
phosphorylated α-synuclein (p-α-synuclein) in dopaminergic neurons. Although increasing evidence supports the
‘gut-first’ hypothesis of PD, suggesting that early pathological events in PD originate in the gut, the regional
susceptibility within the gastrointestinal tract and the vulnerable cell populations remain poorly understood. Here, we
show that enteric nervous system (ENS) cells in the distal colon are more severely affected by α-synuclein pathology
than those in the proximal colon, accompanied by preferential accumulation of p-α-synuclein. To comprehensively
characterize molecular alterations across the colon following injection of α-synuclein preformed fibrils (PFFs), we
performed Multiplexed Error-Robust Fluorescence in situ Hybridization (MERFISH) on Swiss-rolled colon tissues
combined with digital unrolling. At an early stage after PFF injection in mice, significant transcriptional changes were
observed exclusively in distal colonic ENS cell subtypes. Furthermore, immunohistochemical analysis revealed that
distal enteric neurons harbor significantly higher p-α-synuclein levels compared with those in the proximal colon.
These findings suggest that spatial niches within the gastrointestinal tract influence susceptibility to α-synuclein
pathology. Together, our findings provide a spatial framework for understanding the gut-first hypothesis of PD.
posters.P274:
Pusan National University
Reliable cell type labels are often available for only a subset of profiles in single-cell studies, while unlabeled profiles
may still contain useful expression structure. We developed scTrans-SVD, a split-specific dual-view framework
combining measured gene expression with a training-derived low-rank representation for cell type annotation under
limited label supervision. Within each training split, truncated SVD initializes robust matrix factorization using training
expression only, preventing held-out cells from influencing representation learning. The low-rank representation is
treated as an alternative view of the same RNA measurements rather than recovered molecular truth or an additional
modality. Measured and low-rank profiles are divided into aligned gene-subvector tokens and processed using shared
Transformer and classifier weights, with predictions combined by fixed logit averaging. We evaluated scTrans-SVD on
13 public single-cell transcriptomic datasets using matched held-out folds, five fixed seeds, and a class-aware 10%
total-label budget. Seven annotation methods were evaluated using identical revealed-label pools. scTrans-SVD
achieved an aggregate Macro-F1 of 0.8820 versus 0.8442 for the strongest comparator and ranked highest on 9 of 13
datasets. Results suggest that measured and low-rank views provide complementary predictive structure, supporting
split-specific low-rank representations for limited-label cell type annotation.
posters.P275:
Patient phenotype prediction from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) requires processing large numbers of cells,
resulting in substantial computational and memory demands. Although metacells can reduce this burden by
aggregating similar cells, conventional metacell construction is independent of the downstream prediction objective.
We propose PhenoMeta, a patient-wise framework that learns phenotype-aware metacells for resource-efficient
phenotype prediction. PhenoMeta integrates pretrained scGPT representations with patient-specific neighborhood
structure using an autoencoder. Patient-specific anchors are then initialized and refined, and cell-to-metacell
assignments are determined using usage-balanced similarity and a learnable assignment gate. Through straight￾through hard assignment, patient-level prediction loss directly guides metacell membership. Metacells are constructed
from mean input gene expression profiles and aggregated into patient representations using size-aware attention. To
stabilize training, final memberships are frozen using the best validation checkpoint before retraining the predictor.
Across five public disease datasets, PhenoMeta achieved competitive predictive performance and consistently
outperformed CloudPred, ScRAT, and scPhase. It also required the least GPU memory among GPU-based methods and
showed low CPU and system memory usage, supporting resource-efficient patient-level prediction from scRNA-seq
data.
posters.P276:
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables the characterization of cellular heterogeneity at single-cell resolution.
Clustering is fundamental for identifying cell populations, but conventional methods require a predefined cluster
number or resolution parameter despite the underlying population number being generally unknown. Moreover,
adaptive clustering approaches may still emphasize discrete population assignments, insufficiently reflecting
continuous cell states and transitional populations.
We propose D-MELT, a twin contrastive framework that preserves transcriptional continuity through false-negative￾aware instance learning and uses DPMM posterior assignments to adaptively guide cluster-level optimization without
fixing the final cluster number. This allows cluster structure to adapt to the learned representation while retaining
relationships among transcriptionally similar cells. Across nine scRNA-seq datasets, D-MELT achieved strong NMI and
ARI performance, outperforming existing adaptive clustering methods on most datasets.

Endocrine glands rely on specialized vasculature to orchestrate hormone trafficking and tissue homeostasis; however,
the transcriptomic landscape underlying endothelial cell (EC) heterogeneity across these organs remains poorly
understood. Here, we constructed a comprehensive single-cell atlas of ECs from four endocrine organs, utilizing liver
and brain tissues as structural references. Our analysis not only distinguishes capillary ECs by their fenestrated,
non-fenestrated, and sinusoidal architectures but also reveals distinct organotypic programs: vascular remodeling in
the adrenal gland and kidney versus stress responsiveness in the pituitary gland and thyroid. Strikingly, we identified
that the thyroid displays a unique restriction in endothelial–immune communication, mirroring the immune-privileged
phenotype of the brain. This protective vascular interface is compromised during aging and tumorigenesis. These
findings define the molecular basis of endocrine vascular specialization and offer new perspectives on the role of
endothelial plasticity in aging and cancer.
posters.P278:
Structural variants (SVs) are typically identified using whole-genome sequencing data using both short and long reads.
We identify the untapped potential of SV detection using short-read single-cell RNA-seq data, focusing on SV
detection in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Here we present a computational pipeline to detect mtDNA SV,
especially large-scale deletion, using secondary aligned reads (SA) and clipped reads. Candidate deletion events are
sorted into tier 1 (SA and clipped read matched), tier 2 (SA only) and tier 3 (clipped read only). By using dynamic
Z-score peak calling (Z ≥ 3), we were able to identify statistically significant breakpoint hotspots using clipped reads
corresponding to SA reads. We demonstrate the use of this pipeline using a paired tumour and normal adjacent
sample from a nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patient. The paired clipped read analysis allowed us to recover more
than half of the deletion candidates not identified by SA reads alone. We observe conserved genomic regions for
deletion hotspots in the mtDNA across all cell types in both normal and tumour samples with increased deletion
signatures: ~2.5 kb, ~8.5 kb, and ~10 kb. Our results also suggest deletion signatures specific to cell type clusters in
both normal and tumour samples.
posters.P279:
Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) involve complex spatial and cellular heterogeneity that
remains poorly understood. Here, we identify AD-risk spatial niches in the human hippocampus as a spatially
organized multicellular context shaped by glial inflammatory and stress-related programs. To further assess the
generalizability of these spatial molecular features, we integrated multiple MERFISH datasets spanning neurotypical
and disease samples across diverse brain regions and species. These niches showed distinct glial compositions,
including spatial associations between disease-associated microglia-like cells and other glial populations. Integration
with single-nucleus RNA-seq further resolved molecular programs within these niches, while cell–cell communication
analysis suggested inflammatory microglia–astrocyte signaling and complement-associated stress in oligodendrocytes.
We are further integrating single-nucleus ATAC-seq and gene regulatory network analyses to connect these
transcriptional states with AD genetic risk and identify candidate upstream regulators for subsequent validation.
Together, our findings suggest that AD-risk niches represent spatially organized multicellular environments in which
AD-associated transcriptional programs, genetic risk, and coordinated glial responses are spatially coupled.
posters.P280:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression profiles within tissues, but the limited gene
coverage of imaging-based platforms restricts the analysis of unmeasured genes. We propose GEIST, a gene-informed
conditional diffusion framework for spatial gene expression imputation. GEIST constructs gene-specific spatial context
by integrating spatial information with target gene priors obtained from pretrained Geneformer embeddings. These
priors encode gene-specific characteristics and contextual relationships among genes. The resulting gene-specific
spatial context is combined with target gene scRNA-seq information to form a unified representation for
reconstruction. GEIST treats each target gene as a sample and uses a Diffusion Transformer to reconstruct its spatial
expression through iterative denoising, conditioned on the diffusion timestep, scRNA-seq representation, and gene
embedding. We evaluated GEIST on three public imaging-based ST datasets with corresponding single-cell references
and an in-house Xenium skin disease dataset comprising 22 tissue cores. Across most datasets, GEIST achieved higher
Pearson correlation coefficients than baseline methods while maintaining comparable RMSE and overall expression
distributions. These results suggest that incorporating gene prior knowledge into spatial context improves
reconstruction of target-gene spatial expression and supports gene-level imputation in spatial transcriptomics across
diverse tissues and experimental settings.
posters.P281:
Bioinformatics
Therapy response in the tumor microenvironment depends on three coupled factors: the functional state of local
tissue domains, their spatial organization, and how these states shift under treatment. Spatial transcriptomics captures
functional and spatial heterogeneity, but most cohorts lack direct response supervision. Perturbational atlases such as
LINCS/CMAP measure drug-induced transcriptional shifts, but lack tissue-scale spatial context.
We present StructRx, a graph transformer framework for drug-conditioned spatial tissue-state modeling. Each spatial
transcriptomics slide is converted into a tissue-domain graph, where nodes represent spatially coherent segments
described by pathway-level program scores and edges encode local adjacency. A label-free graph pretraining stage
learns spatially contextualized tissue-state representations. A second stage links each tissue segment to a mixture of
CMAP reference states and predicts drug/time-conditioned program shifts at the segment level, without using
cohort-specific response labels.
StructRx then summarizes segment-level evidence into a predefined label-free tissue readout that integrates current
functional state, bounded predicted shift and graph-based spatial coupling. Across retrospective Visium cohorts of
hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma and glioblastoma, and an in-house pre-treatment Xenium HCC cohort,
StructRx preserved response-ranking signal across distinct treatment settings, sample timing and spatial platforms. The
informative readout differed by context, indicating that response is not captured by a single whole-slide average, but
by how functional state, treatment-shift direction and spatial organization combine within tissue. StructRx provides an
interpretable framework for label-free, drug-conditioned spatial response ranking in tumor tissue.
posters.P282:
Spatial transcriptomics captures gene expression while preserving tissue organization, but existing methods primarily
model spatial context at the spot level and do not explicitly account for differences in the local spatial context of the
same gene across spots. We address this by learning a global gene representation shared across the tissue section
and adapting it to each spot using its local spatial context, producing spot-specific gene representations. These
representations are incorporated into pretrained spot representations to improve spatial representation learning.
Across 12 human DLPFC sections, our framework improved spatial domain identification and revealed domain-specific
gene associations, supporting the benefit of spot-specific gene representations
posters.P283:
Although single-cell RNA sequencing has enabled the investigation of complex cellular interactions, existing cell-cell
communication approaches often lose cell-specific signals through aggregation or rely on dropout-prone expression
of surface signaling molecules. We introduce PULSO (Predictive Upstream Ligands using Single-cell transcriptOmics), a
computational framework for inferring upstream ligand signaling activity at single-cell resolution from transcriptomic
data.
PULSO employs a two-step approach. First, a batch-corrected latent representation is incorporated into attention
operations to capture intercellular relationships. Positive and negative sampling are used to train a classification model
that generates cell-specific gene importance scores by integrating gene expression with cellular relationships, enabling
the recovery of weak biological signals obscured by transcriptional dropout. Second, these scores are integrated with
a curated ligand-target gene relationship database to predict upstream ligand activity in individual cells.
We benchmarked PULSO against existing approaches and found that it effectively captures cell-specific ligand
signaling activity while preserving biological structure. We further applied PULSO to psoriasis vulgaris to characterize
disease-associated multicellular signaling programs. PULSO identified biologically relevant ligand signaling patterns
across cellular populations, demonstrating its ability to resolve cell-specific communication signals that may be missed
by conventional approaches.
posters.P284:
Motivation: Spatial domain identification is a central step in spatial transcriptomics. Existing neighbourhood summaries
are first-order or single scale, yet niches with near-identical mean expression can differ sharply in how genes covary,
and tissue organization is hierarchical.
Results: We redefine a cell’s niche as its neighbourhood gene–gene covariance across multiple spatial scales; the
matrix square root of the fused covariance yields a Bures–Wasserstein motivated Euclidean feature, so standard PCA
and Leiden identify domains without training. Across 7 datasets, 25 sections and 5 platforms, CoSMIM ranks first
overall, significantly outperforming first-order and single scale covariance neighbourhood features, and ablations
attribute the gain to multi-scale aggregation. Unlike first-order embeddings, its per-domain covariance is directly
readable as domain-specific co-regulation.

Blood-tumor barrier (BTB) heterogeneity limits treatment of glioblastoma (GBM), yet barrier remodeling is commonly
reduced to an open-versus-closed phenotype. We performed donor-aware analyses of 38 histopathology-annotated
spatial transcriptomic sections from six donors, a separately analyzed endothelial single-nucleus layer from 12 tumors,
and complementary external cohorts to resolve vascular programs alongside malignant-state plasticity. A
THSD1-FLT4-associated Recognition score increased from leading edge to infiltrative tumor (median adjusted effect,
+0.0287; 4/4 donors), while Priming increased across this boundary (+0.1481; 3/4) and declined toward cellular tumor
(-0.1641; 0/4 positive). Gate remodeling increased from infiltrative to cellular tumor (+0.2130; 4/4). Within-region
stratified permutations further showed THSD1-positive malignant-enriched niches neighbored FLT4-positive
vascular-enriched niches in 4/4 donors. Remodeled endothelium was PLVAP-high and MFSD2A-low: PLVAP
pseudobulk expression increased in 11/12 donors (+1.6178 log1pCPM), whereas MFSD2A decreased in 10/12
(-0.7145). Patient-paired GSE162631 and anatomically resolved Ivy GAP data independently supported regional
vascular/BTB remodeling; GSE131928 supported malignant-state architecture and an exploratory within-tumor
continuum. These findings identify spatially partitioned vascular/BTB transcriptional states that coexist with
malignant-state plasticity and provide a donor-anchored map for functional testing. Recognition-Priming-Gate is a
cross-sectional framework and does not imply temporal progression, causal tumor-vascular signaling, or measured
permeability.
posters.P286:
Understanding how cells respond to radiation across different experimental conditions requires both well-organized
data and computational approaches that can capture complex molecular response patterns. We developed a research
portal that integrates publicly available single-cell transcriptomic radiation datasets, exploratory response signatures,
and model-development results within a standardized framework.
Using standardized transcriptomic profiles together with experimental-context information, we are developing machine
learning and deep learning models to learn radiation-associated molecular patterns and predict cellular responses
across experimental settings. The framework is designed to support systematic model training, baseline comparison,
and evaluation using held-out data.
The portal currently serves as a research and model-development platform rather than a validated prediction service.
Predictive performance will be assessed using predefined evaluation criteria and independent test data, while
additional experimental datasets will be incorporated after appropriate curation and quality control.
Ultimately, this framework is intended to provide a foundation for data-driven modeling of radiation responses and
for future studies of how drugs and other treatment-modifying compounds influence responses to radiation and
anticancer therapies.
posters.P287:
Single-cell foundation models trained on millions of cells can learn gene expression patterns across diverse contexts.
However, for predicting genetic perturbation effects they often underperform simple regression models. We
hypothesize two potential limitations: targets defined on dropout-prone absolute expression, and pretraining objectives
that reconstruct static co-expression rather than encoding how genes co-regulate under expression changes. We
introduce , a perturbation-specific pretraining framework that predicts log fold-changes (logFC) conditioned on basal
expression, thereby learning how gene sets co-vary across expression-change contexts at scale. To obtain reliable
estimates of expression change under technical sparsity, we compute logFC from scVI-denoised expression and restrict
pretraining to genes with robust detection. Pretrained on 6.28 million expression-change profiles from 66.6 million
human cells and fine-tuned on five Perturb-seq datasets, scDEBART achieves mean enrichment factor (EF) of 11.96, 4-7
higher than scGPT and GEARS (mean EF 1.74-2.99), and 71.4% top-1 accuracy for reverse perturbation identification
compared to near-zero accuracy for prior models. In cross-modal transfer to drug perturbations (SCIPLEX), the model
shows dose-dependent improvement in directional alignment (cosine similarity 0.04→0.30) with above-random DEG
enrichment (EF 2.91-4.32), suggesting partial transfer of learned regulatory patterns across modalities. Overall, these
results indicate that large-scale pretraining on scVI-denoised expression-change profiles provides a useful inductive
bias for perturbation prediction.
posters.P288:
Pohang University of Science and Technology
Gene signature scoring is widely used in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to quantify pathway and cellular
program activity. Existing methods typically summarize gene expression using mean-based, control-subtracted, or
rank-based statistics. Although useful for comparisons within a dataset, these scores are not standardized against an
explicit null distribution and therefore remain sensitive to dataset-specific differences in gene expression, making their
scores difficult to compare across batches, platforms, and atlases. Here, we introduce Null-Calibrated Signature Score
(NCSS), a signature scoring method that calibrates each cell’s observed signature score against a batch-specific
matched-gene null distribution. Within each batch, NCSS generates random gene sets matched to the target signature
by mean expression, estimates the corresponding null mean and variance for each cell, and expresses the observed
signature score as a z-score. This approach is designed to reduce dataset-specific baseline effects while preserving
biological variation. In simulated scRNA-seq datasets, NCSS showed greater robustness than existing scoring methods
across a range of batch-effect magnitudes. We further evaluated its transferability in two cross-dataset settings. First,
age-associated signatures derived from one peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) atlas were reproduced in an
independent PBMC atlas, demonstrating cross-atlas reproducibility. Second, inter-tumor heterogeneity defined in a
colorectal cancer (CRC) scRNA-seq atlas were recovered in CRC VisiumHD spatial transcriptomic data, demonstrating
transferability across measurement platforms. Furthermore, NCSS scored 2.5 million cells in approximately one minute,
substantially faster than existing methods. Together, these results show that NCSS enables reproducible and
transferable gene signature scoring across batches, datasets, and platforms, making it well suited for integrative
analyses of large-scale single-cell and spatial atlases.

Single-cell studies are commonly organized around discrete experimental stages, while cells collected within the same
stage can occupy heterogeneous and continuously varying states. Existing trajectory inference methods, including
supervised pseudotime approaches, typically impose a separate ordered trajectory on each dataset, without
establishing either its continuity or cross-dataset comparability. Here, we present scTrace, which treats discrete stage
labels as coarse, potentially noisy anchors. We employ triplet-based contrastive learning to construct a latent space
that preserves local cellular heterogeneity while incorporating global structure of ordered stages. Rather than
assuming a valid continuous ordering in every dataset, scTrace evaluates whether a consistent continuous component
exists across datasets and extracts a disentangled disease-relevant axis enabling quantitative cross-dataset analysis.
Applied to multiple atherosclerotic mouse models, scTrace captures a continuous disease-relevant trend shared across
models while preserving model-specific variation. These comparisons allow us to pinpoint shared intermediate states
and divergent modules that discrete stage labels would otherwise mask. When extended to human data, the
framework offers a potential basis for further cross-species calibration. Overall, our results support the identification of
continuous cell-level disease traces to resolve biological variation hidden by discrete experimental sampling, and
provide a valuable framework for cross-model state alignment in complex disease systems.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) induces systemic immune remodeling but how immune states are
coordinated across hematopoietic, circulating, and tumor compartments over disease progression remains poorly
understood. Here, we constructed a longitudinal single-cell atlas spanning bone marrow, peripheral blood, and tumor
to model PDAC-associated myeloid remodeling as a cross-tissue temporal process. We first observed a sequential shift
from monocytic to granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell states during cancer progression. By aligning
transcriptional states across tissues and time, we found that circulating and tumor myeloid populations share a
common progression-associated program but increasingly diverge after entry into the tumor microenvironment,
indicating substantial local reprogramming. Integrating these dynamics with malignant cell states further revealed that
changes in myeloid composition and transcriptional state coincide with stage-dependent shifts in tumor–immune
communication. We next asked whether these progression-associated myeloid changes leave a transcriptional signature
detectable in circulation. Cross-compartment transcriptional pattern modeling identified a conserved myeloid program
in peripheral blood that was reproducible in independent human PDAC single-cell datasets. Together, these findings
reveal how systemic myeloid states are progressively reshaped across anatomical compartments during PDAC
progression and identify a circulating transcriptional program that reflect tumor-associated immune remodeling.
posters.P291:
RNA velocity is a powerful method to estimate the direction of transcriptional change but is high-dimensional, noisy,
and difficult to interpret at the gene level. We introduce Program Velocity (PV), a low-dimensional representation that
models expression as cNMF programs over a fixed basis and estimates changes in program usage through
ridge-regularized decomposition of gene-wise velocity.
We evaluated PV using a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) to induced endoderm progenitor (iEP) reprogramming
scRNA-seq dataset with inferred successful and dead-end fates. Despite compressing gene-wise dynamics into a small
number of transcriptional programs, PV consistently outperformed raw gene-wise velocity in a CellRank-style fate
prediction at day 12, 15, and 21 for day-28 fate prediction. Paired bootstrap analysis with 1,000 resamples showed
AUROC improvement of +0.0676, +0.0745, and +0.0169 at day 12, 15, and 21, respectively, over raw velocity. Also,
program-level analyses revealed fate-associated directional signals not apparent from current program usage alone
and remained biologically interpretable in the context of cell-state transitions.
These results suggest that Program Velocity provides a compact and interpretable representation of transcriptomic
dynamics while retaining, and potentially improving, information relevant to downstream cell-fate inference.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits marked malignant heterogeneity within a complex tumor
microenvironment (TME). Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) contribute to tumor–stroma communication, yet the
malignant cell states that drive or accompany sEV secretion in human PDAC remain poorly characterized.
We integrated human PDAC single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, including primary and metastatic tumors, using scVI,
classified malignant epithelial cells from transcriptomic and inferred copy-number features, and resolved recurrent
malignant transcriptional programs by consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF). SEVtras was applied to
estimate sEV secretion activity at single-cell resolution, and CellChat was used to infer ligand–receptor communication
between malignant cells and fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune populations. sEV secretion activity varied across
malignant programs, and cells with high sEV-associated activity displayed distinct predicted ligand–receptor
communication patterns with stromal and endothelial compartments.
Comparison of primary and metastatic tumors further suggested disease-associated remodeling of malignant
programs and their predicted cell–cell interactions. Together, this integrative analysis links malignant transcriptional
heterogeneity to sEV secretion and TME communication in human PDAC, and highlights candidate tumor cell states
and signaling axes for experimental validation.

Spatial host–microbe sequencing is increasingly used to profile host gene expression while mapping microbial
biogeography in tissue. However, sparse and unevenly captured microbial reads complicate the distinction between
meaningful spatial organization, low support, and measurement-associated structure. We present SPIRA (Spatial
Pattern Inference with Residual Adjustment), a framework for identifying sufficiently supported, technically adjusted
taxon-level spatial patterns and reporting their biological context, taxonomic resolution, and physical scale. SPIRA first
quantifies per-taxon testability, then tests spatial pattern after adjustment for user-defined technical covariates. SPIRA
reports host- or boundary-associated taxa as independent contextual flags and summarizes taxonomic-resolution
stability and cluster scale. In controlled simulations and real-background semi-simulations, SPIRA maintained
calibrated false discovery rates and recovered structured taxa across read-depth regimes. Applied to intestinal Visium
and high-resolution Stereo-seq data, SPIRA identified interpretable microbial hotspots. SPIRA provides an auditable
toolkit for prioritizing spatial microbial signals while preserving biologically informative context.

Dietary nutrient composition and availability regulate cellular bioenergetics and biosynthetic programs, shaping tissue
metabolic adaptation and systemic homeostasis. However, how cellular functional states vary across tissues and
samples under diverse dietary conditions remains incompletely understood. Here we present a multi-tissue single-cell
transcriptomic atlas comprising 497,227 cells from 17 mouse datasets spanning diverse dietary conditions. We applied
non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) independently to each sample and consolidated related gene expression
programs into meta-programs (MPs). Mapping MPs onto cell types and subclusters revealed functional transcriptional
programs that were not fully captured by cluster-based classification. Distinct MP patterns across samples within the
same cell type further revealed functional heterogeneity beyond shared cellular identity and discrete subcluster
boundaries. Building on these findings, we aim to examine associations among MPs predominant in specific cell types
across tissues to explore candidate axes of inter-tissue functional coordination. This atlas provides a reference for
comparing cellular responses to dietary interventions and prioritizing diet-responsive transcriptional programs and
inter-tissue relationships. By extending cell-type annotation to encompass functional transcriptional states, this
resource offers a framework for investigating how nutritional environments shape cellular and tissue function,
informing mechanistic studies and the design of dietary intervention experiments.

Tumor-associated macrophages are key regulators of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression, yet the functional
significance of TREM2-positive macrophages remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA
sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, bulk liver transcriptomic datasets, multiplex immunohistochemistry, and secretome
proteomics to characterize TREM2-positive macrophages in HCC. TREM2-positive macrophages were enriched in HCC
tissues compared with normal and adjacent non-tumor liver tissues and were elevated across tumor grades. Analysis
of bulk liver transcriptomic datasets indicated an increased immunosuppressive score in HCC, while patient plasma
analysis showed elevated IL-4 levels. In U937-derived macrophages, IL-4/IL-13 stimulation induced alternative
activation, STAT6 phosphorylation, TREM2 expression, and secretome remodeling. Secretome proteomics identified
MMP12 as a prominently upregulated extracellular matrix-remodeling factor. TREM2 overexpression enhanced
IL-4/IL-13-induced STAT6 phosphorylation and MMP12 expression and secretion, indicating that TREM2 amplifies
macrophage responses to IL-4/IL-13. Conditioned medium from IL-4/IL-13-treated macrophages promoted xenograft
tumor growth and increased CXCL3 and CXCL8 expression in HCC cells, whereas MMP12 inhibition attenuated these
responses. PLAUR knockdown also reduced CXCL3 induction. These findings define a TREM2–STAT6–MMP12
macrophage axis associated with HCC progression.

Organoids have opened new possibilities for disease modeling, drug screening, and personalized therapy, but moving
this technology from academic settings to industrial scale requires a quantitative measure of how faithfully the model
recapitulates its target tissue. Here we present an end-to-end computational framework that scores organoid fidelity
from single-cell RNA sequencing data. Our framework draws ideas from random matrix theory, Bayesian
nonparametrics, and combinatorial optimization to then measure the multi-point distance between the organoid and
its native tissue. Whole blood samples serve as a negative control for tissue-specific similarity. Independently profiled
normal colon samples scored 99.05% and 97.98%, indicating the empirical ceiling for matched tissue identity. Four
independently generated colon organoid datasets spanned 88.98% to 12.50%. Decomposition of the lowest score
traced the deficit to stromal and endothelial populations absent from the organoid. By ranking organoids on a
common scale and localizing each deficit to its cellular source, our framework provides the quantitative basis for
standardized quality control of organoid manufacturing.
posters.P297:
Fudan University
Encoding spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) data serves to identify the biological semantics of RNA expression
within the tissue while preserving spatial characteristics. Depending on the analytical scenario, one may focus on
different contextual structures of tissues. For instance, anatomical regions reveal consistent patterns by focusing on
spatial homogeneity, while elucidating complex tumor micro-environments requires more expression heterogeneity.
However, current spatial encoding methods lack consideration of the tissue context. Meanwhile, most developed SRT
technologies are still limited in providing exact patterns of intact tissues due to limitations such as low resolution or
missed measurements. Here, we propose STForte, a novel pairwise graph autoencoderbased approach with
cross-reconstruction and adversarial distribution matching, to model the spatial homogeneity and expression
heterogeneity of SRT data. STForte extracts interpretable latent encodings, enabling downstream analysis by accurately
portraying various tissue contexts. Moreover, STForte allows spatial imputation using only spatial consistency to
restore the biological patterns of unobserved locations or low-quality cells, thereby providing fine-grained views to
enhance the SRT analysis. Extensive evaluations of datasets under different scenarios and SRT platforms demonstrate
that STForte is a scalable and versatile tool for providing enhanced insights into spatial data analysis.

Multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing from multiple donors is an effective strategy to reduce batch effects and
lower experimental costs. Existing genotype-based methods reconstruct the donor of origin for each cell but can be
sensitive to sample pooling ratio and sequencing depth. Here we present dropbucket, a robust demultiplexing
method that employs a weighted fuzzy mixture model to enable accurate cell assignment even under extreme pooling
conditions. Using simulated pooled datasets derived from real data, we show that dropbucket outperforms existing
demultiplexing methods not only under baseline pooling conditions but also extreme pooling conditions. We further
demonstrate its utility in maternal–fetal interface and donor–recipient transplant datasets, highlighting the broad
applicability for genetic demultiplexing scenarios.

Medical Science, The Catholic Medical Center of the Catholic University of Korea, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Understanding the complex spatial architecture of the tumor microenvironment (TME) across diverse malignancies
remains a critical challenge in cancer biology. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive pan-cancer spatial
transcriptomics analysis to delineate universal "function-guided niches" across multiple cancer types. To characterize
this spatial heterogeneity, we constructed a comprehensive pan-cancer spatial atlas by assembling a large-scale cohort
of 739 Visium samples across 17 different cancer types. By evaluating spatially resolved functional pathways, we
identified 15 distinct function-guided spatial niches based on spatially resolved functional pathway activity. These
niches captured diverse metabolic, stromal, and immune-associated functional states and revealed recurrent spatial
patterns across cancer types. The resulting functional niche atlas provides a framework for characterizing conserved
and cancer-specific features of the tumor spatial microenvironment and for investigating how distinct cellular and
functional states are organized within tumors. Together, our findings establish a function-guided framework for
systematically characterizing spatial heterogeneity across diverse tumor microenvironments. This pan-cancer spatial
atlas provides a foundation for investigating the functional organization and cellular interactions underlying distinct
tumor niches across cancer types.
posters.P300:
AI-agent-curated repositories such as scBaseCount can expand access to public single-cell RNA-sequencing data, but
disease terms inferred from study-level descriptions may be propagated to healthy controls. We designed an
evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that separates a study’s disease context from the phenotype of individual
samples. Specialized agents resolve SRA, BioSample, GEO, and publication links; retrieve structured and textual
evidence; normalize diseases to MONDO; and assign sample polarity as present, explicitly absent, mixed, or unknown.
A critic agent reconciles source conflicts and abstains when sample-specific evidence is insufficient. In a preliminary
audit of a single-cell metadata benchmark, 61 disease records labeled absent or normal were excluded from
conventional positive-only ontology scoring. The system nevertheless assigned a positive MONDO disease term to 34
of these records (55.7%), and their exclusion increased apparent accuracy from 52.1% to 63.3%. Across 423 training
and development instances, only 98 (23.2%) contained direct or ontology-synonym textual support in leakage-safe
inputs. These findings show that positive-only evaluation can conceal disease-label propagation and reward
unsupported predictions. We are applying the framework to scBaseCount to quantify and repair study-to-sample
propagation, supporting safer cohort construction and more reliable training data for single-cell foundation models.

Introduction:Microsatellite stable (MSS) gastric cancer (GC) represents the majority of gastric cancer cases and poses a significant therapeutic challenge due to its limited response to standard treatments, including immune checkpoint blockade
(ICB) therapies. The tumor microenvironment is thought to contribute to this resistance, yet when and how its stromal
component begins to change during the development of MSS GC remains poorly characterized. In this study, we aimed to
define how fibroblasts change along the stepwise progression from normal mucosa through adenoma to early gastric
cancer.Material and Method:To achieve this aim, we built a single-cell atlas by performing single-cell RNA sequencing
(scRNA-seq) on fresh tissues from 12 Helicobacter pylori-infected patients with MSS gastric neoplasia. A total of 20 specimens were collected and classified into four stages of disease progression: normal (n=8), low-grade adenoma (LA, n=6), high-grade
adenoma (HA, n=2), and early gastric cancer (EGC, n=4). A public gastric cancer scRNA-seq dataset was additionally
analyzed.Result and Discussion:Our single-cell atlas showed that heterogeneity centered on cancer-associated fibroblasts
(CAFs) was already evident at the adenoma stage, accompanied by remodeling of the tumor microenvironment as disease
progressed. This remodeling included stage-dependent shifts in the composition of immune and stromal cell populations.
Subclustering identified seven fibroblast subsets, and this heterogeneity reflected changes in both abundance and
transcriptional state: some subsets expanded with disease stage, whereas others remained stable in abundance but shifted
toward distinct transcriptional states. Similar fibroblast changes were also observed in the public dataset compared with
normal stomach.Conclusion:These findings suggest that CAF-centered remodeling of the tumor microenvironment in MSS
gastric carcinogenesis is already underway at the precancerous stage, before invasive cancer develops.
posters.P302:
Peptide therapeutics offer high specificity and low toxicity, reaching protein-protein interfaces inaccessible to small
molecules. However, computational peptide design remains challenging because both the peptide and its target
binding site are flexible. Conventional structure-based peptide design approaches, however, represent the target
protein as a rigid structure, ignoring the induced fit that accompanies peptide binding. To address these limitations,
we developed FlexPep, the first peptide design framework to explicitly model binding-induced conformational
changes in the target protein. Given an apo structure, FlexPep generates a candidate peptide together with the holo
conformation induced in the target upon binding. FlexPep learns a mapping from an apo structure and a noised
peptide to the corresponding holo-peptide complex using an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network and invariant
point attention. To this end, we constructed a dataset of apo–holo–peptide structural triplets by generating the apo
state for each holo protein with ESMFold2. We show that FlexPep generates peptides with favorable binding energy
while accurately capturing the conformational change induced in the target, performing competitively with existing
methods. These results suggest that co-designing the peptide and the target’s conformational response provides a
practical method to peptide drug discovery from apo structures, with no peptide-bound template.
posters.P303:
Southeast University School of Medicine
Aging is characterized by progressive functional decline across organ systems, yet the molecular programs
coordinating systemic aging remain poorly defined. ZMPSTE24 catalyzes the final cleavage of farnesylated prelamin A,
and its loss causes accumulation of unprocessed prelamin A and multisystem progeroid phenotypes. To identify
shared and organ-specific responses to ZMPSTE24 deficiency, we performed pan-organ transcriptomic profiling and
network modeling across 12 major tissues from ZMPSTE24-knockout and wild-type mice, with three biological
replicates per genotype and tissue, totaling 72 samples. Differential expression analysis, using a linear model with
mouse identity as a blocking factor, identified 52 unique DEGs across the 12 tissues. Weighted gene co-expression
network (WGCNA) analysis identified 36 modules, including M4 and M22, which were enriched for
knockout-associated DEGs. Integration of M4 with recurrent pan-organ DEGs yielded a protein–protein interaction
network enriched in extracellular matrix organization, focal adhesion, integrin signaling, and cytoskeletal regulation.
Mapping network genes onto a mouse whole-body single-cell transcriptomic atlas showed preferential enrichment in
mesenchymal stromal cells and fibroblasts, implicating these populations as candidate cellular sources of the shared
response. These findings define a cross-organ molecular framework for ZMPSTE24-associated progeria and nominate
fibroblast-associated stromal remodeling as a candidate mechanism linking tissue-specific response to systemic aging.
posters.P304:
Genome‑scale metabolic models (GSMMs) provide a framework to study how nutrient availability shapes human
metabolism, yet predictions remain highly sensitive to constraint design. Invariant versus variable metabolic functions
were quantified in the Human GEM across baseline, fixed, and randomized dietary contexts. Baseline essentiality
analysis identified 93 reactions critical for growth, dominated by transport and exchange subsystems, with additional
contributions from glycolysis, amino acid metabolism, and lipid activation. Under amino acid‑rich, fatty acid‑rich, and
glucose‑rich diets, essentiality persisted but redistributed: transport reactions remained critical in glucose‑rich
conditions, while fatty acid oxidation and amino acid metabolism contributed under fatty acid‑ and amino acid‑rich
contexts. Across 300 randomized diets, classification into glucose‑dominant (n=88) and fatty‑dominant (n=212) subsets
revealed condition‑specific essentiality patterns, highlighting redundancy and metabolic flexibility. Growth feasibility
was universal (rate=1.0), with ATP maintenance nearly invariant (CV=2.4×10⁻⁶) and modest variability in individual
ATP‑consuming reactions (CV≈0.003). Vitamin and mineral restriction diets (folate, zinc, iron, phosphate) produced
flux distributions indistinguishable from balanced and high‑fat diets, confirming structural insensitivity to micronutrient
limitation. These findings demonstrate that Human GEM maintains feasibility across diverse diets but redistributes
essential reactions, underscoring the importance of physiologically meaningful constraint design for nutrition and
systems biology.

The mineralocorticoid hormone, aldosterone, regulates blood pressure through the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron
(ASDN) in the kidney. Chronic aldosterone exposure promotes tubular remodeling, interstitial fibrosis, and inflammation,
contributing to the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, the cellular regulatory networks underlying
aldosterone-mediated pathophysiological progression remain unclear.
We profiled mRNA and miRNA transcriptomes in both in vitro and in vivo models of chronic aldosterone exposure and
explored a comprehensive regulatory mRNA-miRNA network associated with renal changes during CKD progression.
RNA-Seq of the kidney ASDN cell model identified 2,783 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) altered by aldosterone
treatment. Pathway analyses revealed that upregulated DEGs were significantly enriched for ion transport and
hormonal response. Conversely, downregulated DEGs were strongly enriched in the regulation of cell cycle and
proliferation. In miRNA profiling, aldosterone induced significant changes in the expression of 63 miRNAs (P < 0.05),
including the miR-466-669 family. Target prediction analysis revealed that miRNA-target genes were significantly
enriched in cell cycle/proliferation pathways and inflammatory responses. Additionally, comprehensive mRNA-miRNA
interaction analysis using a CLIP-Seq database revealed a regulatory network including miRNAs targeting cell cycle
regulation in response to aldosterone.
Our findings provide novel insight into the cellular mRNA-miRNA networks associated with aldosterone-mediated CKD
progression.
posters.P306:
National Institute for Basic Biology(NIBB)
We have developed a method to integrate transcriptomic co-expression networks across diverse experimental
conditions within a single species. Our framework expands previous pan-network approaches into a hypergraph-based
pan-network. It first identifies co-expressed gene clusters within each individual dataset and extracts frequently
co-expressed gene sets across multiple datasets using a frequent itemset mining algorithm. This process yields a
hypergraph where each hyperedge is assigned a frequency (universality, U). We then extracted a subnetwork
comprising high-universality hyperedges as the core network and formed modules within it. Applying our method to
106 Escherichia coli transcriptome datasets from the GEO database, we found that the modularity of the core network
increases and reaches its maximum at a universality cutoff of 15. Approximately 70% of the resulting core modules
correspond to operons, and conversely, approximately 70% of all operons are covered by these core modules. We
visualized the core network via an inter-modular network and analyzed core module–dataset relationships using a
modularity profile matrix. Based on these analyses, we successfully visualized the dynamic reorganization of the
co-expression network in response to environmental changes in bacteria.
posters.P307:
Convergent Analytical Science, University of Science and Technology, Daejeon 34113, Republic of Korea
Liver disease encompasses a broad spectrum of etiologies, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis
(MASH), alcoholic hepatitis (AH), and viral hepatitis, that converge toward fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
However, most studies examine these etiologies in isolation and mainly at advanced stages, leaving early,
etiology-specific features poorly defined, particularly for MASH, a rapidly growing global burden. To address this gap,
we performed a multi-cohort transcriptomic comparison across eight public datasets spanning four etiologies (two
cohorts each) and identified differentially expressed genes versus controls (|log2FC| ≥ 0.585, padj < 0.05). Robust Rank
Aggregation was applied to extract consensus genes within each etiology, and cross-comparison of these genes
yielded etiology-specific genes. Gene Ontology analysis showed that MASH-specific genes were enriched in lipid and
sterol biosynthesis and glucose metabolism, whereas AH-, HBV-, and HCV-specific genes reflected extracellular matrix
remodeling, mitochondrial and ribosomal stress, and antiviral immunity, respectively. Protein-protein interaction and
Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of MASH-specific genes converged on a cholesterol biosynthesis axis, including hub genes
HMGCS1, MVD, SQLE, FDFT1, NSDHL, and TM7SF2, which correlated significantly with the upstream regulator SREBF2.
As these genes were specifically and consistently identified in MASH, they represent strong candidates for future
mechanistic studies elucidating their functional roles in MASH pathogenesis.
posters.P308:
Indian Institute of Technology Bombay
Public metabolomics repositories contain thousands of studies, but two barriers limit reuse: studies are difficult to
discover, and deposited matrices vary in their suitability for supervised learning. We address these through two
analyses. HARMONY harmonizes 4,118 Metabolomics Workbench (MW) and 2,712 MetaboLights studies by recovering
evidence study by study and mapping eight metadata nodes to shared ontology concepts while retaining original
terms. Its search layer combines exact ontology matching with dual-encoder dense retrieval. Harmonization increased
cross-repository retrievability from 75.5% with deposited strings to 89.6%, led by separation method, ionization source,
and mass analyzer type. MERIT-ML then evaluates whether MW datatable, mwTab, and untarg_data matrices support
supervised classification, scoring 21 metrics across five readiness dimensions and feasibility gates for every deposited
analysis. Among 6,696 analyses from 4,121 studies, 96.5% yielded at least one matrix; only 35.5% of studies were
ML-ready, while 34.5% were ready-with-caveats, and 26.1% were class-support-limited. Matrix source, class support,
missingness, dimensionality, and annotation determined reuse. Together, HARMONY and MERIT-ML distinguish two
often conflated questions: can a study be found, and can its matrix support supervised classification? Separating these
questions provides a basis for study selection and benchmark construction.

Mechanistic foundation models that integrate genomic, structural, and transcriptomic evidence under explicit
physicochemical constraints remain scarce for extremophiles, limiting quantitative understanding of how dominant taxa
sustain metabolism in hypersaline ecosystems. We addressed this gap for Haloquadratum walsbyi, the haloarchaeon
dominating thalassohaline hypersaline communities, by building a multi-omics-integrated genome-scale metabolic
model (GSMM) as a mechanistic foundation layer for its metabolism. Genome reannotation, sequence homology, and
AlphaFold2/RoseTTAFold-based structural inference resolved functional assignments for 212 previously uncharacterized
proteins, yielding a curated network (iHQW-TK; 1,820 reactions, 1,323 metabolites). On this foundation, we layered a
non-ideal, energy-dependent thermokinetic formalism — Pitzer-corrected chemical activities, thermodynamic feasibility
constraints, and electrochemically driven transport kinetics — cast as a regularized mixed-integer optimization problem
with a provably unique optimal flux solution, in contrast to classical flux balance analysis. This mathematically principled
architecture identified glycerol- and pyruvate-supported metabolism as the energetically feasible states under
hypersaline conditions; integrating independent transcriptomic data confirmed these routes are transcriptionally active
in vivo, while dihydroxyacetone-based alternatives remain latent. The resulting three-tier model — genomic encoding,
thermodynamic restriction, transcriptional selection — offers a reusable, extensible foundation for multi-omics￾constrained metabolic modeling across physicochemically extreme microbial systems.
posters.P310:
Rapid assessment of radiation exposure is essential for effective medical management following radiological or nuclear
incidents. Proteomics-based biodosimetry offeres a promising approach for identifying circulating biomarkers
associated with absorbed radiation dose. This study aimed to characterize dose-responsive plasma a protein signature
following ex vivo ionizing radiation exposure.
Peripheral blood samples form 8 healthy donors were exposed ex vivo to cobalt-60 gamma radiation across nine
doses ranging form 0 to 6 Gy. Plasma proteins were profiled using the Olink Explore HT platform, measuring more
than 5,000 proteins. Dose responses were evaluated using baseline-corrected NPX changes relative to 0 Gy. No robust
sex-dependent dose-response differences were detected after multiple-testing correction: therefore, subsequent
exploratory analyses were conducted using the combined cohort.
Dose-specific analyses identified significant changes in IKBKG, CCL17 and CXCL5 at 0.1Gy, 0.25Gy, and 0.5 Gy,
respectively. Linear dose-response modeling identified 36 proteins with significant dose-dependent trends, including
EVI5L, SNX29, RAB28, APPL2, and CHUK. Functional annotation implicated immune regulation, inflammatory signalling,
cellular stress responses, and intracellular signaling. A candidate 30-protein signature was selected based on statistical
significance and feature-selection frequency. Exploratory machine learning analyses supported preliminary potential for
dose-estimation modeling, although predictive performance was limited by the small small size and lack of
independent validation. These findings identify candidate plasma protein signatures for radiation bio-dosimetry and
support further validation in independent cohorts using orthogonal analytical platforms.
posters.P311:
Conventional time-series transcriptomic analyses identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways at
individual time points, but provide limited insight into how gene modules are maintained, reorganized, or
redistributed over time. This study develops a computational framework for detecting temporal transitions of gene
modules in transcriptomic data. As a representative application, differential expression analysis is performed on bulk
RNA-sequencing dataset GSE122380 at each time point relative to Day 0. Differentially expressed genes are mapped
onto a high-confidence STRING protein interaction network restricted to Reactome pathway genes. HiDeF is then
applied to derive a fixed hierarchical community structure shared across all time points, enabling temporal changes to
be assessed without redefining module composition. Candidate features for quantifying module activity include gene
enrichment, fold enrichment, statistical significance, community size, and network topology. Transitions between
modules at adjacent time points are formulated as a network-flow optimization problem, with transition costs
incorporating gene overlap, inter-community connectivity, functional similarity, and expression direction. Preliminary
analyses suggest that this framework can capture temporally varying module-level patterns beyond conventional
time-point-wise enrichment analysis. The approach provides an interpretable basis for characterizing dynamic
transcriptomic responses and for identifying biologically meaningful module transitions across time in complex
biological systems and disease processes.
posters.P312:
, Min Jung Kim3,4
, Min Ji Kim3,4

1Department of Physiology, Ajou University School of Medicine. 2Department of Biomedical Sciences, Graduate School of Ajou
University. 3College of Pharmacy, Ajou University. 4Department of Biohealth Regulatory Science, Graduate School of Ajou University
Alveolar macrophages (AMs) take their identity from the lung niche, making them challenging to generate outside the
tissue. While GM-CSF is required for AM differentiation, it cannot reconstitute AM identity on its own. To investigate
which other signals are needed, we analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from the induced alveolar assembloid, a
model that combines human pluripotent stem cell-derived alveolar epithelial organoids with induced macrophages.
Unsupervised clustering identified an AM-like population that expanded only in the assembloid. These cells expressed
AM identity genes and were enriched for lipid metabolism and phagocytosis pathways, whereas monoculture
macrophages retained monocyte-derived features. Through this, we selected the four top-ranked ligands including
GM-CSF, which exhibited the highest AM marker gene regulatory potential. We discovered some of these ligands
were supplied by the alveolar epithelium through paracrine signaling, while others were produced by the AM-like
macrophages themselves, indicating the complex cellular crosstalk of the native lung niche essential for AM identity.
Collectively, AM differentiation in this model depends on the synergistic action of both epithelial and macrophage￾derived cytokines, demonstrating that both signaling sources must be reconstituted to successfully rebuild the AM
program in vitro.
posters.P313:
, Sunjae Lee2
1 Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST). 2Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a progressive liver disease accompanied by extensive
metabolic reprogramming. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) enable the integration of transcriptomic data with
metabolic networks to investigate such alterations at the reaction and flux levels. However, generic GEMs may contain
permissive exchange, transport, and alternative reactions that are not physiologically relevant to the liver, potentially
allowing unrealistic flux distributions and obscuring disease-associated metabolic changes.
To characterize hepatic metabolic alterations in MASH more accurately, we refined a mouse liver metabolic model
using physiological information from the Human2 whole-body metabolic model and manual curation of exchange and
transport reactions. The refined network was then integrated with liver RNA-seq data from a GAN diet mouse model
comprising 27 normal metabolism and 54 MASH samples. Sample-specific metabolic models were reconstructed using
ftINIT, and metabolic flux distributions were inferred using SPOT by integrating reaction-level gene expression with
stoichiometric constraints. Comparative analysis of the resulting flux profiles was used to characterize metabolic
pathways and reactions altered during MASH progression. This approach provides a physiologically informed view of
disease-associated hepatic metabolic reprogramming beyond transcriptomic changes alone.
posters.P314:
and Biochemistry, Yale University. 3Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Yale University
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) offers a less invasive window into brain biology and contains diverse molecular signals that
can inform biomarker discovery for neurodegenerative disease. However, disease-related information may be
distributed across molecular layers and between soluble CSF and extracellular-vesicle compartments. Analyzing these
data separately can obscure shared biological variation. We integrated matched whole-CSF and extracellular vesicle
and nanoparticle (EVps) proteomes from 48 ROS/MAP participants using Joint and Individual Variation Explained
(JIVE). Integration improved biological concordance across compartments and increased the detection of Alzheimer’s
disease (AD)-associated candidates. Notably, the joint signal recovered as many brain-related biomarker candidates as
CSF proteomic studies using substantially larger cohorts, demonstrating that paired analysis can maximize information
from limited clinical samples. We are extending this interpretable framework to matched CSF miRNA and protein
profiles. Complementary joint/individual and latent-factor models characterize shared and modality-specific variation,
while fused graphical modeling estimates AD and control conditional-dependence networks simultaneously, preserving
common structure while identifying condition-specific miRNA–protein and within-omic connections. Together, these
approaches provide an interpretable strategy for distinguishing convergent, compartment-specific, and network-level
AD signals across CSF molecular layers and may enable more efficient biomarker discovery in small, deeply profiled
cohorts.
posters.P315:
, Sukjoon Yoon1,2
1 Sookmyung Women's University. 2CBiS
Gene-level omics data reflect the outcome of many interacting molecular processes. Here, we introduce NetCrafter, a
new framework that reconstructs context-specific functional gene networks directly from the molecular state of each
sample.
NetCrafter combines biological knowledge from ontologies with measured omics signals while removing redundant
functional information. The relevance of each biological term in a sample is distributed among its genes according to
their relative omics contributions, creating a unique functional weight (w) for every gene. Shared functional weights
are then summarized as Tw, a quantitative score representing the functional relationship of each gene pair.
Because every gene has its own functional weight, genes measured using different technologies, such as RNA
expression and CRISPR dependency, can be directly connected within a single network. NetCrafter therefore reveals not
only altered genes, but also disease-specific gene pairs, functional modules, cross-omics target–biomarker relationships
and interaction hotspots. It prioritized mutation-specific CRISPR vulnerabilities, identified high-Tw core networks
enriched for cancer hallmark genes, and detected tumor-specific gene relationships associated with patient survival.
By transforming conventional omics measurements into biologically interpretable gene-pair maps, NetCrafter provides
a new framework for mechanism discovery, precision medicine, multi-omics integration and ontology-guided AI. Its
gene-pair relationships are also being used to train Bio-LDM from limited omics datasets. NetCrafter is available
through the Q-omics platform (https://qomics.ai).
posters.P316:
Research, Kyoto University. 3Department of Information Science, Faculty of Science, Toho University
Exploring how network control is distributed among interacting cell types may provide insight into cellular
communication and disease-related mechanisms. Maximum-matching-based structural controllability requires directed
networks, whereas many cell–cell interaction networks are assembled from undirected protein–protein interaction data.
Minimum Driver Orientation (MDO) addresses this mismatch by assigning edge directions to minimize the number of
driver nodes. MDO was formulated as an integer linear programming (ILP) problem and applied to oligodendrocyte– macrophage (OM) and oligodendrocyte–T-cell (OT) networks associated with multiple sclerosis, containing 3,562 and
8,150 nodes, respectively. Despite its larger size, the OT network required approximately half the driver-node fraction
of the OM network, reflecting differences in the MDO-induced path–cycle cover structure. Driver nodes also exhibited
distinct localization patterns in the OM and OT networks, indicating differences in their underlying control
organization. These results show that MDO can reveal distinct structural patterns of network control in undirected
PPI-based cell–cell interaction networks. In this presentation, we discuss these MDO findings together with ongoing
methodological extensions that broaden the framework toward the analysis of larger and more complex cell–cell
interaction networks.
posters.P317:
2Biomedical Research Institute, Kyungpook National University Hospital, Deagu, Republic of Korea
Aging and metabolic stress are major risk factors for atherosclerosis, yet how they jointly reshape vascular cell states
and regulatory landscapes remains unclear. We performed time-course single-nucleus multiome profiling of aortas
from Ldlr-deficient mice fed normal chow (NCD) or high-fat diet (HFD), initiated at young or old age and maintained
for 12, 24, or 36 weeks. The resulting atlas of 67,944 nuclei revealed distinct transcriptional and chromatin accessibility
states across endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and macrophages. HFD increased Dkk2+
inflammatory endothelial cells, phenotypically modulated smooth muscle cells, and Trem2+
foam-like macrophages
regardless of age at diet initiation. Notably, these HFD-associated populations were also enriched in old mice
maintained on NCD. Both aging under NCD and HFD exposure induced inflammatory and remodeling-related
changes in gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Moreover, transcriptional changes appearing only after 36
weeks of HFD in young mice were already evident at 24 weeks of HFD in old mice, suggesting that aging accelerates
transcriptional responses to dietary stress. Ongoing analysis of differentially accessible regions aims to identify
regulators linking age-associated epigenetic priming to atherosclerosis susceptibility. Together, our study provides a
single-cell multiomic framework for understanding increased atherogenic vulnerability in aged vasculature.
posters.P318:
Transcriptional profiling of drug-treated cells enables systematic pharmacological comparison using resources such as
the Connectivity Map (CMap) L1000 dataset. However, gene-level drug signatures are high-dimensional and
confounded by cell line-specific expression, obscuring pharmacological signal. Existing pathway-level methods reduce
dimensionality but lack a shared reference coordinate system, limiting cross-dataset comparison.
We present PATHMOR (PATHway-based Mechanism-Of-action Representation), which constructs a reference-anchored
latent space enabling projection of drug signatures across experimental contexts. PATHMOR applies pathway-wise
PCA with a data-driven variance threshold to extract biologically interpretable axes while reducing cell line-specific
variation. A context-aware two-track projection strategy supports embedding across novel contexts.
Across nine cancer cell lines and 35 MoA categories, PATHMOR outperformed ssGSEA, VEGA, and MAYA in MoA-level
separability (Cohen’s d = 2.805) and drug-level consistency. Cross-dataset validation preserved compound identity
across an independent RNA-seq platform, while cross-species validation against rat DrugMatrix transcriptomics
showed significant drug-relationship concordance in kidney tissue (Mantel r = 0.41, p < 0.05). Ginseng extract
signatures were enriched toward calcineurin and topoisomerase inhibitor MoAs, consistent with reported activities.
PATHMOR provides a generalizable MoA representation framework for drug repurposing and characterization of
poorly annotated compounds.

Cancer cachexia is a complex metabolic syndrome characterized by progressive muscle and fat loss accompanied by
systemic inflammation, which directly affects the prognosis of cancer patients, yet no approved therapeutic agent
currently exists. While muscle wasting in cachexia has been primarily studied in the context of tumor-derived factors,
the complex mechanisms involving immune cell-mediated pathways remain poorly understood. In this study, public
transcriptomic datasets covering diverse cancer types and experimental conditions were integrated to overcome
inter-dataset heterogeneity. A transcriptomic signature commonly defining cachexia across multiple conditions was
identified, from which DEGs representing core gene expression changes in cachexia were systematically selected.
