evaluate candidate drugs capable of reversing cachexia-associated transcriptomic patterns. Through this approach,
lead candidates that consistently ranked among the top candidates across multiple cachexia datasets could be
selected. Taken together, this study proposes a transcriptomics-based drug repositioning framework for identifying
therapeutic candidates in cancer cachexia. Such a strategy may serve as an effective and scalable starting point for
exploring novel treatment options in diseases where mechanistic understanding remains incomplete.

them. We reprocessed public skeletal-muscle bulk RNA-seq from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, cancer cachexia,
sarcopenia, pre-sarcopenia, inflammatory myositis and scoliosis under a single differential-expression framework,
represented each condition as a log2 fold-change vector over the union DEG feature set, and performed PCA. The
functional meaning of the principal axes was resolved by loading-level enrichment. Knowledge-graph-based drug
repurposing (DREAMwalk on a multiscale interactome) was then applied to side-specific signatures of idiopathic
scoliosis (IS), a disease for which no pharmacological treatment option currently exists. The first two components
captured 48.0% and 16.6% of the variance and ordered the conditions along a reproducible disease gradient. The IS
concave-side signature localised within the atrophic region defined by sarcopenia, pre-sarcopenia and cachexia,
whereas the convex-side signature separated from it. Repurposing returned 19 concave-side and 52 convex-side

Neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by the progressive loss of neurons in the central nervous system. Many
approaches, such as genome-wide association studies and high-throughput drug screening, have been applied to
identify novel drug candidates to counteract neuronal loss. However, there still remains a discrepancy between the
molecular information from postmortem brain tissue and the diagnostic information during disease progression. To
address this challenge, we predicted metabolite-based dementia drug candidates by screening a genome-scale
metabolic model (GEM) constructed from large-scale single-nucleus transcriptomes of neurodegenerative disorders.

tissues, including patients with synucleinopathies and Alzheimer's disease. We constructed disease-specific GEMs by

thereby enhancing metabolite prediction at single-cell resolution. Collectively, our framework establishes a scalable,
single-cell-resolved strategy for metabolite-based drug discovery that bridges brain pathology and plasma metabolomics
in neurodegenerative disorders.

Transcript abundance from RNA sequencing methods is quantified differently depending on modalities. Not only do
bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), and the emerging spatial transcriptomics yield systematically different
expression profiles from one another, but substantial variation also exists among protocols within each modality,
across sample preprocessing, sequencing chemistries, capture strategies, and library preparation methods. These issues
are widely observed yet no validated correction method currently exists. Here, we show that inter-modality
transcriptomics bias has a consistent molecular basis. Using matched bulk and single-cell based RNA-seq data from
multiple independent datasets including in-house and public datasets, we derived per-gene detection signals and
found that some transcript features, such as gene length, GC content, and intron length are associated with
inter-modality detection bias. These patterns are consistent across tissues, protocols, and datasets, indicating that
detection bias is largely transcript-intrinsic rather than platform- or sample-specific. Building on these findings, we are
developing Intrans: toward debiasing Inter-modality Transcriptomic signals that can potentially improve the reliability
of any integrative analysis bridging multi-modality RNA sequencing data.

Autoimmune connective tissue diseases (CTDs), including Sjögren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, and systemic lupus
erythematosus, are clinically distinct but often share interstitial lung disease (ILD) as a common pulmonary lung
comorbidity. This shared pulmonary comorbidity suggests that these different diseases may converge on a common
transcriptomic profile that drives lung injury and fibrosis. This study aimed to identify the autoimmune transcriptomic
programs shared across CTD ILD and to connect their immune components to systemic drug response signatures.
Single cell lung transcriptomic data from CTD ILD and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis were used to define the
transcriptomic programs shared across autoimmune CTD ILD. Methotrexate (MTX) is widely used as a first line
treatment for these autoimmune diseases, but a substantial proportion of patients do not respond well to MTX
treatment. These patients whose autoimmune activity is not controlled by first line treatment may contribute to
comorbidities such as ILD. This raises the possibility that the immune program shared across CTD ILD reflects the
same systemic immune state that separates the responders from nonresponders to MTX or TNF inhibitors (TNFi).
To examine this, RA PBMC drug response data from GSE229449 were used to find out whether the shared
autoimmune immune programs aligned with MTX or TNFi response signatures. This comparison identified
inflammatory cytokine response, leukocyte activation, and myeloid injury programs as the immune features related to
drug response. In contrast, epithelial injury, mitochondrial stress, and fibrotic remodeling were understood as lung
responses that occur downstream of the shared autoimmune profile. Together, these findings suggest that
autoimmune CTD ILD shares immune transcriptomic programs that can be connected to systemic drug response
signatures, while lung injury and fibrosis represent tissue consequences of this autoimmune program.

approaches rely on normalization decisions. In RT-qPCR, reference-gene stability can vary with tissue type and disease
state. We compared bulk RNA-seq findings from a human cartilage cohort with RT-qPCR results for a selected target
panel in a separate, larger specimen set. Six RNA-seq libraries were analyzed, three from non-arthritic and three from
osteoarthritic cartilage. RNA-seq counts were normalized for library size before group comparisons. The RT-qPCR data

reference gene showed a larger between-group shift than the other. Most detectable RT-qPCR targets retained the

comparison was significant under one normalization but not the other. The RNA-seq cohort was small and only one
target panel was examined, so these observations are exploratory. In this dataset, expression calls for a subset of

Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) exhibits substantial molecular and cognitive heterogeneity, which cannot be fully
explained by traditional single-gene analyses. Network approaches based on statistical associations were developed to
characterize coordinated molecular variation from a systems perspective. As discrepancy in cell type responses across
brain regions was indicated in AD progression, conventional population-level bulk-tissue networks obscure cell type
dependencies and regional coordination while average away individual variation. A multiregional framework is needed
to characterize the organization underlying heterogeneous AD progression.

construct the network of networks spanning 7 cortical regions and 16 cell types, modeling the coordination within and
across brain regions. Bootstrap network reconstruction combined with jackknife-after-bootstrap was used to derive
donor-level network representations. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis integrated network features with cell composition,
gene-module and pathophysiological phenotypes.

across four pathological stages. Factors summarized the consistency between donor-level states and molecular responses
across pathological contexts, highlighting system states relating network reconfiguration to cognitive variation.

smaller, soluble Aβ-oligomers (sAβo) are the main cause of AD. In this study, we used a Caenorhabditis elegans model

Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is characterized by chronic sinonasal inflammation and polyp
formation and frequently co-occurs with inflammatory conditions of the lower respiratory tract. The basis of this
interdependence remains unclear. We performed single-cell and spatial transcriptomics on sinonasal tissues from

Despite advances in LC–MS instrumentation and computation, conventional lipidomics workflows often rely on MS/MS
from a single adduct, leaving complementary structural information from other adducts underutilized. This limitation
complicates sphingolipid identification, particularly for isomeric and isobaric species. We developed MA-MS², a
rule-guided framework for sphingolipid annotation through multi-adduct MS/MS integration.

experimental MS/MS spectra acquired across multiple adducts from mouse ear, brain, and liver tissues and NIST SRM
1950 plasma. Its reliability was supported by ECN–retention time relationships, with R² ≥ 0.98 for 20 of 25 subclasses.

feature-specific diagnostic ions. The algorithm reports MS2-spectrum cosine similarity, evaluates matches between
rule-derived and observed ions for each adduct, and integrates evidence across adducts.

Workbench ST002195. Of these, 65.1% had MS/MS spectra for at least two adducts. Retention times of matched lipid
species correlated strongly with MA-MS² library across eight sphingolipid groups (r = 0.978–1.000). This framework
enabled reliable annotation and in-depth identification by routine LC–MS/MS.

analytical infrastructure and mismatched clinical contexts hamper the reuse of public data. Here, we proposed a
robust workflow for data reuse, integration, and interpretation in clinical metabolomics by evaluating the reusability of
Korea Metabolomics Data Repository KAP242412 in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) experimental cohort.

Lupus nephritis (LN) is one of the most severe complications of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and can progress to
end-stage renal disease without appropriate treatment. Current standard induction therapies include immunosuppressive
agents such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and cyclophosphamide. However, a substantial proportion of patients
fail to achieve complete remission, and reliable biomarkers for predicting treatment response before therapy remain
limited. In this study, we analyzed pretreatment glomerular transcriptomic profiles from kidney biopsies of patients
with LN to identify gene expression signatures associated with renal treatment response. Differential expression
analysis revealed distinct pretreatment glomerular gene expression patterns between responders and non-responders.
These differentially expressed genes were used as candidate features to compare five machine-learning models,
among which Elastic Net showed the best overall performance (mean AUC = 0.953). A transcriptomic risk score
derived from the Elastic Net coefficients clearly distinguished responders from non-responders. Furthermore, the
signature maintained its discriminatory ability in an independent external LN biopsy cohort (AUC = 0.889). These
findings suggest that pretreatment kidney transcriptomic profiling may help stratify patients with LN according to their
likelihood of treatment response and support more personalized therapeutic decision-making in lupus nephritis.

inherits research ascertainment bias. Transcriptional effects of gene perturbation, in contrast, require no prior
knowledge. We hypothesized that foundation-model embeddings of these effects would predict lifespan effects with

model pretrained on large-scale cross-species transcriptomes, and evaluated prediction on 116 manually validated
genes (59 increasing, 57 decreasing). Perturbation embeddings separated the two classes with a leave-one-out AUROC

an LLM-based workflow that reads lifespan assays reported as text, tables or survival curves and infers lifespan
change. The workflow matched manual curation for 16 of 18 genes and is extending labels to 174 genes (94

Single-cell drug screening is difficult to scale across combinations of cell lines, perturbations, and doses. Artificial
intelligence models can easily predict single-cell gene expression responses under unmeasured conditions for drugs
observed during training. However, for unseen drugs, existing models usually rely on chemical structure, which does
not directly reflect drug mechanisms. Here, we propose BINDR (Biologically Informed Network for Drug Response), a
generative framework that embeds biological knowledge into drug and gene representations without structural
information. BINDR learns a disentangled basal cell state through adversarial training, to which covariate and drug
vectors are added. The drug module extracts mechanism-centered subgraphs from the Precision Medicine Knowledge

post-treatment expression. On sci-Plex3 with nine fully held-out drugs, BINDR achieved an overall R² of 0.939 and

from 0.923 while reducing decoder parameters. As a structure-independent framework, BINDR could extend in silico

Aging impairs redox homeostasis and energy metabolism in brown adipose tissue (BAT), but molecular targets linking
these alterations to systemic metabolic decline remain unclear. We integrated temporal bulk transcriptomics,
single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and paired BAT transcriptomic and plasma metabolomic profiling to identify and
characterize candidate regulators. Functional validation involved adipocyte-targeted Acss1 restoration in BAT of

Prior-fitted networks (PFNs) predict survival curves in context without per-dataset training; their accuracy should
depend on how well the synthetic pretraining prior covers the data-generating process. We pretrained a
4.5M-parameter SurvPFN-architecture transformer under a Weibull-only or a mixed prior (Weibull, log-normal,
piecewise-exponential), two seeds each, and compared it with the public SurvivalPFN checkpoint, linear Cox, DeepSurv,

crossing hazards, log-normal AFT) at 20% and 60% censoring, 10 datasets per condition. We report integrated
squared error (ISE) against true survival curves as paired geometric-mean ratios (GMR). Under crossing hazards (20%
censoring), the mixed-prior PFN reduced ISE versus Cox-Time (GMR 0.31, 95% CI 0.25-0.39) and SurvivalPFN (0.43,

0.74-1.52) but trailed Cox-Time under nonlinear PH (1.23, 1.03-1.48). Broadening the prior helped mainly the added
families (crossing 0.72, log-normal 0.92, PH about 1.0). Harrell's C from predicted survival at t=12 scored the true

context, facilitating the examination of cellular interactions and the context-dependent effects of local tissue
microenvironments on cellular states. However, existing foundation models are primarily pretrained on single-cell RNA

transcriptional variability and facilitates the identification of niche-specific gene signatures associated with cell–cell
communication. This approach provides a scalable and generalizable solution for decoding spatial transcriptomic
landscapes and offers new opportunities to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying tumor heterogeneity
and microenvironmental regulation.

Thyroid cancer is a highly heterogeneous disease, with its characteristics varying depending on various mutations. To
understand this complexity, numerous studies have been conducted at the transcriptome level, yet the epigenetic
landscape remains poorly understood. In this study, single-nucleus ATAC-seq (snATAC-seq) was obtained from 9
samples of three different subtypes, including follicular thyroid cancer (FTC), papillary thyroid cancer (PTC), and
anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC). Malignant epithelial cells were classified using established thyroid cancer-related gene
sets—specifically, thyroid differentiation (TDS) and ERK signaling scores—revealing heterogeneous distributions across
cancer subtypes and patient samples. Identification of cell type-specific transcription factors revealed unique
regulatory mechanisms shaping cellular identity and tumor behavior. Integration of external methylation datasets
demonstrated a clear association between chromatin accessibility at CpG sites and DNA methylation status.
Furthermore, enhancer-driven regulation varied by cell type, and promoter-enhancer interactions supported by
predicted Hi-C data indicated changes in 3D genome structure. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of
the distinct epigenetic regulation of thyroid cancer subtypes and is expected to contribute to the development of
subtype-specific therapeutic strategies.

Gene expression is regulated by multiple epigenetic factors including chromatin structure. Single cell chromatin
accessibility data combined with transcription factor (TF) binding motif information enhances our understanding of
gene expression regulation. However, enhancer-driven gene regulation remains limited due to the lack of promoter￾enhancer interaction data. Here, we developed TENET+, a tool for reconstructing enhancer-driven gene regulatory
networks (eGRN) by integrating single cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data. By leveraging causal
relationship inference based on pseudo-time-ordered gene expression and chromatin accessibility, TENET+ predicts
interaction between TF expression, target gene expression, and open chromatin regions including long-range enhancer.
Applying TENET+ to a paired scRNAseq and scATACseq dataset of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, we
identified critical regulators and their epigenetic regulations. Interestingly, TENET+ exhibited a superior performance to
predict promoter-enhancer interactions provided by cell type-specific Hi-C datasets compared with other motif-based
GRN reconstruction tools. Notably, TENET+ demonstrates competitive performance in ChIP-seq validation compared to
other tools, even without relying on motif information We identified key regulatory factors in CD4 T cell, and
subsequent siRNA knockdown experiments confirmed that their target genes were indeed regulated by these identified
factors. Overall, TENET+ provides a robust framework for reconstructing eGRN with a single-cell resolution.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains one of the most fatal global health challenges, ranking second only to cancer.
Understanding the complexities of CVD requires high-resolution analysis at the cellular level, as traditional bulk
sequencing is limited to providing averaged gene expression profiles that obscure critical shifts in specific cell
populations like cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts.
In this study, we constructed a comprehensive multi-omic single-cell atlas to identify disease-specific gene expression
patterns and chromatin structures. By integrating scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, VisiumHD, and scDNAmethylation-seq, we
characterized genetic diversity within cardiac pathologies and identified specific cardiomyocyte clusters associated with
cardiac aging. Notably, we pinpointed potential stem cell populations exhibiting high expression of differentiation￾related genes. Pathway-based gene set scoring revealed that these progenitor-like clusters are characterized by
elevated YAP signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers.
Furthermore, trajectory analysis using scATAC-seq data highlighted key transcription factors, such as TRPS1, that play
a pivotal role in cellular transitions. Finally, by applying the Horvath gene list, we successfully identified aging-specific
cell clusters from an epigenetic perspective. These findings provide a high-resolution molecular roadmap for
understanding the progression of heart disease and the mechanisms of cardiac aging.

Tumor tissues are composed of malignant subclones with diverse genetic profiles. Reconstructing the evolutionary
trajectory of these subclones is crucial for understanding how tumors acquire malignant traits. However, current
approaches to subclonal tree reconstruction are limited either by their reliance on single-cell DNA sequencing
(scDNA-seq) which involve a small number of cells and thus yield low-resolution results, or using single-cell RNA
sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, which despite including larger cell populations, remain susceptible to bias from high
dropout rates and technical noise. Here, we introduce CluVar, an autoencoder-based framework for inferring the
phylogeny of cancer subclones from scRNA-seq data using mutation profile analysis. To address the extensive missing
variant information inherent in scRNA-seq datasets, CluVar incorporates a customized loss function and multiple
hidden layers optimized for clustering. CluVar demonstrated superior performance in reconstructing phylogenetic trees
of cancer subclones under a range of erroneous conditions. When applied to cancer scRNA-seq data, the phylogenetic
tree predicted using CluVar aligned well with the transcriptomic profiles. These findings highlight its utility for tracing
evolutionary trajectories and identifying novel variants associated with cancer progression.

posters.P074:
Postzygotic mosaic variants can establish cancerized fields within normal tissues, providing a genetic basis for field
cancerization. Patients harboring such variants would be classified as sporadic cases, lacking family history and
germline variant findings, potentially leaving their cancer susceptibility underrecognized. However, conventional
tumor-normal analysis often misses these variants because shared signals are removed during germline subtraction
and low-VAF alleles are difficult to call at standard coverage. To address this, we developed a tumor-informed
detection pipeline for standard-depth WES (~50–100×) that recovers tumor-normal shared variants in cancer driver
genes while distinguishing them from germline variants, technical artifacts, and tumor-in-normal contamination.
Applied to the TCGA breast cancer cohort (n=661), the pipeline identified candidate mosaic driver variants in a subset
of patients, including PIK3CA and MLLT10. Because tumor-normal sharing alone cannot establish a genuine cancerized
field, we further evaluated variants to distinguish true field formation from independent hotspot recurrence and
non-carcinogenic clonal expansion in normal tissue. This framework enables systematic recovery and evaluation of
mosaic field events and, when extended across cancer types, could define their contribution to tumor initiation and
clarify how cancers arise from precancerized normal tissue.

talks.title: Efficient Pretraining of Cell Foundation Models through Metacell Compression
talks.speaker: Yurim Jung
talks.text:
Seoul 03722, Republic of Korea
Single-cell foundation models learn transferable representations from large-scale transcriptomic
data, but conventional pretraining processes tens of millions of sparse cells independently,
creating substantial computational redundancy. We present MetacellFormer, a foundation
model pretrained on biologically structured metacells. We compressed 43.4 million human
scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq training cells from 1,223 sources into 799,562 metacells, reducing
the number of training examples 54.3-fold. Structured metacells preserved coherent
biological structure and showed stronger cell-type homogeneity and recovery of functional
gene relationships than size-matched random pooling. One complete corpus pass required
approximately 3.5 hours with metacells versus 203 hours with individual cells. Under
matched cumulative wall-clock budgets, metacell pretraining consistently outperformed
single-cell pretraining across six representative benchmarks spanning cell-level tasks (cell
annotation and cross-study drug-response prediction), gene-level tasks (HumanNet and
pathway retrieval), and perturbation-level tasks (exact and functional perturbation retrieval).
Against Geneformer v1/v2, scGPT, and scFoundation, MetacellFormer ranked within the top
two models in five of six benchmarks, including best performance in HumanNet,
cross-study drug-response prediction, and both perturbation retrieval tasks. These results
establish biologically structured metacell compression as an efficient strategy for scaling
single-cell foundation model pretraining.

talks.title: Skiver: Reference-free quality control of metagenomic sequencing datasets using (k,v)-mer sketches
talks.speaker: Gu Zhenhao
talks.text:
, Puru Sharma1
, Limsoon Wong1
, Niranjan Nagarajan1,2
1National University of Singapore
2Genome Institute of Singapore
Background. Quality control of sequencing datasets is an important first step in numerous
bioinformatics pipelines such as mapping, variant calling, and assembly. Existing methods
typically rely on alignment results or quality scores. However, the reference genome is not
always available for mapping, and uncalibrated quality scores may yield biased estimates
of error rates.
Results. We present skiver, a reference-free and alignment-free algorithm that estimates
sequencing error rates and calibrates Phred quality scores using (k,v)-mer sketches. By
identifying the consensus from the sketched (k,v)-mers, skiver estimates survival and
hazard rates that capture positional information of sequencing errors. Across simulated
and real datasets from various sequencing platforms, skiver accurately recovers sequencing
error rates and the proportion of different error types. We further demonstrate its ability
to calibrate Phred scores. It also reliably handles complex datasets containing multiple
strains, alleles, and repetitive regions through an iterative outlier filtering strategy. Skiver is
computationally efficient and supports tools that need accurate sequencing error rate
estimates or quality scores as prior knowledge.

Noisy Reads for DNA Data Storage

present GACHA, a scalable clustering framework based on the observation that a read
need not admit a single globally reliable similarity representation; instead, repeated

clustering passes. GACHA combines randomized multi-strobe candidate generation,

talks.title: Enhancing gene annotation completeness in insects and expanding to challenging gene families
talks.speaker: Takako Mochizuki
talks.text:
Advances in genome sequencing have generated genomic resources for an increasing
number of insect species. However, understanding the molecular basis of insect diversity
requires accurate identification of gene loci, structures, and functions across a broad range
of species, beyond well-established model organisms such as Drosophila melanogaster.
Despite the growing availability of insect genome assemblies, incomplete gene annotations
remain a major obstacle to understanding species-specific biological characteristics.
This presentation focuses on two major challenges in insect gene annotation and our
approaches to overcoming them. The first is the limited availability of transcriptomic
evidence, which can lead to the omission of genes expressed only in specific tissues or
developmental stages. We address this issue in the ladybird beetle Harmonia axyridis by
integrating publicly available RNA-seq datasets to re-evaluate gene models. The second
challenge concerns gene families with low sequence conservation or short functionally
important regions, which are difficult to identify accurately using conventional automated
annotation methods. Using neuropeptides and their receptors in the two-spotted cricket
Gryllus bimaculatus as an example, we present approaches to refining gene structures,
developing curated annotation datasets, and identifying candidate neuropeptide–receptor
pairs through AI-based three-dimensional protein structure prediction.
Together, these studies demonstrate how integrating diverse transcriptomic evidence,
targeted gene annotation, and AI-assisted structural analysis can improve the completeness
and functional utility of insect genome annotations, providing more reliable genomic
resources for comparative and functional studies.

talks.title: Drug development using network medicine
talks.speaker: Sanguk Kim
talks.text:
A major challenge in drug development is the limited translatability of preclinical toxicity
findings to human outcomes, largely owing to biological differences between humans and
model organisms. This gap contributes to high attrition rates in clinical trials and
post-marketing drug withdrawals. Existing toxicity prediction methods rely primarily on
chemical properties and typically do not account for these interspecies differences. We
developed a machine-learning framework that incorporates genotype-phenotype differences
(GPDs) between preclinical models (cell lines and mice) and humans to improve the
prediction of human drug toxicity. Clinical risk information for drugs (e.g., clinical trials or
post-marketing surveillance) was obtained without bias from published reports, data sources,
and databases. GPDs in drug targets were assessed across three biological contexts: gene
essentiality, tissue expression profiles, and network connectivity. We benchmarked the
GPD-based model against state-of-the-art toxicity predictors and evaluated its performance
using independent datasets and chronological validation. Our model outperformed
state-of-the-art models based on chemical structure and demonstrated a practical ability to
anticipate future drug withdrawals in real-world settings. Interpretation: Incorporating
differences in genotype-phenotype relationships offers a biologically grounded strategy for
predicting drug toxicity. Our framework enables the early identification of high-risk drugs in
clinical development. This approach could reduce development costs, improve patient safety,
and increase the success rate of therapeutic approvals. We further develop computational
methods to predict patient-specific drug responses using network biology.

talks.title: MoE-Bind: Guiding De Novo Protein Binder Generation with Sparse Experts
talks.speaker: Dipayan Sarkar
talks.text:
Computational Systems Biology Lab, Department of Bioinformatics, University of North Bengal
De novo protein binder design remains dominated by structure-based pipelines requiring
pre-resolved three-dimensional target conformations and substantial per-design compute.
Sequence-only generative models offer a lighter alternative but remain uniformly dense,
unlike sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures favoured in language models for
decoupling capacity from per-token compute, and many reintroduce structural
computation at inference via external predictors for candidate selection, reinstating that
dependency and latency. We present MoE-Bind, an autoregressive protein binder
generator combining Multi-head Latent Attention with a sparse MoE, generating and
ranking binders intrinsically from sequence alone, without external structure prediction.
Despite activating less than half the per-token parameters of compute-matched dense
baselines, MoE-Bind matches or exceeds them on receptor-conditioned binder generation,
validated under Boltz-2 and AlphaFold2-Multimer, achieving a 24.4% hit rate and reducing
training compute by over 56%, and transfers without peptide-specific training to short
peptide design, recovering reference-level peptide binders. Routing analysis reveals
interpretable expert specialization at the amino acid and biochemical group level, with
dedicated experts for charged and aromatic residues, indicating that biological routing
diverges fundamentally from the diffuse specialization reported in natural language MoE
models. These findings collectively demonstrate that sparse architectural design delivers
fast, interpretable, structure-free binder generation, complementing structure-based design
pipelines.

talks.title: Scale-Resolved Diagnostics Reveal the Operational Boundaries of Plant Genomic Language Models
talks.speaker: Dasol Kim
talks.text:
Genomic language models (gLMs) are increasingly used to score genomic variants, but
the biological scale they represent remains uncertain. Sequence constraint, molecular
consequence, and phenotype association are related but distinct quantities. We
investigated where zero-shot plant gLM scores remain informative and where their signal
stops. Using the Plant gLM Evaluation Framework, we evaluated GPN, PlantCaduceus, and
AgroNT across sequence, molecular, and phenotype scales in rice (227 accessions, six
traits), Arabidopsis (1,001 accessions, eight traits), and maize (~233 lines, three traits). At
the sequence scale, the models captured codon grammar and generalized across the
angiosperm phylogeny. The single-nucleotide models achieved approximately 85% accuracy
in identifying codon position, compared with 69% for the 6-mer model, but this signal
did not consistently extend to higher biological scales. Gene-level variant-effect scores
showed minimal correspondence with genome-wide association statistics (|ρ| ≤ 0.07).
Embedding-based prediction provided no phenotype information beyond genotype
relatedness and outperformed genomic best linear unbiased prediction only when the
genotype baseline was near zero. Supervised probing recovered codon grammar but
added at most 0.03 over a codon-only baseline. A reported gLM–LD enrichment was
largely explained by linkage disequilibrium. These results define a scale-bounded role for
plant gLMs: they are useful for interpreting sequence-level information and prioritizing
rare, coding, and conserved variants, whereas breeding applications will require trait-aware
supervision.

talks.title: Scalable genomic approaches to investigate cellular dynamics in aging and disease
talks.speaker: Junyue Cao
talks.text:
Cell populations change across the lifespan through coordinated shifts in abundance,
state, proliferation, and molecular regulation, yet these dynamics remain difficult to
measure systematically across tissues, time, and space. We have developed scalable
genomic approaches that combine high-throughput single-cell profiling, spatial genomics,
and multiplexed genetic perturbation to investigate these processes in mammalian aging
and disease. Using EasySci-based single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling across
multiple organs and ages, we mapped age-associated changes among more than 500
primary cell types and 2,000 cellular subtypes. These studies revealed nonlinear, stage-like
population dynamics, including early waves of cell depletion followed by later expansions,
together with coordinated changes among related lineages across organs. Spatial mapping
with IRISeq further identified tissue niches enriched for aging-associated cell populations
and their interactions, providing anatomical context for organism-wide changes. To move
from descriptive atlases toward mechanism, PerturbSci-Kinetics and Perturb-Fate integrate
pooled genetic perturbation with single-cell multimodal readouts and measurements of
transcriptome dynamics, enabling direct interrogation of regulators that control cell-state
transitions and population behavior. Together, these technologies provide a framework for
connecting cellular dynamics across time and space to the regulatory programs that drive
them. I will discuss how these approaches reveal shared principles of mammalian aging,
define interactions between immune and tissue-resident populations, and support
systematic investigation of disease-associated cellular states.

talks.title: Towards a Causal Map of Human Cell-State Dynamics
talks.speaker: Jong-Eun Park
talks.text:
Comprehensive maps of human cell states must capture both population-scale diversity
and the regulatory mechanisms that drive state transitions. We developed PANGEA, a
cross-tissue single-cell and spatial atlas assembled through automated retrieval and uniform
reprocessing of raw sequencing data from more than 500 studies and over 2,000 datasets.
Harmonized metadata and hierarchical cell classification enable robust comparison across
organs, diseases, and individuals and reveal conserved as well as context-dependent
cell-state programs. Building on this atlas, we developed Sceleto, a suite of atlas-informed
algorithms for marker discovery and scalable batch correction. Sceleto uses the breadth
and harmonized structure of PANGEA to identify reproducible cell-type and cell-state
markers across heterogeneous datasets, improving annotation and cross-study
comparability. To move from descriptive mapping to causal inference, we performed
large-scale perturb-seq experiments in human dermal fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem
cells, overexpressing 200 transcription factor open reading frames. These perturbations
mapped gene regulatory networks controlling fibroblast activation and lineage plasticity
and distinguished broadly shared regulatory programs from cell-context-specific
mechanisms. Together, PANGEA, Sceleto, and fibroblast perturb-seq connect comprehensive
observational maps with computational interpretation and experimental perturbation,
providing an integrated framework for predicting human cell identity, plasticity, and
disease-associated state transitions and advancing the development of virtual cell models.

talks.speaker: Jae Kyoung Kim
talks.text:
The reliability of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis is often hindered by
subjective parameter tuning and stochastic inconsistencies, which pose significant
challenges for the reproducibility of large-scale studies. To overcome these limitations and
establish a rigorous foundation for single-cell foundation models, we propose a fully
data-driven analysis framework based on mathematical and physical theories. Centrally, we
introduce scLENS, which utilizes Random Matrix Theory (RMT) to distinguish biological
signals from random noise. By employing RMT-based noise filtering and a signal
robustness test, scLENS enables the objective determination of signal dimensions without
manual intervention, ensuring high-fidelity feature extraction even in sparse datasets.
Complementing this, scICE evaluates clustering consistency through the Inconsistency
Coefficient (IC), providing a scalable and efficient way to identify stable cellular identities
across tens of thousands of cells. By replacing subjective heuristics with robust,
theory-based signal detection and evaluation, this integrated approach provides the
essential high-quality, standardized data processing required to train and deploy reliable,
large-scale single-cell foundation models in the era of artificial intelligence.

talks.title: Uncalling Structural Variant Artifacts
talks.speaker: Heng Li
talks.text:
Structural variants (SVs) have significant genetic consequences but remain challenging to
detect accurately. Although many long-read SV callers have been published, they suffer
from high error rates in low-complexity regions and often lack the precision required to
call rare somatic or de novo SVs. In this talk, I will showcase various artifacts in germline
and somatic SV calling and explain the underlying mechanisms behind them. I will then
present effective computational strategies, including assembly and pangenome-based
approaches, to substantially alleviate these SV calling errors to an accuracy practical for
downstream applications.

talks.title: High nitrogen-induced changes in rhizosphere microbial community structure can modulate disease susceptibility to the rice blast
talks.speaker: Junhyun Jeon
talks.text:
Nitrogen-induced susceptibility (NIS) in rice, where excess nitrogen (N) enhances
vulnerability to Magnaporthe oryzae, has been observed but remains mechanistically
unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the rhizosphere microbiome plays a central role in
mediating NIS. Using an experimental system that separates nitrogen effects from plant
growth changes, we found that high N levels significantly reshape bacterial and fungal
community composition, enrich salicylate-degrading and effector-secreting microbial
functions, and suppress key defense genes including OsPAL06 and OsPR10b. Our findings
revealed that both nitrogen treatment and pathogen infection significantly influence
rhizosphere community composition, with a strong interaction between the two factors.
Network analysis further revealed reduced microbial connectivity and loss of keystone taxa
under high N and infection conditions. Strikingly, microbiome transplant from high-N,
infected plants to standard-N reproduced the NIS phenotype and immune suppression,
highlighting a microbiome legacy effect. These findings suggest that excess nitrogen
selects for functionally immune-suppressive microbial consortia that persist independently
of nutrient status, and position the rhizosphere microbiome as a key determinant of NIS,
with implications for microbial diagnostics and nutrient-informed disease management.

talks.title: A Machine Learning Model for Discrimination of Plant Abiotic Stresses Using Transcriptomic Profiling Data
talks.speaker: Minkyu Park
talks.text:
Abiotic stresses are primary constraints on global crop productivity, reducing yields by up
to 80%. While traditional phenotypic sensing detects stress only after physiological
symptoms emerge and often fails to discriminate specific stressor types, transcriptomic
profiling offers a high-dimensional solution, capturing rapid and sensitive molecular shifts.
In this study, we developed AbiOmics, the first end-to-end machine learning pipeline
specifically designed to identify and discriminate among multiple stressors. This approach
represents a previously undocumented method for stress specification using large-scale
transcriptomic big data. We identified 320 stress-specific marker genes using a curated
collection of 1,243 transcriptomes of Arabidopsis samples treated with four major abiotic
stresses, salt, cold, heat, and drought. A single-layer perceptron model trained on these
features achieved 91% accuracy during five-fold cross-validation and 93% accuracy on an
independent test set. The model demonstrated an unprecedented capacity to generalize
to multi-stress conditions, identifying concurrent signatures in combinatorial salt-and-heat
treatments. By integrating marker identification with SHAP-based biological interpretation,
AbiOmics provides a rigorously validated diagnostic tool superior to conventional sensing.
This framework establishes a high-confidence labeling strategy for AI-driven crop
management and precision breeding to mitigate climate change impacts.

talks.title: From Immune Networks to OsWAK16: New Insights into Rice Resistance to Bacterial Leaf Streak
talks.speaker: Siwaret Arikit
talks.text:
Bacterial leaf streak (BLS), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola (Xoc), is an
emerging bacterial disease that threatens sustainable rice production worldwide. Despite
its increasing importance, the molecular basis of host resistance remains poorly
understood, limiting the development of resistant cultivars. In this seminar, I will present
our recent efforts to elucidate the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying BLS
resistance by integrating transcriptomics, genomics, and functional genetics. Comparative
transcriptome analysis of resistant and susceptible rice genotypes following Xoc infection
revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming associated with immune signaling,
protein quality control, reactive oxygen species homeostasis, and cell wall-associated
defense. These findings established a comprehensive framework of rice defense responses
and highlighted several promising candidate genes involved in BLS resistance. To identify
causal resistance genes, we subsequently combined whole-genome resequencing with
QTL-seq analysis in a segregating population derived from Thai rice germplasm. This
approach identified a major resistance locus on chromosome 2 and led to the discovery
of OsWAK16, a previously uncharacterized wall-associated kinase associated with BLS
resistance. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of OsWAK16 significantly increased susceptibility
to Xoc, providing direct functional evidence that this gene plays an essential role in host
resistance. Together, these studies establish a pipeline from genome-wide discovery to
functional validation and identify OsWAK16 as a novel genetic resource for rice
improvement. The findings advance our understanding of rice immunity against bacterial
leaf streak and provide new opportunities for developing durable disease-resistant rice
cultivars through molecular breeding.

talks.title: Grounding Foundation Models in Population-Scale Variation for Soybean Predictive Breeding
talks.speaker: Kyung Do Kim
talks.text:
Crop improvement now depends on integrating genomic, phenotypic, and environmental
data generated at very different scales. Large language models (LLMs) and genomic
foundation models (FMs) — pretrained on large unlabeled text or sequence corpora to
yield transferable representations — offer a way to link such heterogeneous evidence. It
remains unclear, however, how these general-purpose models can be grounded in
species-specific variation so their outputs become testable breeding hypotheses. Here I
review recent progress in LLMs and FMs for plant breeding and show that a
population-scale variation catalog in soybean (Glycine max) provides the substrate such
grounding requires. From 2,737 resequenced global accessions, 2,503 passed filtering and
yielded 6,751,716 SNPs for population structure and domestication analysis; read-depth
profiling added 2,172 genic large deletions and 529 gene-containing CNV regions,
including Rhg1, GA2ox8, and Ps. This joint SNP–structural variation space can be encoded
as model input for genotype representations supporting imputation, allele-effect inference,
and cross-germplasm trait prediction. The framework outlines a route from population
variation to model-generated, experimentally testable hypotheses.

Extracellular vesicles (EVs) circulate systemically, but unbiased identification and molecular
characterization of recipient cells in vivo remain challenging. We developed DNA-barcoded
EVs (tagged EVs) compatible with single-cell RNA sequencing, enabling simultaneous
quantification of EV-associated barcodes and recipient-cell transcriptomes. Following systemic
administration of MC38 colorectal cancer-derived tagged EVs in mice, analysis of scRNA-seq
data detected barcodes in 68.3% of cells and revealed cell-type-specific variation in EV
uptake. High-barcode cells were enriched for myeloid populations, while smooth muscle
cells (SMCs) emerged as previously unrecognized recipients. Barcode–gene expression
correlation and trajectory analyses associated increasing barcode load in SMCs with a
distinct trajectory characterized by vascular contractility and remodeling programs. Spatial
and endothelial analyses further identified an SMC-associated vascular niche in which EV
enrichment coincided with endothelial states linked to permeability and vascular remodeling.
Application to liver and spleen resolved tissue-specific recipient-cell hierarchies, demonstrating
applicability beyond the lung. These findings establish tagged EVs as a quantitative,
sequencing-compatible approach for connecting EV uptake with recipient-cell identity and
transcriptional state in vivo. Its adaptable barcode design may support uptake tracing of
EVs derived from different cancer types across diverse target organs, providing a broadly
applicable framework for investigating EV biodistribution and cell-specific responses.

talks.title: Large-scale Single-Cell and Bulk Transcriptomic Integration Reveals Aging-Associated Cell States and Shared Molecular Signatures in Human Skeletal Muscle
talks.speaker: Xiaohang Zhang
talks.text:
Skeletal muscle aging is marked by declining contractile and regenerative capacity, yet the
cellular states driving these changes remain incompletely understood. Although single-cell
sequencing resolves cellular heterogeneity, findings from individual studies are limited by
sample size and technical variation. We therefore integrated human skeletal muscle
scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq datasets from 42 younger and 56 older donors, totaling
approximately 700,000 cells and nuclei. Cross-cohort harmonization was performed with
scVI while accounting for donor- and platform-associated effects. The integrated atlas
identified ten major cell populations, with focused analyses of muscle stem cells (MuSCs),
fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs), and myofibers. Among three MuSC subclusters, TNF+
MuSCs were enriched in younger muscle but depleted with age. PRG4+ FAPs increased in
older donors and displayed extracellular-matrix remodeling, hypoxia, mTORC1, apoptosis,
and p53 programs, whereas MME+ FAPs declined, indicating loss of an immune-responsive
stromal state. Aging myofibers showed increased SAA1+ and myotendinous-junction
states, alongside reduced neuromuscular-junction-associated and type II states. Integration
with three independent bulk RNA-seq cohorts identified ANXA1, BGN, PLXNB2, SFRP1, and
CDKN1A as shared aging-associated genes. Together, these findings reveal coordinated,
cell-type-specific stromal remodeling, regenerative impairment, and metabolic–contractile
decline in human skeletal muscle aging.

Multiome RNA-velocity methods emit several per-gene quantities — a transcription rate α, a degradation rate γ, and a chromatin-to-transcription lag — each proposed as a
biological readout. A derived quantity is usable only if it is reliable: reproducible across
algorithms and consistent with independent measurement. Across up to five velocity arms
(an RNA-only scVelo floor plus MultiVelo, MultiVeloVAE, MoFlow and CRAK-Velo) on
human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (10x Multiome), we tested each output
on four axes: cross-method reproducibility, a causal within-lineage ATAC-shuffle control,
replication in five external multiomes, and anchoring to measured synthesis and
degradation rates. Only α reproduced across methods (Spearman ρ=0.88); the lag
reproduced weakly in magnitude (strongest pair +0.163), only at chance in sign (54.6%),
and was unchanged by ATAC shuffling, marking it model-structural. γ was fragile (ρ≈−
0.1) and ran reversed against measured half-life (−0.224). Fitted α tracked measured
synthesis (+0.24 to +0.29), but transcript abundance tracked it at least as strongly (+0.410
versus +0.262) — consistency evidence, not α-specific accuracy. The α-over-lag ordering
held in all six systems; the sixth was preregistered and passed six-of-six, sealed before
fitting. Trust α against an abundance baseline; treat lag, sign, timing and γ as requiring
orthogonal validation.

The evolutionary trajectory of glioblastoma (GBM) is a multifaceted biological process that
extends beyond genetic alterations alone. Here, we perform an integrative proteogenomic
analysis of 123 longitudinal glioblastoma pairs and identify a highly proliferative cellular
state at diagnosis and its replacement by activation of neuronal transition and
synaptogenic pathways in recurrent tumors. Proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses
reveal that the molecular transition to a neuronal state at recurrence is marked by
post-translational activation of the wingless-related integration site (WNT)/planar cell
polarity (PCP) signaling pathway and BRAF protein kinase. Consistently, multi-omic analysis
of patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models mirrors similar patterns of evolutionary
trajectory. Inhibition of B-raf proto-oncogene (BRAF) kinase impairs both neuronal
transition and migration capability of recurrent tumor cells, phenotypic hallmarks of
post-therapy progression. Combinatorial treatment of temozolomide (TMZ) with the BRAF
inhibitor, vemurafenib, significantly extends the survival of PDX models. This study
provides comprehensive insights into the biological mechanisms of glioblastoma evolution
and treatment resistance, highlighting promising therapeutic strategies for clinical
intervention.

talks.title: Comprehensive proteogenomic characterization of medulloblastoma
talks.speaker: Youngwook Kim
talks.text:
Current treatment strategies for medulloblastoma remain ineffective owing to extensive
tumor heterogeneity. We generated five platforms of omics data including liquid
chromatography and mass spectrometry-based proteome and performed integrated
multi-omic characterization to improve the conventional molecular classification of
medulloblastoma. We identified seven refined distinct subtypes. The sonic hedgehog (SHH)
group was reclassified into two subgroups, SHHα and SHHβ, whereas group 4 was
divided into three subgroups, G4α, G4β, and G4γ. SHH and group 4 subtypes exhibit two
distinct neuronal differentiation trajectories: granular neuron and unipolar brush cell
differentiation (SHHβ and G4γ, respectively), both of which associated with more favorable
clinical outcomes. Furthermore, we uncovered unique proteomic and kinomic properties
that conferred increased treatment vulnerabilities to targeted therapeutic interventions
against each of the three medulloblastoma subtypes associated with poor clinical
outcomes. We demonstrated the therapeutic potential of exploiting these vulnerabilities by
utilizing a proteasome inhibitor and subtype-specific agents, including CDK1/2, PARP,
CLK1, and MET inhibitors. Mechanistic insights were further elucidated through in-depth
proteome analyses. Our study qualifies the use of proteomic signatures and activation of
neuronal differentiation trajectories to tailor selective therapeutic opportunities for distinct
subgroups of patients with medulloblastoma.

talks.title: Integrating Multi-omics and Clinical Data into Practice: The Multi-omics Journey to Decoding Precision Medicine for Breast Cancer
talks.speaker: Yeon Hee Park
talks.text:
Asian breast cancer exhibits distinct biological features, including a higher proportion of
luminal B disease, a more immune-active tumor microenvironment, and greater prevalence
of BRCA1/2 and TP53 alterations. However, landmark genomic studies have predominantly
involved Western cohorts. We present the CUBRICS study, a whole-genome sequencing
(WGS) analysis of 1,364 Korean breast cancers integrated with clinical outcomes (Kim R
and Park YH et al., Nature 2026). We identified 41 driver genes, including four novel
drivers, and characterized mutational signatures, homologous recombination deficiency
(HRD, 23.1%), structural variants including ERBB2 enhancer hijacking, extrachromosomal
DNA (28.4% of tumors), and copy-number alteration timing indicating that genomic
instability begins decades before diagnosis. Notably, the APOBEC3A/3B germline deletion
was markedly enriched in Koreans (31.8% vs 8.5% in Europeans), modifying tumor
mutagenesis. Clinically, HRD showed context-dependent implications: superior disease-free
survival with adjuvant chemotherapy in triple-negative disease, yet strong resistance to
CDK4/6 inhibitors in HR-positive disease. ERBB2 copy number (≥33) and chromothripsis
predicted pathologic complete response to neoadjuvant TCHP, while high MATH score
predicted anti-HER2 therapy failure. These findings demonstrate how WGS-based multi-omic
profiling can guide biomarker-driven treatment decisions in practice.

The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the urgent need for rapid, systematic, and broadly
applicable strategies to identify antiviral targets against emerging pathogens. Conventional
approaches that rely on detailed viral characterization and large-scale drug screening
remain too slow to meet this challenge. Here, we introduce a transcriptome-based
computational framework that integrates genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) with
dimensionality reduction to discover host metabolic vulnerabilities supporting viral
replication. Infection-specific GEMs are reconstructed from publicly available RNA-seq data,
and single-gene knockout simulations are embedded via UMAP to identify genes whose
knockout shifts the infected metabolic profile toward the uninfected state. The framework
identified porphyrin metabolism for HCoV-229E and oxidative phosphorylation for
HCoV-OC43, with genetic or pharmacological inhibition markedly suppressing replication in
cells and organoids. Extending the framework to SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV revealed
pyrimidine catabolism as a conserved antiviral pathway; inhibiting its rate-limiting enzyme
DPYD with eniluracil suppressed replication in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) organoid
models. Notably, these antiviral targets were undetectable by conventional differential￾expression or enrichment analyses. Together, this work establishes a generalizable, rapid

talks.speaker: Sisi Xie
talks.text:

Chemotherapy resistance is a leading cause of treatment failure in breast cancer. To
identify drivers of chemoresistance, here we present a multi-scale computational
framework integrating bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, transfer learning–based
phenotype inference (scPAS), protein–protein interaction (PPI) network topology, and in
silico perturbation analysis. A predictive model trained on neoadjuvant chemotherapy
response data was projected onto single-cell transcriptomes, enabling resolution of
resistant and sensitive cellular states across tumor and microenvironmental compartments.
Integration of differential expression signatures with network topology enabled
prioritization of key regulatory genes. A topology-aware in silico knockout strategy
quantified phenotypic reversibility using a State Transition (ST) score. This analysis
identified cancer drivers TP53, EGFR, BRCA1 while novel high-impact regulators, UBE2M,
DAPL1, CCND1 showed top ranking reversal effect and significant association with poor
overall survival in TCGA-BRCA cohorts. These results suggest that chemoresistance is a
network-level property and highlight key genes for potential therapeutic considerations in
breast cancer chemotherapy resistance.

ancestry-specific T2D polygenic risk scores (PRSs) and eight mechanism-partitioned PRSs

talks.title: Skiver: Reference-free quality control of metagenomic sequencing datasets using (k,v)-mer sketches
talks.speaker: Zhenhao Gu
talks.text:
, Puru Sharma1
, Limsoon Wong1
, Niranjan Nagarajan1,2
1National University of Singapore
2Genome Institute of Singapore
Background. Quality control of sequencing datasets is an important first step in numerous
bioinformatics pipelines such as mapping, variant calling, and assembly. Existing methods
typically rely on alignment results or quality scores. However, the reference genome is not
always available for mapping, and uncalibrated quality scores may yield biased estimates
of error rates.
Results. We present skiver, a reference-free and alignment-free algorithm that estimates
sequencing error rates and calibrates Phred quality scores using (k,v)-mer sketches. By
identifying the consensus from the sketched (k,v)-mers, skiver estimates survival and
hazard rates that capture positional information of sequencing errors. Across simulated
and real datasets from various sequencing platforms, skiver accurately recovers sequencing
error rates and the proportion of different error types. We further demonstrate its ability
to calibrate Phred scores. It also reliably handles complex datasets containing multiple
strains, alleles, and repetitive regions through an iterative outlier filtering strategy. Skiver is
computationally efficient and supports tools that need accurate sequencing error rate
estimates or quality scores as prior knowledge.

present GACHA, a scalable clustering framework based on the observation that a read
need not admit a single globally reliable similarity representation; instead, repeated

talks.title: Metabuli and Metabuli App: A Fast, Accurate, and Easy-to-Use Metagenomic Taxonomic Classifier
talks.speaker: Jaebeom Kim
talks.text:
6Artificial Intelligence Institute, Seoul National University
Existing taxonomic classifiers analyze either DNA or amino acid (AA) sequences, choosing
between strain-level resolution and remote homology detection, and thus fail to capture a
metagenome's full diversity. Many also require command-line proficiency and high￾performance computing. To address this, we developed Metabuli for joint DNA-AA
analysis and the Metabuli App to remove technical barriers.
For the joint analysis, we designed the metamer, a k-mer encoding an AA 8-mer and its
codons. Comparing metamers lets Metabuli identify exact AA matches for sensitivity while
using DNA identity for specificity. The Metabuli App, a cross-platform GUI (Windows/
macOS/Linux) for standard desktops, supports database curation, raw-read QC,
classification, visualization, and read extraction for taxa of interest.
Metabuli consistently excelled across DNA- and AA-favored benchmarks, capturing >97%
of the classification union of top DNA- and AA-based tools on the CAMI 2 soil dataset.
In pathogen detection, it uniquely succeeded at both variant-specific detection and novel
pathogen identification. Classifying ~7 Gbp human metagenomes against 36,203 genomes
took <10 minutes on a server and <1 hour on standard desktops.
By combining DNA- and AA-based analysis with an accessible, end-to-end desktop workflow,
Metabuli and the Metabuli App aim to accelerate discoveries in clinical diagnostics and
ecological studies.

talks.title: Advancing drug discovery through structure-based drug design: Discovery of PTP1B Inhibitors
talks.speaker: Sanghwa Yoon
talks.text:
Protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) is a key regulator of glucose homeostasis and
cellular signaling pathways, making it an attractive therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes,
obesity, and cancer. However, the development of effective PTP1B inhibitors remains
challenging due to the structural characteristics of its active site and the limitations of
conventional phosphomimetic inhibitors. To address these challenges, we employed an
integrated structure-based molecular modeling approach to identify novel non￾phosphomimetic bidentate inhibitors and investigate their binding interactions and
conformational behavior. Among the identified candidates, COM68 and COM63 exhibited
stable binding modes with favorable binding free energies. However, further structural and
conformational analyses revealed differences in their interaction dynamics and the stability
of key binding residues. Subsequent in vitro assays confirmed the inhibitory activity of
COM68, whereas COM63 showed no inhibitory activity at the tested concentrations. These
findings suggest that evaluating the dynamic behavior of protein–ligand interactions can
provide additional insights beyond conventional binding affinity assessments. Overall, this
study demonstrates the potential of integrating structure-based molecular modeling with
experimental validation to support the discovery and evaluation of novel PTP1B inhibitors.
Such an approach may contribute to more informed candidate prioritization and
optimization, providing a practical strategy for advancing structure-based drug discovery.

talks.title: Interaction-specific imputation reveals multi-scale chromatin organization in single cells
talks.speaker: Minhee Park
talks.text:
Imaging-based chromatin tracing provides a powerful view of 3D genome organization at
single-cell resolution, but frequent stochastic dropout limits the analysis of fine-scale
structural heterogeneity. Existing imputation approaches can reduce sparsity, yet often
smooth away cell-specific structural features.
Here, we present Cooperative Pair-based Imputation and Reconstruction (CoPAIR), a
framework designed to recover missing spatial information while preserving single-cell
heterogeneity. CoPAIR leverages interaction-specific relationships across cells while
reconstructing missing structures based on the observed geometry of each individual cell.
Across multiple chromatin tracing datasets, CoPAIR improves reconstruction accuracy and
better preserves structural variation compared with existing approaches. CoPAIR recovers
localized chromatin interactions associated with cell identity and reveals coordinated
structural variation across different scales of genome organization. Together, these results
demonstrate that CoPAIR is not only an imputation method, but also a framework for
extracting previously obscured biological information from single-cell 3D genome imaging
data.

talks.title: Regulatory Logic of Enhancer RNAs in Stem Cell Fate Transitions
talks.speaker: Seung-Kyoon Kim
talks.text:
Enhancers are cis-regulatory elements that orchestrate spatiotemporal gene expression
through chromatin interactions and coordinated recruitment of transcriptional machinery.
Active enhancers can also produce enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), which contribute to
transcriptional regulation through diverse mechanisms. Despite growing evidence for their
regulatory functions, how eRNAs derived from different enhancer contexts contribute to
dynamic gene regulation in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and during early differentiation
remains incompletely understood. In this talk, I will present our recent findings on the
regulatory logic of eRNAs in stem cell state transitions. Using integrative multi-omics and
functional perturbation approaches, we identified intergenic and intragenic enhancers that
generate distinct eRNAs with temporal, strand-specific, and stimulus-responsive activation
patterns. These eRNAs are dynamically and sequentially activated during early
differentiation and contribute to target gene transcription, pluripotency maintenance, and
differentiation. In particular, intragenic enhancer-derived eRNAs exhibit strand-specific
functional contributions, while distinct external stimuli engage different combinations and
temporal patterns of eRNA activity, accompanied by coordinated changes in enhancer
chromatin state and transcription factor occupancy. Together, these findings support a
model in which enhancer activity operates through temporally ordered and context￾dependent eRNA programs that integrate chromatin state, transcription factor occupancy,
and external stimuli to fine-tune transcriptional outputs. This work provides a broader
regulatory framework for understanding how enhancer-derived RNAs connect epigenetic
dynamics with gene regulation during stem cell state transitions.

talks.title: Spatially Resolved Multi-omics: From Transcriptome to Proteome Profiling in the Same Tissue
talks.speaker: Yoonyoung Lee
talks.text:
Spatial biology has transformed our understanding of tissue heterogeneity by revealing
how cellular identity and molecular function are organized within complex tissue
architectures. However, conventional bulk and single-cell approaches often lose critical
spatial information, while many spatial profiling technologies remain limited in their ability
to perform comprehensive multi-omics analyses on precisely defined cell populations.
To address these challenges, we introduce SLACS (Spatially-resolved Laser Activated Cell
Sorting), a technology that enables precise, automated isolation of spatially defined cells
directly from tissue sections using an infrared laser. By integrating image-guided cell
isolation with downstream molecular profiling, SLACS provides a flexible approach for
investigating genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic characteristics of specific cellular
populations while retaining their spatial origins.
In this seminar, I will highlight applications of SLACS in spatially resolved molecular
profiling across diverse biological and clinical contexts, including breast cancer, osteoporosis,
and head and neck cancer. These studies demonstrate how selective isolation of spatially
distinct cell populations can reveal disease-associated molecular signatures, cellular
heterogeneity, and potential therapeutic targets.
Building on these applications, I will focus on recent advances in integrating spatial
transcriptomics and proteomics within the same tissue. Using triple-negative breast cancer
as an example, we demonstrate how transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of spatially
defined cancer stem cell-associated populations reveals distinct molecular programs and
differences in RNA–protein relationships. These findings highlight the importance of
integrating multiple molecular layers to better understand cellular states and functional
heterogeneity that cannot be fully captured by transcriptomic analysis alone.
Finally, I will discuss the potential of combining SLACS-based multi-omics profiling with
AI-assisted tissue analysis to bridge spatial tissue architecture and molecular function,
providing new opportunities for biomarker discovery and precision medicine.

talks.title: Decoding Tumor Microenvironment Heterogeneity and Therapeutic Response via Advanced Transformer Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics
talks.speaker: Junil Kim
talks.text:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has revolutionized our understanding of tissue architecture by
profiling gene expression within its native context. However, capturing complex spatial
dependencies and directly linking these architectural features to functional drug responses
remain critical challenges. In this presentation, I introduce two complementary,
transformer-based frameworks designed to scale from foundational spatial modeling to
interpretable therapeutic prediction within the tumor microenvironment (TME). First, I
introduce VirtualTissue, a transformer-based foundation model specifically engineered for ST
data. Leveraging high-resolution Xenium data across multiple cancer types (lung, breast,
pancreatic, and ovarian), VirtualTissue learns spatially informed representations by predicting
local neighborhood structures and spatial density. Without relying on explicit coordinates, it
effectively captures niche-driven transcriptional variability and uncovers cell–cell communication
signatures associated with tumor heterogeneity. Second, to translate these spatial
architectures into clinical insights, I introduce DrugGTN, an interpretable graph transformer
framework. DrugGTN bridges the gap between ST data and external drug-perturbation
priors (LINCS/CMAP) by converting tissue slides into segment graphs. A graph transformer
encoder learns contextualized tissue-state representations, mapping them to drug-induced
program shifts to calculate a sample-level 'ResponseScore' that integrates immune
activation, suppressive burden, and spatial accessibility. Validated across retrospective HCC,
RCC, and Visium cohorts, StructRx demonstrates that spatial accessibility acts as a critical,
context-dependent modifier of drug efficacy, especially in immune-exclusion settings.
Together, these frameworks provide a robust, scalable paradigm for leveraging spatial
transcriptomics—moving from foundational decoding of TME landscapes to the precise,
interpretable prediction of microenvironmental drug responses.

talks.title: AI-Driven Approaches to Single-Cell RNA-seq Data Analysis: Integrating Biological Knowledge
talks.speaker: Minsik Oh
talks.text:
Single-cell RNA sequencing has become a standard tool for resolving cellular
heterogeneity, yet its analysis pipeline still rests on decisions that are difficult to
standardize, including clustering resolution, marker gene selection, and cell type labeling.
This talk introduces three recent studies from our group, each integrating biological
knowledge into AI models at a different stage and in a different form.
The first study encodes knowledge as an assumption within the learning objective,
excluding likely false negatives from the contrastive negative pool to preserve
transcriptional continuity within cell types while maintaining separation between them. The
second draws on human-curated knowledge, combining expression-based evidence with
tissue-specific marker resources to stabilize marker selection for LLM-based cell type
annotation. The third borrows knowledge already learned by a foundation model, refining
expression-space clusters within a pretrained embedding space and aggregating them
through hierarchical multiple instance learning for annotation-free phenotype prediction.
These studies illustrate several complementary ways of integrating biological knowledge
into AI models for single-cell analysis.

talks.title: Virtual Tissue Pharmacology: spatial omics and AI for predicting intratumoral drug distribution and response
talks.speaker: Sungwoo Bae
talks.text:
Oncology drug development faces exceptionally high clinical attrition, with more than 95%
of candidates failing in trials. Much of this failure is driven by the heterogeneity of the
tumor microenvironment. Factors such as irregular vasculature, dense stromal barriers, and
uneven antigen expression create steep drug gradients within a single tumor, resulting in
highly variable drug exposure. Although recognized as a key contributor to inconsistent
drug responses, intratumoral heterogeneity is rarely incorporated into preclinical
assessments. Traditional pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) models assume
that tissue acts as a well-mixed compartment. Because they report only average
concentrations, these models cannot resolve microscopic drug distribution or the localized
responses of target cells.
Spatial omics provides the precise resolution needed to capture these micro-scale
dynamics. Leveraging this capability, we developed Virtual Tissue Pharmacology (VTP), a
computational framework designed to simulate drug transport and tissue effects prior to
experimental testing. VTP utilizes tissue architectures drawn either from PortraiATLAS, our
extensive spatial omics database of analysis-ready patient samples, or from synthetic
alternatives. We focus this framework primarily on therapeutic modalities requiring precise
physical delivery, such as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and radiopharmaceutical
therapies (RPTs), for which efficacy requires that a sufficient concentration of payload or
radioisotope reach the target cells.
Structurally, VTP comprises two layers: an architectural layer that defines the tissue, and a
simulation layer that models drug behavior on it. The architectural layer supplies the tissue,
either sourced directly from PortraiATLAS or generated via the VGL (Vision-Gene-Language)

Suite, a multimodal model trained to predict gene expression levels from paired
histopathology images. The simulation layer, implemented as the Microscopic Suite, then
executes functional simulations on this tissue and consists of two complementary models.
Microscopic-PK, a deterministic mechanistic model, computes extravasation, interstitial
diffusion, target binding, internalization, and dose deposition at single-cell resolution.
Microscopic-PD, a deep-learning model, predicts the resulting localized cellular survival
and drug sensitivity. In this presentation, we will share preliminary VTP results for ADC
and RPT applications. We will also discuss expanding this approach to virtual patient

talks.title: BLITSFR: Scalable comparative microbial genomics with a self-contained, interactive, single-file report
talks.speaker: Budi Permana
talks.text:
Comparative microbial genomics routinely requires the alignment of query genomes
against a reference to delineate conserved and variable regions, yet existing tools often
produce static visualisations or necessitate centralised web services and data uploads. To
address this, we present BLITSFR (BLAST Interactive Tracks in Single-File Report), a
command-line tool that compares query genomes against a reference and returns a single
interactive HTML file. The report opens in any modern browser, requiring no server or
data upload, and lets users explore conserved and variable regions across the genomes.
BLITSFR handles both assembled genomes and raw reads, and processes hundreds of
genomes in minutes on a standard laptop with genome tracks sorting, filtering, and
colouring by metadata are performed within the report, without requirement for re-running
the analysis. We demonstrate its utility by analysing vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus
faecium ST78 genomes to confirm the conservation of Tn1549-like transposons and a case
of β-lactam-resistant Corynebacterium diphtheriae, where coverage depth resolved
resistance transposon copy number. BLITSFR and SCIFR are freely available at the provided
GitHub repositories (https://github.com/nalarbp/blitsfr, https://github.com/nalarbp/scifr)

Nucleotide substitution spectra can reveal the molecular, epigenetic, and ecological
processes shaping genome evolution, but most studies have focused on humans and a
few model organisms. Here, we applied EvoSubster, an automated comparative genomics
pipeline that infers lineage-specific substitutions from three-species comparisons, to
non-coding regions of 60 trios spanning 120 spectra across seven major eukaryotic
lineages. Most groups showed high frequencies of C↔T substitutions, particularly CG>TG,
whereas this signature was weak or absent in arthropods, consistent with their low

observed recurrent neighboring-base-dependent T>C patterns. ATA>ACA substitutions were
enriched in most species, while NTA>NCA and NTG>NCG were prominent in
mushroom-forming fungi, corals, anthozoans, and arthropods. Unlike related human T>C
signatures, ATT>ACT was not similarly enriched, suggesting a distinct mutational
mechanism. These results demonstrate that comparative substitution spectra can reveal
lineage-specific and recurrent mutational patterns across eukaryotes. Broader taxonomic
sampling may reveal additional mutational processes and clarify how environmental and
evolutionary forces shape genome-wide mutation patterns.

talks.title: Comprehensive discovery of RNA modification sites in the human transcriptome at single-molecule resolution
talks.speaker: Daehyun Baek
talks.text:
RNA modifications (RMs) are critical for diverse biological processes, but the lack of
accurate, quantitative detection methods has limited their study. A large-scale and
high-quality training dataset is an essential component for accurate deep learning, but
such dataset has been absent for RM detection, resulting in low accuracies. We developed
DeepRM (Deep learning for RNA Modification), a sophisticated deep learning framework
powered by Nanopore sequencing. DeepRM dataset is a massive-scale, three orders of
magnitude larger than the comparable previous ones, and unprecedentedly high-quality
dataset that closely mirrors endogenous transcript environments. Accordingly, DeepRM
detects RM sites and measures their modification stoichiometries with a near-perfect
accuracy. Using DeepRM, we constructed a comprehensive human m6A atlas that reveals
a large number of previously underappreciated non-canonical m6A sites and differentially
modified transcripts, highlighting the complexity and dynamic nature of the human
epitranscriptome. DeepRM is freely available, providing a unique, powerful opportunity for
understanding the biological functions of RMs. DeepRM can also be expanded to various
other RMs and organisms, potentially becoming a future standard for investigating the
epitranscriptome.
