talks.title: RNA Modifications in Viral Life Cycle
talks.speaker: Man-Seong Park
talks.text:
Viral studies have predominantly been focused on the structure and function of either the
viral proteins or genomes, virus-host interactions, and host immune responses. This has
largely been due to technical limitations that have confined the boundaries of research
beyond that of conventional sequence-based analyses. One of such has been in the field
of epitranscriptomics, in which functional studies of RNA modifications in viral genomes
are relatively unknown and the dynamic nature of RNA modifications have yet to be
understood. Several studies have been able to predict distribution patterns and functions
of RNA modifications either with the use of known writer and eraser enzymes, or through
antibodies that specifically recognize these modifications. Through these studies, we have
come to realize that RNA modifications not only contribute to the stability of mRNA
molecules but also play key roles such as immune evasion that contribute to the success
of viral propagation. For these reasons, RNA modifications have emerged as potential
therapeutic targets and have become an important consideration in mRNA vaccine design.
Approximately 170 types of RNA modifications have been identified to date, but very few,
such as m6A(N6-methyladenosine), m5C(5-methylcytosine), and pseudouridine, have been
extensively studied. In SARS-CoV-2, m6A modifications are predominantly distributed in
the ORF1ab region and the 3’ untranslated region, with differences in their distribution
being reported across lineages. However, it is unclear whether these RNA modification
patterns change throughout the viral life cycle and it is likely that they may differ
depending on the host environment. In addition, RNA viruses with segmented genomes
exhibit distinct RNA modification patterns within each genomic segment. Recently,
nanopore-based direct RNA sequencing has facilitated study within this field and has helped
identify the locations and types of RNA modifications in native RNA molecules. Our aim is
to investigate the correlation between viral RNA modifications and biological phenomena,
and hope that through identification and characterization of RNA modifications we may
uncover the mechanisms behind viral evolution, fitness, and pathogenesis.

talks.title: A multiomic transformer model for gene regulatory network inference with single-cell data
talks.speaker: Yasin Uzun
talks.text:
Gene expression is regulated through complex transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms
that can be modeled using gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Recent single-cell multiome
technologies integrate both modalities within the same cell. However, existing
computational approaches remain limited in accurately inferring regulatory interactions.
To address this challenge, we developed MTGRN, a transformer-based deep learning
framework for GRN inference from single-cell multiome data. The first level models
TF-DNA binding by integrating TF sequence and structural features with DNA sequence
information using convolutional neural networks and bidirectional cross-attention. This
module predicts TF binding to regulatory regions near target genes. The second level
models TF-target gene interactions by combining chromatin accessibility, peak distance,
and gene expression information through dense layers and cross-attention mechanisms to
estimate regulatory relationships.
We evaluated MTGRN using seven samples from four multiome datasets: mouse
embryonic stem cells, mouse hepatocytes, human macrophages and the K562 cell line. Two
training strategies were applied: self-training using chromosome splits and cross-training
across samples. Performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristics,
precision-recall curves, F1 score and early precision rate. Assessment with multiple datasets
and metrics showed that MTGRN achieved top performance, outperforming existing
methods, demonstrating reliability and robusticity of inference.

talks.title: Efficient Pretraining of Cell Foundation Models through Metacell Compression
talks.speaker: Yurim Jung
talks.text:
Seoul 03722, Republic of Korea
Single-cell foundation models learn transferable representations from large-scale transcriptomic
data, but conventional pretraining processes tens of millions of sparse cells independently,
creating substantial computational redundancy. We present MetacellFormer, a foundation
model pretrained on biologically structured metacells. We compressed 43.4 million human
scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq training cells from 1,223 sources into 799,562 metacells, reducing
the number of training examples 54.3-fold. Structured metacells preserved coherent
biological structure and showed stronger cell-type homogeneity and recovery of functional
gene relationships than size-matched random pooling. One complete corpus pass required
approximately 3.5 hours with metacells versus 203 hours with individual cells. Under
matched cumulative wall-clock budgets, metacell pretraining consistently outperformed
single-cell pretraining across six representative benchmarks spanning cell-level tasks (cell
annotation and cross-study drug-response prediction), gene-level tasks (HumanNet and
pathway retrieval), and perturbation-level tasks (exact and functional perturbation retrieval).
Against Geneformer v1/v2, scGPT, and scFoundation, MetacellFormer ranked within the top
two models in five of six benchmarks, including best performance in HumanNet,
cross-study drug-response prediction, and both perturbation retrieval tasks. These results
establish biologically structured metacell compression as an efficient strategy for scaling
single-cell foundation model pretraining.

talks.title: Liquid biopsy using plasma cfRNA for early cancer detection: from EV biomarkers to an AI-ready transcriptome cohort
talks.speaker: Yunui Bae
talks.text:
Pancreatic cancer is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage, underscoring the need
for minimally invasive tools for early detection. Liquid biopsy approaches based on
circulating nucleic acids and extracellular vesicles (EVs) offer a promising route, and
machine learning models built on plasma transcriptomes have shown potential to capture
tumor-derived signals. However, the performance of such models depends heavily on the
quality and consistency of the underlying data, which are strongly influenced by pre￾analytical and analytical variables.
Previously, we investigated EV-derived small RNAs as disease biomarkers in multiple
biofluids, including plasma, and gained hands-on experience with how sample handling
and RNA isolation shape the resulting profiles. Building on this work, we are now
extending our focus to total plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), which encompasses both
vesicular and non-vesicular RNA and offers greater scalability and reproducibility for large
cohort studies.
Here, we present the design and current progress of a multicenter plasma transcriptome
project for early detection of pancreatic cancer, conducted with Seoul National University
Hospital, Asan Medical Center, and the National Cancer Center. The cohort aims to enroll
approximately 1,200 participants across three groups: pancreatic cancer, benign pancreatic
disease, and non-pancreatic disease controls. We are establishing standardized workflows
for plasma processing, cfRNA extraction, and total RNA library preparation. In this talk, we
will discuss key pre-analytical considerations for generating reliable plasma transcriptome
data, and outline how these standardized datasets will serve as the foundation for
AI-based early detection models.

talks.title: Toward multimodal multiscale tissue foundation model
talks.speaker: Joo Sang Lee
talks.text:
Understanding tissue function and disease requires connecting molecular states, cellular
interactions, and tissue architecture. Spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, and digital
pathology provide complementary insights, but integrating them across resolutions and
platforms remains challenging. In this talk, I will discuss our ongoing efforts toward a
tissue foundation model that integrates histological images with spatial molecular
measurements through self-supervised learning, cross-modal alignment, and multiscale
modeling. Key challenges include predicting molecular states from morphology,
accommodating heterogeneous molecular panels, and distinguishing cell-intrinsic
information from tissue context. I will highlight evaluation strategies emphasizing biological
fidelity and generalization across patients and technologies, with applications in tumor
microenvironment characterization and treatment response prediction. This framework aims
to support mechanistic hypothesis generation and precision oncology.

talks.title: Recent Trends and Case Studies in Process Modeling for the Amino Acid Biomanufacturing Industry
talks.speaker: Jun-Woo Kim
talks.text:
Amino acids are among the largest products of microbial biomanufacturing and are widely
used in feed additives, foods, pharmaceuticals, and chemical materials. Their industrial
production relies on combinations of unit operations such as fermentation, membrane
separation, evaporation, crystallization, chromatography, distillation, and drying. Each unit
operation is designed and optimized using process models that are built on a fundamental
understanding of the thermodynamic properties of the process streams, electrolyte phase
equilibria, thermal degradation, fluid dynamics, and heat transfer. This presentation reviews
the latest developments in bioprocess modeling over the past three years, drawing on
real cases from the amino acid biomanufacturing industry. In particular, we present an
advanced cascade evaporation and reverse osmosis process applied to L-methionine
commercial plant for the efficient recovery of ammonium acetate as a byproduct, together
with the results of its implementation at the plant. We also introduce a practical
application of compartment modeling, which combines a conventional fermentation model
with computational fluid dynamics (CFD), to simulate an amino acid fermentation process
that uses fresh raw materials and recycled byproducts simultaneously as substrates. Finally,
technoeconomic analysis and life cycle assessment are used to demonstrate that these
modeling results translate into real economic and environmental value in the amino acid
market.

talks.title: From Single Bases to Megabases: Structure-Guided Discovery of New Genome Editing Systems
talks.speaker: Jungjoon Lee
talks.text:
Genome editing enzymes have historically been discovered and engineered via sequence
homology and random mutagenesis, approaches that overlook proteins with structure-only
functional conservation. Here, we demonstrate that AI-based structure prediction
overcomes these limitations at both base- and megabase-editing scales. First, structural
modeling and alanine scanning of a compact bacterial cytidine deaminase identified a
constricted DNA-binding pocket. Combining rational pocket expansion with bacterial
directed evolution yielded an editor with restored substrate control, achieving higher
endogenous activity, reduced indels and cytotoxicity, and a narrower editing window than
benchmark editors. Second, pairwise structural clustering of insertion sequences uncovered
a distinct subclade of bridge recombinases lacking detectable sequence homology.
Following bridge-RNA engineering, our lead recombinase significantly outperformed the
established benchmark at an endogenous human locus. Thus, structure-guided mining and
engineering provide a universal paradigm for discovering and optimizing diverse genome
editing systems.

talks.title: Sensitive Identification of Low-Frequency Somatic Mobile Element Insertions via End-to- End Segmentation and Classification of Long-Read Sequencing
talks.speaker: Xiaowei Zhu
talks.text:
Mobile elements (MEs), such as LINE-1, Alu, and SVA elements, can undergo
retrotransposition in human neural stem cells, creating brain somatic mobile element
insertions (MEIs) in simple or complex forms. Specific ME segments, such as LINE-1 5'
promoters and 3' poly(A) signals, are implicated in gene dysregulation and may contribute
to the etiology of neurological diseases. While long-read sequencing facilitates the
complete identification of complex MEIs and improves detection within repetitive
sequences, the direct detection of low-frequency somatic MEIs in bulk tissues remains
constrained by sequencing artifacts and a poor signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we propose
that the precise arrangement of ME segments is not only essential for predicting
functional consequences but also critical for distinguishing true MEIs from technical
artifacts. We present a novel two-step deep learning framework: an initial module that
performs single-base-resolution annotation of ME segments within long sequencing reads,
followed by a second network that classifies the insertion as a true or false MEI based on
the structural arrangement of those segmented labels. Trained on over 5 million labeled
sequencing reads from 155 individuals with diverse genetic backgrounds, our method
achieves average precision exceeding 0.99 across all ME subtypes for both segmentation
and classification, despite relying on only a single supporting read. This high accuracy,
combined with a minimal requirement for supporting reads, makes it ideal for discovering
somatic mutations in bulk sequencing datasets. Thus, our approach provides a powerful,
high-resolution computational tool to advance the comprehensive profiling of somatic
variations led by MEs, and has the potential to provide further insights into the functional
and pathological implications of somatic retrotranspositions.

talks.title: Comprehensive resolution of cryptic variants in undiagnosed rare diseases via long-read sequencing
talks.speaker: Se Song Jang
talks.text:
Current standard genetic testing often fails to reach a diagnosis in rare diseases due to
technical limitations in detecting structural and epigenetic variation. To address this, we
implemented a long-read sequencing (LRS) workflow coupled with pangenome graph analysis
in a cohort of undiagnosed Korean patients.
By generating high-quality de novo assemblies, we resolved complex genomic regions
inaccessible to short-read sequencing. This approach established a molecular diagnosis in
a substantial fraction of previously unsolved families. The identified mechanisms spanned
complex structural variants, tandem repeat expansions, and methylation outliers, with
causality supported by orthogonal evidence including haplotype phasing and allele-specific
methylation.
Our results illustrate that LRS-based pangenome analysis substantially increases diagnostic
yield by uncovering cryptic variants and providing haplotype-resolved information. This
framework offers a practical route for patients on long diagnostic odysseys and expands
the interpretable variant space in complex genetic disorders.

talks.title: Unveiling the Full Transcriptomic Landscape of Disease with Long-Read Sequencing
talks.speaker: Jihwan Park
talks.text:
Conventional short-read next-generation sequencing (NGS) predominantly captures only
the 3’ ends of mRNAs, leaving full-length transcript architectures largely unresolved. Given
that over 90% of human genes undergo alternative splicing to generate distinct isoforms —with aberrant splicing driving numerous hereditary diseases and cancers—the traditional
gene-centric paradigm obscures critical genomic complexity. Long-read sequencing (LRS)
circumvents the bottlenecks of transcript assembly by directly reading intact, full-length
molecules, thereby driving a fundamental paradigm shift toward high-resolution, isoform￾centric genomic profiling. In the first part of this presentation, we introduce Ouro-seq, a
novel circularization-based targeted single-cell RNA-seq framework designed to overcome
sample-wasting artifacts in current workflows. Ouro-seq dramatically enriches cell-barcode￾containing full-length cDNA molecules up to 91.1% and efficiently spans transcripts up to
6 kbp at single-cell resolution. Utilizing this technology, we established the Mouse
Single-Cell Splicing Atlas, profiling 103,304 single cells across 12 major organs in adult
mice, thereby capturing a previously unappreciated dimension of functional heterogeneity
across individual cell populations. In the second part, we highlight the integration of
long-read single-cell transcriptomics with spatial multi-omics to decode the functional
impacts of isoform diversity in complex diseases. By cross-referencing cell-type-specific
isoforms discovered in the brain and kidney, we designed isoform-specific probes to map
their spatial distribution in situ using the MERSCOPE platform. Furthermore, we
demonstrate how disease-associated shifts in isoform usage structurally alter key proteins,
consequently modulating transcription factor (TF) activity and intracellular cell signaling
pathways. Concurrently validated with computational structure prediction, our results
establish that integrating long-read technological frameworks with spatial architectures
provides critical mechanistic links to clinical phenotypes, ultimately empowering precise
patient stratification and isoform-aware drug discovery.

talks.title: Agentic AI for Drug Discovery with Physical and Biological Priors
talks.speaker: Jaewoo Kang
talks.text:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how therapeutic targets are identified and how chemical
and biological design space is explored. Drawing on work at AIGEN Sciences, this talk
describes an AI-driven discovery framework in which LLM-based agents coordinate
domain-specific foundation models across target prioritization, hypothesis generation,
molecular design, and iterative optimization.
A recurring theme is that structure prediction is becoming commoditized infrastructure,
while experimental labels linking a designed molecule to its function remain scarce for the
modalities of greatest current interest. Progress therefore depends on encoding physical
and biological priors directly into the generative process rather than applying them as
post hoc filters.
We illustrate this across three modalities — molecular glue degraders, therapeutic
peptides, and antibodies — each of which requires different structural and biological
constraints to be respected during generation. We close with the problems that remain
hardest: the scarcity of measured binding and degradation labels, the gap between
computational energy proxies and experimental affinity, and the accuracy limits of
complex structure prediction.

talks.title: Beyond Open Access: The Future of Data Sharing
talks.speaker: Masanori Arita
talks.text:
Open access and the FAIR data principles have become widely accepted norms in scientific
research. Nowadays, however, they are increasingly challenged from the viewpoints of equity
and sustainability. This shift is particularly evident in the context of personal genomes, where
compliance with laws and privacy regulations is becoming stricter. It is worth remembering
that during the Human Genome Project, all data were made fully open without restriction. A
similar tightening of restrictions may arise across other areas as basic science becomes more
intertwined with society. We have been accustomed to the idea that genetic information
should be freely accessed without limitation, but this condition is actually exceptional when
compared to other research fields. In many disciplines, beneficiary liability is the standard,
raising the critical question of whether genetic information should be a public good for the
sake of education and welfare. Moreover, data sovereignty is becoming a dominant concern,
and the CARE principles are now frequently cited alongside FAIR in international forums. In
this talk, I will introduce the challenges facing traditional open access principles and discuss
how we can maintain academic freedom regarding genetic resources.

The company's platform—anchored by the UG200™ Series—utilizes an open-wafer substrate
paired with a flow-based, "mostly natural" sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry. Integrated with
the automated Solaris 2.0 workflow, the system simplifies sample preparation down to a single
touchpoint with minimal hands-on time. This architecture significantly lowers the cost barrier
for whole-genome sequencing (WGS) while ensuring uniform coverage across challenging
GC-rich regions and enabling sub-24-hour turnaround times.
Engineered for 24/7 automated production and BioAI applications, Ultima’s technology acts as
a biological data factory purpose-built for massive research initiatives. The platform powers
large-scale endeavors, including population genomics, the UK Biobank proteomics project, and
single-cell virtual cell atlases such as the Billion Cells Project. Beyond high-volume genomics,
its low base-substitution error rates optimize it for ultra-sensitive clinical applications, including
liquid biopsy, minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring, and early risk screening.

The rapid expansion of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other data-intensive life

studies increase in scale and complexity, researchers are expected to generate larger volumes
of high-quality data within shorter timelines—often while working with limited sample material,

conditions, successful data generation is no longer determined solely by the performance of
an individual instrument. It requires an integrated strategy that considers the entire workflow,
from experimental design and sample preparation to data acquisition, analysis, interpretation,
and reporting.

talks.title: Accelerating Data Generation: Thermo Fisher Scientific’s Strategy for Producing More Data, Faster
talks.speaker: Yu sung Jang
talks.text:
The rapid expansion of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other data-intensive life
science disciplines is transforming both biological research and clinical development. As
studies increase in scale and complexity, researchers are expected to generate larger volumes
of high-quality data within shorter timelines—often while working with limited sample material,
constrained resources, and increasingly demanding quality requirements. Under these
conditions, successful data generation is no longer determined solely by the performance of
an individual instrument. It requires an integrated strategy that considers the entire workflow,
from experimental design and sample preparation to data acquisition, analysis, interpretation,
and reporting.
This presentation introduces Thermo Fisher Scientific’s perspective on accelerating data
generation across life science research workflows. The central principle is that producing more
data, faster, should not come at the expense of data quality, reproducibility, or biological
relevance. Instead, meaningful improvements in productivity can be achieved by reducing
workflow complexity, increasing analytical throughput, minimizing avoidable variability, and
enabling researchers to move efficiently from samples to actionable biological insights.
From Thermo Fisher Scientific’s perspective, the next stage of productivity improvement will
depend on connecting instruments, reagents, automation, software, and scientific expertise into
cohesive end-to-end workflows. This integrated approach can help laboratories adapt to
changing project requirements, expand experimental scale, and shorten turnaround times while
maintaining confidence in their results. The objective is not simply to generate a larger
quantity of data, but to generate data that are reproducible, interpretable, and directly aligned
with the intended research outcome.
As an example of this integrated approach, the presentation will introduce the recently
opened Korea AI Automation Innovation Center (K-AIC) in Korea, showcasing a vision for the
laboratory of the future that combines automation for large-scale sample processing and
analysis with AI-powered data interpretation.

talks.speaker: Seungyoon Nam

This presentation introduces the mission, strategic milestones, and mid-term progress of
the GastroTransformer Research Consortium, a multi-year initiative funded by the National
Bio and Medical Technology Development Program from 2025 through 2028. Integrating
complex, heterogeneous multimodal data—spanning medical imaging, genomics,
transcriptomics, pharmacological profiles, and hospital Electronic Health Records (EHR)—
requires highly sophisticated architectures. To address this, our consortium has pioneered
advanced Multimodal Transformer-based frameworks designed to seamlessly fuse these
diverse data streams, capturing both global clinical contexts and highly localized molecular
or lesion features. As the lead organization, this 15-minute overview highlights our core
foundational achievements, mid-term R&D momentum, and our overarching roadmap
toward clinical validation. This presentation will be sequentially followed by two detailed,
15-minute technical sessions led by two of our Co-Principal Investigators (Co-PIs), who will

talks.title: GastroTransformer: A Multimodal Foundation Model for Predicting Chemotherapy Response and Recurrence Risk in Gastric Cancer
talks.speaker: Giltae Song
talks.text:
Patients with gastric cancer respond very differently to the same chemotherapy. The data
that could guide treatment choice (tumor transcriptomics, CT, clinical records and regimen
information) are rarely all available for the same patient. We present GastroTransformer, a
multimodal model built on a Modality-Slot Q-Former. It places pathway-level transcriptomic
(ssGSEA-512), drug (ChemBERTa), CT and EMR (CT-CLIP) and regimen embeddings in a
shared latent space and works with whichever modalities are present. The backbone was
pretrained on about 127,000 transcriptomes (bulk RNA-seq, microarray, cell-line and
single-cell) as a single-modality stream, plus smaller paired drug–transcriptome, CT–EMR,
and drug-set–EMR datasets. Pretraining used contrastive, cross-source alignment and
masked-reconstruction objectives, and no outcome labels.
For drug-response prediction on GDSC–CCLE, the model achieved R² = 0.776 (Pearson r =
0.883) on 11,473 held-out pairs from unseen cell lines, outperforming Ridge regression
(0.759) and a drug-mean baseline (0.740). In the TCGA-STAD and ACRG cohorts, its
transcriptome representation ranked survival risk better than raw pathway features in 20
of 27 conditions (pooled DFS C-index 0.614 vs. 0.550). Applying the cell-line-trained model
to TCGA-STAD tumors, we inferred patient-level virtual IC50s for the drugs each patient
actually received and grouped patients into tertiles by predicted sensitivity. Among 129
chemotherapy-treated patients, observed recurrence rose from 22% to 37% to 56% across
the predicted sensitive, intermediate and resistant groups (log-rank p = 0.003; adjusted HR
= 1.62 per SD, p = 0.031). Predicted 5-FU resistance showed the same gradient (HR =
1.46 per SD, p = 0.008), which was absent in untreated patients (interaction p = 0.043),
suggesting a treatment-related rather than purely prognostic signal.

talks.title: Extending the capacity of RNA therapeutics
talks.speaker: Young-suk Lee
talks.text:
The utility of messenger RNA (mRNA) as a therapeutic modality has been widely
demonstrated with the containment of COVID-19, yet the decisions in sequence design in
the untranslated regions (UTRs) remain largely unexplored, especially in preclinical models.
Here, we focus on the 5' UTR of mRNA and discover sequences that improve therapeutic
potential in mouse models of aging and obesity. Bioinformatic analysis of RNA
sequencing (RNA-seq), single-cell RNA-seq, ribosome profiling, and crosslinking and
immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing data revealed that ribosomal protein (RP)
mRNAs are abundant and ubiquitous but undergo distinct translational regulation by
LARP1 and LARP4. Of 11 RP mRNAs, we find that the 5' UTRs of RPL18, RPL35, and RPS9
improve the protein output of synthetic mRNAs in human and mouse cells. Investigation
of mutant 5' UTRs indicates that this improvement is independent of its terminal
oligopyrimidine motif but strong in cells with high levels of reactive oxygen species. In
aged mice and mice receiving a high-fat diet, synthetic mRNAs with the 5' UTR of RPS9
resulted in improved protein expression and enhanced humoral immunity through T
helper cell 2 cytokines when encoding viral antigens. Altogether, our results highlight the
importance of UTR sequence in expanding the therapeutic potential of synthetic mRNAs
for aged individuals and those diagnosed with obesity.

talks.title: Deciphering cell-type specific gene programs of colorectal cancer from single-cell data
talks.speaker: Quan Wang
talks.text:
Colorectal cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, arises from the stepwise
accumulation of genetic alterations in colonic epithelial cells, accompanied by dynamic
remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. While the adenoma-carcinoma sequence is
widely recognized, the cell type-specific gene programs and their interactions with the
tumor microenvironment that drive malignant transformation remain poorly understood. In
this study, we analyzed single-nucleus data from colorectal carcinoma and matched
unaffected tissues, revealing dysregulated gene programs at the level of individual cell
types. In epithelial cells, we identified two activated modules linked to enhanced stemness
and two repressed modules associated with apoptosis and chronic inflammatory signaling.
Transcription factors analysis highlighted CEBPB and RUNX1 as key activated regulators,
while FOXP1 and POU5F1 were repressed in cancerous cells. Further investigation of
intercellular communication uncovered disrupted crosstalk between epithelial cells and
tumor microenvironment components, which may underlie these gene program alterations.
Additionally, we observed functional reprogramming within the tumor microenvironment,
including extracellular matrix remodeling by stromal fibroblasts and impaired B
cell-mediated immunity. Together, these findings improve our understanding of the
molecular and cellular mechanisms driving colorectal tumorigenesis and may bring new
opportunities for the development of therapeutic strategies.

talks.title: Defining Age-Stratified Dermatologic Reference Cohorts through Population-Scale Profiling of the Healthy Skin Microbiome
talks.speaker: Woo Jun Sul
talks.text:
Here, we present two complementary large-scale skin microbiome cohort studies designed
to address distinct but interconnected needs: defining population-level ecological variation
in the healthy skin microbiome across Asian populations and establishing a standardized
Korean metagenomic reference resource for comparative dermatologic research.
First, we performed a large-scale, integrative metagenomic cohort study of the healthy
skin microbiome in 1,947 women from Korea, Thailand, and Indonesia. By combining
bacterial and fungal amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, skin physiology
measurements, lifestyle metadata, and host genetic profiles, this study systematically
characterized the ecological and host-associated factors shaping healthy skin microbial
variation. Second, we are developing a standardized Korean skin microbiome reference
resource based on a large-scale 2,200-participant dermatologic cohort. This cohort is
designed to capture both age-stratified healthy variation and disease-associated microbial
deviations in major dermatologic conditions, including atopic dermatitis, acne, and
wound-associated skin infections. The resource integrates harmonized clinical and lifestyle
metadata with standardized sampling of healthy, lesional, non-lesional, and matched
control skin sites, together with full-length 16S rRNA profiling and shotgun metagenomic
sequencing. Together, these two large-scale metagenome-centered cohort studies highlight
the importance of distinguishing natural population- and site-associated variation in the
healthy skin microbiome from disease-associated dysbiosis. By integrating ecological
discovery across healthy Asian populations with a standardized Korean dermatologic
reference cohort, this work provides a robust foundation for comparative skin microbiome
analysis, disease biomarker discovery, and future precision dermatology application.

talks.title: Protein analysis from multimers to metagenomes
talks.speaker: Milot Mirdita
talks.text:
Protein analysis rests on detecting evolutionary relationships, and recent advances in AI have
made that detection fast, accurate and accessible, reshaping how biologists work with proteins.
This talk presents advances spanning the acceleration of structure prediction, the largest-scale
prediction of protein complexes to date, and structure-level search at metagenomic scale.
ColabFold made AlphaFold2 structure prediction accessible to everyone, with over 100 million
uses. To accelerate prediction further, MMseqs2 was adapted for GPUs, cutting multiple
sequence alignment generation from minutes to seconds and making large-scale prediction
feasible.This enables a proteome-scale expansion of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database
with high-confidence protein complexes, selected from over 31M homo- and heterodimers
predicted across 4,777 proteomes including model and WHO global-health organisms.
Calibration against recent, post-training PDB structures established high-confidence thresholds,
yielding 1.74M high-confidence homodimers and 79K high-confidence heterodimers, exceeding
experimentally determined complexes by orders of magnitude. Recurrent folds are largely
anchored in known structures, while a fraction of structural clusters span multiple domains of
life, suggesting conserved building blocks of cellular life. All complexes are openly available
through alphafold.ebi.ac.uk.
Foldseek enables structure-level homology search by encoding each residue as a token in the
3Di structural alphabet. Foldseek2 adds a second, orthogonally trained alphabet that further
improves the sensitivity of remote-homology detection. Because structure prediction remains
too slow and costly to apply exhaustively at metagenomic scale, both alphabets can also be
inferred directly from amino acid sequence through a protein language model, running orders
of magnitude faster than structure prediction and bringing sensitive structure-level search
within reach of the largest sequence collections available.
Through deep evolutionary relationships, these methods and resources enable the interpretation
of protein structure at the scale of life.

talks.title: Qoka: An AI-Powered Research Environment for Bioinformatics and Reusable Analysis Workflows
talks.speaker: Jeongbin Park
talks.text:
The growing availability of biological data creates opportunities for discovery, yet
translating these resources into research outcomes often requires navigating disconnected
tools, configuring computational environments, and managing complex analysis workflows.
These technical barriers can limit data reuse, particularly for researchers with limited
programming experience. Here we introduce Qoka, an AI-powered desktop research
environment that brings literature exploration, research planning, data analysis, and
manuscript preparation into a unified workspace. Qoka enables researchers to interact with
Claude or Codex through natural language, connecting AI agents to research modules
through integrated Model Context Protocol tools and extensible skills. The platform
combines research notebooks, a paper library, manuscript editing and review, and
project-specific and cross-project memory. Integrated execution environments support
running analysis code while reducing the burden of environment setup. A central
component, Autopipe, supports packaging analyses into reusable pipelines and facilitates
their discovery, sharing, and re-execution through Autopipe Hub. Researchers can inspect
analysis code and outputs within the same workspace, linking computational work with
research documentation. We discuss the design and implementation of Qoka, with
particular emphasis on natural-language interaction and reusable analysis workflows. We
also explore how this approach could help bridge the gap between access to biological
data and its practical use, and outline its potential role in supporting research around
shared biodata resources within K-BDS.

talks.title: AI-Powered Histopathology: Dissecting the TME to Predict Patient Response Using Spatial Single-Cell and H&E Images
talks.speaker: Sanghyuk Lee
talks.text:
Histopathology relies on visual inspection of H&E slides, where accurately identifying
single-cell phenotypes remains subjective and challenging. To bridge this gap, we present
two Vision Transformer (ViT)-based models that predict cell types (HNE2Cell) and cell
densities (HNE2Space) directly from standard H&E images. Leveraging 35 Xenium datasets
spanning ~10 million cells across 8 organs, our framework couples pretrained pathology
foundation models with hierarchical decoders. HNE2Cell accurately classifies 15 distinct cell
types, achieving strong F1-scores for malignant cells (0.936) and fibroblasts (0.755).
Concurrently, HNE2Space predicts 11 cell densities with robust spatial correlations, notably
for malignant cells (Spearman’s r = 0.805) and fibroblasts (0.603). By integrating these
predictions across tumor compartments (core, edge, stroma), we generated over 1,000
spatial tumor microenvironment (TME) features. Validated on TCGA-BRCA (n = 1,023) and
cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma immuno-oncology (IO) cohorts (n = 45), these spatial
features strongly correlated with patient survival and immunotherapy response. Overall,
our scalable approach transforms routine histology slides into virtual spatial maps, offering
a cost-effective platform for biomarker discovery and precision oncology.

talks.title: Six Years of the Korea BioData Station (K-BDS): Building a National Analysis Infrastructure for Bio Data and the Road Ahead
talks.speaker: Junehawk Lee
talks.text:
and analyzing data produced by publicly funded bio R&D. Launched in 2021 by the
Ministry of Science and ICT, it is operated jointly by KOBIC, which leads data
standardization and curation, and KISTI, which builds and operates the computing
infrastructure and research environment. This talk reviews what the program has delivered
on the infrastructure side from 2021 to 2026 and outlines where it goes next. Over six
years we have built an integrated analysis system dedicated to bio data: a GPU cluster
with 55 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, more than 2 PB of high-performance storage, a cloud
environment, and a dedicated research network that links K-BDS with ministry data
centers. On top of this we provide curated public databases, analysis tools contributed
through open calls, and pretrained AI models such as AlphaFold. Since 2022 the K-BDS
Utilization Support Program has offered these resources free of charge to researchers in
universities, research institutes, hospitals, and industry, supporting more than 200 projects
in genomics, protein structure prediction, drug discovery, and biomedical AI. With about
2.3 million data entries (roughly 13 PB) now registered in K-BDS and resource utilization
near 90%, demand has clearly outgrown the current system. The next phase therefore
shifts the focus from collecting data to making it usable by AI. In line with the 4th Basic
Plan for National Bio Research Resources (2026–2030), we are planning AI-ready data
conversion and quality control, AI-agent-based services for data discovery and analysis, a
trusted research environment for sensitive data, and a dedicated high-performance
computing infrastructure for bio AI that works together with ministry data centers. I will
share the lessons learned from operating K-BDS, the plans now taking shape, and how
the bioinformatics community can take part in shaping them.

talks.title: Spatial proteomics to understand diseases
talks.speaker: Min-Sik Kim
talks.text:
Diseases are characterized by complex spatial heterogeneity arising from interactions among
distinct cell types and their surrounding microenvironments. Therefore, understanding
disease mechanisms requires not only identifying molecular changes, but also determining
where these changes occur and how they are organized within the tissue context. Spatial
proteomics has emerged as a powerful approach to address these challenges by mapping
protein expression and molecular states while preserving the spatial architecture of tissues.
In this seminar, I will introduce recent advances in high-resolution mass spectrometry￾based spatial proteomics and its applications in understanding human diseases. Mass
spectrometry-based approaches enable comprehensive and unbiased characterization of
tissue proteomes with high molecular specificity and, when combined with spatial information,
provide an opportunity to investigate disease-associated molecular heterogeneity at
unprecedented depth.

talks.title: Beyond Single Cells: Toward Robust Foundation Models for Cellular Representation
talks.speaker: Insuk Lee
talks.text:
Foundation models are rapidly transforming single-cell transcriptomics by enabling the
learning of transferable cellular representations from millions of cells. However, the
sparsity and technical noise inherent to single-cell measurements fundamentally limit the
fidelity of learned representations and constrain their biological generalization. Addressing
these limitations is essential for the next generation of cellular foundation models. In this
talk, I will present a new framework for cellular foundation modeling that aims to learn
more robust and biologically faithful representations by overcoming the limitations of
sparse and noisy single-cell observations. I will discuss our recent results demonstrating
improved representation learning and downstream performance, and outline future
directions toward scalable and generalizable foundation models for cellular biology.

talks.title: Translational Research on Patient-Derived Tumor Organoids (PDOs)-based High-Throughput Screening (HTS) Platform for Precision Oncology and New Drug Development
talks.speaker: Sang-Yun Lee
talks.text:
Recently, cancer organoid-based drug sensitivity tests have been studied to predict patient
responses to anticancer drugs. The area under curve (AUC) or IC50 value of the
dose-response curve (DRC) is used to differentiate between sensitive and resistant patient‘s
groups. This study proposes a multi-parameter analysis method (cancer organoid-based
diagnosis reactivity prediction, CODRP) that considers the cancer stage and cancer cell growth
rate, which represent the severity of cancer patients, in the sensitivity test. On the CODRP
platform, patient-derived organoids (PDOs) that recapitulate patients with pan-cancers (lung,
ovarian, head and neck) were implemented by applying a mechanical dissociation method
capable of high yields and proliferation rates. A disposable nozzle-type cell spotter with
efficient high-throughput screening (HTS) has also been developed to dispense a very small
number of cells due to limited patient cells. A drug sensitivity test was performed using PDO
from the patient tissue and the primary cancer characteristics of PDOs were confirmed by
pathological comparision with tissue slides. The conventional index of drug sensitivity is the
AUC of the DRC. In this study, the CODRP index for drug sensitivity test was proposed
through multi-parameter analyses considering cancer cell proliferation rate, the cancer
diagnosis stage, and AUC values. The proposed CODRP index-based drug sensitivity test
predicted the drug responses and clinical prognosis and was verified to be consistent with the
clinical drug treatment follow-up results. Therefore, the PDO-based HTS and CODRP index
drug sensitivity tests described in this paper may be useful for predicting and analyzing
promising anticancer drug efficacy for patients with lung cancer and can be applied to a
precision medicine platform.

talks.speaker: Lana Garmire

Copy number variations (CNV) are key drivers of cancer progression, yet methods for
predicting spatial CNVs directly from haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images are currently
lacking. We introduce HisToSpatialCNV, a multiscale deep-learning framework that integrates
histopathological features from H&E-stained images to infer spatial CNV patterns. Combining
interpretable feature extraction with graph neural networks and multihead self-attention, our
approach captures both local and global tissue contexts. Applied to HER2+ breast cancer, skin
cancer and brain cancer datasets, HisToSpatialCNV outperformed existing methods for spatial
gene expression inference and showed strong concordance between predicted CNVs and gene
expression. In addition, it enabled tumour subclone identification, phylogenetic reconstruction
and detection of pathway alterations linked to tumour progression. HisToSpatialCNV generalized
across Visium and Xenium spatial transcriptomics platforms, on HER2+ patients. Applying the
HisToSpatialCNV HER2+ model to TCGA HER2+ histopathology data identified spatial-molecular
subtypes associated with distinct survival outcomes in TCGA HER2+ patients. By connecting
histopathology to spatial genomics, HisToSpatialCNV offers a powerful, cost-effective tool for
studying intratumour heterogeneity using only routine pathology images.
